subtopic_detail: Observation rather than treatment for isolated thrombocytopenia with cutaneous bleeding only
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy brought in by his father because of bruises. Over three days he has developed dozens of bruises on both shins and forearms and a rash of tiny red spots across his chest and back that do not fade when pressed.

He had a runny nose and cough a fortnight ago that settled without treatment. He had one nosebleed yesterday that stopped after five minutes of pressure. He has been running around the waiting room and eating a sandwich while you take the history. There is no fever today, no bone or joint pain, no night waking and no weight loss. There is no lymphadenopathy and no palpable liver or spleen edge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae over trunk and limbs, bruises over both shins and forearms, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 121 g/L (110-140), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), neutrophils 3.1 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), blood film shows large platelets with normal red and white cell morphology and no blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin followed by early outpatient review
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin raises the count within 24 to 48 hours and is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding or an urgent need to raise the count, neither of which applies to a single self limiting nosebleed (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Oral prednisolone for four days with early outpatient review
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is an alternative first line agent when treatment is indicated, but giving it before the marrow has been considered risks partially treating an undiagnosed leukaemia and altering its appearance (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Platelet transfusion followed by admission for overnight observation
options.rationale: Transfused platelets are destroyed by the same autoantibody within hours, so transfusion is reserved for life threatening haemorrhage alongside immunoglobulin and corticosteroid (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate before any treatment decision is made
options.rationale: Marrow examination is the near pair and is indicated when there are atypical features such as anaemia, neutropenia, blasts on the film, organomegaly or bone pain, and this child has an otherwise entirely normal count and film (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Observation with written safety advice and early outpatient review
options.rationale: Treatment is directed at bleeding rather than at the platelet count, and a well child with skin and mild mucosal bleeding only is managed expectantly with written advice about avoiding contact sport and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, since around 80 per cent recover spontaneously within six months (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Immune thrombocytopenia in children is typically a post viral, self limiting illness with an abrupt onset in a child who is otherwise entirely well, which is precisely what distinguishes it from marrow failure or infiltration. The count often sits below 20 x10^9/L, but serious bleeding is uncommon and intracranial haemorrhage occurs in well under one per cent, so the decision to treat is driven by the bleeding phenotype rather than the number. Features that should prompt marrow examination include any other cytopenia, abnormal cells on the film, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain or systemic symptoms. Families need written information because the reassurance that a very low count is compatible with home management is counterintuitive and often gets lost.
key_points: Treatment is based on bleeding severity, not on the platelet count alone.
A well child with skin and mild mucosal bleeding is managed with observation.
Anaemia, neutropenia, blasts, organomegaly or bone pain point away from the diagnosis and towards marrow examination.
Around 80 per cent of children recover spontaneously within six months.
Advice covers avoidance of contact sport, non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and aspirin.
explanation.pearls: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and aspirin are avoided for the duration of the thrombocytopenia because they add a functional platelet defect to a quantitative one, and paracetamol is the analgesic of choice in these children.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Acting on an intermediate predictor score in an irritable hip rather than waiting for every criterion
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 3 year old boy who has refused to stand since yesterday morning. His mother says he screams if anyone moves his right leg and that he had a runny nose last week that has settled.

He lies with the right hip flexed and turned outwards and cries with any attempt to move it. He is drinking and interactive between examinations. There is no rash, no other joint involvement and no history of trauma. A hip ultrasound performed in the department shows a moderate right hip effusion with no effusion on the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, right hip held flexed and externally rotated, marked pain on passive internal rotation, no rash and no other joint involvement
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.5 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/hr (less than 15), blood culture collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent ultrasound guided hip aspiration before antibiotics are given
options.rationale: Three of the four clinical predictors are met with a C reactive protein of 42 mg/L, which alone carries a high likelihood of infection, and joint fluid must be obtained before antibiotics because culture yield falls sharply once treatment starts (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin now and arrange aspiration tomorrow
options.rationale: Treating first is understandable but sterilises the joint fluid and leaves the organism and its sensitivities unknown for a course that will run for several weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit for observation with analgesia and repeat bloods in 12 hours
options.rationale: Observation is the pathway for transient synovitis, but that child is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers and will weight bear, and delay here risks femoral head destruction within a day (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and general practice review in 48 hours
options.rationale: A temperature just below one predictor threshold does not make the overall picture benign, and discharging a febrile child who will not weight bear with a raised C reactive protein is the classic error in this presentation (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before aspiration
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the near pair and is valuable for detecting adjacent osteomyelitis or a pelvic collection, but it requires sedation and should not delay aspiration when the joint effusion is already demonstrated (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: The irritable hip in a young child sits on a spectrum from transient synovitis, which needs analgesia and review, to septic arthritis, which needs washout within hours. The four predictors of fever, refusal to weight bear, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/hr and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L were derived to help, but they were never intended to be applied as a pass or fail rule, and a child meeting three of four has a probability of infection well above 90 per cent in the original series. C reactive protein was not in the original set and has since emerged as the single strongest laboratory predictor, with values above 20 mg/L substantially raising the odds. Aspiration before antibiotics preserves the culture, and delayed treatment in a septic hip leads to avascular necrosis and permanent joint destruction because the femoral head blood supply runs inside the capsule.
key_points: Refusal to weight bear plus fever plus raised inflammatory markers indicates aspiration, not observation.
The four predictor score is a probability aid rather than a threshold rule.
C reactive protein above 20 mg/L is the strongest single laboratory predictor.
Joint fluid is obtained before antibiotics wherever possible to preserve culture yield.
The intracapsular femoral head blood supply makes delay in the hip particularly damaging.
explanation.pearls: In a child under three months, or one who is immunised incompletely or immunosuppressed, empirical cover is broadened beyond staphylococcal cover because Kingella kingae and Haemophilus influenzae type b become realistic pathogens and both are easily missed on routine culture.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Deciding oral against intravenous therapy for eyelid cellulitis on the basis of eye examination findings
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 5 year old girl with two days of a red swollen right upper eyelid that started after her mother noticed an insect bite there.

The swelling has increased so that she now holds the eye half closed, though she opens it fully when asked. Her mother has held her home from school but reports she has eaten normally and been her usual self. Holding the lids apart, the conjunctiva is white, the eye moves fully in all directions without pain, the pupil reacts briskly with no relative afferent defect, and she reads the same line on the chart with each eye. The globe does not protrude and the redness stops at the bony rim of the orbit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right upper lid swelling and erythema confined within the orbital rim, no proptosis, full painless extraocular movements, no relative afferent pupillary defect, equal visual acuity both eyes, no chemosis
data_table.Investigations: Immunisations up to date including Haemophilus influenzae type b

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol drops with review again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Topical treatment reaches the conjunctival surface rather than the eyelid soft tissue, and the conjunctiva here is white, so the target of the drops is not the site of infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Referral to ophthalmology for examination within the next week
options.rationale: A week is far too long an interval for a condition that can cross the septum within a day, and the eye examination that ophthalmology would perform has already been completed and is normal (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Oral antibiotics as an outpatient with review again in 24 hours
options.rationale: Infection confined anterior to the orbital septum in a systemically well child over one year, with a fully assessable and normal eye, is treated with oral antibiotics and mandatory review the next day to detect progression (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Admission for intravenous antibiotics and review again in 24 hours
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy is indicated where the eye cannot be assessed, the child is under one year or systemically unwell, or any orbital sign is present, and none of those applies here (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Computed tomography of the orbits before any antibiotic is started
options.rationale: Imaging is the near pair reserved for suspected postseptal disease or a subperiosteal collection, signalled by proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, chemosis or reduced acuity, and it delivers a radiation dose to the developing lens for no benefit here (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: The orbital septum is the anatomical divide that determines management of periocular infection. Anterior to it, infection is confined to the lid and behaves like any soft tissue cellulitis; posterior to it, infection sits in the orbit, threatens the optic nerve and can spread to the cavernous sinus. The distinction is clinical, resting on proptosis, pain or restriction of eye movement, chemosis, reduced acuity and a relative afferent pupillary defect, and it is unreliable if the child will not allow the lids to be parted. Preseptal disease most often follows local trauma, an insect bite or a lid lesion, whereas postseptal disease usually arises from ethmoid sinusitis, which is why the two present at different ages and with different histories.
key_points: Painless full eye movements, normal acuity and absent proptosis place the infection anterior to the septum.
Oral therapy with 24 hour review is appropriate for a well child over one year with a normal eye examination.
Intravenous therapy is required if the eye cannot be assessed or any orbital sign is present.
Imaging is reserved for suspected postseptal infection or a subperiosteal collection.
Preseptal disease follows local skin breach; postseptal disease usually follows ethmoid sinusitis.
explanation.pearls: If a distressed child will not let you open the lids, that alone converts the case to the intravenous pathway, because an unassessable eye must be treated as though it harbours postseptal disease until proven otherwise.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Using a raised gonadotrophin to redirect the investigation of short stature with absent puberty
stem: A 14-year-old girl is the shortest in her year and has not menstruated. Her height is 143 cm, below the 1st centile, with falling height velocity since age eight.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 1 breast with stage 3 pubic hair, low posterior hairline, broad chest, cubitus valgus
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 68 IU/L (1-9), luteinising hormone 24 IU/L (0.1-6), oestradiol less than 40 pmol/L, thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send coeliac serology with thyroid function tests
options.rationale: Coeliac disease and hypothyroidism are the standard screens for short stature with delayed puberty and are the near pair here, but the thyroid function is already normal and neither raises the follicle stimulating hormone (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Send a peripheral blood sample for karyotyping
options.rationale: A markedly raised follicle stimulating hormone places the defect in the ovary rather than the pituitary, and primary ovarian failure with short stature and these physical features in a phenotypic girl is investigated by karyotype, which also identifies mosaicism and any Y chromosome material (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
options.rationale: Imaging the pituitary is the right move when gonadotrophins are low or inappropriately normal alongside a low oestradiol, and hers are high, which excludes a central cause (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

options.text: Arrange a growth hormone stimulation test first
options.rationale: Growth hormone deficiency is the tempting explanation for a falling height velocity, but the insulin like growth factor 1 is normal and it would not explain the raised gonadotrophins or the physical features (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

options.text: Start transdermal oestradiol and review in a year
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement will be needed, but starting it before the karyotype forfeits the chance to plan growth promoting treatment and to screen for the cardiac, renal and autoimmune associations that the diagnosis carries (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

explanation.summary: Short stature with absent puberty is separated first by the gonadotrophins: high values indicate primary gonadal failure, while low or normal values indicate a hypothalamic or pituitary cause or constitutional delay. Turner syndrome affects around one in 2500 live born girls and is frequently diagnosed late, because the physical features can be subtle and adrenarche proceeds normally, so pubic and axillary hair develop and give a false impression that puberty has begun. Growth failure typically becomes evident in mid childhood, well before the absent breast development declares itself, and growth hormone therapy started early adds several centimetres to adult height. Diagnosis triggers a defined surveillance program covering the bicuspid aortic valve and aortic coarctation, renal tract anomalies, hearing, thyroid autoimmunity, coeliac disease and later fertility planning.
key_points: A raised follicle stimulating hormone localises the problem to the gonad and excludes a central cause.
Adrenarche is normal in Turner syndrome, so pubic and axillary hair can mislead.
Karyotype identifies mosaicism and Y chromosome material, which carries gonadoblastoma risk.
Cardiac, renal, thyroid, coeliac and hearing surveillance all begin at diagnosis.
Growth hormone therapy started early increases final adult height.
explanation.pearls: Around 5 to 10 per cent of girls with Turner syndrome have aortic coarctation and up to 30 per cent a bicuspid aortic valve, so echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging are arranged at diagnosis even when femoral pulses and four limb blood pressures are normal.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choosing a scabicide that is age appropriate for a young infant while treating the household
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6 week old boy whose parents say he has been squirming and crying for the past fortnight and has a rash that is spreading.

He has small red bumps and some blistery spots across his trunk, and his mother shows you the same spots on the soles of both feet, the palms of both hands and across his scalp. Both parents describe intense itching at night that keeps them awake, and you can see thin wavy lines between the fingers of the mother's right hand. The baby is feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile and has no fever. There is no honey coloured crusting and no surrounding spreading redness.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous papules and vesicopustules over trunk, palms, soles and scalp, burrows visible in the mother's finger web spaces, no impetiginised crusting, no cellulitis, weight tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Oral ivermectin for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
options.rationale: Ivermectin is not used in children under 15 kg or under five years because safety data are lacking, and it is a second line agent even in adults with ordinary scabies (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Topical corticosteroid for the baby and permethrin for the parents
options.rationale: A corticosteroid settles the itch but leaves the mite in place and allows continued transmission, and unopposed steroid can convert ordinary scabies to the crusted form (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Oral cefalexin for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment is added when there is secondary bacterial infection with honey coloured crusting or surrounding cellulitis, and neither is present on this examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Sulfur ointment for the baby and permethrin for household contacts
options.rationale: Permethrin is not recommended below two months of age in Australia, so sulfur in a soft paraffin base applied for three consecutive nights is the preferred scabicide for this infant, while all household members are treated simultaneously whether or not they are itching (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Permethrin 5 per cent cream for the baby and all household contacts
options.rationale: Permethrin is the correct agent for everyone else in this household but is outside its approved age range for a 6 week old, which is the specific reason the infant needs a different preparation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult pattern in distribution: the scalp, face, palms and soles are involved in babies and spared in older children and adults, and vesicles and pustules are far more common. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by finding burrows in a household contact, and treatment failure is far more often due to untreated contacts or incorrect application than to genuine resistance. Every household member and every recent close physical contact is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms, because the incubation period before itching starts is up to six weeks in a first infestation. Itch persists for two to four weeks after successful treatment because it is a hypersensitivity response to mite antigen, and this is the commonest reason families believe treatment has failed and re treat unnecessarily.
key_points: Infants have scalp, face, palm and sole involvement that older children do not.
Permethrin is not recommended below two months of age in Australia.
All household and close contacts are treated on the same day regardless of symptoms.
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and does not indicate treatment failure.
Application must cover the entire body including under the nails, and be left on overnight.
explanation.pearls: Bedding, towels and clothing used in the previous two days need hot washing or sealing in a plastic bag for at least three days, because the mite survives away from skin for around 24 to 36 hours at room temperature.

subtopic_detail: Reading periorbital bruising with an abdominal mass as metastatic disease rather than injury
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3 year old girl whose mother felt a lump in her tummy while bathing her three days ago.

Over the past month she has been pale and grizzly, has stopped wanting to walk to the park and has been limping on and off without any fall the family can recall. She has purple discolouration around both eyes that her mother assumed came from tripping over a toy a fortnight ago. On examination there is a firm irregular mass in the left upper abdomen that extends across the midline and does not move with respiration. Her blood pressure is normal for age and there is no blood on urine dipstick.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular fixed abdominal mass extending across the midline, bilateral periorbital ecchymoses with no lid swelling or tenderness, pallor, no hepatomegaly, antalgic gait
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), urine dipstick negative for blood and protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a full blood count and arrange orthopaedic review of the limp
options.rationale: The blood count is already available and shows an anaemia that needs explaining, and treating the limp as an isolated orthopaedic problem ignores the abdominal mass that unifies the presentation (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Arrange coagulation studies and review the bruising in one week
options.rationale: A coagulopathy would produce bruising at varied sites rather than a symmetrical periocular distribution, and the platelet count is normal, so this pathway would waste a week (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Send urinary catecholamine metabolites and arrange abdominal imaging
options.rationale: A fixed irregular mass crossing the midline with bone pain, anaemia and bilateral periorbital bruising from orbital bone metastases indicates a catecholamine secreting tumour of neural crest origin, and urinary homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid with cross sectional imaging is the pathway (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Arrange abdominal ultrasound and send urine for microscopy only
options.rationale: The near pair is a renal embryonal tumour, which characteristically gives a smooth mass that does not cross the midline, with hypertension and haematuria, and neither the blood pressure nor the dipstick supports it here (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey for non accidental injury before imaging
options.rationale: Bilateral symmetrical periorbital bruising without lid swelling or tenderness is characteristic of orbital metastatic deposits rather than trauma, and attributing it to injury is the classic delay in this diagnosis (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood, with a median age at diagnosis of around 18 months, and more than half of children have metastatic disease when they present. It arises anywhere along the sympathetic chain, most often in the adrenal gland, and the abdominal mass characteristically crosses the midline because it originates retroperitoneally rather than within an organ. Bone and bone marrow are the commonest metastatic sites, producing pain, limp, pallor and the striking bilateral periorbital ecchymoses that come from orbital bone deposits. Around 90 per cent of tumours secrete catecholamines, so urinary metabolites provide a simple non invasive screening test, and staging uses meta iodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy alongside cross sectional imaging.
key_points: A mass crossing the midline and fixed to the retroperitoneum suggests neural crest rather than renal origin.
Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis without swelling reflects orbital bone metastases.
Around 90 per cent of tumours secrete catecholamines detectable in urine.
The renal embryonal tumour gives a smooth mass that respects the midline, with hypertension and haematuria.
Bone and marrow are the commonest metastatic sites, causing limp, pain and anaemia.
explanation.pearls: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome, with chaotic eye movements and jerky limb movements, is a paraneoplastic presentation that occurs in around two per cent of children and can appear before any mass is palpable, so it always prompts a search for an occult neuroblastoma.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Treating household threadworm when the index child is below the age threshold for anthelmintics
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 month old girl whose 4 year old brother was diagnosed with threadworm a week ago and treated at the pharmacy.

Her mother says the baby has been waking and squirming after midnight for the past four nights, and two nights ago she saw several fine white threads moving around the baby's bottom when she changed her. The baby is feeding well and has gained weight along her centile line. There is no diarrhoea, no blood in the nappy and no fever. The perianal skin is slightly red from scratching with no discharge, no ulceration and no crusting.

data_table.Examination: Mild perianal erythema, no excoriation breach, no discharge, no lymphadenopathy, weight tracking along the 40th centile
data_table.Investigations: Household of five including two adults and three children aged 5 months, 4 years and 7 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Permethrin cream for the baby and mebendazole for the household
options.rationale: Permethrin is a topical scabicide with no activity against intestinal helminths, so it targets the wrong organism entirely despite also being a nocturnal itch treatment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Faecal microscopy for the baby before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Eggs are deposited on perianal skin rather than passed in faeces, so stool microscopy is insensitive and unnecessary when adult worms have already been seen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Hygiene measures for the baby and mebendazole for the household
options.rationale: Anthelmintic treatment is not recommended below six months of age, so this infant is managed with hygiene measures alone while every other household member is treated simultaneously to remove the reservoir that keeps reinfecting her (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Mebendazole for the baby and for all household members now
options.rationale: Treating the whole household simultaneously is correct, but mebendazole is outside its recommended age range at five months and safety data below six months are inadequate (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Mebendazole for the baby now and a repeat dose in two weeks
options.rationale: The two week repeat dose is the correct schedule because the drug does not kill eggs, but it compounds rather than corrects the age problem and leaves the rest of the household untreated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Threadworm is extremely common in Australian households with young children and spreads by the faecal to oral route when eggs deposited on perianal skin at night are transferred to hands, bedding and surfaces. Eggs remain viable in the environment for two to three weeks, which is why a single dose fails and why the whole household is treated together with a repeat dose two weeks later. Diagnosis is made by seeing the worms, usually two to three hours after the child falls asleep, or by an adhesive tape preparation applied to the perianal skin in the morning; stool examination is unhelpful. In infants below the treatment age threshold, the practical approach is to eliminate the reservoir in the rest of the household and rely on hygiene measures until the child is old enough.
key_points: Anthelmintic treatment is not recommended below six months of age.
All household members are treated at the same time, with a repeat dose after two weeks.
The drug kills adult worms but not eggs, which is why the repeat dose is needed.
Eggs are laid on perianal skin, so stool microscopy is insensitive.
Hygiene measures cover morning bathing, nail trimming, handwashing and hot washing of bedding.
explanation.pearls: In girls, migrating worms can reach the vulva and cause vulvovaginitis or recurrent urinary symptoms, so nocturnal perianal itch in a girl presenting with unexplained vulval irritation is worth asking about before urine is sent.

subtopic_detail: Radiographic hip surveillance interval in a non ambulant child with spastic cerebral palsy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a complex care clinic reviewing a 5 year old girl with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy. She has never taken independent steps, is transported in a moulded seating system and needs support to sit.

Her parents say she seems comfortable, sits happily in her chair through a school day and does not cry with nappy changes or dressing. Passive hip abduction is 45 degrees on each side with no fixed deformity and her legs are the same length. Her last pelvic radiograph was at eighteen months of age and reported no abnormality. She has had no hip imaging since, because she has never complained of pain.

data_table.Examination: Passive hip abduction 45 degrees bilaterally, no leg length discrepancy, no pain on hip range of movement, unable to sit unsupported
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic radiograph at eighteen months of age reported as normal, no imaging since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management of her hips?

options.text: Pelvic radiograph now and every six months with migration percentage measured
options.rationale: A child who cannot walk sits in the highest risk group for progressive hip displacement, and Australian surveillance schedules call for six monthly radiographs with measured migration percentage from two years of age through the years of fastest displacement (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

options.text: Pelvic radiograph only when hip pain or loss of abduction is noticed
options.rationale: Displacement is silent until it is advanced, and waiting for pain or restricted abduction means most hips are already beyond the range in which preventive surgery works (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips now and again at skeletal maturity
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging characterises cartilage and soft tissue but is not the surveillance instrument, since the decision rule is built on a measurement taken from a standardised plain radiograph (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips every six months to avoid repeated radiation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the tool for the infant hip before the femoral head ossifies, and by five years the ossified head makes it unreliable for measuring displacement (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Refer for botulinum toxin to the hip adductors and review clinically in a year
options.rationale: Adductor injection can help spasticity and positioning but does not prevent displacement, and using it in place of imaging removes the measurement that triggers timely surgery (Source: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy).
source_refs: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy

explanation.summary: Hip displacement occurs in about a third of children with cerebral palsy overall and in the large majority of those who never walk, and it is a mechanical consequence of muscle imbalance rather than a congenital abnormality. The risk is stratified by gross motor function, so surveillance frequency is set by motor level rather than by symptoms: children who walk independently need little or no radiographic follow up, while non ambulant children are imaged six monthly through early childhood. Migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying outside the bony acetabulum, is the measured variable, and a value above 30 per cent or an increase of more than 10 per cent a year triggers orthopaedic referral. Detected early, displacement is managed with soft tissue surgery, while a dislocated painful hip in adolescence requires major reconstructive or salvage surgery and causes lasting pain and difficulty with seating and hygiene. Pain is a late and unreliable signal, and many children with communication difficulty cannot report it at all.
key_points: Surveillance frequency is set by gross motor function, not by symptoms.
Non ambulant children need six monthly pelvic radiographs through early childhood.
Migration percentage above 30 per cent or a rise above 10 per cent a year triggers orthopaedic referral.
Hip displacement is silent until advanced, so waiting for pain forfeits preventive surgery.
Ultrasound is the infant tool and is unreliable once the femoral head has ossified.
explanation.pearls: Migration percentage rising more than 10 percentage points in a year predicts progression to dislocation more reliably than any single absolute value, so serial measurements on comparable radiographs matter more than the number on any one film.

sources.label: Australian hip surveillance guidelines for children with cerebral palsy
RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: Interpreting raised transaminases of muscle origin in a boy with motor delay
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver blood tests found while investigating tiredness. He walked at 19 months and his mother says he still cannot keep up in the playground and asks to be carried home from kindergarten.

To stand from sitting on the floor he rolls onto his front, pushes up onto his hands and feet and then walks his hands up his thighs. His calves feel firm and look larger than expected for his build. He speaks in short sentences and his kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about his language. Abdominal examination finds no hepatomegaly, an abdominal ultrasound is normal and his gamma glutamyl transferase is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Rises from the floor by climbing up his own legs, waddling gait, firm enlarged calves, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 310 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 285 U/L (less than 45), gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits, creatine kinase 14200 U/L (less than 200), abdominal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with electromyography of the proximal muscles
options.rationale: Electrodiagnostic testing separates neuropathic from myopathic weakness, a question already answered by a creatine kinase in the tens of thousands, and it is uncomfortable for a preschool child (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunohistochemistry and western blot
options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is negative or ambiguous, since it requires anaesthesia in a child with a myopathy and adds nothing when the mutation is identifiable on blood (Source: RCH Melbourne: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy to characterise the raised transaminase pattern
options.rationale: Alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are present in skeletal muscle as well as liver, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase with a normal ultrasound points away from hepatic disease entirely (Source: RCH Melbourne: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to investigate the language delay
options.rationale: Cognitive and language delay accompanies this condition in about a third of boys because the gene product is expressed in brain, so the delay is explained rather than requiring separate imaging (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene for deletions and duplications
options.rationale: Deletions or duplications of one or more exons account for about three quarters of cases and are identified on a blood sample, so molecular testing confirms the diagnosis, defines the mutation for treatment eligibility and enables carrier testing in the family (Source: RCH Melbourne: Duchenne muscular dystrophy).

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is frequently diagnosed late, and one of the commonest detours is an incidental finding of raised transaminases that leads to a hepatic workup, because clinicians forget that these enzymes are abundant in skeletal muscle. Requesting a creatine kinase alongside any unexplained transaminase elevation in a boy is the step that redirects the investigation. Clinical clues are motor delay, a waddling gait, difficulty with stairs, calf pseudohypertrophy and the characteristic manoeuvre of climbing up the legs to stand from the floor. Cognitive and language delay occur in about a third and are part of the condition. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids prolong ambulation, cardiac and respiratory surveillance begins in childhood, mutation specific therapies depend on knowing the exact variant, and the family needs genetic counselling since about two thirds of mothers are carriers.
key_points: Raised alanine and aspartate aminotransferase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase can be muscle in origin.
Check creatine kinase in any boy with unexplained transaminase elevation or motor delay.
Genetic testing on blood identifies about three quarters of cases and has displaced biopsy as the first test.
Cognitive and language delay affects about a third and is part of the condition.
Diagnosis unlocks corticosteroid therapy, cardiac surveillance and family genetic counselling.
explanation.pearls: Creatine kinase in this condition runs at ten to a hundred times the upper limit of normal from birth, so a value in the tens of thousands in a boy with motor delay is close to diagnostic before any genetic result returns.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Timing the first retinal examination in an extremely preterm infant
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar on the special care nursery round. A girl born at 24 weeks and 2 days gestation weighing 620 g is now 28 days old and stable on continuous positive airway pressure in 25 per cent oxygen.

Her mother asks when her daughter's eyes will be checked, because a friend's baby had eye examinations in hospital. The infant received supplemental oxygen from birth, has had two courses of antibiotics for suspected sepsis and is tolerating expressed breast milk feeds. Growth is tracking along the third centile for corrected age. No ophthalmology review has been arranged so far.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 52/30 mmHg, respiratory rate 54 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in 25 per cent oxygen, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (140-220 at birth), cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: When should her first retinal examination be performed?

options.text: Now, since she has already reached four weeks of postnatal age
options.rationale: Four weeks postnatal age is one half of the rule, but in an extremely preterm infant this arrives at 28 weeks postmenstrual age, before the retinal vasculature has developed enough for the examination to be informative (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: Only if supplemental oxygen is still required beyond 28 days of life
options.rationale: Oxygen exposure modifies risk but screening eligibility is set by gestation and birthweight, and disease occurs in eligible infants who never received prolonged supplemental oxygen (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At term corrected age, when the retina has completed vascularisation
options.rationale: Treatable disease develops and can progress to retinal detachment well before term, so waiting until 40 weeks misses the window in which laser or intravitreal therapy preserves vision (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: In the week before discharge home, with outpatient follow up afterwards
options.rationale: Screening is timed to the biology of retinal vascularisation rather than to the discharge date, and an infant of this gestation may remain an inpatient for months (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At 31 weeks postmenstrual age, which for her falls in about three weeks
options.rationale: The first examination occurs at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever comes later, and for an infant born at 24 weeks the postmenstrual criterion is the later of the two (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity).
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity results from arrested retinal vascularisation followed by disordered neovascularisation, and it remains a preventable cause of childhood blindness in survivors of extreme prematurity. Australian screening covers infants born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing less than 1250 g at birth, with the first examination at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later. Examinations continue at one to three weekly intervals depending on the zone and stage found, until the retina is fully vascularised or the disease has regressed. Treatment thresholds are defined by zone, stage and the presence of plus disease, and laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor therapy is delivered within days of reaching them. Even treated infants need long term follow up for myopia, strabismus and amblyopia.
key_points: Screen infants born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing under 1250 g.
First examination at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later.
The postmenstrual criterion governs for the most preterm infants, the postnatal one for larger babies.
Repeat examinations continue until full vascularisation or regression.
Treatment thresholds rest on zone, stage and plus disease, and are acted on within days.
explanation.pearls: Plus disease, meaning dilation and tortuosity of the posterior pole vessels, is the feature that converts an observation interval into a treatment decision, and its presence in zone I mandates treatment within about 72 hours.

sources.label: RANZCO: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity
Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

subtopic_detail: Escalating beyond phototherapy when neurological signs accompany severe hyperbilirubinaemia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department for a 4 day old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth. His mother says he has gone a deep yellow colour, has fed poorly since yesterday and has a cry she describes as sharp and different from before.

He was discharged at 36 hours of age when he looked well. Today he is difficult to rouse for a feed, and when you lift him his neck arches backwards and his back stiffens before he settles. Intensive phototherapy was started twenty minutes ago on arrival. His mother is blood group O positive and the baby is A positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 465 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 12 micromol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (140-220), reticulocytes raised, direct antiglobulin test positive, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue intensive phototherapy alone and repeat the bilirubin in four hours
options.rationale: Phototherapy lowers bilirubin over hours, and the arched posture with a high pitched cry signals bilirubin already crossing into the brain, so a four hour observation period accepts ongoing neuronal injury (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin and continue intensive phototherapy
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has a role in isoimmune haemolysis where the bilirubin is rising despite phototherapy and approaching the exchange threshold, but it works too slowly to be the answer once encephalopathy is evident (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Stop breastfeeding, give formula feeds and continue intensive phototherapy
options.rationale: Improving enteral intake reduces enterohepatic recirculation and is worth doing, but substituting formula addresses a minor contributor while the acute neurological emergency goes untreated (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Arrange urgent exchange transfusion while intensive phototherapy continues
options.rationale: Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, here lethargy with retrocollis and a high pitched cry, mandate exchange transfusion irrespective of where the value sits on the treatment chart, and phototherapy runs throughout the preparation (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Commence phenobarbital to induce hepatic conjugation and observe overnight
options.rationale: Enzyme induction takes days to alter conjugation and has no place in acute severe hyperbilirubinaemia, and sedating an encephalopathic newborn masks the very signs being monitored (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in the first week is managed on a chart that plots the value against postnatal age and risk factors, with separate lines for phototherapy and for exchange transfusion. That chart is overridden by clinical signs: lethargy, hypotonia, a high pitched cry, poor feeding, retrocollis and opisthotonos indicate that unbound bilirubin is already crossing the blood brain barrier, and exchange transfusion becomes immediate regardless of the number. ABO incompatibility with a positive direct antiglobulin test, as here, is a common Australian cause of early haemolytic jaundice in a group O mother, alongside rhesus disease and glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Early discharge before the bilirubin peaks is a recurring contributor, which is why a review within 48 hours of discharge is arranged for babies who go home before 72 hours. Kernicterus, the chronic sequel, produces choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss and upward gaze palsy, and is entirely preventable.
key_points: Neurological signs override the treatment chart and mandate immediate exchange transfusion.
Retrocollis, opisthotonos, a high pitched cry and lethargy are the acute encephalopathy signs.
Continue intensive phototherapy while the exchange is being organised.
Immunoglobulin is for isoimmune haemolysis approaching threshold, not for established encephalopathy.
Discharge before 72 hours requires a review within 48 hours because the bilirubin has not yet peaked.
explanation.pearls: Double volume exchange, about 160 to 180 mL per kilogram, removes roughly 85 per cent of circulating red cells and around half the total body bilirubin in a single procedure, which is why nothing pharmacological substitutes for it once encephalopathy has begun.

subtopic_detail: Managing a self limiting viral skin eruption in a child with coexisting dermatitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 5 year old boy whose mother is upset about spots that keep spreading. They started as three bumps behind his knee eight weeks ago and there are now about thirty across his trunk, arms and both knee creases.

The lesions are 2 to 4 mm, dome shaped, skin coloured and each has a small central dimple. Several sit within patches of dry, scaly, itchy skin that his mother treats intermittently with a moisturiser she buys at the supermarket. He is otherwise well, eats and plays normally, and has not been unwell. His mother has been told by the swimming school that he cannot return until the spots are gone, and she asks you to freeze them off today.

data_table.Examination: Approximately thirty dome shaped umbilicated papules 2 to 4 mm across the trunk, arms and popliteal fossae, surrounding dry scaly erythematous patches, no pustules, no surrounding cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for ten days to cover secondary bacterial infection
options.rationale: Antibiotics are for secondary infection with pustules, spreading erythema or systemic features, and the surrounding change described here is eczematous rather than infective (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Treat each lesion with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy at today's appointment
options.rationale: Cryotherapy is painful, poorly tolerated in a preschool child and risks hypopigmentation and scarring for a condition that resolves without any treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Molluscum contagiosum).

options.text: Prescribe topical imiquimod cream applied three nights a week for sixteen weeks
options.rationale: Randomised evidence shows no benefit over vehicle for this condition in children while producing application site irritation, so it is not recommended despite being widely requested (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Explain the natural course and treat the surrounding dermatitis with topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: The eruption clears spontaneously over months to two years and no exclusion from swimming is required, while treating the surrounding dermatitis reduces scratching, which is what spreads lesions and causes secondary infection (Source: RCH Melbourne: Molluscum contagiosum).

options.text: Refer for curettage of all lesions under general anaesthesia within the month
options.rationale: Anaesthetic risk for a benign self limiting condition is disproportionate, and new lesions typically appear after curettage because the virus is already seeded in adjacent skin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the epidermis that spreads by direct contact and by autoinoculation from scratching, and it is one of the commonest reasons a preschool child is brought to a doctor for skin. Lesions are dome shaped, umbilicated papules that appear in crops over months and then resolve completely without scarring, typically within twelve to eighteen months and sometimes up to two years. Children with atopic dermatitis develop more numerous and more widespread lesions because the barrier is impaired and scratching seeds new sites, so treating the dermatitis is the intervention that most reduces spread. An inflammatory reaction with redness and tenderness around lesions commonly heralds resolution and is frequently mistaken for bacterial infection. Australian guidance does not require exclusion from school, childcare or swimming, though covering lesions with clothing or a dressing during swimming is reasonable.
key_points: The eruption is self limiting and resolves without scarring over months to about two years.
Coexisting dermatitis drives spread through scratching, so treating it is the priority.
Exclusion from school, childcare or swimming is not required.
Inflammation around lesions usually signals impending resolution rather than bacterial infection.
Destructive treatments risk scarring and pain for a condition that clears on its own.
explanation.pearls: A crop of lesions turning red, swollen and tender at around the nine to twelve month mark is the beginning of the end rather than a complication, and reassurance at that point prevents an unnecessary course of antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: Napkin eruption that involves the skin folds and has not responded to barrier and steroid
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 7 month old girl whose mother says her bottom has been raw for a fortnight and is getting worse rather than better. She has been changing the nappy more often and applying a zinc barrier cream at every change, and has used 1 per cent hydrocortisone ointment twice daily for the last five days.

The napkin area shows confluent beefy red erythema that extends deep into both inguinal creases and the natal cleft, with a scattering of small red papules and a few pustules on normal looking skin several centimetres beyond the main rash. There are no erosions, no bullae and no perianal fissures. She finished a course of amoxicillin for otitis media three weeks ago. She is afebrile, feeding well and thriving.

data_table.Examination: Confluent erythema involving both inguinal creases and the natal cleft, satellite papules and pustules on adjacent normal skin, oral cavity clear
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Change to a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied twice daily for a week
options.rationale: Potent steroids are avoided under an occlusive nappy because absorption is high and atrophy follows, and escalating steroid potency in an untreated candidal infection makes it worse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue the barrier preparation alone and change the nappy more frequently
options.rationale: Barrier and frequent changes are the treatment for irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the flexures because the skin there is not in contact with urine and faeces (Source: RCH Melbourne: Napkin rash).

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole as a single weight based dose with review in a week
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal therapy is reserved for extensive, recurrent or immunocompromised disease, and topical treatment clears an uncomplicated napkin candidiasis without systemic exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Apply topical mupirocin ointment three times daily for seven days to the area
options.rationale: Antibacterial treatment addresses impetiginised dermatitis with honey coloured crusting or bullae, and the pustules here sit on erythematous satellite lesions typical of yeast rather than staphylococcal infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Apply a topical imidazole antifungal cream at each nappy change with the barrier
options.rationale: Involvement of the depths of the flexures with satellite papules and pustules distinguishes candidal infection from irritant dermatitis, and a topical imidazole applied under the barrier is the treatment, particularly after a recent antibiotic course (Source: RCH Melbourne: Napkin rash).

explanation.summary: Napkin dermatitis is usually irritant in origin, caused by prolonged contact with urine and faeces under occlusion, and it characteristically affects the convex surfaces while sparing the depths of the flexures. When the rash goes into the creases, spreads beyond the nappy line as separate satellite lesions, or fails to respond to barrier treatment within a few days, secondary candidal infection is the usual explanation and recent antibiotic exposure makes it more likely. Persistent napkin eruptions that resist both barrier and antifungal treatment should prompt consideration of psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, zinc deficiency and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, the last suggested by petechiae and erosions. Low potency hydrocortisone is safe under a nappy for a short course, but potent corticosteroids are not, because occlusion greatly increases absorption. Persistent perianal fissuring or unusual bruising in the area should raise the question of non accidental injury.
key_points: Irritant dermatitis spares the flexures; candidal infection involves them.
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash are the diagnostic clue to yeast.
Recent antibiotic exposure substantially raises the risk of secondary candidal infection.
Only low potency corticosteroids are used under an occlusive nappy, and only briefly.
A rash resistant to both barrier and antifungal treatment needs a wider differential.
explanation.pearls: Check the mouth as well as the nappy area, since oral thrush and napkin candidiasis frequently coexist in an infant after antibiotics and treating only one end leaves a reservoir that reseeds the other.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of recurrent apnoea in a stable preterm infant
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a boy born at 28 weeks and 3 days gestation, now 11 days old and 1180 g. Nursing staff report six episodes over the last 24 hours in which he stops breathing for around 20 seconds, the heart rate falls into the 80s and the saturation dips, each recovering with gentle tactile stimulation.

The episodes began on day three and have been gradually more frequent. He is in room air with no increased work of breathing between episodes, tolerating full enteral feeds of expressed breast milk, and gaining weight. A septic screen two days ago including blood culture was negative and his C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage, his blood glucose has been consistently normal and his haemoglobin is 132 g/L. He has not yet received any respiratory stimulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute between episodes, blood pressure 54/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), blood culture no growth at 48 hours, haemoglobin 132 g/L, glucose within normal limits, cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin pending cultures
options.rationale: New or abruptly worsening apnoea in a preterm infant does demand a sepsis workup, but a negative screen two days ago with a normal C reactive protein and a gradual course over eight days argues against infection here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal handbook).

options.text: Commence caffeine citrate with a loading dose followed by daily maintenance
options.rationale: Caffeine is the first line respiratory stimulant for apnoea of prematurity, reducing apnoea frequency within a day and also reducing bronchopulmonary dysplasia and cerebral palsy at follow up in preterm infants (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal handbook).

options.text: Commence nasal continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cm of water pressure
options.rationale: Positive pressure is the next step when apnoea persists despite caffeine or when there is an obstructive component, and applying it to an infant comfortable in room air adds feeding and nasal trauma risk (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn).
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor and thicken feeds to treat gastro oesophageal reflux
options.rationale: Reflux has not been shown to cause apnoea of prematurity, and acid suppression in preterm infants increases necrotising enterocolitis and late onset sepsis (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn).
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude seizures presenting as apnoea
options.rationale: Seizures can present as apnoea but are usually accompanied by other stereotyped movements or eye deviation and by a normal or rising heart rate, whereas apnoea of prematurity is accompanied by bradycardia (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal handbook).

explanation.summary: Apnoea of prematurity reflects immaturity of the brainstem respiratory centre and of the chemoreceptor response to carbon dioxide, and its incidence rises steeply as gestational age falls, affecting nearly every infant born before 28 weeks. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so sepsis, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, intracranial haemorrhage, seizure, necrotising enterocolitis and temperature instability are considered whenever the pattern changes abruptly rather than evolving gradually. Bradycardia accompanying the pause distinguishes it from the tachycardia usually seen with seizure related apnoea. Caffeine is given until roughly 34 weeks postmenstrual age with a symptom free period before discharge, and it is one of the few neonatal drugs with a demonstrated benefit on long term neurodevelopmental outcome. Positive airway pressure is added when episodes continue despite caffeine, and intubation is reserved for infants whose apnoea does not respond to both.
key_points: Apnoea of prematurity is a diagnosis of exclusion; an abrupt change in pattern prompts a sepsis workup.
Caffeine citrate is first line and reduces bronchopulmonary dysplasia and cerebral palsy at follow up.
Continuous positive airway pressure is the next step when caffeine alone is insufficient.
Acid suppression for presumed reflux does not help and raises sepsis and necrotising enterocolitis risk.
Bradycardia with the pause suggests apnoea of prematurity rather than seizure.
explanation.pearls: Caffeine has a wide therapeutic index and a half life of about 100 hours in the preterm infant, so routine plasma level monitoring is unnecessary and a single loading dose covers the first several days on its own.

sources.label: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn
Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Imaging an infant with hip risk factors after the neonatal examination signs have disappeared
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 10 week old girl at her first specialist appointment. She was born at 39 weeks in the frank breech position by caesarean section, and her mother was treated for hip dysplasia as a baby.

Her newborn examination in hospital was documented as normal, and no imaging was arranged because no clunk was felt. Today Ortolani and Barlow tests produce no clunk on either side. There is an extra skin crease on the left thigh compared with the right, hip abduction is 70 degrees on the right and 55 degrees on the left, and with the hips and knees flexed the left knee sits slightly lower than the right. She feeds and grows normally and moves both legs.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow negative bilaterally, left hip abduction 55 degrees and right 70 degrees, asymmetric left thigh crease, left knee lower on Galeazzi testing
data_table.Investigations: No imaging performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents, since the neonatal and current examinations were both normal
options.rationale: The provocation tests lose sensitivity after about eight to twelve weeks as soft tissues tighten, so a negative examination at this age carries far less weight than the asymmetric abduction and crease (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph before the orthopaedic appointment
options.rationale: The femoral head is still largely cartilaginous at this age, so a radiograph is difficult to interpret and becomes the imaging of choice from about four to six months when ossification is established (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound and refer to a paediatric orthopaedic service
options.rationale: Ultrasound images the cartilaginous infant hip and quantifies acetabular development and femoral head coverage, and breech presentation with a first degree family history plus asymmetric abduction is precisely the combination that requires it (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Fit a Pavlik harness now and review the hip clinically in six weeks
options.rationale: Harness treatment follows an imaging diagnosis, since applying it to a normal hip carries risks of avascular necrosis and femoral nerve palsy for no benefit (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Repeat the clinical examination at six months of age and image only if abnormal
options.rationale: Waiting until six months forfeits the window in which simple harness treatment works, after which the alternative is closed or open reduction under anaesthesia (Source: RACGP: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in general practice

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip spans a spectrum from a shallow acetabulum to frank dislocation, and it is the commonest cause of hip arthritis requiring replacement in young adults when missed. Australian practice screens clinically at birth, at the six week check and at subsequent well child visits, and adds targeted ultrasound for infants with risk factors, principally breech presentation in the third trimester, a first degree family history and an abnormal or equivocal examination. Provocation tests are most informative in the first weeks and become unreliable after about three months, at which point limited abduction, asymmetric thigh creases and apparent femoral shortening become the important signs. Ultrasound is the modality until the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months, after which plain radiography takes over. Treatment before six months is usually a Pavlik harness worn for six to twelve weeks with ultrasound monitoring, and success rates fall substantially once walking has begun.
key_points: Breech presentation and a first degree family history are the two strongest risk factors.
Ortolani and Barlow tests lose sensitivity after about eight to twelve weeks.
Limited abduction, asymmetric creases and apparent femoral shortening dominate after that.
Ultrasound is the imaging modality until about four to six months, then plain radiography.
Harness treatment starts only after imaging confirms the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Asymmetric abduction with a difference of more than about 20 degrees is a stronger predictor than an asymmetric thigh crease, which occurs in a substantial minority of entirely normal infants and on its own does not justify imaging.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
RACGP: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in general practice
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Newborn hip assessment

subtopic_detail: Imaging the hip when an adolescent presents with knee pain and a limp
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12 year old boy brought by his mother with six weeks of aching in the left knee that is worse at the end of a school day. He weighs 74 kg and his body mass index sits well above the 97th centile.

He has not fallen or been tackled and the pain came on without an injury. He walks with the left foot turned outwards and swings the leg through rather than bending it normally. The left knee looks and feels the same as the right, with no effusion, no joint line tenderness, full flexion and extension and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip, the leg rotates outwards on its own and he stops you at about 60 degrees because of groin discomfort. He is afebrile and his C reactive protein is 3 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), knee examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Anteroposterior and frog leg lateral radiographs of both hips
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with referred knee pain is the classic presentation of a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, the lateral view detects early slips missed on the frontal view, and both hips are imaged because the other side slips in a substantial minority (Source: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the symptomatic left knee
options.rationale: Imaging where the pain is felt is the specific trap in this condition, since hip pathology refers to the knee through the obturator nerve and a normal knee film falsely reassures (Source: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee to assess for a meniscal tear
options.rationale: A meniscal injury would follow a twisting mechanism and produce joint line tenderness or an effusion, and none of those features is present on a normal knee examination (Source: RCH Melbourne: The limping child).

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips to look for an effusion in the joint
options.rationale: Ultrasound answers the question of effusion in suspected septic arthritis or transient synovitis, and an afebrile boy with a normal C reactive protein and a six week history does not fit either (Source: RCH Melbourne: The limping child).

options.text: No imaging, with referral to physiotherapy for anterior knee pain rehabilitation
options.rationale: Patellofemoral pain is a diagnosis of exclusion in this age group and does not explain restricted hip flexion with obligate external rotation, and continued weight bearing risks progression to an unstable slip (Source: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: A slipped upper femoral epiphysis occurs when the femoral head displaces posteriorly and inferiorly through the growth plate, typically in an overweight adolescent during the growth spurt, and it is one of the diagnoses most reliably delayed in paediatric practice. Between a fifth and a half of patients complain only of knee or thigh pain because the hip refers along the obturator nerve, so hip examination is mandatory in every adolescent with knee pain and no injury. The physical signs are loss of internal rotation and obligate external rotation as the hip is flexed. Radiographs must include a frog leg lateral view, because a mild slip can look normal on the frontal projection alone. Management is urgent non weight bearing and surgical fixation in situ, since progression from a stable to an unstable slip raises the risk of avascular necrosis from a few per cent to close to half. Endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency are considered in a child who is young, short or thin for this diagnosis.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain and no injury.
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the signature physical sign.
A frog leg lateral view is required because early slips are missed on the frontal view alone.
Image both hips, since the contralateral side slips in a substantial minority.
Make the child non weight bearing immediately, as progression to an unstable slip risks avascular necrosis.
explanation.pearls: Avascular necrosis complicates under about 5 per cent of stable slips but approaches 50 per cent once the slip becomes unstable, which is why crutches and a bed are ordered from the emergency department rather than after the orthopaedic review.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Treating a mite infestation across a household rather than the presenting child alone
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3 year old boy whose mother says he scratches himself raw every night and barely sleeps, though he seems settled during the day. The rash started about five weeks ago.

There are excoriated red papules across his trunk and limbs, and on close inspection short wavy grey lines a few millimetres long between the fingers and along both wrist creases. There are firm red nodules in both axillae. His mother says her own arms have started itching this week and his 6 year old sister has been scratching for a fortnight. He is otherwise well, afebrile, and there is no honey coloured crusting or surrounding cellulitis. He weighs 15 kg.

data_table.Examination: Burrows in the finger webs and wrist flexures, excoriated papules on the trunk and limbs, nodules in both axillae, no crusting or spreading erythema
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply 5 per cent permethrin cream to the child and every household member on one day
options.rationale: Topical permethrin is the first line treatment in Australian practice, and treating the whole household simultaneously whether or not each person itches is what prevents the reinfestation cycle that follows treating the index child alone (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Apply 5 per cent permethrin cream to the child alone and review him in one week
