options.rationale: Treating only the symptomatic child leaves untreated contacts who are already infested, and reinfestation follows within weeks, which is the commonest reason a course appears to have failed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Give a single weight based dose of oral ivermectin repeated after two weeks
options.rationale: Oral treatment is reserved for crusted disease, institutional outbreaks or failed topical therapy, and it is not recommended for children under 15 kg or under five years of age (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Apply undiluted 25 per cent benzyl benzoate emulsion overnight to the whole family
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is an alternative but must be diluted for young children because the undiluted preparation causes marked burning and irritant dermatitis at this age (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe a moderately potent topical corticosteroid and an oral antihistamine at night
options.rationale: Suppressing the itch without killing the mite allows the infestation to continue and to spread, though a steroid does have a place alongside treatment for the itch that persists afterwards (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Scabies is a mite infestation transmitted by prolonged skin to skin contact, and the intense nocturnal itch is a delayed hypersensitivity response that takes four to six weeks to develop on first exposure and only days on reinfestation. Burrows in the finger webs, wrist flexures, axillae, umbilicus and genitals are the diagnostic sign, and in infants and young children the palms, soles, scalp and face are also involved, so treatment in that age group covers the whole body rather than stopping at the neck. Every household member and any recent close contact is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms, and bedding and clothing from the preceding days are hot washed or sealed for a week. The itch commonly persists for two to four weeks after successful treatment and is managed with emollients, topical corticosteroid and antihistamine rather than with repeated scabicide. Crusted scabies, seen with immunosuppression or in remote community settings, carries an enormous mite burden, is highly transmissible and needs combined oral and topical therapy.
key_points: Treat every household member and close contact on the same day, whether or not they itch.
In children under two the application covers scalp, face, palms and soles as well as the body.
Wash bedding and clothing in hot water or seal it for at least a week.
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and is not a sign of treatment failure.
Oral ivermectin is reserved for crusted disease, outbreaks or failed topical therapy.
explanation.pearls: A second application of permethrin seven days after the first is standard practice because the cream is not reliably ovicidal, and eggs surviving the first treatment hatch within that week.

subtopic_detail: Selecting the test that a chromosomal microarray will not detect in developmental delay
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a developmental clinic reviewing a 4 year old boy referred with global developmental delay. He said his first words at three, flaps both hands when excited, avoids looking at faces and covers his ears at the kindergarten music session.

His mother mentions that her brother lives in supported accommodation and has never been given a diagnosis, and that her own mother stopped having periods at 38 and now has a hand tremor and an unsteady walk. His face is long with prominent ears and his finger joints hyperextend. A chromosomal microarray requested by the general practitioner has returned with no pathogenic copy number variants. Newborn screening was normal and his hearing test at three was normal.

data_table.Examination: Long face with prominent ears, joint hypermobility, hand flapping, reduced eye contact, no dysmorphic features of a recognised chromosomal syndrome
data_table.Investigations: Chromosomal microarray with no pathogenic copy number variants, newborn screening normal, audiology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum creatine kinase with thyroid function and a full blood count
options.rationale: Creatine kinase screens for a muscular dystrophy in a boy with motor delay, and his delay is predominantly in language and social communication without weakness or a waddling gait (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: Standard karyotype with G banding on a peripheral blood sample
options.rationale: Karyotype detects aneuploidy and large structural rearrangements at a resolution well below that of the microarray already performed, so it adds nothing here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated for microcephaly or macrocephaly, focal neurological signs, seizures or regression, none of which is described, and it requires anaesthesia for a low yield in isolated delay (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids with an acylcarnitine profile
options.rationale: Metabolic testing is directed at regression, episodic decompensation, organomegaly or consanguinity, and normal newborn screening with steady if slow progress makes it low yield (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: FMR1 CGG repeat analysis performed on a peripheral blood sample
options.rationale: A trinucleotide repeat expansion is invisible to a chromosomal microarray, so a normal array does not exclude it, and the maternal family pattern of undiagnosed intellectual disability with premature ovarian insufficiency and a late onset tremor and ataxia is the pedigree signature of premutation carriers (Source: RCH Melbourne: Fragile X syndrome).

explanation.summary: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and the commonest single gene cause of autism, and it results from expansion of a CGG repeat in the FMR1 gene that silences the gene when the repeat exceeds about 200. Because this is a repeat expansion rather than a copy number change, chromosomal microarray does not detect it, and targeted repeat analysis must be requested separately even when array testing has been done. The physical phenotype of a long face, prominent ears, joint hypermobility and, after puberty, enlarged testes is subtle in early childhood, so the family history often carries more diagnostic weight than the examination. Premutation carriers with 55 to 200 repeats are not intellectually disabled but are at risk of premature ovarian insufficiency in women and of a late onset tremor and ataxia syndrome in both sexes, which is why the maternal grandparents' health is informative. Diagnosis alters family planning for the extended maternal line, since carrier females have a 50 per cent chance of transmitting the expanded allele.
key_points: Chromosomal microarray does not detect trinucleotide repeat expansions.
Request FMR1 repeat analysis specifically in unexplained developmental delay or autism in a boy.
Long face, prominent ears and joint hypermobility are subtle before puberty.
Premutation carriers develop premature ovarian insufficiency or a late onset tremor and ataxia syndrome.
Diagnosis has implications for the whole maternal line, not only the immediate family.
explanation.pearls: A maternal grandmother with menopause before 40 and a later tremor with gait ataxia is a premutation pedigree until proven otherwise, and that combination in the family history should trigger FMR1 testing even before the child's own phenotype looks convincing.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Genetic testing

subtopic_detail: Oxygen saturation target in established chronic neonatal lung disease before discharge
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar planning discharge for a boy born at 26 weeks and 5 days gestation who is now 38 weeks postmenstrual age and 2.6 kg. He remains on 0.15 L per minute of nasal prong oxygen and has needed supplemental oxygen every day since birth.

He feeds fully by breast and bottle, has had no apnoeas for three weeks and caffeine was stopped a fortnight ago. In air he settles at saturations of 89 to 91 per cent while asleep, and on his current flow he sits at 95 per cent. His weight has crossed from the 25th to the 5th centile over the last month despite fortified feeds of 160 mL per kilogram per day. A recent echocardiogram shows normal right ventricular pressures. His parents live four hours from the tertiary centre and are keen to go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on 0.15 L per minute nasal prong oxygen, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram with normal right ventricular pressure and no tricuspid regurgitation jet, haemoglobin 118 g/L, chest radiograph with diffuse haziness and coarse interstitial markings

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for his oxygen therapy?

options.text: Wean to room air before discharge and accept saturations of 89 to 91 per cent
options.rationale: Sustained saturations below the low 90s in chronic neonatal lung disease are associated with poor weight gain and with progressive pulmonary hypertension, so accepting them to achieve discharge in air trades a short admission for a worse outcome (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

options.text: Continue oxygen at saturations of at least 93 per cent and arrange home oxygen
options.rationale: In established chronic neonatal lung disease the target shifts upward to 93 per cent or more, because adequate oxygenation supports growth and prevents hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, and a home oxygen program allows that target to be met outside hospital (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

options.text: Commence a tapering course of systemic dexamethasone to allow oxygen weaning
options.rationale: Late systemic corticosteroid facilitates extubation and weaning but carries adverse neurodevelopmental effects, and it is reserved for infants who cannot be weaned from positive pressure ventilation rather than for low flow oxygen at term (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia).

options.text: Start long term oral furosemide with potassium supplementation and wean oxygen
options.rationale: Diuretics give a short term improvement in lung mechanics without evidence of lasting benefit, and long term use brings hypokalaemia, nephrocalcinosis and hearing loss (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia).

options.text: Increase the flow to target saturations above 97 per cent until the growth improves
options.rationale: Higher targets do not improve growth further and increase exposure to oxygen toxicity and to retinopathy in an infant whose retinal screening is not yet complete (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

explanation.summary: Chronic neonatal lung disease is defined by a continuing oxygen requirement at 36 weeks postmenstrual age in an infant born before 32 weeks, and it reflects arrested alveolar and vascular development rather than simple lung injury. Saturation targets change with the stage of care: during the neonatal period lower targets reduce retinopathy, but once chronic lung disease is established the target rises to at least 93 per cent because chronic hypoxaemia diverts energy from growth and drives hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction towards pulmonary hypertension. Faltering growth on adequate calories is often the first clinical sign that the saturation target is set too low. Home oxygen programs allow infants who are otherwise well, feeding and thermally stable to complete their oxygen requirement at home with community nursing support and scheduled review. Follow up covers growth, respiratory syncytial virus prophylaxis where funded, immunisation on schedule by chronological age, and neurodevelopmental surveillance.
key_points: Chronic neonatal lung disease is an oxygen requirement at 36 weeks postmenstrual age after preterm birth.
The saturation target rises to at least 93 per cent once chronic lung disease is established.
Faltering growth on adequate calories suggests the target is set too low.
Home oxygen is appropriate for an otherwise stable, feeding infant with community support.
Late systemic corticosteroid and long term diuretics carry harms that outweigh their short term gains here.
explanation.pearls: Immunise on chronological rather than corrected age, since these infants have the highest morbidity from pertussis and influenza and delaying vaccines to the corrected schedule leaves them unprotected through the months of greatest risk.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

subtopic_detail: Collapse on day five in a term baby with weak femoral pulses and a pre and post ductal saturation difference
stem: A 5-day-old term boy fed poorly since yesterday and went grey and floppy during a feed. Blood cultures are taken and 10 mL/kg of sodium chloride given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176 /min, respiratory rate 68 /min, SpO2 96% right hand and 88% left foot
data_table.Examination: Mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, barely palpable femoral pulses, liver 3 cm palpable
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18, lactate 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Give repeated fluid boluses and antibiotics for septic shock
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given because sepsis cannot be excluded, but repeated volume loading in an obstructed left heart worsens pulmonary oedema and the acidosis. The differential pulse and saturation findings identify a mechanical cause that fluid cannot fix (Source: RCH Melbourne: The collapsed neonate).

options.text: Intubate and ventilate with a high inspired oxygen concentration
options.rationale: High inspired oxygen lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and hastens closure of the duct, diverting flow away from the systemic circulation he depends on. Airway support may still be needed, but with careful oxygen targeting rather than maximal concentrations (Source: RCH Melbourne: The collapsed neonate).

options.text: Start prostaglandin E1 and involve paediatric cardiology
options.rationale: Presentation in the first fortnight with shock, absent femoral pulses and a saturation gradient across the duct indicates a duct dependent systemic circulation, and prostaglandin reopens the closing duct to restore lower body perfusion. Treatment is started on clinical grounds before echocardiography because the window between duct closure and death is short (Source: RCH Melbourne: The collapsed neonate).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide to offload the circulation
options.rationale: Diuresis reduces preload in a baby whose systemic output depends on ductal flow and will deepen the shock. It has a role only after the duct is reopened and the circulation stabilised (Source: RCH Melbourne: The collapsed neonate).

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram in the morning and continue supportive care
options.rationale: Waiting for imaging in a baby with a closing duct risks irreversible end organ injury or death within hours. Echocardiography confirms the anatomy and guides surgery but follows rather than precedes prostaglandin in a shocked infant (Source: RCH Melbourne: The collapsed neonate).

explanation.summary: Duct dependent lesions present when the arterial duct closes over the first one to two weeks, which is typically after discharge, so the collapsed neonate returning from home is the classic scenario. Left sided obstruction such as coarctation, interrupted arch, critical aortic stenosis and hypoplastic left heart produces shock with poor lower body perfusion, weak femoral pulses and a pre to post ductal saturation gradient, whereas right sided obstruction produces cyanosis. Sepsis is the main differential and looks identical at first glance, which is why antibiotics are given while the cardiac cause is addressed. Prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency and is started before echocardiography when the clinical picture fits, with the team prepared for apnoea, hypotension and fever as its recognised effects. Pulse oximetry screening before discharge is designed to detect some of these lesions but does not catch every case.
key_points: Duct dependent lesions present with collapse as the duct closes in the first one to two weeks
Weak femoral pulses with a pre to post ductal saturation gradient signals left sided obstruction
Prostaglandin is started on clinical grounds before echocardiography confirms the anatomy
High inspired oxygen and diuresis both worsen a duct dependent systemic circulation
Antibiotics are given concurrently because neonatal sepsis presents identically
explanation.pearls: Have airway equipment ready before the prostaglandin runs, since apnoea occurs in roughly 10 to 15 per cent of infants started on it and is most likely within the first hour at higher infusion rates.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

subtopic_detail: Eye surveillance planning for a young girl with antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular arthritis
stem: A 4-year-old girl has had a swollen right knee for ten weeks with morning stiffness. She has no eye symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with 15 degree fixed flexion contracture, small left ankle effusion, eyes white and quiet
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her eyes?

options.text: Review only if her eyes become red, painful or photophobic
options.rationale: The uveitis associated with this pattern of arthritis is characteristically asymptomatic and white, so symptom based review means it is detected only once cataract, synechiae or band keratopathy have developed. Symptom triggered review is appropriate for the acute painful uveitis of spondyloarthropathy (Source: RCH Melbourne: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis).

options.text: Arrange annual optometry review of her visual acuity
options.rationale: Visual acuity testing does not detect anterior chamber inflammation, which requires slit lamp examination, and annual intervals are far too long for her risk category. Yearly community review is inadequate surveillance for this group (Source: RCH Melbourne: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis).

options.text: Refer for slit lamp examination now, then three monthly
options.rationale: A girl under seven with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody is in the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, which is silent and can cause permanent visual loss before any symptom appears. Australian practice is slit lamp screening every three months in this group, spacing out only after several years of quiescent disease (Source: RCH Melbourne: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis).
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Uveitis screening guidance

options.text: Screen her eyes at the same interval as her joint reviews
options.rationale: Uveitis activity runs independently of joint activity and can appear or progress while the arthritis is in remission, so tying eye review to joint control misses cases. Screening intervals are set by risk category and disease duration, not by the state of the joints (Source: RCH Melbourne: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone and rely on it to suppress the eyes
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is not the standard first treatment for oligoarticular disease, where intra articular injection and methotrexate are preferred, and it would not remove the need for screening. Steroids also carry their own ocular risks including cataract and raised intraocular pressure (Source: RCH Melbourne: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis).

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis complicates juvenile idiopathic arthritis in a significant minority of children and is the main cause of long term disability in the oligoarticular subtype. The highest risk group is young girls with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody, in whom inflammation is asymptomatic with a white quiet eye, unlike the painful red eye of spondyloarthropathy related uveitis. Because it cannot be detected clinically or by acuity testing, surveillance depends on regular slit lamp examination, most intensively in the first years after diagnosis when risk is highest. Untreated disease leads to posterior synechiae, cataract, band keratopathy, glaucoma and permanent vision loss. Treatment is escalated from topical corticosteroid through methotrexate to biological agents, and adalimumab has substantially improved outcomes in refractory disease.
key_points: Young antinuclear antibody positive girls with oligoarticular disease are at highest uveitis risk
The inflammation is asymptomatic with a white eye and requires slit lamp detection
Three monthly screening applies to the highest risk group in the early years after diagnosis
Ocular and joint activity are independent, so remission of arthritis does not permit relaxed screening
Untreated disease causes synechiae, cataract, band keratopathy and permanent visual loss
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate used for the arthritis also reduces the incidence and severity of the uveitis, which is one reason it is favoured over repeated systemic corticosteroid in antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular disease.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Uveitis screening guidance

subtopic_detail: Low pre feed glucose at two hours of age in an asymptomatic small for gestational age term baby
stem: A girl born at 38 weeks weighing 2350 g, below the third centile, is 2 hours old. She latched briefly but tired quickly.

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal tone and strong suck, no jitteriness or distress
data_table.Investigations: Pre feed blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L on a laboratory calibrated analyser

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous glucose bolus and maintenance infusion in the nursery
options.rationale: Intravenous treatment is reserved for babies with clinical signs such as seizures or apnoea, glucose below about 1.5 mmol/L, or failure of oral measures, and it separates mother and baby unnecessarily. Escalating first removes the chance for a feeding based approach to work (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal hypoglycaemia).

options.text: A formula top up alone, repeating glucose before the next feed
options.rationale: A feed alone raises glucose more slowly than gel plus a feed and introduces formula without addressing this measurement promptly, which matters when the mother intends to breastfeed. Feeding alone is appropriate when the glucose sits just below target without other risk factors (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Continue skin to skin care and recheck before the next feed
options.rationale: A value of 1.9 mmol/L in an at risk baby is below the operational threshold and requires action now rather than observation, since neuroglycopenic injury can occur without clinical signs. Watchful waiting suits a baby with a glucose at or above the threshold (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Buccal dextrose gel with a feed, rechecking glucose in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel combined with a feed is first line for asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk baby who can feed, and it reduces admissions to the neonatal unit and separation from the mother. The recheck at 30 minutes determines whether a second dose or escalation to intravenous therapy is needed (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: Lancet: Sugar Babies trial of dextrose gel for neonatal hypoglycaemia

options.text: Send a critical sample for insulin, cortisol and ketones first
options.rationale: A critical sample is collected when hypoglycaemia is persistent, severe or unexplained by recognised risk factors, and it must never delay treatment in a baby whose low glucose is explained by growth restriction. Her poor glycogen stores account for the finding at this age (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal hypoglycaemia).

explanation.summary: Babies who are small for gestational age, preterm, large for gestational age or born to mothers with diabetes are screened for hypoglycaemia because their glycogen stores or insulin regulation put them at risk in the transitional period after birth. Australian units generally use an operational threshold of 2.6 mmol/L, with values below that prompting intervention and values below about 1.5 mmol/L or any clinical sign prompting intravenous treatment. Buccal dextrose gel with a feed has changed practice since trial evidence showed it reduces treatment failure and admission for intravenous glucose without harm, and it keeps mother and baby together. Measurements must be made on a laboratory calibrated analyser rather than a ward glucometer designed for adults, since bedside meters are inaccurate at low values. Persistent or unexplained hypoglycaemia beyond the first day requires a critical sample and endocrine assessment for hyperinsulinism or a metabolic disorder.
key_points: At risk babies include small and large for gestational age, preterm, and infants of diabetic mothers
The usual operational threshold is a blood glucose of 2.6 mmol/L
Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is first line for asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in a baby able to feed
Clinical signs or a glucose below about 1.5 mmol/L prompt intravenous glucose
Bedside glucometers are unreliable at low values and results need laboratory confirmation
explanation.pearls: Recheck the glucose 30 minutes after dextrose gel, since a second dose may be given but persistent values below the threshold after two doses is the trigger to move to intravenous glucose rather than continuing to repeat the gel.

sources.label: Lancet: Sugar Babies trial of dextrose gel for neonatal hypoglycaemia

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of early morning headache with vomiting and a new head tilt in a school aged child
stem: An 8-year-old boy has had six weeks of headaches that wake him before dawn, with vomiting twice a week that eases the headache. For a fortnight he has held his head tilted to the left.

data_table.Examination: Left sixth cranial nerve palsy, unsteady tandem gait, indistinct optic disc margins, normal power and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start migraine prophylaxis and review the diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Migraine does not produce a cranial nerve palsy, a persistent head tilt, ataxia or blurred disc margins, and prophylaxis would delay diagnosis by weeks. A prophylactic trial is reasonable in a child with frequent headaches and a normal examination (Source: RCH Melbourne: Headache).

options.text: Refer to an optometrist for vision assessment and glasses
options.rationale: The visual change here reflects a cranial nerve palsy and probable papilloedema rather than refractive error, and optometry review would not address raised intracranial pressure. Refractive assessment is appropriate for isolated visual difficulty with a normal neurological examination (Source: RCH Melbourne: Headache).

options.text: Prescribe an antiemetic and reassure that the pattern will settle
options.rationale: Vomiting that relieves headache is a feature of raised intracranial pressure rather than a primary gastrointestinal problem, and symptomatic treatment masks a progressive lesion. An antiemetic would be reasonable in cyclical vomiting with a normal examination between episodes (Source: RCH Melbourne: Headache).

options.text: Lumbar puncture for opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture before imaging in a child with focal signs and probable papilloedema risks fatal herniation if a posterior fossa mass is present. Pressure measurement has a role only after imaging has excluded a mass lesion (Source: RCH Melbourne: Headache).

options.text: Urgent same day neuroimaging with immediate neurosurgical discussion
options.rationale: Morning headache with vomiting, a new head tilt, a sixth nerve palsy, ataxia and indistinct disc margins together indicate raised intracranial pressure from a posterior fossa lesion until proven otherwise. Same day imaging with immediate specialist discussion is required because hydrocephalus can decompensate rapidly (Source: RCH Melbourne: Headache).
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Childhood brain cancer referral guidance

explanation.summary: Brain tumours are the commonest solid malignancy of childhood and the majority in this age group sit in the posterior fossa, where they obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and present with the features of raised intracranial pressure rather than with focal weakness. The red flag pattern is headache that is present on waking or wakes the child, vomiting that relieves the headache, a progressive course over weeks, and any objective neurological sign. A sixth nerve palsy is a false localising sign of raised pressure, and a persistent head tilt reflects either fourth nerve involvement or tonsillar herniation and is easily dismissed as musculoskeletal. Papilloedema is a late sign and its absence never excludes the diagnosis. Any child with these features needs urgent imaging, and lumbar puncture must not precede it because of herniation risk.
key_points: Headache on waking with vomiting that relieves it suggests raised intracranial pressure
A sixth nerve palsy is a false localising sign and a new head tilt is a posterior fossa red flag
Papilloedema is a late sign and its absence does not exclude a mass lesion
Lumbar puncture before imaging risks herniation in a child with focal signs
Progressive symptoms over weeks with any objective sign mandate urgent imaging
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the headache is present on waking and whether vomiting relieves it, because that combination has a far higher yield for an intracranial mass in children than headache severity, which correlates poorly with the underlying cause.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Childhood brain cancer referral guidance

subtopic_detail: Joint pains and fever after a sore throat in a child from a high incidence community with echocardiographic valve changes
stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a high incidence remote community had an untreated sore throat two weeks ago. For five days he has had migratory aching in both knees, both ankles and one wrist. No joint is swollen, red or hot.

data_table.Investigations: ESR 62 mm/h, antistreptolysin O markedly elevated, PR interval 220 ms
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiogram: mild mitral regurgitation meeting pathological criteria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Acute rheumatic fever; four weekly benzathine benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: In a high incidence population, echocardiographic carditis counts as a major criterion even without a murmur, and polyarthralgia, fever, raised inflammatory markers and a prolonged PR interval each count as minor criteria, so he meets the diagnostic threshold. Long acting four weekly penicillin as secondary prophylaxis is the single intervention that prevents recurrences and the progression to established valve disease (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever).
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Streptococcal pharyngitis; ten days of oral penicillin
options.rationale: Clearing residual streptococcal carriage is part of the initial treatment but does nothing to prevent the recurrent infections that drive cumulative valve damage. Primary treatment of pharyngitis alone is what is offered when the diagnosis is streptococcal sore throat without rheumatic fever (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever).
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Reactive arthritis; non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires the absence of carditis and other criteria, and it typically follows the infection more quickly with a non migratory persistent arthritis. His echocardiographic valve involvement and prolonged PR interval place him in a different category (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever).
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Defer diagnosis; repeat echocardiography in four weeks
options.rationale: Delaying the diagnosis delays prophylaxis during the period when recurrence risk is highest, and the echocardiographic criteria are designed to be applied at presentation. Repeat imaging is used to follow progression once treatment has started (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever).
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Viral illness; review at the community clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: A markedly raised antistreptolysin O titre, sustained inflammatory response and pathological mitral regurgitation are not explained by a viral illness, and a missed diagnosis in this setting carries a lifetime of valve disease. Observation without a plan also fails a family who have travelled a long distance for assessment (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever).
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever remains far more common in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in northern and central Australia than in the general population, and the Australian guideline applies modified diagnostic criteria in these high incidence settings. Two changes matter most: echocardiographic carditis without a murmur counts as a major criterion, and monoarthralgia or polyarthralgia counts as a minor criterion, both of which lower the threshold appropriately in a population where the consequences of a missed diagnosis are severe. Diagnosis requires evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus two major or one major and two minor criteria. Treatment of the acute episode uses anti inflammatory therapy for symptoms and penicillin to clear the organism, but the intervention that changes the natural history is four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin for at least ten years or until a specified age. Cases are notifiable in the jurisdictions with control programs and are entered on a register that supports delivery of every dose.
key_points: High incidence population criteria allow echocardiographic carditis as a major criterion
Polyarthralgia and a prolonged PR interval both count as minor criteria in that setting
Diagnosis needs preceding streptococcal evidence plus two major or one major and two minor criteria
Four weekly benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis is the intervention that prevents progression
Cases are notifiable and entered on a register that supports adherence to every dose
explanation.pearls: Secondary prophylaxis continues for a minimum of ten years or until age 21, whichever is longer, and extends further when established valve disease is present, because recurrence risk is highest in the first few years and each recurrence adds valve damage.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

subtopic_detail: Bedwetting five nights a week in a seven year old who has never been reliably dry overnight
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a seven year old boy and his mother about bedwetting. He wets on about five nights a week and has never had more than three consecutive dry nights.

He has no daytime wetting, no urgency and no straining, and he opens his bowels daily with soft stools. He drinks most of his fluid after school because he does not like the school toilets. He is otherwise well, growing along the fiftieth centile and doing well at school, and he has recently started refusing sleepovers with his cousins. Examination of his abdomen, spine, lower limb neurology and external genitalia is normal, and his urine dipstick shows no glucose, protein, blood, nitrites or leucocytes. His mother is willing to be woken at night and the family is committed to a treatment plan.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable faecal loading, normal lumbosacral spine with no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose, protein, blood, nitrites and leucocytes; bladder diary shows normal daytime voiding frequency and volumes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe desmopressin each night and continue it until he has been dry for three consecutive months
options.rationale: Desmopressin works while it is being taken but relapse after cessation is common, so it is chosen for short term cover such as a camp or when an alarm has failed or cannot be used. It also carries a hyponatraemia risk requiring evening fluid restriction (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Start oxybutynin at night to increase his functional bladder capacity while he is asleep
options.rationale: Anticholinergic therapy targets overactive bladder, which typically produces daytime urgency and frequency that he does not have. It is added for children with proven detrusor overactivity resistant to first line measures (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Arrange an enuresis alarm program with structured family support and review after several weeks
options.rationale: The alarm is first line for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a school aged child, with the highest sustained dry rate because it produces conditioned waking rather than temporary symptom suppression. Success requires a motivated family who will wake with the child, which is present here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Advise that he drinks nothing after four in the afternoon and reassess the pattern in three months
options.rationale: Restricting evening fluid without addressing his poor daytime intake reduces total intake and shrinks functional bladder capacity, making matters worse. Redistributing fluid across the school day is helpful, but as an adjunct rather than a treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric urologist for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic assessment first
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, abnormal urinary stream, neurological signs or treatment failure, none of which apply to uncomplicated night time wetting. Referral first delays a treatment that most families can start immediately (Source: RCH Melbourne: Enuresis).

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis is described as monosymptomatic when there are no daytime urinary symptoms, and it affects a substantial minority of children at school entry with spontaneous resolution at roughly 15 per cent per year. Assessment focuses on excluding daytime symptoms, constipation, an abnormal stream, neurological signs, and the polyuria of diabetes, all of which change the pathway. Constipation is the most commonly missed contributor and treating it alone resolves wetting in many children. Alarm therapy has the best sustained outcomes and works by conditioning arousal to bladder fullness, but requires a committed family and typically several weeks before dryness is achieved. Desmopressin gives faster symptomatic control and is useful for short term needs, while combination therapy is used when either alone is insufficient.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis has no daytime urinary symptoms and needs no imaging
Exclude and treat constipation before starting specific therapy
The alarm is first line with the highest sustained dry rate but takes weeks and requires family commitment
Desmopressin gives rapid short term cover and relapses commonly on cessation
Evening fluid restriction without daytime redistribution reduces functional bladder capacity
explanation.pearls: Continue an alarm until the child achieves fourteen consecutive dry nights before stopping, because ceasing at the first run of dry nights is a leading cause of relapse.

subtopic_detail: Immunisation planning for a well four year old newly arrived in Australia with no written vaccination records
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a four year old girl who arrived in Australia six weeks ago with her family after two years in a refugee camp. She is being enrolled in kindergarten next month.

Her mother believes she received some injections as a baby but has no documentation and no way of contacting the clinic that gave them. The child is thriving, has had no serious illness and takes no medication, and she has never had an allergic reaction to a vaccine or to egg. Her examination is normal and her growth is on the twenty fifth centile for height and weight. Her mother is anxious that the child should not receive injections she has already had.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and thriving, no chronic illness, no immunosuppression, no scars suggestive of previous vaccination, no allergies
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination normal, no immunisation record available on the Australian Immunisation Register

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her immunisation?

options.text: Wait until documentary evidence of her previous vaccinations can be obtained from her country of origin
options.rationale: Records are frequently unobtainable and waiting leaves a susceptible child unprotected while she enters group care. Documentation is used when it is available and reliable, but its absence must not delay the schedule (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Perform serology for every vaccine preventable disease and immunise only against those she lacks
options.rationale: Serology is not available or interpretable for all antigens, delays protection and is more expensive and distressing than vaccinating. It has a defined role for a few conditions such as hepatitis B and varicella in older children rather than as a blanket strategy (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give one vaccine at each visit at monthly intervals to minimise the chance of an adverse reaction
options.rationale: Multiple vaccines can be safely administered at the same visit at separate sites, and spacing them out prolongs susceptibility and increases the chance the schedule is never completed. Separation is required only for specific live vaccine timing rules (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Treat her as unvaccinated and begin an age appropriate catch up schedule at today's visit
options.rationale: A child without written documentation is presumed unvaccinated and started on a catch up schedule determined by age, because repeating doses already received is safe while leaving gaps is not. Doses are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, which also underpins her family assistance and childcare enrolment requirements (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
source_refs: Department of Health: Catch up immunisation calculator

options.text: Give only the vaccines required for kindergarten entry now and complete the remainder after she settles
options.rationale: A partial schedule leaves her unprotected against diseases with significant morbidity and relies on a return visit that often does not happen in newly arrived families. Entry requirements set a minimum administrative standard rather than a clinical target (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Newly arrived refugee and migrant children frequently have absent or unreliable immunisation records, and the Australian Immunisation Handbook directs that any dose without written documentation be considered not given. Repeat doses of routine childhood vaccines in an already immune child carry no additional risk beyond local reactions, whereas assuming protection that does not exist has serious consequences. Catch up schedules are calculated by age using the online calculator, with minimum intervals between doses rather than the routine intervals, and multiple vaccines are given at the same visit at separate sites. Refugee health assessment also includes screening for tuberculosis, hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus, strongyloides, schistosomiasis where relevant, and iron and vitamin D deficiency. All doses are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, which matters for childcare enrolment and family payments.
key_points: Undocumented doses are treated as not given and a full catch up schedule is started
Repeat doses of routine childhood vaccines are safe in an already immune child
Multiple vaccines may be given at the same visit at separate injection sites
Catch up schedules use minimum rather than routine intervals and are calculated by age
Serology has a limited targeted role rather than a blanket one
explanation.pearls: Use the national catch up calculator rather than the routine schedule, because it applies the shortened minimum intervals that let a child complete a multi dose course in weeks instead of months.

sources.label: Department of Health: Catch up immunisation calculator

subtopic_detail: Short stature with absent pubertal signs in a fourteen year old boy whose bone age is markedly delayed
stem: A 14-year-old boy is the smallest in his year. He has grown 4.5 cm in each of the past two years, parallel to but below the third centile. His father did not shave until 19.

data_table.Examination: Height 149 cm on the third centile, testicular volume 3 mL, full visual fields
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology and thyroid function normal; bone age 11 years 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence growth hormone, monitor growth velocity
options.rationale: Growth hormone is indicated for proven deficiency or for specific conditions on defined criteria, and his normal insulin like growth factor 1 with a preserved growth velocity argues against deficiency. Treating a normal variant exposes him to injections and cost for no gain in final height (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
options.rationale: Imaging is prompted by headache, visual field loss, growth velocity failure, diabetes insipidus or a discordant clinical picture, none of which is present. His normal fields, fundi and preserved velocity make an intracranial lesion very unlikely (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Request a karyotype and gonadotropin levels
options.rationale: Karyotyping is indicated for dysmorphic features, disproportionate stature or a girl with unexplained short stature, and gonadotropins are hard to interpret before the pubertal window has passed. A family history of delayed puberty with delayed bone age points elsewhere (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Give three months of low dose testosterone
options.rationale: A short androgen course is a legitimate option when delay is causing significant psychological distress, which he does not report, and it advances puberty without increasing final height. It is offered after discussion rather than as routine management of a normal variant (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

options.text: Explain the pattern and review six monthly
options.rationale: A normal growth velocity tracking parallel to the centiles, a bone age delayed by more than two years, prepubertal testicular volume at 14 and a family history of late puberty describe constitutional delay of growth and puberty, which reaches a normal adult height without treatment. Regular review confirms the expected pubertal progression and detects the minority whose velocity falters (Source: RCH Melbourne: Short stature).

explanation.summary: Short stature is assessed by plotting serial heights, calculating growth velocity, comparing with the mid parental target range and obtaining a bone age, since the pattern over time discriminates far better than any single measurement. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the commonest cause of a short prepubertal adolescent boy, characterised by a delayed bone age, a normal growth velocity, a positive family history and eventual attainment of a height within the target range. Growth failure, defined by crossing centiles downward or a velocity below the expected range, points instead to pathology such as hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, growth hormone deficiency, chronic illness or an intracranial lesion. Basic screening includes full blood examination, renal and liver function, thyroid function, coeliac serology and insulin like growth factor 1. Psychological impact is asked about explicitly because it, rather than the height itself, most often drives the decision to intervene.
key_points: Growth velocity and bone age matter more than a single height measurement
Delayed bone age with normal velocity and a family history indicates constitutional delay
Crossing centiles downward signals pathology and prompts investigation
Growth hormone is for proven deficiency or specific defined indications
A short androgen course is reserved for significant psychological distress
explanation.pearls: A bone age delayed by more than two years alongside a normal growth velocity predicts a final height within the mid parental target range, which is the specific reassurance families need rather than a general statement that he will catch up.

subtopic_detail: Imaging decisions after a first febrile urinary tract infection that responded promptly in an eight month old
stem: An 8-month-old girl is reviewed ten days after her first urinary tract infection: three days of fever to 39.2 degrees C, a catheter specimen growing Escherichia coli, and afebrile within 30 hours of oral antibiotics. Antenatal ultrasound scans were normal.

data_table.Examination: Well, thriving on the 50th centile, normal abdomen and blood pressure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: No routine imaging; advise prompt urine testing with any future fever
options.rationale: A first urinary tract infection in an infant over six months that is caused by Escherichia coli and responds within 48 hours is a typical infection, for which routine imaging is not required in Australian paediatric guidance. The family instead receives clear advice to seek early urine testing with future febrile illness, since recurrence is the trigger for imaging (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound now to exclude a structural abnormality
options.rationale: Ultrasound is recommended for infants under six months with a first infection, for atypical infections and for recurrent infections, none of which describes her. Ordering it in a typical infection yields little and generates incidental findings and further tests (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Dimercaptosuccinic acid scan in four to six months for renal scarring
options.rationale: Cortical scintigraphy is reserved for children with recurrent or atypical infection, or where an abnormal ultrasound raises concern about scarring. Performing it after a single typical infection exposes a well infant to radiation without changing management (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram to look for vesicoureteric reflux
options.rationale: This invasive study is used for atypical or recurrent infection, an abnormal ultrasound, or a strong family history of reflux, and it requires catheterisation with radiation exposure. Identifying low grade reflux after a single typical infection does not alter outcomes (Source: RCH Melbourne: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Nightly trimethoprim prophylaxis until her second birthday
options.rationale: Prophylaxis after a single typical infection provides minimal reduction in recurrence and selects resistant organisms, and it is considered only for high grade reflux or frequent recurrences. Prompt treatment of recurrences protects the kidney better than continuous low dose therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Australian practice has moved away from imaging every child after a first urinary tract infection, because most abnormalities detected do not alter management and investigation carries radiation, catheterisation and incidental finding costs. An infection is classified as atypical when the child is seriously ill or septic, has poor urine flow, an abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, a non Escherichia coli organism, or fails to respond within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. Ultrasound is recommended for infants under six months with a first infection, for any atypical infection and for recurrent infection, with cortical scintigraphy and cystourethrography reserved for narrower indications. The most valuable intervention for a well infant after a typical infection is family education about testing urine early during future febrile illness. Age under three months, systemic toxicity or inability to tolerate oral therapy remain indications for intravenous treatment at the time of infection.
key_points: Typical infection means Escherichia coli with a response within 48 hours in a child who is not septic
Ultrasound is indicated under six months of age, for atypical infections and for recurrent infections
Cortical scintigraphy and cystourethrography have narrower recurrent or atypical indications
Prophylaxis is not routine after a single typical infection
Early urine testing during future febrile illness is the highest yield family advice
explanation.pearls: Collect the specimen by catheter or suprapubic aspirate in a non toilet trained child, since bag specimens have a false positive rate high enough that a positive bag culture should never be used to diagnose infection or to trigger imaging.

subtopic_detail: Sudden severe scrotal pain overnight in an adolescent with an absent cremasteric reflex
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 14 year old boy who woke at two in the morning with severe left scrotal pain and has vomited twice. It is now five hours since the pain began and he is pale and reluctant to walk.

He has had no dysuria, no urethral discharge, no fever and no recent trauma, and he is not sexually active. He describes a similar but briefer episode three months ago that settled after twenty minutes. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and exquisitely tender with the testis sitting higher than the right and lying transversely. There is no cremasteric reflex on the left and elevating the testis does not relieve his pain. His urine dipstick is negative for nitrites and leucocytes. The on call surgical team is in the hospital and theatre is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left testis high riding and transverse, exquisitely tender, absent left cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation, right testis normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and act on the findings when they are available
options.rationale: Imaging in a case with this clinical picture only delays surgery and can be falsely reassuring in early or intermittent torsion where flow is preserved. Ultrasound is helpful when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and would not otherwise lead to exploration (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

options.text: Refer him for immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum with bilateral fixation as indicated
options.rationale: Sudden severe pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is torsion until proven otherwise, and salvage falls sharply after about six hours of ischaemia. Exploration allows detorsion with fixation of both testes, since the anatomical predisposition is usually bilateral (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

options.text: Start oral antibiotics for epididymo orchitis and review him in the clinic within 48 hours
options.rationale: Epididymo orchitis is rare in a prepubertal or non sexually active adolescent, develops over days with dysuria or pyuria, and is typically relieved by elevating the testis. His negative dipstick and sudden onset point away from infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give strong analgesia and reassess him in the morning when the surgical clinic list is running
options.rationale: Any delay of hours in a testis that has already been ischaemic for five hours converts a salvageable organ into an infarcted one. Analgesia is given while theatre is prepared, never as a reason to wait (Source: RCH Melbourne: Acute scrotal pain).

options.text: Send a first pass urine sample for nucleic acid testing and treat according to the result obtained
options.rationale: Sexually transmitted infection testing is appropriate for a sexually active young man with a subacute painful epididymis, not for this presentation. Waiting for a result would waste the remaining window for testicular salvage (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time critical diagnosis with two incidence peaks, in the neonatal period and around puberty, and salvage rates fall from above 90 per cent within six hours to well under half beyond twelve. The classic features are abrupt severe pain often waking the patient from sleep, nausea and vomiting, a high riding transversely lying testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, and a history of prior self limiting episodes suggests intermittent torsion. Doppler ultrasound is useful when the picture is equivocal but must never delay exploration when the clinical suspicion is high, since preserved arterial flow can be seen in partial or early torsion. The main differentials are torsion of the appendix testis, which produces a localised upper pole tenderness with a blue dot sign, and epididymo orchitis, which develops over days with urinary symptoms. Fixation is performed bilaterally because the underlying bell clapper anatomy is usually present on both sides.
key_points: Abrupt pain with vomiting, a high riding transverse testis and absent cremasteric reflex indicates torsion
Salvage rates fall sharply beyond six hours of symptom onset
Doppler flow may be preserved in partial or intermittent torsion, so imaging must not delay theatre
Prior brief self limiting episodes suggest intermittent torsion and support urgent exploration
Both testes are fixed at operation because the predisposing anatomy is usually bilateral
explanation.pearls: Manual detorsion by rotating the testis outward like opening a book can restore flow while theatre is prepared, but it relieves pain in only some patients and never replaces exploration with fixation.

subtopic_detail: Loose soiling most days of the week in a well grown six year old who opens his bowels fully only every eight to ten days
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general outpatient clinic seeing a six year old boy whose parents have brought him because he has been soiling his underwear four or five days a week for three months. They describe the soiling as loose and runny and think he has ongoing diarrhoea, and his teacher has twice sent him home from school.

He opens his bowels fully into the toilet about once every eight to ten days, and his mother says those motions are so large they block the toilet. He passed meconium on the first day of life and his weight and height have tracked along the 50th centile throughout. His lower back and neurological examination are normal, and his abdomen is soft with a firm mass palpable in the left iliac fossa. His general practitioner prescribed a fixed low dose stool softener which the family gave for four weeks without any change.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with a firm non tender mass in the left iliac fossa, normal perianal appearance and anal position, normal lower back with no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes
data_table.Growth: Weight and height both on the 50th centile with no change in centile over two years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange an abdominal radiograph to confirm the extent of faecal loading
options.rationale: A radiograph adds nothing when a faecal mass is already palpable, and radiographic loading scores correlate poorly with the clinical picture, so it delivers radiation without changing the plan. Imaging is reserved for genuine diagnostic doubt or a suspected obstructive complication (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Refer for a rectal suction biopsy to exclude an aganglionic segment
options.rationale: The condition this test looks for declares itself with meconium passage beyond 48 hours, poor growth and a narrow empty rectum that decompresses explosively on examination, none of which fit a child on the 50th centile who passed meconium on day one. Overflow soiling is in fact distinctly uncommon in aganglionosis, which argues against it rather than for it (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Start an escalating oral macrogol regimen with a scheduled toileting plan
options.rationale: Runny soiling with infrequent enormous stools and a palpable faecal mass is overflow around a retained load, and no maintenance dose will work until that load is cleared, which an escalating macrogol course achieves at home over three to seven days. Pairing it with sitting on the toilet after meals treats the withholding behaviour that keeps the cycle going (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation).

options.text: Give a phosphate enema now before starting any maintenance treatment
options.rationale: Rectal disimpaction sits second in the Australian sequence because oral macrogol clears the same load without a rectal procedure in a child who is already withholding, and paediatric phosphate enemas can cause hyperphosphataemia with hypocalcaemia. It becomes reasonable only after an adequate oral course has failed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Prescribe a daily stimulant laxative alone and review him in six weeks
options.rationale: A stimulant without a disimpaction phase repeats the mistake of the earlier fixed low dose trial, because driving peristalsis against an impacted rectum increases the soiling and the pain that reinforces withholding. Stimulants earn their place added to maintenance macrogol once the load has cleared (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for more than 95 per cent of childhood constipation and the diagnosis is clinical, resting on stool frequency, calibre, withholding behaviour and an abdominal or rectal faecal mass. Soiling in this setting is almost always overflow rather than true diarrhoea, and families and schools routinely misread it as a behavioural problem or gastroenteritis. Treatment has two distinct phases that are frequently collapsed into one: clearing the retained load, then a maintenance dose continued long enough for a stretched rectum to regain sensation. Red flags that shift the workup are delayed meconium, failure to thrive, bilious vomiting, an abnormal sacral or neurological examination and onset in the first month of life. Relapse is the norm when maintenance is stopped as soon as things improve.
key_points: Runny soiling with infrequent large stools is overflow around a retained faecal load
Disimpaction must precede maintenance or the maintenance dose appears to fail
Oral macrogol is first line for disimpaction in Australia, ahead of rectal treatment
Radiographs correlate poorly with clinical constipation and are not needed to diagnose it
Passage of meconium on day one with normal growth argues strongly against aganglionosis
explanation.pearls: Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is titrated up daily over three to seven days for disimpaction, then continued at a maintenance dose for at least two months after a soft daily stool is established, because stopping as soon as the soiling settles is the single commonest reason it comes back.

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of knee pain and a limp in a heavy twelve year old whose knee examination is entirely normal
stem: A 12-year-old boy has six weeks of worsening left knee pain and a limp, with no injury. His weight is above the 97th centile. A knee radiograph two weeks ago was normal.

data_table.Examination: Normal left knee; the hip flexes into obligate external rotation and internal rotation is painful
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee and review with the result
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging of a joint with a completely normal examination will be normal, and the finding that matters lies proximal to it. Referred pain along the obturator nerve means knee pain in a child of this age demands examination and imaging of the hip before the knee is investigated further (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

options.text: Ultrasound of the left hip to look for a joint effusion
options.rationale: Ultrasound answers a different question, distinguishing transient synovitis from septic arthritis in an acutely febrile child with a hip effusion, whereas this boy has six weeks of pain, a normal temperature and normal inflammatory markers. A negative ultrasound would also not exclude the bony displacement that is actually present (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

options.text: Simple analgesia and activity modification with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Continued weight bearing over another four weeks risks progression from a stable to an unstable displacement, which raises the rate of avascular necrosis from under 5 per cent to as high as 50 per cent. A gradual six week history is characteristic of the condition rather than reassuring against it (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Urgent pelvis radiographs and strict non weight bearing
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with weeks of knee pain points to displacement through the proximal femoral physis, and anteroposterior plus frog leg lateral views of the pelvis are the diagnostic test because early slips are visible only on the lateral projection. Non weight bearing is started immediately on clinical suspicion because progression to an unstable slip is the event that destroys the femoral head (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics for a joint infection
options.rationale: Bone and joint infection is argued against by six weeks of gradual symptoms with a normal temperature, a C reactive protein of 3 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 8 mm/h. Empirical antibiotics would also delay the imaging and weight bearing restriction that actually change his outcome (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp).

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and its reputation for delayed diagnosis rests almost entirely on referred knee pain, since roughly one in four affected children present complaining only about the knee or distal thigh. Risk factors are obesity, male sex, age around the pubertal growth spurt and endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency, and bilateral involvement occurs in about 20 to 40 per cent either at presentation or later. Anteroposterior and frog leg lateral pelvis radiographs are diagnostic, with Klein's line failing to intersect the femoral head on the affected side, and early slips can be invisible on the anteroposterior view alone. Treatment is urgent in situ screw fixation, and the single strongest determinant of outcome is whether the slip is stable at the time of surgery. Avascular necrosis and chondrolysis are the complications that produce lifelong disability.
key_points: Around a quarter of slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents as isolated knee pain
Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the key bedside finding
Anteroposterior plus frog leg lateral pelvis views are required, as early slips hide on the anteroposterior view
Non weight bearing starts on clinical suspicion, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
Normal inflammatory markers over a six week history argue against infection and transient synovitis
explanation.pearls: Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck on the anteroposterior view should intersect part of the epiphysis, and any child under about sixteen presenting with knee pain and a limp needs a hip examination before the knee is imaged.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: A lumbosacral dimple with a hair tuft found at the newborn check in a baby with a normal neurological examination
stem: A 2-day-old term boy has a mark on his lower back noted at the newborn check. He feeds well and has passed urine and meconium.

data_table.Examination: Single midline lumbosacral dimple 6 mm across, base not visible, 35 mm above the anal verge, adjacent tuft of dark hair; normal tone and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents that no imaging or follow-up is needed
options.rationale: A simple dimple that is small, sited within 25 mm of the anal verge, with a visible base and no other cutaneous marker needs no imaging, but this one is larger, higher, blind ending and accompanied by two additional skin markers. Two or more cutaneous markers substantially raise the probability of an underlying spinal cord anomaly (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the definitive study but in a neonate requires sedation or anaesthesia, and it is reserved for babies with abnormal or equivocal ultrasound findings or with neurological signs. Going straight to it exposes a well newborn to an anaesthetic that ultrasound will usually make unnecessary (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.text: Review at the six-week check and image only if symptoms appear
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms means waiting for neurological injury, since tethering typically declares itself through leg weakness, gait abnormality or bladder dysfunction that may not fully recover after release. The point of screening is to detect the anomaly before that occurs (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.text: Plain radiograph of the lumbosacral spine before discharge
options.rationale: Plain films show bony vertebral anomalies but not the spinal cord, the filum terminale or an intraspinal lipoma, which are the structures that matter. It differs from ultrasound in imaging the wrong tissue while adding radiation (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

options.text: Spinal ultrasound within the first three months of life
options.rationale: An atypical dimple with additional cutaneous markers warrants imaging, and ultrasound is the first line study because the posterior vertebral elements have not yet ossified, which allows the conus and filum to be visualised without sedation or radiation. The window closes at around three to six months as ossification progresses, after which magnetic resonance imaging becomes necessary (Source: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

explanation.summary: Occult spinal dysraphism includes a tethered cord, intraspinal lipoma, dermal sinus tract, split cord malformation and thickened filum terminale, and it is frequently signalled by a cutaneous marker over the lumbosacral spine long before any neurological sign appears. Reassuring features of a simple sacral dimple are a diameter under 5 mm, a position within 25 mm of the anal verge, a visible base, a midline location within the gluteal cleft and the absence of any other skin marker. Markers that raise concern are a hair tuft, a subcutaneous lipoma, a haemangioma or other vascular lesion, a skin tag or appendage, a deviated gluteal cleft, an atypical or multiple dimple, and any discharge from the lesion, and the presence of two or more markers is a particularly strong predictor. Ultrasound is the first line investigation in the first three months while the posterior elements remain cartilaginous, with magnetic resonance imaging for abnormal or equivocal results or for older infants. Detection before symptoms matters because neurological deficits from tethering, particularly bladder dysfunction, often persist after surgical release.
key_points: Simple dimples are under 5 mm, within 25 mm of the anus, midline with a visible base and no other marker
Hair tufts, vascular lesions, lipomas, skin tags and a deviated gluteal cleft are concerning markers
Two or more cutaneous markers substantially raise the risk of dysraphism
Ultrasound is first line before three months while the posterior elements are unossified
Waiting for neurological symptoms risks deficits that do not fully reverse after release
explanation.pearls: Measure the distance from the dimple to the anal verge rather than judging it by eye, because a lesion more than 25 mm above the anus lies above the level of the sacrococcygeal segment and is far more likely to communicate with the spinal canal.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sacral dimples and spinal dysraphism

subtopic_detail: Deciding whether a six year old using reliever three to four times a week has crossed the threshold for regular preventer treatment
stem: A 6-year-old boy with asthma uses salbutamol via spacer as needed, with no preventer. Over three months he has used it three or four times most weeks, wakes coughing twice a month, has missed two school days and stops partway through soccer. Spacer technique is correct.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear with no wheeze at rest, SpO2 98 per cent in air

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue as-needed salbutamol and recheck technique
options.rationale: Reliever use on three or more days a week, night waking and exercise limitation together define poor symptom control, which is precisely the trigger for adding a preventer rather than for another period of observation. His technique has already been directly observed and is correct, so there is no remediable cause to review (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start an inhaled corticosteroid and long acting beta2 agonist
options.rationale: Combination therapy is the next step up if symptoms persist despite regular low dose inhaled corticosteroid, not the entry point, and long acting beta2 agonists are not recommended as initial preventer treatment in children of this age. Starting here also makes it impossible to know whether the corticosteroid alone would have sufficed (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start montelukast 5 mg each evening as preventer
options.rationale: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a second line preventer in children, less effective than inhaled corticosteroid, and carries a Therapeutic Goods Administration warning about neuropsychiatric effects including sleep disturbance and behavioural change. It is reserved for children who cannot use an inhaled corticosteroid (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start a two week course of oral prednisolone and review
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids treat acute exacerbations over three days, and a fortnight of systemic steroid for stable interval symptoms exposes him to adrenal suppression and growth effects without altering the underlying airway inflammation. Nothing in the current examination indicates an exacerbation (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start a regular low dose inhaled corticosteroid
options.rationale: Symptoms or reliever use on more than two days per week, any night waking due to asthma, or activity limitation each independently indicate poorly controlled asthma and warrant a regular preventer, and he meets all three. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is the first line preventer for a child of this age and is delivered through the spacer he is already using correctly (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Australian asthma control in children is assessed over the preceding four weeks against four questions covering daytime symptoms, reliever use, night waking and activity limitation, with more than two days a week of symptoms or reliever use marking the boundary of good control. A child with any of these features is not adequately managed on reliever alone, and low dose inhaled corticosteroid is the first line preventer for children aged six and over. Before escalating any preventer, adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure such as household smoking, and comorbid rhinitis should be reviewed, and a written asthma action plan updated. Growth is monitored because inhaled corticosteroids produce a small reduction in growth velocity in the first year of use, largely without affecting final adult height, whereas poorly controlled asthma itself suppresses growth. Response is reassessed at four to eight weeks with a view to stepping down after several months of good control.
key_points: Symptoms or reliever use on more than two days a week indicates poor control in a child
Night waking or exercise limitation each independently indicate the need for a preventer
