Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is first line preventer treatment from age six
Long acting beta2 agonists are not appropriate as initial preventer therapy in this age group
Confirm technique, adherence and trigger exposure before every step up
explanation.pearls: Reassess a child four to eight weeks after starting a preventer and consider stepping down once control has been maintained for at least three months, because the commonest cause of an apparently unresponsive preventer at that review is a spacer that is never actually used at school.

subtopic_detail: Jaundice persisting at four weeks in a thriving breastfed baby whose parents describe pale nappies and dark wee
stem: A four-week-old exclusively breastfed girl is still jaundiced and has gained 780 g since birth. Her parents report pale creamy stools for two weeks and urine that stains the nappy dark yellow.

data_table.Examination: Alert, jaundiced sclerae, liver edge 2 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 62 micromol/L; newborn screening normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer today to a paediatric liver service for urgent investigation
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or above 20 per cent of the total is never physiological and never breast milk jaundice, and pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed biliary flow that must be investigated before the surgical window closes. Outcomes after portoenterostomy fall sharply once the infant passes 60 days of age, so the referral is measured in days rather than weeks (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Reassure this is breast milk jaundice and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is common at this age in a thriving baby but is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normally pigmented stools, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after the conjugated fraction is confirmed normal. Pale stools and a conjugated bilirubin of 62 micromol/L exclude it outright (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Start phototherapy and repeat the serum bilirubin in twelve hours
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water soluble isomers and does nothing for a conjugated fraction, and in cholestasis it can additionally produce the bronze baby discolouration. Repeating the total alone also misses the fraction that carries the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Check thyroid function and repeat the bilirubin in one week
options.rationale: Congenital hypothyroidism and galactosaemia are part of the prolonged jaundice screen but both cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and her newborn screening was normal. A week of waiting on a time critical surgical diagnosis is the harm here (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice).

options.text: Request an outpatient abdominal ultrasound at the next appointment
options.rationale: Ultrasound forms part of the specialist workup and may show a small or absent gallbladder or the triangular cord sign, but a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis and a routine outpatient slot loses weeks. The investigations that matter are arranged by the receiving unit rather than sequentially in the community (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Prolonged neonatal jaundice

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant, or beyond twenty one days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin as the first investigation, and the single question that determines urgency is whether the conjugated fraction is raised. Unconjugated prolonged jaundice is usually breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, ongoing haemolysis, urinary tract infection or Gilbert syndrome, and is investigated at a routine pace. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in this age group means biliary atresia until proven otherwise, along with choledochal cyst, neonatal hepatitis, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and metabolic disease. Biliary atresia occurs in roughly one in fifteen to twenty thousand births and its outcome depends almost entirely on the age at Kasai portoenterostomy, with native liver survival substantially better when surgery occurs before 60 days. Because affected babies feed well and gain weight normally, well appearance is the trap rather than reassurance.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term baby requires a split bilirubin
A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or 20 per cent of total is always pathological
Pale stools with dark urine indicate obstructed biliary flow
Affected infants typically thrive, so good weight gain is not reassuring
Outcomes after portoenterostomy deteriorate sharply after 60 days of age
explanation.pearls: Ask the parents to photograph a dirty nappy on their phone rather than describing the colour, because acholic stools are often reported as normal by parents who have never seen a pigmented stool and the photograph resolves the ambiguity in seconds.

subtopic_detail: A groin lump that comes and goes with crying in a six week old born at 32 weeks, alongside an incidental umbilical swelling
stem: A 6-week-old boy born at 32 weeks has a right groin lump, first seen four days ago, that appears when he cries and disappears when he settles. He is thriving.

data_table.Examination: Soft easily reducible swelling above and lateral to the right pubic tubercle, non-tender; testes descended; 15 mm reducible umbilical swelling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the groin swelling?

options.text: Reassure and review both swellings at twelve months
options.rationale: Spontaneous closure is the expected course for the umbilical swelling, which is why that one is observed to school age, but the groin swelling arises through a patent processus vaginalis that does not close and can trap bowel. Applying the umbilical rule to the groin is the error this pairing is built around (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the groin before deciding on referral
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical when a reducible swelling appears with straining above and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and imaging is reserved for an equivocal examination or for distinguishing a hydrocele of the cord. Waiting for a scan adds days of incarceration risk without changing the plan (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for repair within days
options.rationale: Incarceration risk is highest in the first months of life and higher again in infants born preterm, running at roughly 30 per cent in the first year for this age group, so repair is arranged promptly rather than electively. Reducibility today does not lower that risk, since incarceration is an unpredictable event rather than the endpoint of a gradual process (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Refer for elective repair after his first birthday
options.rationale: Routine listing is appropriate for an older child in whom incarceration risk has fallen substantially, but a six week old born at 32 weeks sits in the highest risk group. An incarcerated hernia in this age group threatens both the bowel and the testis (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Apply a supportive binder and review him in six weeks
options.rationale: Trusses and binders have no role in children, do not prevent incarceration and can cause skin breakdown and pressure injury to the cord structures. They also give false reassurance to parents who then delay presenting when the swelling becomes irreducible (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

explanation.summary: Inguinal hernia in infancy is almost always indirect and results from failure of the processus vaginalis to obliterate, so it never resolves spontaneously and always requires operative repair. Incidence is around 1 to 5 per cent of term infants and rises to 10 to 30 per cent in those born preterm, with boys affected far more often than girls. The urgency comes from incarceration, which is commonest under one year of age and carries risks of bowel ischaemia, testicular infarction from compression of the cord vessels and, in girls, strangulation of an ovary within the sac. An incarcerated hernia that cannot be reduced needs immediate surgical attention, while one reduced successfully is usually repaired on that admission after a period of settling. The umbilical hernia is managed entirely differently, closing spontaneously in the great majority and only being repaired if it persists beyond about four to five years or complicates, which is very rare.
key_points: Infant inguinal hernia never closes spontaneously and always needs repair
Incarceration risk is highest under one year and higher again after preterm birth
The diagnosis is clinical and does not require imaging when the examination is typical
Umbilical hernias close spontaneously and are observed until about four to five years
Trusses and binders have no place in paediatric hernia management
explanation.pearls: A groin swelling above and lateral to the pubic tubercle that extends towards the scrotum is a hernia, whereas one that is confined to the scrotum, transilluminates and does not extend up the cord is a hydrocele, and only the first needs a surgical appointment within days.

subtopic_detail: A toddler refusing to use an arm after being swung by the hands, but with elbow swelling and bony point tenderness
stem: A 2-year-old girl was swung by her hands between two adults and has not used her left arm since. Her grandmother adds she also came off a slide onto grass.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held adducted, forearm pronated; swelling and marked point tenderness over the lateral bony prominence of the elbow; no wrist tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hyperpronation manoeuvre, then reassess the arm after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Reduction is appropriate for the classic presentation, which has a clear axial traction mechanism with no swelling and no bony tenderness, and manipulating an undiagnosed fracture risks displacing it. Swelling and focal tenderness over the lateral condyle are precisely the findings that remove this option (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

options.text: Elbow radiographs before attempting any reduction manoeuvre
options.rationale: Radial head subluxation produces no swelling and no bony point tenderness, so their presence together with an added fall from a slide means a lateral condylar or supracondylar fracture must be excluded before any manipulation. Lateral condylar fractures are intra articular, are easily missed on a single view and displace if managed as a pulled elbow (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

options.text: Broad arm sling with review in the fracture clinic next week
options.rationale: Deferring assessment for a week risks displacement of an undiagnosed intra articular fracture, which converts a cast into an operation. Immobilisation without imaging also leaves both the diagnosis and the neurovascular monitoring plan undefined (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

options.text: Supination and flexion manoeuvre, then a collar and cuff
options.rationale: This is the alternative reduction technique, differing from hyperpronation only in success rate and comfort, and it carries the same objection here because the examination does not fit radial head subluxation. Splinting afterwards would also mask the failure of a manoeuvre that should not have been attempted (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow).

options.text: Ultrasound of the elbow to look for a joint effusion first
options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate an effusion but does not characterise the fracture line, its displacement or the involvement of the articular surface, all of which determine management. Plain films answer the question that has been raised (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the elbow region

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation is the commonest elbow injury in children under five and follows sudden axial traction on a pronated forearm, classically when a child is lifted or swung by the hand. The diagnosis rests on a typical mechanism with a completely normal examination apart from refusal to use the arm, and radiographs are unnecessary when that pattern is clear because reduction is both diagnostic and therapeutic. What makes the diagnosis unsafe is any swelling, bruising, deformity or bony point tenderness, or a mechanism involving a fall, since lateral condylar and supracondylar fractures present in the same age group with a similarly held arm. Lateral condylar fractures are Salter Harris type IV injuries that cross the articular surface, are frequently subtle on the anteroposterior view and progress to non union and cubitus valgus if missed. Documented neurovascular status before and after any manipulation is part of the record in every case.
key_points: Radial head subluxation shows no swelling, bruising or bony tenderness
Any swelling or point tenderness mandates radiographs before manipulation
A fall as part of the mechanism removes the classic history
Lateral condylar fractures are intra articular and are easily missed on one view
Reduction is diagnostic and therapeutic only when the presentation is typical
explanation.pearls: After a successful reduction a child with radial head subluxation usually begins using the arm again within five to ten minutes, and continued refusal to use the arm at thirty minutes should prompt radiographs rather than a repeat manoeuvre.

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of nappy area rash unresponsive to barrier cream that now involves the skin creases with satellite lesions
stem: A 9-month-old boy has had a nappy rash for three weeks despite a thick zinc barrier cream at every change. It improved briefly and has since spread.

data_table.Examination: Confluent bright erythema over buttocks and perineum extending into the inguinal and gluteal creases; satellite papules and pustules on the lower abdomen; adherent white plaques on the tongue

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: A topical imidazole antifungal cream at every nappy change
options.rationale: Involvement of the skin creases with satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash, together with adherent oral plaques, indicates candidal infection rather than the irritant dermatitis that barrier cream treats. A topical imidazole applied at each change under the barrier cream is first line, with oral treatment added for the mouth (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

options.text: A potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily
options.rationale: Potent corticosteroids are avoided in the nappy area because occlusion under a nappy greatly increases absorption, risking skin atrophy and adrenal suppression, and they worsen an untreated fungal infection. A short course of hydrocortisone 1 per cent is the only steroid used here, and only for stubborn inflammation alongside antifungal treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

options.text: Oral cefalexin for five days with the barrier cream
options.rationale: Bacterial infection of the nappy area presents with pustules, honey coloured crusting, erosions or surrounding cellulitis, none of which is present, and satellite lesions with crease involvement point elsewhere. Oral antibiotics would also further disturb the flora that allows overgrowth (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Continue the barrier cream and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Barrier preparations treat irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the creases because urine and faeces do not reach them, and three weeks of adequate use has already failed. Persisting adds another fortnight of discomfort without addressing the organism (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash).

options.text: A single dose of oral fluconazole with the barrier cream
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal treatment is reserved for extensive, recurrent or immunocompromised disease because topical treatment clears uncomplicated candidal nappy dermatitis, and a single dose would in any case not cover the treatment period needed. It differs from the preferred option mainly in exposing him to systemic drug effects for no added benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Nappy rash is most often an irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and faeces, and it characteristically affects the convex surfaces of the buttocks, thighs and pubic area while sparing the depths of the skin creases. Secondary candidal infection is common after about three days of any nappy rash and is recognised by bright confluent erythema that fills the creases, satellite papules and pustules outside the main area, and often coexisting oral plaques. Bacterial infection, seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, scabies and, rarely, zinc deficiency or Langerhans cell histiocytosis are the other diagnoses to hold in mind, and a rash that is eroded, ulcerated or fails to respond to appropriate treatment should prompt reconsideration. Management always includes frequent nappy changes, nappy free time, gentle cleansing without soap and a barrier preparation, with a topical imidazole added when candidal features are present. Potent corticosteroids are avoided because the nappy acts as an occlusive dressing.
key_points: Irritant dermatitis spares the skin creases while candidal infection fills them
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash indicate candida
Topical imidazole under a barrier preparation is first line treatment
Potent topical steroids are avoided because the nappy occludes and enhances absorption
Oral plaques point to a coexisting oral infection needing separate treatment
explanation.pearls: Treat the mouth at the same time as the nappy area with oral miconazole gel or nystatin, because an untreated oral reservoir passes through the gut and reinfects the nappy area within days of stopping the topical cream.

subtopic_detail: A long narrow head with a palpable ridge in a five month old whose ears are symmetrical and whose head circumference is tracking normally
stem: A 5-month-old boy is referred because his head has looked long and narrow since six weeks of age and has not changed with repositioning. He was born at term and his development is normal.

data_table.Examination: Elongated narrow skull with frontal prominence and occipital pointing, ears symmetrically placed, firm midline sagittal ridge
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 75th centile, tracking since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise repositioning and tummy time, review in three months
options.rationale: Repositioning treats deformation from external pressure, which produces a parallelogram shaped head with the ear and forehead on the flattened side pushed forward, and it cannot alter a skull constrained by a fused suture. A further three months also passes through the period of most rapid brain growth when surgical correction is most effective (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric craniofacial service
options.rationale: A boat shaped skull that is long and narrow with a palpable midline ridge and symmetrical ears indicates premature fusion of the sagittal suture rather than positional moulding, and the diagnosis is confirmed and managed in a specialist unit. Referral is time critical because minimally invasive endoscopic techniques are generally restricted to infants under about six months, after which open cranial vault remodelling is required (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet fitted over one month
options.rationale: Helmet therapy reshapes a skull whose sutures are all open by directing growth away from the prominent areas, and it has no capacity to release a fused suture. It differs from the correct option in treating the shape rather than the constraint that produces it (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a normal variant
options.rationale: A palpable ridge over a suture with a skull shape that has not responded to repositioning is not a normal variant, and untreated single suture fusion can lead to raised intracranial pressure in a minority as well as a permanent cosmetic deformity. A normal head circumference is expected because compensatory growth occurs along the unfused sutures (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Arrange cranial ultrasound to assess the sutures
options.rationale: Ultrasound through the fontanelle images the brain rather than defining suture fusion and would delay referral without changing the answer. Where imaging is used it is a low dose computed tomogram with three dimensional reconstruction, arranged by the receiving unit (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Craniosynostosis).

explanation.summary: Abnormal head shape in infancy is usually positional in origin and follows the rise in supine sleeping, producing a flattened occiput with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced forward, giving a parallelogram when viewed from above. Craniosynostosis is far less common at about one in two thousand births and produces a characteristic shape determined by which suture has fused, with growth restricted perpendicular to the fused suture and compensatory growth parallel to it. Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single suture form and produces a long narrow skull with frontal bossing and occipital pointing, with symmetrical ear position and often a palpable ridge. Head circumference is typically normal in single suture disease because compensatory growth preserves volume, so a normal measurement is not reassuring. Multi suture and syndromic forms, including Apert and Crouzon syndromes, carry a much higher risk of raised intracranial pressure and are managed in specialist craniofacial units.
key_points: Positional moulding gives a parallelogram with the ear displaced forward on the flat side
Synostosis gives a shape determined by which suture is fused, with symmetrical ears
A palpable ridge over a suture is a key discriminating sign
Head circumference is usually normal in single suture synostosis
Endoscopic correction is generally limited to infants under about six months of age
explanation.pearls: Look at the head from directly above rather than from the front, because the parallelogram of positional moulding and the elongated boat shape of sagittal synostosis are almost indistinguishable face to face and unmistakable from the vertex view.

subtopic_detail: Pallor and irritability in a toddler drinking over a litre of cow's milk daily with a ferritin of 6
stem: A 22-month-old boy has been pale, irritable and tired for three months and no longer wants to walk far. He drinks about 1.2 litres of cow's milk a day and refuses meat and vegetables. His stools are normal.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L, mean cell volume 62 fL, ferritin 6 microg/L, coeliac serology negative with normal total immunoglobulin A

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the full blood count
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, cardiac failure or a haemoglobin below about 60 to 70 g/L with symptoms, and a child who is walking about with a compensated chronic anaemia does not qualify. Transfusing also carries the risk of circulatory overload in slowly developed anaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Arrange a single dose intravenous iron infusion as a day procedure
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for children who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron, or who have ongoing losses outpacing replacement, and it requires a day procedure with a small risk of hypersensitivity. Nothing here suggests oral therapy will fail (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis before any specific treatment
options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait shares microcytosis with this picture but is distinguished by a normal or high ferritin, a normal red cell distribution width and a red cell count that is high for the haemoglobin. A ferritin of 6 mcg/L with a normal C reactive protein already establishes iron deficiency, and electrophoresis performed while iron deplete can also falsely lower the haemoglobin A2 fraction (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Start oral iron and limit cow's milk to 500 mL daily
options.rationale: Excessive cow's milk is the classic Australian cause in this age group, displacing iron rich foods, providing calcium and casein that inhibit iron absorption, and causing occult gut blood loss, so replacement fails unless the intake is capped. Oral elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg per kilogram daily with dietary change corrects the deficiency and is continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises to refill stores (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Refer for upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated when there is overt bleeding, growth failure, gastrointestinal symptoms or failure to respond to adequate oral iron, and he has normal stools, normal growth and negative coeliac serology. An anaesthetic and endoscopy before a trial of treatment inverts the sequence (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow's milk intake is its leading cause, through three separate mechanisms: displacement of iron rich foods, inhibition of absorption by calcium and casein, and occult intestinal blood loss from a milk induced enteropathy. The recommendation is to cap cow's milk at about 500 mL per day from twelve months and to avoid bottles at bedtime. The blood picture is a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a raised red cell distribution width, often a reactive thrombocytosis, and a low ferritin, though ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant so a concurrent C reactive protein is needed to interpret it. Differentials are thalassaemia trait, which has a normal ferritin and a normal red cell distribution width, lead exposure, and coeliac disease. Treatment is oral elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg per kilogram daily continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises, and failure to respond within a month usually means poor adherence, continued milk intake or an unrecognised cause of loss.
key_points: Cow's milk above about 500 mL a day is the leading cause in Australian toddlers
A low ferritin with a normal C reactive protein confirms iron deficiency
Thalassaemia trait has a normal ferritin and a normal red cell distribution width
Oral iron continues for three months after the haemoglobin normalises
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or cardiac failure
explanation.pearls: Expect the reticulocyte count to rise within three to five days and the haemoglobin to climb by around 10 g/L per fortnight, so a repeat count at four weeks that has not moved points to adherence, ongoing milk intake or the wrong diagnosis rather than to a need for a higher dose.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

subtopic_detail: Persistent toe walking at five with bulky calves and a boy who climbs up his own legs to stand
stem: A 5-year-old boy has always walked on his toes. He walked at 18 months, cannot keep up on the oval and needs a rail on stairs. Rising from the floor, he walks his hands up his own thighs.

data_table.Examination: Bulky firm calves, ankle dorsiflexion 5 degrees with knee extended, normal tone and reflexes, downgoing plantar responses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for serial casting to improve ankle range
options.rationale: Serial casting treats a fixed contracture in idiopathic toe walking, which requires a normal neurological examination and no proximal weakness. Immobilising the legs of a boy with an untreated myopathy accelerates the loss of ambulation (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for Achilles tendon lengthening
options.rationale: Surgical lengthening treats the ankle contracture and not the weakness underneath it, and operating before the underlying diagnosis is known risks a significant functional deterioration in a child whose toe walking is compensating for weak hip and knee extensors. It differs from casting only in being irreversible (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

options.text: Measure his serum creatine kinase before any treatment
options.rationale: Toe walking with calf hypertrophy, proximal weakness demonstrated by climbing up his own legs to stand, and mild speech delay points to a dystrophinopathy, in which the creatine kinase is typically ten to a hundred times the upper limit of normal and is the cheapest and fastest screening test available. Australian mean age at diagnosis remains close to five years, and the delay is almost always because toe walking was labelled idiopathic (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy and review in six months
options.rationale: Stretching and physiotherapy form part of long term management of many causes of toe walking, but referring without a diagnosis defers the question for another six months in a boy who already has proximal weakness. A gait that has never normalised with weakness on standing is not the pattern that resolves with stretching (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of his brain
options.rationale: Cerebral imaging is directed at a spastic diplegia from an upper motor neurone cause, which would show increased tone, brisk reflexes and upgoing plantar responses rather than the normal tone and reflexes present here. Spinal imaging would be the relevant study if a tethered cord were suspected, which would produce back or bladder signs (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking).

explanation.summary: Toe walking is common in early childhood and is usually idiopathic, but the label can only be applied after a neurological examination that is entirely normal and where the child can walk with heels down when asked. The differential includes cerebral palsy with spastic diplegia, tethered cord, hereditary spastic paraplegia, autism spectrum disorder and neuromuscular disease, of which Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most time critical to identify. Boys with a dystrophinopathy present between two and five years with delayed walking, difficulty running and climbing stairs, calf pseudohypertrophy from fatty and fibrous replacement, and a positive Gower manoeuvre, and around a third have associated cognitive or language delay. Serum creatine kinase is the screening test, followed by genetic testing for dystrophin gene deletions, duplications and point mutations. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids started before significant decline prolong ambulation, and because cardiac and respiratory surveillance and genetic counselling for the family follow immediately.
key_points: Idiopathic toe walking requires a normal neurological examination and the ability to walk flat footed on request
Calf hypertrophy with proximal weakness points to a dystrophinopathy
The Gower manoeuvre demonstrates proximal weakness at the bedside
Creatine kinase is the screening test and is grossly elevated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Surgical or casting treatment before diagnosis can worsen function
explanation.pearls: Ask any boy who toe walks to stand up from sitting on the floor without using furniture, because the Gower manoeuvre takes ten seconds to elicit and converts a routine gait referral into a creatine kinase request that will usually come back above 10000 U/L.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: A rapidly growing red lesion on the upper eyelid of a three month old that partly closes the eye when she is tired
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a three month old girl whose parents are worried about a mark on her left upper eyelid. It was a faint pink patch at two weeks of age that they were told would fade, and it has been growing steadily since.

It is now a bright red raised lesion measuring 22 mm across the upper lid. Her mother has photographs on her phone showing it has roughly doubled in size in the past six weeks. By the end of the day, when the child is tired, the lesion droops enough that the upper lid covers the top half of the pupil, and her parents have noticed she prefers to look to the right. The lesion is soft, compressible, not ulcerated and not tender. She was born at 34 weeks and is otherwise thriving and developing normally, and there are no other similar lesions on her skin.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible non ulcerated lesion 22 mm across the left upper eyelid causing mechanical ptosis over the superior half of the pupil when tired, no other cutaneous lesions, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Growth: Weight and length on the 25th centile corrected for gestation, development appropriate for corrected age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her when she is twelve months old
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for the majority of these lesions, which involute over several years without treatment, but a lesion obstructing the visual axis during the critical period of visual development causes deprivation amblyopia and astigmatism from pressure on the globe. Vision lost in the first year is not recovered when the lesion later involutes (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Apply topical timolol gel twice daily and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Topical beta blocker is effective for thin superficial lesions of a few millimetres depth and is a reasonable choice where there is no functional threat. It penetrates poorly into a 22 mm lesion with a deep component and is too slow for a sight threatening problem (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Refer her for surgical excision of the lesion in the next few weeks
options.rationale: Surgery during the proliferative phase risks significant bleeding and a worse cosmetic outcome than the scar that follows involution, and it is reserved for residual fibrofatty tissue after involution or for lesions that fail medical treatment. Medical treatment shrinks the lesion faster and without a scar (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Refer her for pulsed dye laser treatment over the coming months
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser penetrates only about a millimetre and is used for ulcerated lesions and for residual telangiectasia after involution, not for a bulky proliferating lesion. It differs from topical treatment mainly in mechanism, sharing the same problem of reaching only the surface (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Refer her urgently for assessment and oral propranolol treatment
options.rationale: Obstruction of the visual axis is one of the accepted indications for systemic treatment, alongside ulceration, airway involvement, disfigurement and high output cardiac failure, and oral propranolol produces measurable shrinkage within days to weeks. It is started after cardiovascular assessment with monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, ideally before the proliferative phase ends at around five months (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas are usually absent or minimally visible at birth, proliferate rapidly through the first three to five months, plateau, and then involute slowly over several years, which distinguishes them from vascular malformations that are present at birth and grow with the child. Most need no treatment, but a minority require systemic therapy because of their site or complications, and the window for intervention is narrow because treatment works best during proliferation. Indications for oral propranolol are obstruction of vision, the airway or the ear canal, ulceration, high output cardiac failure and lesions likely to cause permanent disfigurement, particularly on the central face. Risk factors include prematurity, low birth weight, female sex and multiple gestation, and five or more cutaneous lesions prompt abdominal ultrasound for hepatic involvement. Segmental facial lesions raise the possibility of PHACE syndrome and warrant cardiac, cerebral and ophthalmological assessment before propranolol is started.
key_points: Proliferation occurs over the first three to five months, so treatment decisions are time critical
Obstruction of the visual axis is an indication for systemic treatment
Oral propranolol is first line, started after cardiovascular assessment
Topical timolol and laser reach only superficial lesions
Five or more cutaneous lesions prompt ultrasound for liver involvement
explanation.pearls: Any periocular haemangioma large enough to touch the eyelid margin needs ophthalmology review even if the pupil looks uncovered, because pressure on the globe induces astigmatism and amblyopia without ever obstructing the visual axis.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

subtopic_detail: A head circumference crossing from the 50th to above the 97th centile over three months with a tense fontanelle and vomiting
stem: A five-month-old boy has vomited most mornings for a fortnight. His head circumference was on the 50th centile at three months and is above the 97th today. He has stopped holding his head up.

data_table.Examination: Fontanelle full and tense when upright, prominent scalp veins, downward eye deviation; no retinal haemorrhages
data_table.Growth: Father's head circumference 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that this is benign familial macrocephaly and review monthly
options.rationale: Benign familial macrocephaly runs along a large but parallel centile line in a well infant with a large parent, whereas this head has crossed three centile lines in three months in a child with a tense fontanelle, vomiting and lost skills. His father's head circumference on the 50th centile removes the familial explanation entirely (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Arrange urgent neuroimaging and discuss with a neurosurgical service
options.rationale: Rapid centile crossing with a tense fontanelle when upright, distended scalp veins, downward eye deviation and developmental regression is progressive raised intracranial pressure, and imaging with immediate neurosurgical involvement is required because untreated hydrocephalus causes irreversible visual and cognitive loss. Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle can be obtained within minutes as the first study while the referral is made (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection before imaging
options.rationale: Abusive head trauma is an important cause of rapid head growth in infancy, but it is argued against here by the absence of bruising and of retinal haemorrhages, and by the gradual centile crossing with preserved growth elsewhere. Investigating that possibility first would delay imaging in a child with active signs of raised pressure (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Request an outpatient MRI brain at the next appointment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging gives the best anatomical detail and will be needed, but obtaining it as an outpatient in an infant who requires sedation takes weeks, and the pressure is rising now. It differs from the correct option only in timing, and timing is the whole question (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Measure the head circumference again in four weeks and plot it
options.rationale: Serial measurement is the right approach to isolated macrocephaly in a thriving infant with a soft fontanelle and normal development, none of which describes this child. Another four weeks of untreated raised pressure risks permanent optic atrophy (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

explanation.summary: Head circumference is plotted at every infant health check precisely so that a change in trajectory is detected before the clinical signs of raised pressure appear, and crossing centile lines is far more significant than any single large measurement. Benign familial macrocephaly and benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces are the common benign causes and both feature a well infant with normal development, a soft fontanelle and growth along a parallel line, usually with a large parent. The findings that indicate raised intracranial pressure in an infant are a tense fontanelle when upright and settled, distended scalp veins, sunsetting eyes from pressure on the dorsal midbrain, irritability, vomiting, developmental regression and a high pitched cry. Causes include obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus, intracranial mass, chronic subdural collections including from abusive head trauma, and venous sinus thrombosis. Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle is the fastest first study in an infant, with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging following as directed by the neurosurgical team.
key_points: Crossing head circumference centiles matters more than a single large measurement
A tense fontanelle when upright and settled indicates raised pressure
Sunsetting eyes reflect pressure on the dorsal midbrain
Loss of previously acquired skills is regression and is never benign
Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle is the fastest first investigation
explanation.pearls: Always plot the parents' head circumferences before accepting benign familial macrocephaly, since the diagnosis requires a large parent as well as a well infant, and a normal sized parent converts a reassuring measurement into one that needs explaining.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Raised intracranial pressure

subtopic_detail: rapidly enlarging vascular birthmark over the upper eyelid obscuring part of the visual axis at ten weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10-week-old girl whose parents point out a red raised lesion on her left upper eyelid. It was a faint pink patch at two weeks and has grown noticeably each week since.

The lesion is now 15 mm across, bright red, raised and compressible, and it partly covers the upper half of the pupil when she is upright and relaxed. It is not ulcerated and not bleeding. She was born at term, is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile. There is no other lesion on the skin, no bruit over the liver, no stridor and no other abnormality on examination, and the rest of the eye looks normal with a symmetrical red reflex. Her parents say a relative was told to leave a similar mark alone because it would disappear on its own.

data_table.Examination: 15 mm raised compressible bright red lesion of the left upper eyelid partly covering the upper pupil, no ulceration, symmetrical red reflex
data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Other findings: No additional cutaneous lesions, no hepatic bruit, no stridor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her at the 12 month immunisation visit for regression
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for most of these lesions because the great majority involute without treatment, but one that obscures the visual axis can cause deprivation amblyopia within weeks at this age. Waiting until 12 months risks permanent visual loss on that side. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Apply topical timolol gel twice daily and photograph the lesion weekly at home
options.rationale: Topical beta blockade is useful for small superficial lesions in non-critical sites, but penetration is insufficient for a deep or bulky lesion and absorption near the eye is a further concern. It will not shrink a periocular lesion quickly enough to protect vision. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Refer urgently for oral propranolol with cardiovascular screening and ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Periocular location with interference in the visual axis is one of the standard indications for systemic treatment, and oral propranolol produces visible shrinkage within days to weeks during the proliferative phase that continues to around five months. Referral includes pre-treatment cardiovascular assessment and ophthalmology involvement for amblyopia management. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and neck before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for large segmental facial lesions, where associated structural anomalies of the posterior fossa, arteries, eye and sternum must be sought, or for lesions with functional airway concern. A solitary localised eyelid lesion with no other findings does not require it before treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment as the definitive management of the lesion
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser has a role for ulcerated lesions and for residual telangiectasia after involution, but it treats only the superficial component and does not debulk a proliferating lesion. It cannot clear the visual axis within the window that matters. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate until around five months and then involute slowly over years, so most need nothing beyond explanation and review. Treatment is indicated when the lesion threatens function or life, when it ulcerates, or when it will leave significant disfigurement, and a periocular lesion obscuring the visual axis is among the clearest functional indications because deprivation amblyopia develops quickly at this age. Oral propranolol is the first line systemic therapy and produces rapid shrinkage during the proliferative phase, given after cardiovascular assessment and with feeding and hypoglycaemia advice for parents. Imaging is reserved for large segmental facial lesions or airway concern, and topical timolol is limited to small superficial lesions in non-critical sites.
key_points: Proliferation continues until about five months, which is the window where treatment works fastest
Functional threat, ulceration and disfigurement are the indications for treatment
A periocular lesion touching the visual axis risks deprivation amblyopia within weeks
Oral propranolol is first line; topical timolol suits only small superficial lesions
explanation.pearls: Ask where the haemangioma is before deciding whether it can be left alone: eyelid, nasal tip, lip, airway and perineal lesions all need same-week referral, and for one touching the visual axis oral propranolol plus ophthalmology review is urgent rather than something to revisit at the next immunisation.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Infantile haemangioma

subtopic_detail: loss of consciousness after a sudden fright with pallor preceding the event and a brief stiffening
stem:
You are the doctor in an emergency department. A 16-month-old boy is brought in after an episode at home. He bumped his head lightly on a table, looked startled, went pale and limp within seconds without crying out, and lost consciousness for about 20 seconds with some stiffening of his arms.

He came round on his own and was back to normal within a few minutes, with no drowsiness and no confusion afterwards. His mother says this is the fourth similar episode in three months, always triggered by a sudden fright or minor knock, and always with pallor first. He is thriving and has normal development. His diet is mainly cow milk, about a litre a day, with limited meat. He is afebrile and examination is normal with a soft abdomen, no murmur, no organomegaly and a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Episode description: Sudden fright or minor knock, pallor within seconds, limpness, 20 seconds of unconsciousness with brief stiffening, rapid full recovery
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 68 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (15-150), electrocardiogram with normal intervals
data_table.Development: Normal milestones, thriving, diet mainly cow milk with limited meat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the mechanism, treat the iron deficiency, and give first aid advice for episodes
options.rationale: Reflex anoxic episodes triggered by fright or minor pain, with pallor preceding collapse and rapid recovery, are benign vagally mediated events and iron deficiency is a recognised precipitant whose correction reduces their frequency. Parents need an explanation of the mechanism plus practical advice to lie the child flat and not to shake or resuscitate, since the child recovers spontaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.text: Start sodium valproate and arrange an outpatient electroencephalogram within four weeks
options.rationale: An antiseizure medicine is indicated for epileptic seizures, which are not preceded by pallor triggered by a fright and are usually followed by a postictal period rather than immediate normal behaviour. Treating these episodes as epilepsy exposes him to a hepatotoxic and teratogenic drug for a benign condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.text: Refer for cardiac electrophysiology study to exclude an inherited arrhythmia syndrome
options.rationale: An inherited arrhythmia would be suggested by episodes during exertion or swimming, a family history of sudden death, or an abnormal electrocardiogram, none of which are present with normal intervals on his tracing. Invasive electrophysiology is far beyond what a classical trigger-and-pallor history requires. (Source: RCH CPG: Syncope)

options.text: Admit for continuous video electroencephalographic monitoring to capture a typical event
options.rationale: Prolonged monitoring is useful when episodes are frequent and the diagnosis genuinely remains uncertain after a careful history. Here the trigger, the pallor before collapse and the immediate recovery make the diagnosis clinically, and events triggered by fright are unlikely to occur on demand in hospital. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

options.text: Advise the parents to prevent all episodes by avoiding any situation that startles him
options.rationale: Avoidance is impossible to sustain and drives restrictive parenting that harms the child's development more than the episodes themselves. Explanation with first aid advice achieves far more than attempts to eliminate every trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

explanation.summary: Reflex anoxic episodes are vagally mediated asystolic events in young children, triggered by a sudden fright, minor injury or unexpected pain, in which the child goes pale before losing consciousness. Brief stiffening or a few jerks from cerebral hypoxia are common and often lead to a mistaken diagnosis of epilepsy, but the sequence of trigger, then pallor, then collapse, with rapid full recovery and no postictal phase, distinguishes them. Iron deficiency is a recognised and correctable precipitant, so a full blood count and ferritin are worth checking, and an electrocardiogram is reasonable to exclude a long QT interval. Management is explanation, iron repletion when deficient, and first aid advice to lay the child flat and let the episode terminate on its own.
key_points: Pallor before the collapse, with an identifiable trigger, separates this from an epileptic seizure
Brief stiffening or jerks are hypoxic and do not indicate epilepsy
Iron deficiency is a correctable precipitant and repletion reduces episode frequency
An electrocardiogram excludes a long QT interval; further cardiac testing is rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent what colour the child went and in what order things happened: pallor that precedes the collapse after a bump or a fright is a reflex anoxic episode, and the treatment is explanation plus iron repletion if the ferritin is low, not an antiseizure medicine.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Breath holding and reflex anoxic seizures

subtopic_detail: thin midline membrane joining the labia minora in an asymptomatic preschool girl with a normal urinary stream
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed that her vulva looks different while helping her in the bath. The mother is worried that something is missing or has been damaged.

The girl is toilet trained, passes urine in a single forward stream without spraying, and has never had dysuria, discharge or a urinary tract infection. On examination, with the mother present and after explaining what you are doing, the labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent membrane, with a small opening anteriorly through which urine passes. The vulval skin elsewhere is normal in colour and texture, with no thickened white plaques, no fissures, no bruising and no bleeding. Growth and development are normal.

data_table.Examination: Thin translucent midline membrane between the labia minora with a patent anterior opening, surrounding vulval skin normal
data_table.History: Continent, single forward urinary stream, no dysuria, discharge or previous urinary tract infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric gynaecologist for separation under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgical separation is reserved for adhesions causing urinary obstruction, recurrent infection or symptoms that persist after topical treatment, and it carries a high recurrence rate until oestrogen levels rise at puberty. Operating on an asymptomatic girl with a patent anterior opening exposes her to anaesthesia with nothing to gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Prescribe topical clobetasol ointment once daily to the vulva for four weeks
options.rationale: A potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for vulval lichen sclerosus, which presents with thickened white plaques, fissuring, itch and bruise-like haemorrhage, none of which are described here. Applying it to normal vulval skin risks atrophy without addressing the fused membrane. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

options.text: Apply topical oestrogen cream twice daily for six weeks and review the response
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen does separate adhesions, but it is used for girls with obstructive symptoms, recurrent urinary infection or persistent local discomfort, and it commonly causes local pigmentation and occasionally breast budding. Starting it in an asymptomatic girl treats the parents' anxiety rather than the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Report the finding to child protection services as a possible sign of sexual abuse
options.rationale: Labial adhesions are an ordinary consequence of the low oestrogen state of childhood combined with local irritation, and they are not a marker of abuse; bruising, tears, bleeding or an abnormal disclosure would be. A notification made on this finding alone would be both distressing and unfounded. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Explain the finding, advise simple vulval care, and review only if symptoms develop
options.rationale: Adhesions that do not obstruct urine flow need no active treatment because almost all separate spontaneously as oestrogen rises around puberty, and many resolve earlier. Explaining the mechanism, advising against soap and bubble bath, and naming the symptoms that would warrant review is complete management. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

explanation.summary: Midline fusion of the labia minora is common in the low oestrogen years between infancy and puberty and is usually discovered incidentally by a parent. The decision point is whether the adhesion is obstructing: a single forward stream, continence and no history of urinary infection all indicate that it is not. Asymptomatic adhesions are managed with explanation and vulval care alone, since the great majority separate spontaneously and any treatment carries a high recurrence rate before puberty. Topical oestrogen, and rarely surgical separation, are reserved for obstruction, recurrent urinary infection or persistent symptoms.
key_points: Asymptomatic labial adhesions need explanation and vulval care, not treatment
Urinary stream, continence and infection history determine whether the adhesion is obstructive
Topical oestrogen is reserved for symptomatic or obstructive adhesions and recurs commonly before puberty
White thickened plaques with fissuring and bruising point to lichen sclerosus rather than simple adhesions
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to describe the urinary stream before deciding anything about labial adhesions: a single forward stream with no post-void dribbling and no previous urinary tract infection means the adhesion is non-obstructive, and the correct plan is explanation plus soap-free vulval care with review only if symptoms appear, not a six week course of oestrogen cream.

subtopic_detail: repetitive vomiting and pallor two hours after a first feed of rice cereal with no urticaria or wheeze
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 6-month-old boy is brought in pale and floppy. He has vomited more than ten times over the past hour. His mother says he was completely well this morning and had his first ever bowl of rice cereal two hours before the vomiting started, mixed with his usual formula which he has taken since birth.

He has no rash, no lip or tongue swelling, and his breathing is quiet with no noisy breathing or cough. He is lethargic but rousable and his hands feel cool. There was a similar but milder episode three weeks ago, two hours after his only previous taste of rice cereal, which settled at home over an afternoon and was attributed to a stomach bug. He is afebrile, and there is no diarrhoea, and no one else at home is unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176 beats per minute, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and lethargic, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, chest clear with no wheeze or stridor, skin free of urticaria or angioedema
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glucose 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly into the lateral thigh, repeated if needed
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is the treatment for immunoglobulin E mediated anaphylaxis, which is defined by acute skin or mucosal change with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise, typically within minutes of exposure. The two hour delay, quiet chest and entirely normal skin place this outside that pathway even though the child is shocked. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Normal saline 20 mL/kg as a rapid bolus with intravenous ondansetron, then reassess
options.rationale: This presentation is cell mediated rather than antibody mediated, and the shock comes from massive fluid shift into the gut, so the treatment is aggressive volume replacement with an antiemetic to break the vomiting cycle. Boluses are repeated until perfusion is restored, and most infants improve within hours without any adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone after blood cultures, with a fluid bolus for suspected sepsis
options.rationale: Sepsis is the reasonable default for a shocked lethargic infant, but the child is afebrile, the illness began abruptly two hours after a specific food, and an identical milder episode followed the only previous exposure to that food. Antibiotics can be added if the course deviates, but they do not explain a twice-repeated food-locked pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Oral rehydration solution given in small frequent volumes with review in four hours
options.rationale: Oral rehydration is first line for mild to moderate dehydration in gastroenteritis, but this infant is shocked with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and is vomiting repeatedly, so the oral route will fail. Shock requires intravenous or intraosseous volume regardless of the underlying trigger. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone with a non-sedating oral antihistamine and observation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines treat neither the volume depletion nor the underlying mechanism, and antihistamines are ineffective because histamine release is not the driver of this reaction. Relying on them would leave a shocked infant without the fluid that actually reverses the process. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome

explanation.summary: Profuse repetitive vomiting one to four hours after a food, with pallor, lethargy and hypotension but no urticaria, angioedema or respiratory signs, is the signature of food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome. Rice, oats, cow milk and egg are the usual triggers in Australian infants, and the reaction is cell mediated, so skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are typically negative and adrenaline has little role. The shock is hypovolaemic from fluid sequestration in the gut, and treatment is rapid isotonic fluid replacement with ondansetron. A previous milder episode after the same food is the historical clue that converts a presumed gastroenteritis into a recognised syndrome.
key_points: Delayed onset of one to four hours with no skin or respiratory features separates this from anaphylaxis
Treatment is 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses plus ondansetron, repeated to restore perfusion
Skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are usually negative because the mechanism is cell mediated
A repeat episode after the same food is the clue that the first was not gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: Ask what the infant ate two to four hours before the vomiting started, and whether the same food preceded a previous episode. Repetitive vomiting with pallor and shock but a normal skin and chest, twice after the same grain, is food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome: give 20 mL/kg saline boluses and ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg, not intramuscular adrenaline, and refer to a paediatric allergy service for a supervised food challenge rather than an adrenaline autoinjector.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Food protein induced enterocolitis syndrome
ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis
RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

subtopic_detail: developmental regression with microcytic anaemia and abdominal pain in a child living beside a smelter
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital. A 2-year-old girl is referred with four months of intermittent abdominal pain, constipation and irritability. Her parents say she has stopped using the ten words she had at 18 months and now mostly points. The family moved 18 months ago to a house built in the 1920s, three streets from a lead and zinc smelter, and renovations stripping old paint were done while they lived there.

She eats little meat and drinks about a litre of cow milk each day. There has been no vomiting, no fever, no diarrhoea, and no blood in the stool. On examination she is alert and interactive but quiet, with pale conjunctivae and no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising and a normal neurological examination with no focal deficit and a normal gait. Her weight and length have tracked along the 25th centile throughout.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, abdomen soft with palpable faecal loading, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, normal tone gait and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 66 fL (73-85), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-450), basophilic stippling noted on the film

lead_in: Which investigation should you request to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Venous blood lead level, taken with attention to avoiding external contamination
options.rationale: Residence near a smelter, a renovated pre-1970 house, a history of putting things in the mouth at this age, developmental regression, abdominal pain and a microcytic anaemia with stippled red cells together make lead the unifying explanation, and a venous level is the test that confirms it. Capillary samples are prone to skin contamination and a raised result on a finger prick still requires venous confirmation. (Source: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health)
source_refs: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to look for marrow infiltration or failure
options.rationale: Marrow examination is indicated when an anaemia is accompanied by abnormal white cells or platelets, blasts on the film, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain, and all of those are absent here. An isolated microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin is a peripheral problem, not a marrow one. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Urinary catecholamines with an abdominal ultrasound looking for a solid tumour
options.rationale: Neuroblastoma can present with irritability, anaemia and loss of milestones, but it almost always produces a mass, bone pain, periorbital bruising or hepatomegaly, none of which are found. The environmental history and basophilic stippling point away from malignancy. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis with iron studies to separate thalassaemia from deficiency
options.rationale: Electrophoresis is the right test when a microcytosis is disproportionate to the anaemia and iron stores are normal, whereas this child's ferritin of 9 micrograms/L already shows genuine iron deficiency. Neither result would account for the language regression or the stippled film. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A on a normal gluten containing diet
options.rationale: Coeliac disease is a fair explanation for iron deficiency with abdominal pain, but it does not cause loss of acquired speech, and it produces loose stools or faltering growth rather than constipation with centile-stable growth. It remains a reasonable second line test if lead is not the answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

explanation.summary: Chronic lead exposure in Australian children clusters around smelter towns such as Port Pirie, Broken Hill and Mount Isa, and around disturbed pre-1970 lead paint during renovation. The presentation is deliberately non-specific: colicky abdominal pain, constipation, irritability and loss of language milestones, with a microcytic anaemia that is worsened by coexisting iron deficiency because low iron increases lead absorption. Basophilic stippling is suggestive but neither sensitive nor specific, so the diagnosis rests on a venous blood lead level. Management is source removal and iron repletion, with chelation reserved for high levels or encephalopathy, and notification thresholds follow the national guidance.
key_points: Ask about smelter towns, pre-1970 housing and recent renovation in any child with unexplained regression
Iron deficiency increases gut absorption of lead, so the two commonly coexist and each worsens the other
A venous sample is required because capillary samples are contaminated by skin lead
Source removal and iron repletion come first, with chelation reserved for very high levels or encephalopathy
explanation.pearls: In an Australian toddler with a microcytic anaemia and lost words, the exposure history is the test-selector: a house built before 1970 that has been sanded or stripped, or an address in a smelter town, should trigger a venous blood lead level, and a level at or above 5 micrograms per decilitre is the national threshold for investigating and removing the source rather than simply treating the iron deficiency.

sources.label: NHMRC Information Paper: Evidence on the effects of lead on human health

subtopic_detail: scaly scalp patch with broken hairs and occipital lymph nodes unresponsive to topical antifungal cream
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy whose mother has been treating a patch on his scalp for six weeks. She has used a topical clotrimazole cream from the pharmacy twice daily throughout, and the patch has slowly enlarged.

On examination there is a 4 cm round scaly patch over the left occiput with hairs broken off a few millimetres above the skin, and a few small mobile lymph nodes at the occiput on the same side. The scalp is not boggy, there is no pus, no crusted honey coloured exudate and no fluctuance. He is systemically well and afebrile, and the rest of his skin and his nails are normal. A skin scraping and plucked hairs have been sent for fungal microscopy and culture, with results expected in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Round scaly occipital patch with hairs broken close to the scalp, ipsilateral occipital lymphadenopathy, no boggy swelling or pustules
data_table.Treatment to date: Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for six weeks with progressive enlargement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start oral griseofulvin daily with fatty food and continue it for six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Fungal infection of the scalp involves the hair shaft and follicle, which topical agents cannot penetrate, so oral therapy is required and treatment is started before culture returns when the clinical picture is characteristic. Griseofulvin with a fatty meal to aid absorption remains a standard first line oral agent for this infection in children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Switch to ketoconazole shampoo twice weekly and review the patch in one month
options.rationale: Antifungal shampoo reduces surface spore shedding and is a useful adjunct that limits spread to classmates and siblings, but it does not reach the fungus inside the hair shaft and will not cure the infection. Using it alone repeats the error of the last six weeks with a different bottle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to treat bacterial infection of the hair follicles
options.rationale: Antibiotics would be needed for a boggy pustular inflammatory mass with secondary bacterial infection, but there is no fluctuance, no pus and no systemic upset here. Treating a dermatophyte with cefalexin lets the scarring alopecia progress untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment daily to settle the inflamed scaly patch
options.rationale: A corticosteroid would be the treatment if this were scalp psoriasis or discoid eczema, but those do not break hairs off at the scalp or produce regional lymphadenopathy. Steroid applied to an untreated dermatophyte suppresses the inflammation while the fungus spreads. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Wait for the fungal culture before starting any systemic treatment, and keep him home
options.rationale: Culture takes up to four weeks and guides the choice of agent and duration, but withholding treatment during that wait allows further hair loss and ongoing transmission. Australian practice is to treat on the clinical picture and adjust once the organism is known, and exclusion from school is not required once treatment has begun. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Dermatophyte infections)

explanation.summary: Scalp dermatophyte infection is distinguished from other scaly scalp conditions by hairs broken close to the skin and by regional lymphadenopathy, which are absent in psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis. Because the organism lives within the hair shaft, topical antifungals cannot cure it, and six weeks of a topical cream that has failed is itself part of the pattern. Oral therapy with griseofulvin or terbinafine is started on clinical grounds while culture is pending, with an antifungal shampoo added to reduce shedding and household spread. Untreated infection can progress to a boggy inflammatory mass with permanent scarring alopecia.
key_points: Hairs broken at the scalp surface plus occipital lymph nodes are the clinical signature of scalp dermatophytosis
Topical antifungals fail because the organism is inside the hair shaft
Start oral therapy on clinical grounds; culture refines the agent and duration later
Antifungal shampoo is an adjunct to reduce spore shedding, never the sole treatment
explanation.pearls: Feel for occipital nodes whenever you assess a scaly scalp in a child: their presence alongside hairs broken a few millimetres above the skin makes dermatophyte infection likely enough to start oral griseofulvin the same day, typically for six to eight weeks and given with a fatty meal, rather than waiting the three to four weeks that culture takes.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Skin and soft tissue infections

subtopic_detail: thick fissured hyperkeratotic crusts on palms and soles in a child from a remote community with little itch
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote community clinic in the Northern Territory. A 7-year-old girl is brought in with thick grey crusted plaques on both palms and soles that have built up over several months, with deep painful fissures. Her scalp and back have thick scale as well.

Her grandmother says the girl barely scratches, which is why nobody thought it was the same thing her cousins had. Two other children in the household have an itchy papular rash between the fingers and on the wrists. This girl was treated for nephrotic syndrome last year and is taking prednisolone. She is systemically well, afebrile, with no cellulitis, no discharging sores and no joint swelling. Skin scrapings taken today are reported within the hour as showing numerous mites and eggs.

data_table.Examination: Thick grey hyperkeratotic fissured crusts on palms, soles and scalp, minimal excoriation, no cellulitis or purulent sores
data_table.Household: Two other children with an itchy papular eruption of the finger webs and wrists
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone, ongoing since treatment for nephrotic syndrome last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: A single dose of oral ivermectin today, repeated once in seven days, for this child only
options.rationale: Two doses is the regimen for ordinary scabies, but a heavily crusted infestation carries millions of mites and requires multiple ivermectin doses combined with a topical agent and keratolytic therapy. Treating only the index child also leaves the household reservoir untouched. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies)

options.text: Topical permethrin 5% cream applied once tonight and repeated after one week
options.rationale: Permethrin alone cannot penetrate crusts that are millimetres thick, so mites survive in the deeper layers and the child relapses. It remains part of the regimen, but only alongside keratolytic softening and repeated oral ivermectin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Scabies)

options.text: Multi-dose oral ivermectin with topical permethrin and keratolytic, plus household treatment
options.rationale: Crusted infestation is treated as a combination protocol because the crust shelters an enormous mite burden: a keratolytic such as urea or salicylic acid softens the scale, topical scabicide is applied to the softened skin, and oral ivermectin is repeated on a schedule determined by severity. Simultaneous treatment of every household contact prevents the immediate reinfestation that otherwise follows. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Scabies)

options.text: Oral cefalexin for ten days with daily bleach baths and dressings to the fissures
options.rationale: Antibiotics are added when there is impetigo or cellulitis complicating the infestation, and that matters in this setting because of the risk of subsequent acute rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. There is no pus or cellulitis described, and antibiotics do nothing about the mite burden. (Source: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections)
source_refs: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections

options.text: Cease prednisolone immediately and review the skin in one week before treating the mites
options.rationale: Immune suppression is the reason the infestation became crusted and the steroid dose should be reviewed with her nephrology team, but abrupt cessation risks adrenal insufficiency and relapse of the underlying renal disease. The infestation is treated now, not after a week of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

explanation.summary: Crusted scabies is the hyperinfested form seen in immune suppression, and the diagnostic trap is that itch is minimal or absent, so the appearance is mistaken for eczema or psoriasis. Thick fissured plaques on palms, soles and scalp in a child on prednisolone, with classic burrow rash in other household members, is the recognisable pattern. Because the crust shelters an extremely high mite burden, single-agent treatment fails: the regimen combines a keratolytic to soften scale, topical permethrin, and repeated doses of oral ivermectin, with simultaneous treatment of all contacts. In northern and central Australia this is also a public health matter, since the associated streptococcal skin infection drives acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and acute rheumatic fever.
key_points: Minimal itch does not exclude scabies and is characteristic of the crusted form
Thick crusts shelter mites from topical agents, so keratolytic softening is part of treatment
Repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide is the standard combination for crusted disease
Treat every household contact at the same time or reinfestation is immediate
