explanation.pearls: When a child on immunosuppression has thick crusted plaques and does not scratch, ask what rash the other children in the house have: classic finger web itch in contacts alongside minimal itch in the index case is crusted scabies, and it needs a keratolytic plus topical permethrin plus a multi-dose oral ivermectin schedule with same-day treatment of the whole household.

sources.label: CARPA Standard Treatment Manual: Skin infections

subtopic_detail: clockwork monthly fevers with aphthous ulcers and pharyngitis and complete wellness between episodes
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar in a fever clinic. A 4-year-old boy has had fevers to 39.5 degrees Celsius every four weeks for the past eight months. Each episode lasts four days and his mother can predict the next one on the calendar.

During episodes he has mouth ulcers, a sore throat and tender neck glands, and he looks miserable but is never admitted. Between episodes he is entirely well, attends kindergarten, and his weight and height have tracked steadily along the 50th centile. Two throat swabs taken during previous episodes grew normal flora, and a full blood count during a well period was normal. He has received all scheduled immunisations, has had no rash, no joint swelling, no abdominal pain and no diarrhoea, and there has been no overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile and well today, all vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination during episodes: Temperature to 39.5 degrees Celsius, aphthous oral ulcers, exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymph nodes
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count during a well interval normal, two throat swabs during episodes grew normal flora, growth along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the next episode?

options.text: Prescribe oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for ten days at the start of the next episode
options.rationale: Penicillin treats streptococcal pharyngitis, which would produce positive swabs and a course that does not recur on a monthly timetable. Repeated antibiotic courses for this pattern expose the child without altering the interval. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis

options.text: Arrange genetic testing for familial Mediterranean fever before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Monogenic periodic fever syndromes are considered when episodes involve serositis, rash, arthritis or amyloidosis, or when there is a suggestive ethnic and family history, and their attacks are not calendar-regular. Testing is reasonable if the course deviates, but it should not delay a therapeutic step that is also diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

options.text: Admit during the next episode for bone marrow examination and a whole body scan
options.rationale: Malignancy is the concern behind recurrent fever, but it produces progressive illness, faltering growth, cytopenias or organomegaly rather than eight months of complete wellness between identical four-day episodes. Invasive investigation is not justified by this pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Fever without focus)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral prednisolone at the onset of fever and record the response
options.rationale: A single corticosteroid dose given as the fever starts typically aborts the episode within hours in this syndrome, which makes it both the treatment and a strong diagnostic confirmation. Families are counselled that steroid may shorten the interval between episodes, and that the condition is self limiting over years with normal growth throughout. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

options.text: Refer for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy as the definitive treatment for the syndrome
options.rationale: Tonsillectomy does resolve this syndrome in many children and is a recognised option, but it is a second line consideration for frequent disabling episodes after the diagnosis has been established and the natural resolution explained. Proceeding to surgery before a steroid trial skips the least invasive confirmatory step. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

explanation.summary: Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis is the commonest periodic fever syndrome of early childhood and is defined clinically by its regularity. The three features that make the diagnosis are clockwork recurrence, complete wellness between episodes, and entirely normal growth. Negative throat swabs and a normal interval blood count exclude the alternatives that would otherwise need treatment. A single dose of prednisolone at fever onset usually aborts the attack within hours, which both treats the episode and confirms the diagnosis, although families should be warned that episodes may then recur sooner.
key_points: Calendar regularity with complete wellness between episodes is the diagnostic hallmark
Normal growth and a normal interval blood count argue against malignancy and immunodeficiency
A single dose of prednisolone at fever onset usually aborts the episode within hours
Steroid may shorten the interval between attacks; tonsillectomy is a later option for disabling disease
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to bring the calendar or phone diary: fevers that fall every three to six weeks to the day, each lasting three to five days with mouth ulcers and a sore throat, with a completely well child in between and a normal growth chart, is periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and adenitis, and a single prednisolone dose at onset that aborts the fever within hours seals the diagnosis without any genetic test.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Pharyngitis and tonsillitis

subtopic_detail: choosing seasonal immunisation for a preterm infant approaching their first winter with a well sibling at school
stem:
You are the doctor running a general practice baby clinic in early autumn. A 3-month-old boy born at 32 weeks gestation attends for his scheduled immunisations. He was in the special care nursery for three weeks with no chronic lung disease and has been well since discharge, feeding and growing along the 25th centile.

His mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy but says she was not offered any vaccines during it and received none. His 4-year-old sister is well and fully immunised. There is no family history of immunodeficiency, and the baby has had no wheeze, no admissions and no oxygen requirement since going home. His mother is worried because a neighbour's baby was admitted to intensive care last winter with a chest infection, and she asks what can be done to protect him through the coming season.

data_table.History: Born at 32 weeks, three weeks in special care, no chronic lung disease, no oxygen at home
data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 25th centile since discharge

lead_in: In addition to his scheduled vaccines, what should you recommend today?

options.text: Palivizumab given monthly through the winter season to this infant only
options.rationale: Monthly injections are burdensome and this product has largely been replaced in Australian programs by a single dose long acting monoclonal antibody covering a whole season. Monthly dosing also restricted eligibility to the most severe chronic lung and cardiac disease, which this infant does not have. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: A single dose of nirsevimab before the season, since his mother was not vaccinated
options.rationale: Protection against respiratory syncytial virus in the first season comes either from maternal vaccination in pregnancy or from a long acting monoclonal antibody given to the infant, and this mother received neither, so the infant needs the antibody. A single dose before or early in the season covers approximately five months, and prematurity places him in the group that benefits most. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

options.text: Influenza vaccine for the infant now, with a second dose given four weeks later
options.rationale: Influenza vaccine is recommended from 6 months of age, with two doses in the first year of vaccination, so it is a real part of this family's winter plan but cannot be given at 3 months. Cocooning by vaccinating the household is the interim measure at this age. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Influenza)

options.text: Defer all additional protection until 6 months of corrected age and review then
options.rationale: Correcting for prematurity is right for developmental milestones but wrong for immunisation, which follows chronological age, and deferral would leave him unprotected through the very season in question. Preterm infants are at higher risk of severe bronchiolitis, not lower. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants

options.text: Vaccinate the mother against respiratory syncytial virus now so her milk protects him
options.rationale: Maternal vaccination works by transferring antibody across the placenta in the third trimester, so giving it after birth does not protect an infant already born. Breast milk carries some protection but not the specific antibody titre this strategy relies on. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Protection of infants against respiratory syncytial virus in their first winter now runs along two alternative routes: maternal vaccination in the third trimester, or a long acting monoclonal antibody given directly to the infant. When the mother was not vaccinated during pregnancy the infant route applies, and nirsevimab is given as a single dose before or early in the season to cover roughly five months. Preterm birth increases the risk of severe bronchiolitis and strengthens the indication, while immunisation itself follows chronological rather than corrected age. Influenza vaccine remains part of the winter plan from 6 months of age, with household cocooning until then.
key_points: Either maternal third trimester vaccination or infant monoclonal antibody protects the first season, not both routes by default
Maternal vaccine given after delivery does not protect the infant, since the mechanism is transplacental antibody
Scheduled vaccines for preterm infants follow chronological age, not corrected age
Influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, with two doses in the first year of vaccination
explanation.pearls: For any infant facing their first winter, ask one question first: did the mother receive a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine in the third trimester? If not, the infant needs a single dose of nirsevimab before or early in the season, and the dose is scheduled by chronological age even in a baby born at 32 weeks.

sources.label: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Respiratory syncytial virus
Australian Immunisation Handbook: Vaccination for preterm infants

subtopic_detail: asymptomatic hip migration on surveillance imaging in a non-ambulant child with bilateral spasticity
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric rehabilitation clinic. A 5-year-old girl with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy attends for review. She has never walked and uses a supportive seating system, which corresponds to level four on the standard functional classification.

Her parents report no pain at all, and she tolerates sitting, standing frame sessions and nappy changes without distress. On examination hip abduction in flexion is 35 degrees on the right and 30 degrees on the left, with no fixed flexion contracture and no leg length discrepancy. A surveillance anteroposterior pelvic radiograph performed this month is reported with a migration percentage of 38 per cent on the right and 34 per cent on the left. The films from 12 months ago showed 24 per cent and 22 per cent. She has no scoliosis and her seating has not changed.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral spasticity, hip abduction in flexion 35 degrees right and 30 degrees left, no pain on hip movement, no fixed contracture
data_table.Imaging: Migration percentage right 38 per cent and left 34 per cent, compared with 24 per cent and 22 per cent 12 months ago
data_table.Function: Non-ambulant, supportive seating, level four on the gross motor functional classification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pelvic radiograph in 12 months as part of routine surveillance imaging
options.rationale: Annual imaging is the correct interval for a stable hip in a child at this functional level, but a migration percentage that has risen by 14 points in a year and crossed 30 per cent has already breached the threshold for referral. Continuing to watch risks silent progression to dislocation and later pain. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Prescribe regular oral baclofen and review the hip clinically in three months
options.rationale: Tone reduction is a useful adjunct that can improve comfort and ease of care, but no medical therapy reverses established femoral head displacement. Relying on baclofen would let the migration percentage keep climbing while the window for simpler surgery closes. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Reassure the family that intervention is unnecessary while the hips remain pain free
options.rationale: Displacement in this population is characteristically painless until the hip is subluxed or dislocated, which is precisely why radiographic surveillance exists rather than symptom-triggered imaging. Waiting for pain means intervening after the deformity is established. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics now given the migration percentage and its rate of change
options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent, or a rise of more than 10 percentage points in a year, is the trigger for orthopaedic referral regardless of symptoms, and both criteria are met here. Early referral allows soft tissue surgery or preventive reconstruction before the head displaces far enough to require salvage procedures. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Arrange botulinum toxin injections to the hip adductors as the definitive management
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin can improve adductor tone and sitting comfort and may be used alongside surgical planning, but it has not been shown to prevent progressive displacement on its own. Offering it as the definitive answer substitutes a temporary tone measure for the structural assessment the imaging demands. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

explanation.summary: Hip displacement in cerebral palsy is progressive, painless in its early stages, and closely related to gross motor function, which is why Australian practice uses scheduled radiographic surveillance rather than waiting for symptoms. The measurement that drives decisions is the migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to the lateral margin of the acetabulum. Referral to orthopaedics is triggered by a migration percentage above 30 per cent or a rise of more than 10 percentage points between annual films, and this child meets both. Tone management with baclofen or botulinum toxin supports comfort and care but does not reverse established displacement.
key_points: Surveillance frequency is set by gross motor function level, and non-ambulant children carry the highest risk
Migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral even in a pain free child
A rise of more than 10 percentage points in a year is itself a referral trigger
Tone reduction improves comfort and care but does not prevent progressive displacement
explanation.pearls: Compare the migration percentage with the previous film rather than reading it in isolation: in a non-ambulant child with cerebral palsy, either crossing 30 per cent or gaining more than 10 percentage points in a year warrants orthopaedic referral that day, because these hips are painless until they are already subluxed.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

subtopic_detail: painless ear discharge through a persistent drum perforation for more than six weeks in a remote community child
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote community clinic. A 5-year-old boy is brought in because his right ear has been running for three months. His grandmother says it never hurts him and he never has fever with it, but she has to wipe it most days.

On otoscopy, after you dry the canal with rolled tissue spears, there is a large central perforation of the right tympanic membrane with mucoid discharge coming through it. The canal skin is not swollen and the pinna is not tender to move. The left drum is dull and retracted but intact. He has no facial weakness, no swelling behind the ear, no headache and no neck stiffness, and he is systemically well. His school teacher has reported that he does not respond when called from across the room and has fallen behind with reading.

data_table.Examination: Large central right tympanic membrane perforation with mucoid discharge, non-tender pinna and mastoid, left drum dull and retracted
data_table.Duration: Discharge continuous for three months, painless, no fever
data_table.Function: Teacher reports poor response to speech across the classroom and falling behind with reading

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin for seven days with review at the clinic once the course is finished
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin is the treatment for acute otitis media with an intact drum and systemic symptoms, a picture that includes pain and fever rather than three painless months of discharge. Once a perforation is chronically discharging, oral therapy alone rarely dries the ear because the biofilm sits in the middle ear cleft. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.text: Framycetin with gramicidin and dexamethasone ear drops applied three times daily
options.rationale: This combination is used for infection of the canal skin where the drum is intact, and the aminoglycoside component is avoided when the middle ear is open because of the risk of inner ear toxicity. The non-tender pinna and normal canal skin indicate the problem is not an outer ear infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Otitis media)

options.text: Urgent transfer for intravenous antibiotics and a computed tomography scan of the mastoid
options.rationale: Urgent imaging and admission are for suspected intracranial or mastoid complications, signalled by fever, postauricular swelling, facial nerve palsy, severe headache or vertigo, and none of these are present. Transferring a systemically well child out of community for a chronic problem delays the treatment that actually helps. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.text: Refer for grommet insertion into both ears at the next visiting surgical outreach clinic
options.rationale: A ventilation tube is used for persistent middle ear fluid behind an intact drum, and the right ear is already ventilated by the perforation itself, so a tube adds nothing there. Surgical repair of the drum is considered only after the ear has been dry for a prolonged period and the child is older. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

options.text: Dry mopping with topical ciprofloxacin drops and referral for formal audiology assessment
options.rationale: Discharge through a perforation lasting beyond six weeks is treated by regular cleaning of the canal so that drops reach the middle ear, together with a quinolone preparation that is not toxic to the inner ear when the drum is open. Audiology is mandatory rather than optional because the hearing loss is driving the classroom difficulty and needs measurement and amplification planning. (Source: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children)
source_refs: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

explanation.summary: Painless discharge through a perforation persisting beyond six weeks defines chronic suppurative otitis media, which carries a high burden in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and is a leading cause of preventable childhood hearing loss in Australia. The treatment that changes outcomes is mechanical: dry mopping the canal so that topical antibiotic actually reaches the middle ear, using a quinolone because aminoglycoside drops risk cochlear toxicity through an open drum. Systemic antibiotics have a limited role unless there are signs of complication such as mastoiditis or facial palsy. Audiology referral is an essential part of the plan, since the conductive loss affects language and schooling and may need amplification or classroom sound field support.
key_points: Discharge through a perforation beyond six weeks is chronic, not acute, otitis media
Dry mopping before drops is what allows topical therapy to reach the middle ear
Use quinolone drops rather than aminoglycoside preparations when the drum is perforated
Every child with chronic discharge needs audiology and educational support, not antibiotics alone
explanation.pearls: Treat the hearing as seriously as the discharge: a child with a chronically discharging ear who does not answer when called across a classroom needs formal audiology and school based amplification alongside dry mopping and ciprofloxacin drops, because the conductive loss rather than the infection is what costs them their reading.

sources.label: Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children

subtopic_detail: breast development in a tall adolescent boy whose testes remain small despite advanced pubic hair
stem: A 14-year-old boy has had breast development for 18 months. He is above the 97th centile for height, his parents are average, and his arm span exceeds his height by 7 cm. He needed extra help with reading at school.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical breast tissue, testes 4 mL and firm, advanced pubic hair
data_table.Investigations: Morning testosterone low for age, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Testicular ultrasound for a hormone secreting tumour
options.rationale: A hormonally active testicular tumour is the concern when gynaecomastia is accompanied by a palpable testicular mass or a raised beta human chorionic gonadotropin, and both are absent here. Bilateral small firm testes point to failure of the gonad rather than a tumour within it. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging for a prolactinoma
options.rationale: A pituitary lesion causing hypogonadism would suppress rather than elevate the gonadotropins, so the raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone place the lesion below the pituitary. Imaging the pituitary here would be normal and would delay the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Clinical review in six months without further testing
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for physiological pubertal gynaecomastia, which occurs at mid puberty with normally enlarging testes of 10 mL or more and resolves within two years. Testes of 4 mL alongside advanced pubic hair is a mismatch that excludes the physiological pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Urine drug screen for anabolic androgenic steroids
options.rationale: Exogenous androgen use suppresses the gonadotropins and shrinks the testes, so it belongs in the differential of small testes with gynaecomastia, but the raised gonadotropins here point the other way. The history of no supplement or anabolic use is consistent with that biochemistry. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Karyotype analysis on a peripheral blood sample
options.rationale: Small firm testes with a raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone identify primary testicular failure, and in a tall adolescent with disproportionately long limbs, breast development and learning difficulty the explanation is an additional X chromosome. Karyotype confirms it and opens the discussion about testosterone replacement and fertility preservation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

explanation.summary: The discriminating finding in adolescent gynaecomastia is testicular volume interpreted against the stage of pubic hair. Physiological pubertal gynaecomastia occurs when the testes are already 10 mL or larger and settles within about two years, whereas testes of 4 mL with advanced pubic hair indicates that androgen is coming from the adrenal while the testis has failed. A raised luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone localises the problem to the gonad, and the combination with tall stature, long limbs and learning difficulties is characteristic of an additional X chromosome. Karyotype confirms the diagnosis, after which management involves paediatric endocrinology, testosterone replacement, educational support and early counselling about fertility.
key_points: Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer before attributing gynaecomastia to puberty
Raised gonadotropins localise the defect to the testis rather than the pituitary
Tall stature with long limbs and learning difficulty alongside small firm testes suggests an extra X chromosome
Suppressed gonadotropins with small testes would instead suggest exogenous androgen use
explanation.pearls: Gynaecomastia plus testes under 6 mL in a boy with well developed pubic hair is never physiological: check morning testosterone with luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone, and if the gonadotropins are high, send a karyotype rather than scheduling a six month review.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Delayed puberty and hypogonadism

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease with delayed presentation past day 10
stem: A 3-year-old boy has had fever for eleven days, a truncal rash from day three, cracked lips, red eyes without discharge and a swollen left neck lump. His fingertips are now peeling. Blood cultures are negative at 24 hours.

data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 158 mg/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L; echocardiogram normal coronary arteries and function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold immunoglobulin because he is past day ten, and observe
options.rationale: Fulfilment of four principal criteria with persistent inflammation (CRP 158, platelets 612, hyponatraemia, hypoalbuminaemia) meets the AHA definition of Kawasaki disease presenting late. IVIG is still indicated beyond day 10 when inflammatory markers are elevated OR coronary changes are present, because it lowers aneurysm risk even in the sub-acute phase. Withholding therapy exposes the child to progressive coronary injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge on ibuprofen with paediatric outpatient review in two weeks
options.rationale: Discharge on a non-steroidal without immunomodulation abandons the disease-modifying window entirely. Ibuprofen does not treat vasculitis and worsens the risk profile if aspirin is later required. Inpatient IVIG plus aspirin is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Change to intravenous ceftriaxone and repeat the blood cultures
options.rationale: The clinical pattern is not bacterial sepsis nor EBV (no exudative pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, negative cultures at 24 hours). Antibiotic escalation delays IVIG. Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis and infectious workup should not defer treatment when criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse, holding immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Corticosteroids in Kawasaki disease are adjunctive for predicted IVIG resistance or for genuine IVIG failure (persistent fever 36 hours after first infusion), not as a first-line replacement for IVIG. Steroid monotherapy leaves the coronary risk unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high dose aspirin, repeat echocardiography
options.rationale: This child fulfils four of the five principal criteria (rash, conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, extremity changes, cervical adenopathy >1.5 cm) with persistent fever and strongly elevated inflammatory markers past day 10; RCH and AHA both recommend IVIG plus aspirin in the sub-acute phase provided CRP or coronary artery changes remain. Serial echocardiography detects late aneurysm formation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood; the coronary arteries are the principal target and untreated disease carries a 25% risk of aneurysm formation, falling to under 5% with timely IVIG. RCH and the American Heart Association both treat presentations beyond day 10 with IVIG plus aspirin when systemic inflammation persists (CRP raised, ESR raised, platelets rising, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria) or when the echocardiogram shows coronary changes. Aspirin is used at anti-inflammatory dose while febrile then reduced to antiplatelet dose for six to eight weeks or until inflammatory markers normalise. Follow-up echocardiography at two and six weeks catches late aneurysm development.
key_points: Four of five principal criteria plus fever meet clinical Kawasaki diagnosis; incomplete Kawasaki uses a supplementary lab algorithm.
IVIG 2 g/kg reduces coronary aneurysm risk from roughly 25% to under 5%.
Late-presenting Kawasaki (after day 10) still receives IVIG if CRP raised or coronaries abnormal.
IVIG resistance (fever >36 hours after infusion) is the trigger for adjunctive steroids or infliximab.
Aspirin is used at anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet dose and is one of the paediatric exceptions to the Reye syndrome caution.
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria plus a strawberry tongue plus a platelet count above 450 x10^9/L in a persistently febrile toddler flips the differential from viral exanthem toward Kawasaki disease before the classic extremity peeling appears.

sources.label: American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at-risk newborn
stem: A 2-hour-old boy born at 39+4 weeks to a mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes has fed once with a shallow latch. He is quiet, pink and well perfused. Heel-prick glucose is 1.9 mmol/L (threshold 2.6).

data_table.Examination: Birth weight 4420 g (97th centile); alert, normal tone, no jitteriness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose intravenously and special care admission
options.rationale: IV dextrose bolus is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia OR persistently low glucose despite oral or buccal glucose gel measures. An asymptomatic first low reading at 1.9 mmol/L is treated first with oral 40% glucose gel and a feed, per RCH and Australasian pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Critical hypoglycaemia screen before any further intervention
options.rationale: A hyperinsulinism screen is triggered by hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 hours, requiring glucose infusion rates above 8 mg/kg/min, or occurring outside a recognised risk category. It is not the first response to a single mildly low reading in an infant of a diabetic mother. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: 30 mL/kg of formula by bottle, rechecking in six hours
options.rationale: A 30 mL/kg formula bolus at 2 hours of life is a supra-physiological volume and undermines breastfeeding without addressing the immediate metabolic risk any better than gel plus feed. Testing intervals are pre-feed at 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours for infants of diabetic mothers, not at a six-hour gap. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Repeat the glucose at four hours as a physiological nadir
options.rationale: The physiological glucose nadir in healthy term babies is around 1 hour of life; a value of 1.9 mmol/L at 2 hours in an infant of a diabetic mother is below the RCH intervention threshold of 2.6 mmol/L and requires active management, not observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: 200 mg/kg of 40% buccal dextrose gel and a feed, recheck at 30 minutes
options.rationale: The Sugar Babies/HYPO protocol adopted by RCH treats asymptomatic hypoglycaemia below 2.6 mmol/L in at-risk infants with 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) of 40% buccal dextrose gel plus a supported feed, then rechecks the level 30 minutes after the feed. This avoids unnecessary separation and preserves breastfeeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: Sugar Babies (Harris 2013) buccal dextrose gel trial

explanation.summary: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is managed on a stepped pathway that keeps the mother-baby dyad together where possible. RCH defines a target of at least 2.6 mmol/L pre-feed from 2 hours of age in at-risk infants: infants of diabetic mothers, small or large for gestational age, preterm 35-37 weeks, and those with perinatal stress. Asymptomatic first low readings are treated with buccal 40% dextrose gel at 200 mg/kg plus a supported breastfeed, with recheck 30 minutes after the feed. Failure of two gel-and-feed cycles, symptomatic hypoglycaemia, or a glucose under 1.5 mmol/L escalates to IV dextrose and special-care admission with a target glucose infusion rate that keeps the infant euglycaemic.
key_points: At-risk infants (IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm, perinatal stress) get pre-feed BSL at 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours.
First-line treatment for asymptomatic BSL <2.6 mmol/L is 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) of 40% dextrose gel plus a feed.
Recheck BSL 30 minutes after the feed; if still low, repeat gel plus feed once before IV dextrose.
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL <1.5 mmol/L bypasses gel and goes straight to IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg then infusion.
Persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours or GIR >8 mg/kg/min triggers a hyperinsulinism screen.
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dosed at 200 mg/kg keeps the mother and baby together and reduces NICU admission for hypoglycaemia by about 40% in the Sugar Babies trial - remember 0.5 mL/kg of 40% gel.

sources.label: Sugar Babies (Harris 2013) buccal dextrose gel trial

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia from excess cow's milk intake
stem: An 18-month-old girl looks pale. She drinks about 900 mL of cow's milk daily and refuses meat, egg and vegetables. There is no bleeding or family history of haemoglobinopathy. Iron studies are pending.

data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 82 g/L, mean cell volume 62 fL, platelets 468 x10^9/L
data_table.Blood film: Microcytic hypochromic cells, no basophilic stippling or target cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral iron 3 mg/kg daily, milk under 500 mL daily, plus coeliac serology
options.rationale: The clinical picture (excess milk intake, meat refusal, microcytic hypochromic anaemia without haemolysis or bleeding) is classic dietary iron deficiency. RCH treats with 3-6 mg/kg elemental iron daily and reduces cow's milk to below 500 mL/day. Coeliac serology (transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA) is co-ordered because coeliac disease is a common co-cause of iron deficiency in toddlers. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy before any oral iron therapy is started
options.rationale: Bone marrow biopsy is reserved for suspected marrow failure, refractory anaemia after adequate iron replacement, or when the blood film and history do not fit a common cause. Dietary iron deficiency in an otherwise well toddler does not warrant an invasive procedure as a first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion as first line treatment
options.rationale: IV iron in children under five is reserved for oral iron intolerance, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD), or ongoing losses that outstrip oral replacement. A well toddler with dietary iron deficiency will respond to oral iron; ferric carboxymaltose is not licensed under one year and is second line under five. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis first, deferring iron until thalassaemia excluded
options.rationale: The presentation strongly favours iron deficiency (dietary history, low MCH, high red cell distribution width, no family history of haemoglobinopathy). Iron replacement should not be delayed pending electrophoresis, though electrophoresis is legitimate if the response to iron is inadequate at eight weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: An over the counter paediatric multivitamin containing 4 mg iron daily
options.rationale: A multivitamin containing 4 mg of iron delivers approximately one-fifth of the therapeutic dose required and will not correct clinical anaemia in a reasonable timeframe. Six-month review of a haemoglobin of 82 g/L delays diagnosis of the roughly 20% of iron-deficient toddlers who have an underlying malabsorptive cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is the commonest paediatric anaemia in Australia, peaking between nine months and three years when rapid growth outstrips a milk-heavy diet with limited iron intake. Excess cow's milk (>500 mL/day) both displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss through non-IgE cow's milk protein enteropathy in some children. Assessment includes an iron panel with ferritin (an acute phase reactant that may be falsely normal), coeliac serology, and dietary counselling. Oral ferrous sulfate 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron is first line; expect a haemoglobin rise of about 10 g/L per fortnight and a reticulocyte response within a week. Continue treatment for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation to replenish stores.
key_points: Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day in toddlers to prevent iron deficiency.
First-line oral iron dose is 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron; ferrous sulfate 30 mg = 6 mg elemental.
Co-order coeliac serology because coeliac disease is a common cause of refractory iron deficiency.
Expect Hb rise of about 10 g/L per fortnight; failure to respond triggers investigation for malabsorption or loss.
Continue oral iron for three months after Hb normalises to refill stores.
explanation.pearls: In a well-appearing toddler with dietary iron deficiency, transferrin saturation below 16% and ferritin below 15 microg/L confirm the diagnosis; a rise in reticulocyte count within seven days of starting ferrous sulfate proves the therapy is working before the haemoglobin has moved.

subtopic_detail: Bruising in a non-mobile infant and mandatory reporting
stem: A 4-month-old boy has a bruise on his left cheek, which his mother attributes to the family cat jumping over him. He is not rolling and cannot sit unsupported.

data_table.Skin survey: Left cheek bruise 2 cm x 1 cm; 1 cm linear bruise on the left pinna
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, coagulation profile and blood film normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the mechanism, arrange general practice review and discharge
options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant carries a strong statistical association with inflicted injury regardless of the explanation offered, because the mechanisms available to an infant who cannot roll are extremely limited. Discharge without a full skeletal survey and child protection referral misses occult fractures and abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Admit for skeletal survey, MRI brain and child protection referral
options.rationale: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant is a sentinel injury: TEN-4 FACESp screening puts this in the highest concern category (face and ear bruising, under 4 months). RCH mandates full skeletal survey, neuroimaging for abusive head trauma, ophthalmology fundoscopy, and same-day involvement of the hospital child protection team plus a mandatory report to statutory services. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
source_refs: TEN-4 FACESp bruising clinical decision rule

options.text: Request von Willebrand studies before any further investigation
options.rationale: Bleeding disorders should be excluded but do not replace child protection assessment. Coagulation screening runs in parallel with skeletal survey, neuroimaging and social work involvement, not instead of them. Sequential single-track workup delays safeguarding decisions. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Photograph the bruises, discharge, and request a child health nurse visit
options.rationale: Photodocumentation is important but not sufficient. Discharging a pre-mobile infant with unexplained bruising home before completing the skeletal survey and safeguarding pathway exposes the child to further injury; the child health nurse cannot substitute for the paediatric child protection team. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Radiograph the skull and left ribs; if normal, manage as accidental
options.rationale: A limited two-view series misses the classic metaphyseal lesions, posterior rib fractures, and healing fractures that a full 21-view skeletal survey detects. Statutory notification is mandatory for reasonable suspicion regardless of imaging results in every Australian jurisdiction. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: The mantra 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise' captures the epidemiology: bruising in an infant who cannot yet mobilise (roll, cruise, walk) is exceptional in accidental injury and highly predictive of inflicted trauma. The TEN-4 FACESp decision rule flags bruising to the Trunk, Ear, Neck in any child under four years, Face, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid or Subconjunctivae, or Patterned bruising, and any bruise in a pre-cruiser as a sentinel injury requiring evaluation. Standard RCH workup includes full skeletal survey (repeated at 2 weeks for equivocal findings), MRI brain, dilated fundoscopy, coagulation and full blood count, and same-day involvement of the paediatric child protection team. Mandatory reporting to the statutory child protection agency is triggered by reasonable belief of harm, not diagnostic certainty.
key_points: Pre-mobile infant bruising is a sentinel injury for abusive head trauma and occult fracture.
TEN-4 FACESp flags Torso, Ear, Neck (under 4 years); Face, Angle jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Subconjunctivae; Patterned; and pre-cruisers.
Full skeletal survey (21 views) not a limited two-view study; consider a repeat at 2 weeks.
MRI brain is preferred over CT for abusive head trauma; dilated fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages.
Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable belief, not certainty; runs in parallel with medical workup.
explanation.pearls: A bruise on the ear or the cheek of an infant under 4 months old carries a positive predictive value for inflicted injury above 90% in TEN-4 FACESp derivation cohorts; a full skeletal survey plus MRI brain the same day is standard of care regardless of the explanation offered.

sources.label: TEN-4 FACESp bruising clinical decision rule

subtopic_detail: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and biliary atresia workup
stem: A 5-week-old breastfed girl has prolonged jaundice, pale stools for ten days and dark urine for a week. She is alert, on the 25th centile, with a 2 cm liver edge.

data_table.Bilirubin: Total 152 micromol/L, conjugated 68 micromol/L (reference less than 20)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure about breast milk jaundice and repeat bilirubin in two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is UNCONJUGATED. A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L (or above 20% of total) is always pathological in infancy and cannot be attributed to breastfeeding. Delayed workup misses the Kasai-portoenterostomy window for biliary atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Admit for phototherapy and reassess the total bilirubin at 24 hours
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers; it does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and can cause bronze baby syndrome in the presence of a significant direct fraction. It also anchors decision-making on the wrong pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Admit for urgent hepatology review, hepatobiliary ultrasound and liver biopsy
options.rationale: A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L with pale stool and dark urine in an infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 60 days of life gives the best long-term native-liver survival, so admit, involve paediatric hepatology, and expedite the triple workup of ultrasound, HIDA and liver biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: GESA and Liver Foundation Australia biliary atresia pathway

options.text: Trial two weeks of formula feeding, then repeat both bilirubin fractions
options.rationale: A milk-swap trial is only relevant to distinguishing breast milk unconjugated jaundice; it has no role once the conjugated fraction is elevated. Two weeks of delay in biliary atresia crosses the critical 60-day surgical window. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Send urine culture and thyroid function, referring only if abnormal
options.rationale: UTI and hypothyroidism are recognised causes of prolonged UNCONJUGATED jaundice. Neither typically produces a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L with pale stools. Sequential ruling out of these before hepatology referral delays the surgical window for biliary atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days in a preterm) must have a split bilirubin done. A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L, or above 20% of the total, is always pathological. The differential includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, neonatal hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis, TORCH infection, metabolic disorders and parenteral nutrition associated cholestasis. Biliary atresia is the not-to-miss diagnosis because Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 60 days of life gives the best native-liver survival; every week of delay after that meaningfully worsens outcomes. Standard workup pairs ultrasound (looking for the 'triangular cord sign' and absent gallbladder) with hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA) after phenobarbital priming and, when indicated, liver biopsy plus intraoperative cholangiogram.
key_points: Split bilirubin is mandatory for jaundice persisting beyond 14 days (21 days preterm).
Conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is pathological.
Pale stool plus dark urine is biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life optimises native-liver survival.
Phototherapy has no role and can cause bronze baby syndrome when conjugated fraction is high.
explanation.pearls: Any breastfed baby still jaundiced at two weeks needs a split bilirubin; a direct fraction of 68 micromol/L with pale stools mandates same-week ultrasound and hepatology referral because Kasai portoenterostomy done inside the 60-day window doubles the 10-year native-liver survival.

sources.label: GESA and Liver Foundation Australia biliary atresia pathway

subtopic_detail: Hemiplegic migraine masquerading as acute ischaemic stroke
stem: A 10-year-old girl woke with headache, left lip and hand tingling, then left arm weakness peaking over 45 minutes and present for two hours. A similar left-sided episode six months ago resolved fully over four hours.

data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain normal, glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within the thrombolysis window
options.rationale: Paediatric acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis is not routinely offered in Australia and requires confirmed arterial occlusion on MRI/MRA, exclusion of stroke mimics, and specialist involvement. Empirical thrombolysis of a probable hemiplegic migraine attack carries substantial haemorrhage risk without benefit. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and MRA before treatment
options.rationale: Non-contrast CT is insensitive for early paediatric ischaemic stroke and cannot exclude arterial dissection or basilar occlusion. Diffusion-weighted MRI with MRA is the definitive investigation, distinguishes hemiplegic migraine (typically normal DWI) from ischaemic stroke (restricted diffusion), and drives all subsequent treatment decisions. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)
source_refs: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.text: Give intranasal sumatriptan and defer imaging until the deficit settles
options.rationale: Triptans are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine because of vasoconstrictive potential in the presence of neurological deficit and until stroke is definitively excluded. Family history is supportive but not diagnostic while a fixed hemiparesis is present. (Source: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus)
source_refs: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.text: Load intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg and repeat CT brain in six hours
options.rationale: Phenytoin loading is a status epilepticus treatment; there is no witnessed seizure and no evidence of ongoing epileptiform activity. Waiting six hours for CT changes squanders diagnostic time and risks a genuine stroke going untreated. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

options.text: Start aspirin and clopidogrel and arrange echocardiography before imaging
options.rationale: Empirical dual antiplatelet therapy for undifferentiated paediatric neurological deficit is not supported by evidence and carries bleeding risk if imaging reveals intracranial haemorrhage or dissection with an intramural haematoma. Advanced imaging precedes treatment selection. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

explanation.summary: Hemiplegic migraine is a rare familial migraine subtype defined by aura that includes reversible motor weakness lasting minutes to days, typically alongside visual, sensory or aphasic aura. Paediatric ischaemic stroke is the critical mimic and is missed on non-contrast CT in roughly half of cases at presentation. Diffusion-weighted MRI with MRA is the diagnostic investigation of choice: normal DWI in the presence of hemiparesis strongly supports migraine, while restricted diffusion drives stroke pathways (paediatric-adapted thrombolysis or thrombectomy in select centres). Once stroke and other structural mimics are excluded, hemiplegic migraine attacks are managed with anti-nausea therapy, hydration, analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen, avoiding triptans and ergots) and paediatric neurology follow-up for preventive strategy.
key_points: Hemiplegic migraine causes fully reversible motor aura; diagnosis requires exclusion of stroke.
Non-contrast CT is insensitive for paediatric ischaemic stroke; DWI-MRI plus MRA is the investigation of choice.
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine and while stroke is on the differential.
Familial hemiplegic migraine is autosomal dominant with mutations in CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A.
Attack treatment is supportive: hydration, antiemetic, non-triptan analgesia.
explanation.pearls: In a child under 12 with focal neurological deficit and a normal non-contrast CT, arrange MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging within 60 minutes: the absence of restricted diffusion strongly supports hemiplegic migraine over stroke, while its presence opens the paediatric acute stroke pathway.

sources.label: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

subtopic_detail: Recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula versus anastomotic stricture after primary repair
stem: A 6-week-old girl had repair of type C oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula on day one and a normal contrast study before discharge at four weeks. She now coughs and becomes cyanosed with most feeds, with a witnessed apnoea yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Right lower lobe consolidation; oesophagogram shows an anterior air column above the anastomosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue in the upper oesophageal pouch
options.rationale: The combination of feed-related cyanosis, recurrent right lower lobe pneumonia and a persistent anterior air column above the anastomosis on tube oesophagogram is classic for a recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula. Rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue instilled into the oesophagus and observed on the tracheal side is the reference standard test; it also localises the fistula for the corrective operation. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: A 24-hour multichannel intraluminal impedance and pH study
options.rationale: Gastro-oesophageal reflux is common after oesophageal atresia repair and can contribute to aspiration, but MII-pH testing does not detect recurrent fistula and is not the first investigation when the barium study shows a suspicious air column. Reflux workup follows exclusion of a mechanical airway to oesophagus connection. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scintigraphy for biliary reflux
options.rationale: HIDA scintigraphy assesses biliary tract patency, not tracheo-oesophageal communication, and has no role in evaluating recurrent aspiration after oesophageal atresia repair. The imaging modalities of value are contrast oesophagogram and rigid bronchoscopy. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: An outpatient videofluoroscopic swallow study by speech pathology
options.rationale: Videofluoroscopy assesses oro-pharyngeal swallow safety; it cannot distinguish aspiration from swallow incoordination from aspiration via a recurrent fistula and delays definitive endoscopic diagnosis in a systemically unwell infant with witnessed apnoea and consolidation. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: Fluoroscopic balloon dilatation of a presumed anastomotic stricture
options.rationale: Anastomotic stricture typically presents with progressive dysphagia and food impaction, not feed-triggered cyanosis and pneumonia. Dilating a suspected recurrent fistula site risks converting a small communication into a large one and forces contamination of the mediastinum. Diagnosis precedes intervention. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

explanation.summary: Recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula complicates 5-15% of primary oesophageal atresia repairs, usually presenting between four weeks and six months with feed-triggered coughing, cyanotic spells, recurrent right lower lobe aspiration and failure to thrive. The tube oesophagogram may show a linear air column above the anastomosis but is diagnostically insensitive; rigid bronchoscopy with instillation of methylene blue into the oesophagus, watching for dye appearance on the tracheal side, is the reference standard and simultaneously localises the fistula for repair. Alternative diagnoses include anastomotic stricture (progressive dysphagia rather than aspiration), gastro-oesophageal reflux, laryngeal cleft, and vocal cord dysfunction from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. VACTERL association carries a higher rate of postoperative complications and demands coordinated multidisciplinary follow-up.
key_points: Recurrent TOF classically presents with feed-triggered cyanosis and right lower lobe aspiration.
Tube oesophagogram is insensitive; rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue is the reference standard.
Anastomotic stricture presents with progressive dysphagia and food bolus impaction, not aspiration.
VACTERL infants require coordinated cardiac, renal, orthopaedic, spinal and airway follow-up.
Repair of recurrent TOF may need pleural or pericardial interposition to prevent second recurrence.
explanation.pearls: In an oesophageal atresia infant with new feed-related cyanosis and right lower lobe pneumonia after day 21, ask theatre for rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue down the upper pouch: dye on the tracheal side confirms recurrent TOF and localises it for corrective surgery.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in adolescent girl
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 15 year old girl brought by her mother for tiredness that has worsened over three months. She is falling asleep in afternoon classes and has stopped athletics training. Her periods began at 12 and for the last year have lasted seven days with heavy flow requiring a pad every two hours on the first two days. She eats a self-described vegetarian diet with no red meat and drinks two mugs of tea with lunch.

She reports no bruising, no black stools, no weight loss, no recurrent infections. She is not sexually active. There is no family history of thalassaemia or coeliac disease.

On examination she has pale conjunctivae and mild angular cheilitis; the remainder of the examination including abdominal palpation is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (120-160), MCV 71 fL (80-100), MCH 22 pg (27-32), platelets 384 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), ferritin 6 microg/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 8% (20-45), CRP <5 mg/L (<5), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days with vitamin C and arrange menstrual review
options.rationale: Alternate-day oral iron in confirmed iron deficiency (ferritin 6, transferrin saturation 8%) improves fractional absorpt. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency; RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron daily and repeat full blood count in six weeks
options.rationale: Daily dosing produces a hepcidin rise that halves fractional absorption of the next dose, so alternate-day dosing gives. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion in the day-oncology unit within the week
options.rationale: IV iron in adolescents is reserved for oral intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing loss exceeding oral replacement, or need. (Source: AMH: Iron replacement)

options.text: Refer for upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy before starting iron replacement
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated in adolescents with iron deficiency when there is no identifiable cause and menstrual and dietary. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Trial ferrous sulfate 100 mg twice daily with meals and add proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Twice-daily dosing worsens hepcidin-driven absorption blockade, meals reduce iron uptake, and proton pump inhibitors red. (Source: eTG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Adolescent iron deficiency anaemia is common in menstruating girls and is compounded by vegetarian diet and tannin-rich beverages that block non-haem iron absorption.
key_points: Alternate-day oral iron beats daily dosing for absorption and tolerability in non-pregnant women and.
Vitamin C co-administration doubles fractional iron absorption; tea, milk, calcium and PPIs reduce i.
IV iron reserved for oral intolerance, malabsorption, or losses exceeding oral replacement capacity.
explanation.pearls: Ferrous sulfate 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days achieves better 14-day cumulative absorption than 100 mg daily because hepcidin blocks absorption for ar.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis escalation of respiratory support
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 6 month old boy brought in by ambulance with three days of coryza, cough and worsening breathing since this morning. He is bottle-fed and today has taken only half his usual volumes with brief episodes where he pulls off and pants. He has had no fever, no apnoeas witnessed, and no wheeze audible to the parents. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean and has no comorbidities.

On examination he is alert but working hard: subcostal and intercostal recession, tracheal tug, bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. Capillary refill is under two seconds and he is well perfused.

He has been on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min for two hours since triage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 89% on 1 L/min nasal prong oxygen, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for respiratory syncytial virus; venous blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg (35-45) HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-26) lactate 1.6 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase nasal prong oxygen to 2 L/min and reassess in one hour with a repeat blood gas
options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prongs deliver an unreliable FiO2 above 2 L/min and there is a ceiling effect around 2 L/min in infants. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%
options.rationale: Australian bronchiolitis guidance moves to high-flow at 2 L/kg/min when a child has failed a two-hour low-flow trial wit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess response before escalating support
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended for bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months because there is no consistent evidence of be. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer nebulised 3% hypertonic saline and continue low-flow oxygen for six hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways for emergency department infants because the p. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Proceed directly to CPAP at 6 cmH2O in the emergency department resuscitation bay
options.rationale: CPAP is reserved for infants who fail high-flow nasal cannula, or who have impending respiratory failure with hypercapni. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian bronchiolitis pathways use a stepped escalation model: room air where possible, then low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min targeting SpO2 90% and above, then high-flow n.
key_points: SpO2 target for bronchiolitis is 90% and above (not 92-94% as in some older guidelines).
Low-flow ceiling is 2 L/min in infants; escalate to HFNC 2 L/kg/min after a 2-hour trial fails.
Salbutamol and hypertonic saline are not routine in Australian bronchiolitis care.
explanation.pearls: In Australian ED bronchiolitis care, escalate to high-flow nasal cannula 2 L/kg/min after 2 hours of failed low-flow (SpO2 <90% or worsening work of breathing).

subtopic_detail: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia phototherapy decision
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a term baby girl on the postnatal ward at 54 hours of age. She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery weighing 3.6 kg, is exclusively breastfeeding with good latch, and has passed meconium and urine. Her mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the baby's cord blood group is B positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. There are no dysmorphic features and no cephalhaematoma.

The midwife has escalated because the baby looks visibly yellow to the face and chest today. A transcutaneous bilirubin reading was 305 micromol/L, prompting a serum sample.

Serum total bilirubin is 320 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 8 micromol/L. Weight loss from birth is 7.4%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert baby, moderate jaundice to chest and abdomen, tone and reflexes normal, no cephalhaematoma, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin total 320 micromol/L (conjugated 8), haemoglobin 168 g/L (140-220 neonate), reticulocytes 4.5%, ABO incompatibility with positive direct antiglobulin test

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother and repeat serum bilirubin in 24 hours because ABO incompatibility is usually mild
options.rationale: Positive DAT with ABO incompatibility lowers the phototherapy threshold on Australasian nomograms because ongoing haemol. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange urgent exchange transfusion via the umbilical vein without further phototherapy
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin approaches the exchange line despite intensive phototherapy, or where t. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy now and repeat serum bilirubin in four to six hours
options.rationale: At 54 hours of age, 320 micromol/L in the presence of a haemolysis risk factor (positive DAT with ABO incompatibility) e. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice; ANZCOR)

options.text: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give formula while continuing observation without phototherapy
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding is not the primary intervention here and does not address haemolysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and monitor without phototherapy
options.rationale: IVIG is an adjunct in haemolytic disease of the newborn (isoimmune) with rising bilirubin despite intensive phototherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management in Australia uses gestational-age and postnatal-age nomograms with lower thresholds when haemolysis risk factors are present (positive DAT, isoimmunisa.
key_points: Positive DAT with ABO incompatibility lowers the phototherapy and exchange thresholds.
Intensive phototherapy is first-line above the phototherapy line, with recheck at 4-6 hours.
Exchange transfusion for continued rise despite phototherapy or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
explanation.pearls: In ABO incompatibility with positive DAT at 54 hours, intensive phototherapy is triggered around 30 micromol/L below the standard nomogram line; recheck bilirub.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease with unilateral cervical adenitis pretender
stem: A 4-year-old boy has had fever for six days and a swollen left neck, unimproved after 48 hours of oral cefalexin.

data_table.Examination: 3 cm firm left anterior cervical node, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, truncal rash, normal hands and feet
data_table.Investigations: CRP 132 mg/L, platelets 468 x10^9/L, ALT 62 U/L, albumin 30 g/L, sterile pyuria; blood cultures negative, neck ultrasound shows no abscess

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Continue cefalexin and add clindamycin for atypical adenitis
options.rationale: The clinical picture is inconsistent with staphylococcal or streptococcal cervical lymphadenitis: no fluctuance, no absc. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and repeat ultrasound
options.rationale: Persisting with bacterial adenitis pathway ignores the incomplete Kawasaki disease pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Single dose of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added upfront only in high-risk Kawasaki disease (Kobayashi or Egami scores predicting IVIG resistan. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Echocardiography and intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin
options.rationale: This is incomplete Kawasaki disease: fever for at least 5 days with two of five principal criteria (conjunctivitis, oral. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease; AHA scientific statement)
source_refs: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease

options.text: Excisional biopsy of the node for mycobacterial culture
options.rationale: Atypical mycobacterial cervical adenitis is usually indolent, non-tender, in preschool children with a violaceous overly. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when a child has fever for 5 days or more with 2-3 (rather than 4) of the principal clinical criteria plus a supportive laboratory panel pe.
key_points: Incomplete KD: fever plus 2-3 principal criteria plus supportive lab panel meets AHA treatment thres.
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin is first-line; do not wait for coronary changes on echo.
Cervical adenitis unresponsive to antibiotics, without abscess on ultrasound, plus supportive labs,.
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria plus a cervical node without abscess on ultrasound plus a CRP over 100 in a child febrile past day 5 should prompt IVIG for incomplete Kawasaki d.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement on Kawasaki disease

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in an infant - malrotation with midgut volvulus
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 5 week old boy with three episodes of green vomiting in the last four hours. He was born at term and has been formula-fed since day 4 after breastfeeding did not establish. His mother reports that until today he has been feeding well with progressive weight gain. There has been no diarrhoea, no fever, no unwell contacts.

He cried inconsolably when the ambulance service placed the intravenous cannula, then became quiet, mottled and drowsy en route.

On examination he is pale, floppy and cool peripherally, with a tender-looking distended abdomen; capillary refill is four seconds and he is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178 /min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 58 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Mottled infant, drowsy but rousable, distended and tender abdomen, no visible peristaltic wave, no palpable olive, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L (22-26), lactate 5.8 mmol/L (<2), base excess -12, glucose 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and arrange urgent upper GI contrast study before surgical referral
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in an infant with shock is malrotation with midgut volvulus until surgically excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

options.text: Perform bedside abdominal ultrasound to look for a pyloric olive before considering surgical referral
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Trial oral rehydration solution 10 mL every ten minutes for two hours before any further investigations
options.rationale: Oral rehydration is contraindicated in a shocked drowsy infant with a surgical abdomen and bilious vomiting; aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone empirically and arrange urgent lumbar puncture in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Sepsis is on the differential but the discriminating feature is bilious vomiting in an infant, which is a surgical emerg. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, insert nasogastric tube on free drainage, and phone paediatric surgery
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting plus shock in an infant is midgut volvulus complicating malrotation until proven otherwise, and the pri. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; the feared diagnosis is malrotation with midgut volvulus, which can produce bowel necrosis within hour.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until surgically proven otherwise.
Shocked infant with bilious vomiting: resuscitate and phone surgery, do NOT go to radiology first.
NGT on free drainage decompresses the stomach and reduces vomiting risk.
explanation.pearls: A shocked infant with green vomit goes to theatre for Ladd's procedure, not to the contrast suite; upper GI series is only for the stable, uncertain case.

subtopic_detail: Bruising in a non-mobile infant
stem: A 4-month-old girl is brought in by her mother's partner, who says she rolled off the couch onto a rug. She was not yet rolling at her 4-month check last week.

data_table.Examination: Alert and well perfused; 1 cm yellow-brown left cheek bruise and 2 cm medial right upper arm bruise

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for a full non-accidental injury workup and notify child protection
options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, with an inconsistent mechanism from a non-parent carer, meets criteria for a full NAI w. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Reassure and document the bruises, with general practitioner review
options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant carries a high probability of inflicted injury (TEN-4 rule: bruises in a child under 4 m. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Full blood count and coagulation studies, discharging if normal
options.rationale: A normal coagulation screen does not rule out inflicted injury; it forms one part of the NAI workup alongside skeletal s. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Refuse to release the child until police attend the department
options.rationale: Confrontation is not the doctor's role and may compromise the safety of the mother, the child, and staff. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Discharge to the mother when she arrives and confirms the story
options.rationale: Discharging on a second-hand confirmation of the mechanism does not add clinical information and does not discharge the. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in an infant who is not yet cruising is one of the strongest single features of inflicted injury.
key_points: Bruises in a pre-mobile infant are inflicted injury until otherwise explained.
TEN-4-FACES-p flags bruises requiring NAI workup: torso, ear, neck, or any in under-4-month-olds.
Structured workup: skeletal survey, fundoscopy, coagulation, CT head as indicated, social review.
explanation.pearls: The rule 'if they don't cruise, they don't bruise' means any bruise in an infant under 4 months mandates a full non-accidental injury workup plus notification t.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA with subclinical cerebral oedema
stem: A 7-year-old girl is six hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis. Over 45 minutes she has become withdrawn, with headache, one vomit and incontinence.

data_table.Investigations: Glasgow coma scale 13, pH 7.24, glucose 12 mmol/L (32 earlier), potassium 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Add 5% glucose to the fluids and continue insulin unchanged
options.rationale: Adding glucose is appropriate for the falling blood glucose (transitioning to two-bag or dextrose-added regimen once glu. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes, halving fluids
options.rationale: Falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (Cushing response), headache, vomiting, incontinence and GCS drop in a chi. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ISPAD DKA guideline)

options.text: Stop insulin for 30 minutes and correct the potassium first
options.rationale: Interrupting insulin will halt ketolysis and worsen acidosis; potassium can be replaced through fluids while insulin con. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: A 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus for cerebral perfusion
options.rationale: Additional saline bolus can worsen cerebral oedema by continuing free-water accumulation intracellularly during rapid os. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Increase insulin to 0.1 units/kg/hour to clear the ketones
options.rationale: Insulin escalation would accelerate glucose fall, worsening osmolar shift and cerebral oedema, and is contraindicated du. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates 0.5 to 1% of paediatric DKA episodes and carries around 20% mortality, with survivors often left with cognitive impairment.
key_points: Cushing response (bradycardia plus rising BP) plus GCS drop in DKA equals cerebral oedema until prov.
Give hyperosmolar therapy first (3% saline or mannitol); CT after stabilisation.
Halve IV fluid rate simultaneously.
explanation.pearls: 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes is the Australian first-line for suspected paediatric DKA cerebral oedema when a rising BP with falling pulse plus GCS.

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease presenting after nursery discharge
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 6 day old boy brought in by his parents because he has become mottled and off feeds over the last four hours. He was born at 39 weeks by uneventful vaginal delivery, passed the routine 24-hour saturation screen with pre-ductal SpO2 96% and post-ductal SpO2 95%, and was discharged at 48 hours. Feeding has been described as 'okay' until yesterday when volumes dropped.

Today he is grey, cool and lethargic. Femoral pulses are difficult to palpate; brachial pulses are volume-adequate. Precordium is quiet with no murmur audible. His liver is 3 cm below the costal margin.

A pre-ductal (right hand) SpO2 reads 84% and post-ductal (right foot) SpO2 reads 68% on room air.
