data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172 /min, blood pressure 62/34 mmHg (right arm), respiratory rate 68 /min, temperature 36.2 degC
data_table.Cardiovascular examination: Weak femoral pulses, strong brachial pulses, quiet precordium, no murmur, hepatomegaly 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.14, HCO3 10 mmol/L, lactate 8.4 mmol/L (<2), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, chest X-ray: mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, normal pulmonary vascularity

lead_in: What is the single best immediate intervention?

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 20 minutes and repeat if perfusion does not improve
options.rationale: Volume in a duct-dependent left-sided obstruction (likely coarctation or interrupted aortic arch here) can worsen pulmon. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate with FiO2 1.0 to correct the hypoxia and hyperventilate for pulmonary vasodilatation
options.rationale: High FiO2 in duct-dependent left-sided obstruction is harmful because oxygen constricts the ductus and worsens systemic. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 5 to 10 nanogram/kg/min and prepare for intubation if apnoea develops
options.rationale: Neonatal collapse in the first two weeks of life with weak femoral pulses, a pre-post-ductal saturation gradient greater. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg and lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg for suspected neonatal septic collapse
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are reasonable while workup proceeds because sepsis is a differential, but delaying prostaglandin. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal collapse)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 microgram/kg and prepare for tension pneumothorax needle decompression
options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of tension pneumothorax or anaphylaxis; the picture fits duct-dependent circulation. (Source: ANZCOR: Neonatal)

explanation.summary: Neonates with duct-dependent left-sided obstructions (critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, hypoplastic left heart, critical aortic stenosis) can pass 24-hour saturation s.
key_points: A ductal-arch obstruction can pass the 24-hour saturation screen; collapse comes days later.
Pre- to post-ductal SpO2 gradient greater than 3% with weak femorals equals duct-dependent CHD.
Prostaglandin E1 5-10 nanogram/kg/min reopens the ductus.
explanation.pearls: In a collapsed neonate under 2 weeks with pre-post-ductal saturation difference over 3% and weak femorals, start prostaglandin E1 at 5 nanogram/kg/min immediate.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis - oxygen escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 month old boy admitted overnight with his first episode of coryza followed by wheeze and feeding difficulty. He is exclusively breast fed and is now taking about half his usual volume per feed. His mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy at 39+2 weeks and he has had no previous admissions.

On arrival he is quietly alert with mild subcostal recession, wet cough, wheeze and crackles bilaterally. He has had no apnoeas. He is on room air with continuous SpO2 monitoring.

Over the last hour his oxygen saturations have drifted from 94% to 88% with feeds and 91% at rest. Nasal suction has cleared moderate secretions. Chest signs are unchanged and he is not in extremis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152 /min, respiratory rate 58 /min, SpO2 89% on room air at rest, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Subcostal recession, no head bobbing, no nasal flare, capillary refill 2 s, alert and consolable
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR pending, no chest x-ray performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen therapy?

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe on room air with hourly checks
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids do not shorten bronchiolitis and are not part of the RCH pathway; the immediate issue is hypoxia which needs oxygen, not steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Escalate directly to heated humidified high flow nasal cannula 2 L/kg/min from room air now
options.rationale: The AU PARIS trial and RCH pathway both make HFNC a second line device after failed low flow rather than the first oxygen chosen; jumping straight to HFNC has not been shown to reduce PICU admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg on oxygen and reassess in twenty minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months as there is no consistent benefit on admission length, oxygen need or work of breathing; salbutamol is not the answer to falling saturations. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; AAP Clinical Practice Guideline 2014)

options.text: Start low flow oxygen 1 to 2 L/min via nasal prongs titrated to SpO2 at or above 90%
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance identifies low flow nasal prong oxygen 1-2 L/min as the first line escalation for infants dropping below the SpO2 target of 90%; humidification and heating are not required at these flow rates. HFNC is reserved for failure of low flow after two hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue room air observation with two hourly nasal suction and repeat saturation in one hour
options.rationale: Persistent SpO2 at 89% at rest is below the RCH target of 90% and mandates oxygen now rather than a further period of observation on room air; ongoing hypoxia risks feed failure and apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: This infant meets RCH criteria for oxygen with SpO2 at 89% at rest and 88% with feeds despite airway clearance. The RCH pathway starts oxygen at low flow via nasal prongs 1-2 L/min with a saturation target of 90%. HFNC is reserved for failure of low flow after two hours, not as an initial device. Neither salbutamol nor systemic corticosteroids alter the natural history of viral bronchiolitis and neither addresses hypoxia.
key_points: SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90%, not 92-94%
First line oxygen is low flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min
HFNC is second line after failed low flow, not first
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: The PARIS trial showed early HFNC does not reduce PICU admission compared with rescue HFNC after low flow failure - low flow first is both cheaper and evidence based.

subtopic_detail: Croup - dexamethasone dose selection
stem:
You are the paediatric intern seeing a 22 month old boy in the emergency short stay unit at 2 am with two nights of coryza and a barking cough. His mother reports he woke tonight with a hoarse cry and noisy breathing on inspiration.

He is sitting on his mother's lap alert and interactive. He has audible stridor at rest which improves when he settles. There is mild suprasternal recession. Chest is otherwise clear on auscultation with no wheeze or crackles. He drinks water when offered and there is no drooling.

He was fully immunised on schedule and has had no previous croup admissions. There is no history of foreign body inhalation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest that settles when calm, mild suprasternal recession, no cyanosis, colour normal, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose to give now?

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg single dose now with four hours observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is second line to oral dexamethasone when a child cannot tolerate an oral dose; there is no vomiting or refusal here so the oral route is preferred and cheaper. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose now with four hours observation
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved by RCH for severe croup with stridor and marked recession at rest that does not settle, or with agitation or exhaustion; using it for moderate croup gives no added benefit over 0.15 mg/kg. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now with four hours observation
options.rationale: RCH croup guidance uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose for mild and moderate croup, giving effective symptom relief with the lower dose. The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup. Stridor at rest that settles when calm is moderate. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for three days with GP review tomorrow
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone has weaker evidence than dexamethasone with a shorter duration of action requiring a multiday course, and re-presentation rates in AU emergency data are higher; dexamethasone is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution alone with three hours observation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, and a steroid must still be given because adrenaline effect wears off in 90-120 minutes; adrenaline alone risks rebound stridor without underlying anti-inflammatory cover. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: This child has moderate croup on the RCH scoring - stridor at rest that settles when calm with mild recession and no cyanosis or agitation. Both mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; the 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe presentations. Adrenaline is added only to severe or life threatening croup and always with dexamethasone cover. RCH observes for four hours after steroids or three hours after nebulised adrenaline before discharge.
key_points: Mild and moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral single dose
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline
Nebulised adrenaline dose is flat 5 mL of 1:1000, not per kg
Observe for 3 hours after last adrenaline before discharge
explanation.pearls: The 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone dose is often used reflexively - RCH specifies 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup, which covers most emergency presentations.

subtopic_detail: Gastroenteritis rehydration escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the short stay unit reviewing an 18 month old girl brought in by her father with 24 hours of watery diarrhoea and three episodes of non bilious vomiting. Her older brother had similar symptoms last week that settled. She has been offered clear fluids at home but vomits within ten minutes of each offer and has passed no urine in the six hours prior to arrival.

She is quiet on her father's lap and cries with a few tears. Mucous membranes are dry. Capillary refill is 2 seconds centrally. Her weight three weeks ago at a nurse review was 11.2 kg; today she weighs 10.6 kg.

A single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg was given on arrival forty minutes ago with brief effect; she has since had one further small vomit after 30 mL of oral rehydration solution.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes with tears, capillary refill 2 s, alert, no abdominal tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Repeat oral ondansetron 4 mg and continue small oral sips of rehydration solution every five minutes
options.rationale: The AU ondansetron dose for a child under 15 kg is 2 mg not 4 mg, and repeat dosing is not recommended in the emergency department pathway; further oral only has already failed once. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert an IV cannula, give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and continue at full maintenance rate
options.rationale: IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure; in mild to moderate dehydration NGT is preferred and has lower cannulation failure and complication rates in AU emergency populations. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and rehydrate with oral solution at 25 mL/kg in the first hour then reassess
options.rationale: RCH gastroenteritis pathway makes nasogastric rehydration first line when oral trial fails in mild to moderate dehydration (5-10%); it avoids IV access, has fewer complications and equal efficacy in AU trials. Rate is 25 mL/kg in the first hour then continue over 4-6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Admit for observation on continued small oral offers of dilute apple juice every hour by cup
options.rationale: Continued oral trial without route change ignores the failure of the first oral attempt with antiemetic cover, and diluted juice has an inappropriate electrolyte content and osmolality compared with oral rehydration solution. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give loperamide 0.2 mg/kg orally to slow bowel transit and continue oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are contraindicated in children with acute infective gastroenteritis due to the risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged infection; they are not part of the AU pathway. (Source: AMH: Antidiarrhoeals)

explanation.summary: This child has 5-6% dehydration with failed oral trial after ondansetron. RCH pathway makes NGT rehydration the next step - it has equivalent efficacy to IV in AU trials with fewer complications, no need for cannulation and shorter time to full rehydration. IV is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure. Antimotility agents like loperamide are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line when oral fails in mild to moderate dehydration
IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure
Ondansetron dose is banded by weight: 2 mg for under 15 kg, 4 mg for 15-30 kg
Loperamide is contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis
explanation.pearls: The AGREE trial (Melbourne) showed NGT rehydration was non-inferior to IV with fewer complications - AU practice has shifted decisively toward NGT first.

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media - antibiotic decision
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 22 month old girl brought by her father with two days of low grade fever and pulling at her right ear. She had one episode of vomiting overnight and has been more irritable than usual but is taking her usual fluids and about two thirds of her normal food. She is fully immunised.

On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is red and bulging with loss of normal landmarks. There is no perforation or discharge. The left ear is normal. She has a clear runny nose and a normal oropharynx with no exudate. Chest is clear. There is no neck stiffness and she is not photophobic.

She has no known drug allergies and has not been given any antibiotics in the previous six months. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and lives at home with parents in Adelaide.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane red and bulging with no perforation, left ear normal, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily for seven days as first line antibiotic monotherapy
options.rationale: Amoxicillin clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48-72 hours on amoxicillin, or where there is a high concern for beta lactamase producing organisms; it is never first line in uncomplicated paediatric AOM in the AU pathway. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for five days with a return in 48 hours if not improving
options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are indicated for children under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, systemically unwell children or perforated AOM; a well 22 month old with unilateral AOM does not meet criteria and gains little from immediate treatment. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Analgesia and safety net advice with a delayed antibiotic script to fill only if not improved in 48 hours
options.rationale: RCH and eTG endorse analgesia with delayed antibiotic in non Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children over 6 months without perforation who are systemically well; most cases resolve without antibiotics and delayed scripts reduce use without increasing complications. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media; eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops for seven days without any oral antibiotic and review in one week
options.rationale: Ciprofloxacin ear drops are used for otitis externa or for chronic suppurative otitis media with a perforation; they cannot cross an intact tympanic membrane and have no role in acute otitis media with an intact drum. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Refer to the emergency department for intravenous ceftriaxone and admission for observation
options.rationale: IV antibiotics are reserved for suspected mastoiditis, meningitis or a systemically unwell child not tolerating oral therapy; this child is systemically well with a normal neurological examination and does not need admission. (Source: eTG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: The AU approach to uncomplicated AOM in a well child over 6 months is analgesia with delayed antibiotics. Immediate antibiotics are indicated for children under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children (higher risk of chronic suppurative otitis media), systemically unwell children or a perforated ear. When antibiotics are indicated, amoxicillin is first line at 15 mg/kg/dose three times daily for five days; augmentin is reserved for treatment failure.
key_points: Delayed antibiotic script is first line for well non-Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children over 6 months
Immediate antibiotics: under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, unwell, perforated
Amoxicillin is first line; augmentin only after 48-72 h treatment failure
Ciprofloxacin drops are for otitis externa or chronic suppurative OM with perforation
explanation.pearls: The AU rationale for immediate antibiotics in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children is the substantially higher rate of chronic suppurative otitis media and its consequences for hearing and schooling.

subtopic_detail: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia workup
stem: A 3-week-old breastfed boy has been jaundiced since day 4. His stools have become paler over the past week and his urine is dark. He feeds well and is gaining weight.

data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus, firm liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 168 micromol/L (<26), conjugated bilirubin 42 micromol/L (<15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add ursodeoxycholic acid and review liver enzymes in one month
options.rationale: Empirical ursodeoxycholic acid without a diagnosis delays surgical treatment of biliary atresia; UDCA has a role after diagnosis of specific cholestatic disorders but is never a substitute for urgent structural workup. (Source: NASPGHAN 2017)

options.text: Reassure about breast milk jaundice and review at six weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and cannot explain a conjugated fraction of 42 micromol/L or pale stools; labelling this as breast milk jaundice delays workup for biliary atresia beyond the 60 day Kasai window and worsens outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Start phototherapy and repeat the bilirubin in six hours
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to a water soluble form; it has no effect on conjugated bilirubin and can cause bronze baby syndrome in cholestatic infants. This infant has cholestasis, not unconjugated jaundice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Urgent paediatric hepatology referral for cholangiography this week
options.rationale: A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total in an infant over 2 weeks mandates urgent hepatology workup for biliary atresia; the Kasai portoenterostomy has a much higher success rate if done before 60 days of life. Pale stools plus dark urine with a firm liver make biliary atresia the leading concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice; NASPGHAN 2017)

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound with repeat conjugated bilirubin in one month
options.rationale: An ultrasound is a helpful adjunct but a normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia and a one month delay would push definitive surgery past the 60 day Kasai window when outcomes fall sharply; urgent referral is required regardless of the ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any infant with jaundice beyond 14 days needs a split (conjugated and unconjugated) bilirubin. A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is always pathological and mandates urgent hepatology assessment for biliary atresia. Pale stools, dark urine and a firm liver support this. The Kasai portoenterostomy has a much higher rate of biliary drainage restoration if performed under 60 days of age, and each week of delay reduces success. Do not send this child home on watchful waiting.
key_points: Conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is always pathological
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes fall sharply after 60 days of age
Phototherapy has no role in conjugated jaundice
Pale stools and dark urine are red flags for biliary obstruction
explanation.pearls: The stool colour chart in the RCH resources should be given to every family with prolonged neonatal jaundice - parents can catch progression to biliary atresia earlier than any single blood test.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7 month old boy admitted with six days of persistent fever above 39 degC that has not responded to paracetamol. His mother reports he has been miserable and off his feeds. He had a red rash on his trunk on day three that has faded. His hands looked puffy yesterday.

On examination today he is irritable with bilateral non exudative conjunctivitis and dry cracked red lips. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Hands and feet show mild oedema without desquamation. A chest x-ray on admission was normal. Blood and urine cultures at 48 hours are negative. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone was started three days ago with no improvement.

He has no known allergies and no significant past history. He was fully immunised at 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172 /min, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctivitis without exudate, cracked lips, no lymphadenopathy, hand and foot oedema, systolic flow murmur
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 18.4 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 145 mg/L (<5), ALT 68 U/L (<45), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), urinalysis 30 white cells per HPF with no growth on culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram and give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high dose aspirin now
options.rationale: Six days of fever plus two of five classical features and multiple supportive laboratory findings (albumin below 30, sodium below 135, platelets rising, sterile pyuria, anaemia, raised ALT) meets the AHA algorithm for incomplete Kawasaki disease with more than three lab criteria. Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin without waiting for full classical criteria to prevent coronary aneurysms. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone for a further 48 hours pending viral PCR results and clinical reassessment
options.rationale: Delaying treatment beyond day 10 of illness sharply increases the risk of coronary aneurysm; empirical antibiotics without response and negative cultures should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, not further watchful waiting. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg/day for three days as first line monotherapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added to IVIG only for high risk patients (Kobayashi score high risk, under 12 months in Japanese cohorts) or for IVIG resistance; monotherapy corticosteroids are not first line and IVIG is still required. (Source: AHA 2017 Kawasaki disease scientific statement)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and start empirical intravenous aciclovir for suspected HSV encephalitis
options.rationale: There is no seizure, focal neurology or altered consciousness to raise concern for HSV encephalitis, and the clinical and laboratory picture fits incomplete Kawasaki; empirical aciclovir does not address the coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge home on paracetamol with outpatient paediatric review in one week after clinic booking
options.rationale: A miserable infant with six days of unremitting fever, incomplete Kawasaki features and rising markers cannot be discharged; missed Kawasaki disease can cause life threatening coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when there are five or more days of fever with only two or three classical features plus supportive laboratory findings. This child has bilateral non exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips and extremity oedema plus six supportive lab features. Under the AHA algorithm this warrants IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin. Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply after day 10 of illness so treatment cannot wait for classical criteria. Echocardiography is done at diagnosis and repeated at 1-2 weeks and 4-6 weeks.
key_points: AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria: fever with 2-3 features plus supportive labs
Supportive labs: albumin below 30, sodium below 135, sterile pyuria, anaemia, raised platelets, raised ALT, raised WCC
Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin without waiting for full features
Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply beyond day 10 of illness
explanation.pearls: Infants under 12 months present most often with incomplete Kawasaki and have the highest coronary aneurysm rate - a low threshold for IVIG in this group is life saving.

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis observation duration
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 5 year old girl brought in by ambulance 90 minutes ago after her first known peanut exposure at a friend's house. Within ten minutes of eating a peanut butter biscuit she developed urticaria, facial swelling and audible wheeze.

Paramedics gave a single intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram at the scene with rapid resolution of wheeze and improvement in tachycardia within five minutes. On arrival she was well perfused with clear chest and no stridor. She received a second intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram in the department 30 minutes ago after a brief return of wheeze, again with prompt response.

She has been observed for 90 minutes since arrival with no further symptoms. She is now bright and alert, drinking water, and has passed urine. Her parents have arrived with her ASCIA action plan blank and her EpiPen Jr script filled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 102/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, chest clear, no urticaria, no facial swelling, no stridor, no wheeze

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan from this presentation?

options.text: Admit overnight for a supervised peanut challenge in the paediatric ward the following morning
options.rationale: Deliberate re-exposure to the trigger after an anaphylactic reaction is contraindicated and would not be done as an inpatient challenge; if food challenge is needed it is done later in a supervised immunology setting after negative testing. (Source: ASCIA food allergy guidelines)

options.text: Discharge now with an EpiPen Jr and GP follow up next week to complete the anaphylaxis action plan
options.rationale: ASCIA specifies a minimum observation of four hours after the last adrenaline dose in a child needing more than one dose; discharging at 30 minutes exposes the child to a missed biphasic reaction without adrenaline access at hospital. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

options.text: Admit for 24 hours of hourly observations and oral prednisolone daily for three days as inpatient
options.rationale: A 24 hour admission is not required after a first anaphylaxis that has responded well; oral prednisolone does not reduce biphasic reactions and is not recommended in ASCIA guidance. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

options.text: Observe to four hours after the last adrenaline dose then discharge with ASCIA plan and immunology referral
options.rationale: ASCIA guidance requires a minimum of four hours observation after the last adrenaline dose in a child who had more than one dose or persistent symptoms; the 30 minute mark from the second dose is short of that. Immunology referral is standard for a first anaphylactic reaction to identify the trigger. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024; RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Start an oral antihistamine for three days and dispense an EpiPen 300 microgram for future emergency use
options.rationale: This child weighs 18 kg so the correct device is EpiPen Jr 150 microgram (10-20 kg band); EpiPen 300 microgram is for children 20 kg and above. Antihistamines relieve urticaria but have no role in the immediate anaphylaxis pathway. (Source: ASCIA acute management of anaphylaxis 2024)

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends observation for a minimum of four hours after the last adrenaline dose for children who required more than one dose, had persistent or protracted symptoms, or had features suggesting a biphasic reaction. This child had two doses and needs a further 3.5 hours of observation. On discharge every child needs an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan, a prescription for a weight banded adrenaline autoinjector (EpiPen Jr 150 microgram for 10-20 kg, EpiPen 300 microgram for 20 kg or more) and referral to a paediatric immunology or allergy service.
key_points: Observe a minimum of 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose if 2 or more doses needed
EpiPen Jr 150 mcg for 10-20 kg; EpiPen 300 mcg for 20 kg or more
Oral prednisolone does not reduce biphasic reactions
First anaphylaxis warrants immunology referral to identify the trigger
explanation.pearls: Antihistamines and steroids have never been shown to reduce biphasic anaphylaxis - they treat urticaria but do not replace observation time or adrenaline.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA cerebral oedema
stem: A 9-year-old girl is four hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis with insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour and 48-hour rehydration fluids. She has vomited once and has a headache.

data_table.Neurology: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, from 14 on admission
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.22, glucose 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase insulin to 0.15 units/kg/hour and give 10 mL/kg saline
options.rationale: Increasing insulin and giving further boluses worsen cerebral oedema by lowering osmolality and dropping glucose too fast; the presenting problem is not persistent acidosis but neurological deterioration during resuscitation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg, elevate the head, halve fluids, call PICU
options.rationale: Drowsiness, headache, vomiting, hypertension with relative bradycardia (Cushing response) four hours into DKA fluids in a child under 12 with severe presentation defines clinical cerebral oedema; treatment is hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg 2.7% or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg), head elevation, fluid restriction to 2/3 maintenance and immediate PICU involvement. (Source: BSPED/ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline 2020; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the acidosis faster
options.rationale: Bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk and is contraindicated except for life threatening hyperkalaemia; it will not reverse the neurological deterioration and may worsen it. (Source: ISPAD 2022; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT head before starting any osmotic therapy
options.rationale: Clinical cerebral oedema is a treat first diagnosis - CT is often normal early and delays hyperosmolar therapy; the child should be treated on clinical grounds and imaged only if she stabilises or the diagnosis is unclear. (Source: BSPED/ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline 2020)

options.text: Stop dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour now
options.rationale: Reducing insulin without addressing the raised intracranial pressure does not treat the cerebral oedema, and stopping dextrose risks rebound ketosis; the priority is hyperosmolar therapy and PICU escalation, not a tweak to insulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Clinical cerebral oedema complicates 0.5-1% of paediatric DKA episodes and has a mortality of about 20% with major morbidity in survivors. Risk factors present here include age under 12, new onset, severe acidosis on admission and a rapid rise in corrected sodium. The Muir criteria triad of headache, vomiting and altered conscious state with Cushing response (hypertension and relative bradycardia) mandates immediate hyperosmolar therapy - hypertonic saline 2.7% at 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg - alongside head elevation, halving the fluid rate and PICU escalation. Do not delay for imaging.
key_points: Diagnose cerebral oedema clinically, treat before imaging
Hyperosmolar therapy: 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes OR mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg
Reduce fluid rate to two thirds maintenance, head up 30 degrees
Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except for life threatening hyperkalaemia
explanation.pearls: The classic warning is a rise in blood pressure with a fall in heart rate during DKA resuscitation - it is a Cushing response and not a sign the child is recovering.

subtopic_detail: First UTI imaging in a child under 24 months per RCH CPG
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl in the short stay ward. She was admitted 48 hours ago with a first febrile urinary tract infection, culture positive for Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim, and switched from IV to oral trimethoprim after 24 hours with rapid resolution of fever. Antenatal ultrasounds through the pregnancy were reported as normal with normal kidneys and bladder documented on the 20 week morphology scan. There is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux, no history of poor urinary stream, no palpable abdominal mass and she is now feeding, playing and afebrile for 36 hours.

Her mother works in a rural community two hours from the tertiary centre and asks what imaging her daughter needs before discharge to prevent kidney damage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, playing, abdomen soft, no flank fullness, no back or spinal abnormalities, external genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture Escherichia coli >10^8 CFU/mL sensitive to trimethoprim, creatinine 28 micromol/L, C reactive protein 42 mg/L falling from 96, blood culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No routine renal tract imaging, provide safety net advice about recurrent fever with prompt urine collection
options.rationale: For a first typical urinary tract infection in a child aged 6 to 24 months who responds to antibiotics within 48 hours, has documented normal antenatal kidney imaging and no risk features for atypical infection, RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound; safety netting for recurrence is the appropriate plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during this admission before discharge, with paediatric outpatient follow up
options.rationale: Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection: poor response after 48 hours of antibiotics, non-Escherichia coli organism, sepsis, abdominal or bladder mass, or raised creatinine. None of those apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal cortical scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring
options.rationale: The dimercaptosuccinic acid renal cortical scan is a NICE pathway construct, not part of the RCH imaging cascade. RCH does not use routine dimercaptosuccinic acid to assess scarring in a typical first infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux prior to discharge home to a rural community
options.rationale: Micturating cystourethrogram is invasive, carries a radiation and infection risk, and is not part of the RCH cascade after a first typical urinary tract infection in this age group. Reserve for recurrent infection or a hydronephrotic kidney on ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound plus prophylactic trimethoprim for 6 months to prevent culture proven recurrence
options.rationale: Long term antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a first typical infection in a child of this age without demonstrated high grade vesicoureteric reflux or an abnormal urinary tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: In a child aged 6 to 24 months who has a first typical urinary tract infection with rapid clinical response and documented normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound, dimercaptosuccinic acid or micturating cystourethrogram. Ultrasound during the acute illness is reserved for features of atypical infection, and the dimercaptosuccinic acid and micturating cystourethrogram cascade is NICE, not RCH. Safety netting for recurrent fever and prompt clean catch urine at re-presentation is the appropriate plan. Documented antenatal monitoring and prompt clinical response together carry weight.
key_points: Atypical urinary tract infection triggers ultrasound during illness: poor response at 48 hours, non-Escherichia coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine.
Dimercaptosuccinic acid and micturating cystourethrogram are NOT in the RCH cascade after a first typical infection.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for demonstrated high grade vesicoureteric reflux or recurrence, not routine first infection.
explanation.pearls: For an 18 month old girl with a first Escherichia coli urinary tract infection that responds within 48 hours and normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH advises safety net advice with no routine imaging.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Paediatric urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation per RCH CPG
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a district general emergency department. A 7 month old previously well infant presents with 3 days of coryza, cough and rising work of breathing. His mother reports poor feeding for the last 12 hours and no wet nappy for 4 hours. He has no cyanosis at rest and is not sleepy. On examination he has bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, moderate subcostal recession and tracheal tug. There is no focal consolidation on auscultation.

His nasopharyngeal aspirate later confirms respiratory syncytial virus. He is nursed sitting up in a cot. A junior colleague has already commenced high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.4 within the first 10 minutes of arrival citing severity and pulls you aside asking whether that is correct first line oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 87% on room air, temperature 37.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, subcostal recession, tracheal tug, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate later positive for respiratory syncytial virus; capillary blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 46 mmHg lactate 1.4 mmol/L; chest X ray not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: Continue high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with fraction of inspired oxygen 0.4 as commenced
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants who fail low flow after 2 hours; starting straight on high flow is not the RCH first line and can commit an infant to a higher acuity area unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Low flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 target 90%, review at 60 minutes
options.rationale: First line oxygen for bronchiolitis is low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, titrated to SpO2 target 90% (not 92 to 94%); escalation to high flow is considered if low flow fails after 2 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back with review of oxygen needs after the third dose
options.rationale: Nebulised bronchodilators are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and delay appropriate oxygen and feeding assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent every 4 hours to reduce airway oedema
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway and has no reliable short stay benefit; it does not address the immediate hypoxia. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation because of respiratory rate above 60
options.rationale: Isolated tachypnoea in an infant who is not exhausted, apnoeic or unresponsive is not an indication for intubation; escalate through low flow then high flow first. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH recommends low flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min titrated to an SpO2 target of 90% as the first line for hypoxic bronchiolitis, with review at 60 to 120 minutes. High flow is not the first line and is reserved for children who deteriorate or do not improve on low flow after 2 hours. Salbutamol, hypertonic saline and steroids are not routinely recommended under 12 months. Oxygen is the primary supportive treatment; hydration by nasogastric or intravenous route is added as feeding deteriorates.
key_points: First line oxygen in bronchiolitis is nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, target SpO2 90% under RCH.
High flow nasal cannula is a rescue after failure of low flow at 2 hours, not the initial setting.
Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline and steroids are not routinely used in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: For a 7 month old with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis and SpO2 87%, start low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min to a target 90%; do not open with high flow.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis fluid regimen and cerebral oedema risk
stem: A 9-year-old boy weighing 28 kg has new type 1 diabetes with ketoacidosis. He is drowsy but rousable, 7% dehydrated, and has had one 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus.

data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.05, glucose 34 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: Which fluid and insulin plan is most appropriate?

options.text: 0.9% saline, potassium 20 mmol/L, 7% deficit over 48 hours, insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: The maintenance plus deficit approach is right but the deficit is capped at 5 to 7 percent regardless of clinical estimate and must be replaced over 48 hours using isotonic fluid with potassium; insulin should be at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour and started at least 1 hour after fluids. Adding 20 mmol/L potassium is only appropriate once serum potassium is known to be <5.5 mmol/L and urine output confirmed; the letter is close but the description misses the potassium detail and the insulin dose caveat that is separately assessed in option C. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Two further 20 mL/kg saline boluses now, then immediate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid boluses beyond an initial 10 mL/kg (repeated only for persistent shock) increase the risk of cerebral oedema. Insulin should not be started immediately as it worsens fluid shifts and cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.9% saline, potassium 40 mmol/L, 5 to 7% deficit over 48 hours, insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: RCH and ISPAD advise capped deficit of 5 to 7 percent regardless of estimate, replaced over 48 hours using isotonic fluid with 40 mmol/L potassium once serum potassium is <5.5 mmol/L and urine output established, insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour started 1 hour after fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose, deficit over 24 hours, immediate insulin infusion
options.rationale: Half normal saline as initial fluid and replacement over 24 hours are associated with rapid corrected sodium change and higher risk of cerebral oedema; RCH uses isotonic fluid, spread rehydration over 48 hours, and adds dextrose only once blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.9% saline at twice maintenance for 4 hours, immediate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: Running fluids at 2 times maintenance during initial rehydration exceeds RCH capped rates, increases the risk of cerebral oedema, and starting insulin simultaneously worsens osmotic shift. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis fluid management uses an initial 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus only if perfusion demands, then maintenance plus a capped 5 to 7 percent deficit spread evenly over 48 hours with isotonic fluid containing 40 mmol/L potassium once serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L and urine output is established. Insulin runs at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour, started at least 1 hour after fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk. Dextrose is added when blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L rather than dropping the insulin rate first. The disconfirming feature that kills the more aggressive options is the drowsy state on presentation, which raises baseline cerebral oedema risk.
key_points: Deficit is capped at 5 to 7 percent and replaced over 48 hours to minimise cerebral oedema.
Insulin starts 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Add dextrose when blood glucose falls under 15 mmol/L; do not reduce insulin first.
explanation.pearls: For a 28 kg child with pH 7.05, use isotonic fluid at maintenance plus 5 to 7 percent deficit over 48 hours, potassium 40 mmol/L once safe, insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour started 1 hour later.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus 2022: DKA and hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months investigation choice
stem: A 6-week-old term boy has six hours of fever and is taking half his usual feeds. He is quiet but consolable, with no rash and no focus of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, respiratory rate 46/min, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 18 mg/L, urine dipstick negative, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and review if fever persists
options.rationale: Any infant under 3 months with a temperature >=38.0 degC requires a full septic screen and empirical antibiotics; discharge without treatment carries an unacceptable meningitis and bacteraemia miss rate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin and admission, deferring lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve reliable central nervous system penetration for bacterial meningitis and deferring lumbar puncture undertreats a serious bacterial infection risk in a 6 week old. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime alone, deferring lumbar puncture
options.rationale: C reactive protein trends do not exclude bacterial meningitis in this age group; deferring the lumbar puncture to observe biomarkers is not the RCH pathway for an under 3 month old with fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Lumbar puncture, intravenous cefotaxime, amoxicillin and aciclovir
options.rationale: For any infant under 3 months with fever, RCH advises full septic screen including a lumbar puncture where safe, followed by empirical IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover under 1 month; broadly used to under 2 to 3 months in some pathways) plus IV aciclovir until herpes simplex is excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: High flow oxygen, 20 mL/kg saline bolus and intensive care review
options.rationale: The child is not shocked or hypoxic and does not need high flow or a fluid bolus; the immediate priority is the septic screen and empirical antibiotics, not paediatric intensive care unit transfer. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: A 6 week old with fever >=38.0 degC needs a full septic screen and empirical intravenous antibiotics regardless of how well or unwell they look, because clinical assessment poorly discriminates serious bacterial infection under 3 months. RCH recommends lumbar puncture with cefotaxime plus ampicillin/amoxicillin (for Listeria) plus aciclovir until herpes simplex encephalitis is excluded. Waiting for biomarkers to trend or discharging on oral antibiotics both risk missing bacterial meningitis or bacteraemia. This pathway is stricter than that used in older children where a source-driven approach is acceptable.
key_points: Fever under 3 months: full septic screen including lumbar puncture where safe.
Empirical cover: IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus aciclovir until herpes simplex encephalitis excluded.
Clinical wellness and normal C reactive protein do not exclude serious bacterial infection in this age.
explanation.pearls: A 6 week old with a documented temperature of 38.4 degC gets lumbar puncture plus IV cefotaxime, amoxicillin and aciclovir even if he brightens briefly on the parent's lap.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in neonates and infants

subtopic_detail: Croup severity based dexamethasone dose per RCH
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on evening shift. A 2 year old boy presents with a barking cough for 8 hours and stridor. He has no drooling, is tolerating small sips and is not toxic. His mother reports similar symptoms 6 months ago that settled with a single oral dexamethasone dose from a regional emergency department. He has no allergies and is fully vaccinated. There is no foreign body history. On examination he has occasional inspiratory stridor when upset but no stridor at rest, mild suprasternal recession only when crying, and normal air entry bilaterally.

He becomes calmer sitting on his father's lap. The bedside nurse asks what dexamethasone dose to draw up before you review him again in 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession when crying, no stridor at rest, tolerating oral fluids
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; no chest X ray required in typical croup

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose now, review at 30 minutes and discharge if he remains clinically stable
options.rationale: Prednisolone is used in some services but dexamethasone is preferred for its longer half life and lower recurrence of symptoms in the following 24 hours; RCH lists dexamethasone first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose today with no additional oral steroid required at this visit
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is a second line option when oral dexamethasone is not tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred as first line where available. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 now, observe for 3 hours, no oral steroid required at this visit
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest; steroid should be given in mild and moderate cases and this child qualifies for oral dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose now, arrange urgent retrieval to a tertiary paediatric intensive care unit
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is only indicated for severe croup with stridor at rest and increased work of breathing; this child is mild with stridor only when upset and does not need tertiary retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now, observe for 30 minutes then discharge home with croup advice
options.rationale: Mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; escalate to 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup with stridor at rest. Observation for 30 minutes is standard before discharge if he remains well. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup as a single dose, escalating to 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup with stridor at rest, respiratory distress or agitation. Nebulised adrenaline is added for moderate to severe cases and needs 3 hours minimum observation after the last nebule. The disconfirming finding here is that the stridor is only present when upset and the child settles on his father's lap, which places him in the mild category and rules out the higher dose. Prednisolone is a fallback where dexamethasone is unavailable.
key_points: Mild/moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose.
Severe croup with stridor at rest: 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000, observe 3 hours.
Nebulised budesonide is a fallback when oral steroid cannot be given.
explanation.pearls: Stridor only when upset with normal air entry and no recession at rest is mild croup; give 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone, not 0.6 mg/kg.

subtopic_detail: ASCIA banded adrenaline dose for paediatric anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar on a Sunday afternoon at a suburban emergency department. A 4 year old boy who weighs 16 kg presents 20 minutes after eating a peanut biscuit at a birthday party. He has widespread urticaria, facial swelling, harsh stridor at rest and vomiting. His mother reports mild wheeze at home which is now worse. He has a documented previous mild peanut reaction and carries no adrenaline autoinjector. He is placed supine with legs elevated because he is pale and tachycardic.

An ASCIA action plan is on the ward wall. The intern preparing the drug asks whether to use 10 microg/kg by weight, or the ASCIA banded intramuscular dose. Your consultant emphasises the AU standard. He has no known intercurrent medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Urticaria over the trunk, facial and periorbital swelling, stridor at rest, wheeze, pale, capillary refill 3 s
data_table.Investigations: Not required at this point; peak flow deferred

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of intramuscular adrenaline?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microg into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: ASCIA uses a banded weight table with 150 microg (0.15 mL 1:1000) for children 10 to 20 kg, given intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeatable every 5 minutes as required. This is the AU standard rather than the 10 microg/kg arithmetic approach. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microg into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes
options.rationale: 300 microg (EpiPen dose) is the banded dose for children 20 kg and over; this child is 16 kg and falls into the 10 to 20 kg band, so the 150 microg dose is correct. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 microg/kg = 160 microg via 1:10,000 preparation into the deltoid
options.rationale: 10 microg/kg arithmetic is not the AU banded standard, the 1:10,000 preparation is for intravenous or intraosseous rescue only, and the deltoid site is inferior to the anterolateral thigh in emergency doses. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microg/kg/min immediately without an intramuscular dose
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after intramuscular doses have failed, given in a monitored high dependency or paediatric intensive care setting. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as first line
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis; hydrocortisone is second line and not the first drug. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines use a banded weight table for intramuscular adrenaline: 150 microg for children 10 to 20 kg (equivalent to an EpiPen Junior), 300 microg for 20 kg and over, and 500 microg for large adolescents and adults. Doses are drawn from 1:1000 ampoule (or delivered by autoinjector) and given into the mid anterolateral thigh. Repeat every 5 minutes if the patient has not improved. 1:10,000 adrenaline is reserved for intravenous or intraosseous rescue and 10 microg/kg arithmetic is not the AU standard because banded dosing is faster and safer under stress.
key_points: ASCIA banded intramuscular adrenaline: 10 to 20 kg = 150 microg; 20 kg and over = 300 microg.
Intramuscular route into anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes.
1:10,000 preparation is for intravenous or intraosseous administration only, not intramuscular.
explanation.pearls: A 16 kg child in anaphylaxis gets 150 microg (0.15 mL of 1:1000) intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh - the banded ASCIA dose, not 10 microg/kg arithmetic.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: Refractory paediatric septic shock with severe hypokalaemia after fluid resuscitation
stem: A 3-year-old boy (15 kg) has fever, vomiting and a spreading purpuric rash. After ceftriaxone and 60 mL/kg of 0.9% saline he remains shocked on peripheral adrenaline 0.1 microg/kg/min.

data_table.Investigations: pH 7.22, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, potassium 2.4 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.05 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before retrieval?

options.text: A fourth 20 mL/kg saline bolus with adrenaline increased to 0.3 microg/kg/min now
options.rationale: Further crystalloid beyond 60 mL/kg without addressing severe hypokalaemia risks hyperchloraemic acidosis and pulmonary oedema and does not treat the arrhythmogenic potassium; further volume before correcting potassium is not the appropriate step. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Potassium infusion 0.5 mmol/kg/hour through a large bore line with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe hypokalaemia at 2.4 mmol/L in a shocked child is arrhythmogenic and precipitates cardiac arrest particularly during catecholamine therapy; the correct step is to begin controlled potassium replacement at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour under continuous monitoring while maintaining current inotropic support until central access allows noradrenaline. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mmol intravenously over 15 minutes, then reassess perfusion
options.rationale: Rapid potassium bolus is contraindicated because of high arrhythmia risk; the recommended rate is 0.5 mmol/kg/hour via continuous infusion with cardiac monitoring, not a bolus. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg, deferring potassium replacement
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is reasonable in catecholamine resistant shock but is not the pre eminent step here; ignoring an arrhythmogenic potassium of 2.4 mmol/L exposes the child to sudden arrest and it should be corrected in parallel or ahead of steroid consideration. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Intubation and renal replacement therapy for the lactic acidosis
options.rationale: Intubation and renal replacement are not indicated at present given adequate oxygenation and moderate lactate; both delay the immediate correction of the arrhythmogenic hypokalaemia and could precipitate arrest during induction. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

explanation.summary: A shocked 3 year old with a potassium of 2.4 mmol/L is at high risk of arrhythmia and arrest, particularly under catecholamine infusion. The Australian paediatric sepsis pathway prioritises antibiotics within the hour, up to 60 mL/kg fluid in aliquots and early vasopressor via peripheral or intraosseous route; once refractory, the next competing priorities are correcting severe electrolyte disturbance and moving from peripheral adrenaline to noradrenaline via central access. Rapid potassium bolus is unsafe; instead a monitored infusion of 0.5 mmol/kg/hour balances speed and safety. Steroid, ventilation and renal replacement each have narrower roles and do not address the immediate arrhythmia risk.
key_points: Severe hypokalaemia in septic shock is arrhythmogenic and must be corrected by infusion, not bolus.
Standard paediatric potassium replacement is up to 0.5 mmol/kg/hour with continuous cardiac monitoring.
Central noradrenaline is preferred to escalating peripheral adrenaline once catecholamine resistance emerges.
explanation.pearls: In a shocked child with potassium 2.4 mmol/L, run a monitored potassium infusion at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour and prepare to switch to central noradrenaline; do not bolus potassium or push more crystalloid.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Paediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock

subtopic_detail: Neonate with duct dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease refractory to prostaglandin E1
stem: A 3-day-old term neonate in a regional nursery is cyanosed, SpO2 62 per cent despite 100 per cent oxygen. Prostaglandin E1 has run 20 minutes at 0.1 microg/kg/min without improvement. Retrieval is 90 minutes away.

data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: d-transposition of the great arteries, intact ventricular septum, restrictive foramen ovale, ductus small

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase prostaglandin E1 to 0.4 microg/kg/min and add nitric oxide
options.rationale: In d-transposition with a restrictive atrial septum, further ductal opening does not improve mixing because the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel; nitric oxide can worsen the mismatch. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Cease prostaglandin E1 and commence dobutamine 10 microg/kg/min
options.rationale: Cessation of prostaglandin E1 removes a small source of mixing at the duct; inotrope alone does not treat the parallel circulation and induced hypothermia is not the immediate step for a duct dependent lesion. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Bedside balloon atrial septostomy under echocardiographic guidance
options.rationale: In d-transposition of the great arteries with an intact ventricular septum and restrictive atrial communication, cyanosis is due to inadequate mixing at atrial level; a balloon atrial septostomy performed under echocardiographic guidance improves mixing and is a temporising manoeuvre before the arterial switch. Prostaglandin alone is insufficient when the atrial septum is restrictive. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Intubate and hyperventilate to a pCO2 of 25 mmHg in 100 per cent oxygen
options.rationale: Hyperventilation and hyperoxia in a parallel circulation do not increase mixing and can be harmful; the driver of hypoxia here is inadequate atrial mixing not pulmonary vascular resistance. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Peripheral extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in this nursery
options.rationale: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is not a peripheral bedside procedure in a regional nursery and does not address the anatomical problem; balloon atrial septostomy under echocardiographic guidance is the standard temporising step. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

explanation.summary: d-transposition of the great arteries places the pulmonary and systemic circulations in parallel; adequate mixing depends on the atrial septum, ventricular septum or ductus arteriosus. When the ventricular septum is intact and the atrial communication is restrictive, oxygenation cannot improve with prostaglandin E1 alone because there is minimal ductal mixing available. Emergency balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) under echocardiographic guidance enlarges the interatrial communication, increases mixing and buys time for the arterial switch operation. Prostaglandin continues but is not the answer to persistent cyanosis in this specific anatomy.
key_points: d-transposition: systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel; oxygenation depends on mixing.
Restrictive atrial communication in d-transposition demands balloon atrial septostomy, not more prostaglandin.
Arterial switch is the surgical goal; septostomy is the temporising manoeuvre.
explanation.pearls: For d-transposition of the great arteries with intact ventricular septum and restrictive atrial communication and persistent cyanosis on prostaglandin E1, the temporising manoeuvre is a balloon atrial septostomy.

sources.label: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook
AAP/RCPCH neonatal cyanotic congenital heart disease review

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis after conservative measures
stem: A 7-year-old boy has never been dry at night. Days are dry, with no urgency or constipation. A reward chart over three months has not helped. He leaves for his first school camp in six weeks.

data_table.Examination: Growth on the 50th centile, no palpable bladder or faecal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative

lead_in: Which treatment is most appropriate now?

options.text: Continue the reward chart with evening fluids stopped from 6 pm
options.rationale: Reward charts alone have already failed after a 3 month trial; escalation to an active therapy is indicated with a defined event in 6 weeks. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Nightly enuresis alarm for at least eight weeks, with a parent wake protocol
options.rationale: Enuresis alarms are the most effective first line therapy for durable cure (evidence based number needed to treat around 2) but need at least 8 weeks and are not suited to a 6 week camp deadline. Explain benefits and offer as durable therapy after the camp. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Oral oxybutynin 5 mg at bedtime with evening fluid restriction
options.rationale: Anticholinergics are used in enuresis with detrusor overactivity or when desmopressin plus alarm have failed; they are not first line for primary monosymptomatic enuresis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Oral desmopressin 120 microg wafer at bedtime for the camp, alarm afterwards
options.rationale: In primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis at age 7 with a specific short term social need (camp in 6 weeks), desmopressin sublingual wafer 120 microg (or 200 microg tablet) at bedtime with strict evening fluid restriction is the recommended short term option; the durable therapy is an enuresis alarm and should be planned once the deadline passes. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before any specific treatment
options.rationale: Urodynamics is not indicated in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis with a normal examination and negative urinalysis; workup can be entirely non invasive. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis

explanation.summary: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a school aged child is treated after conservative measures (reward chart, fluid timing, constipation exclusion, sleep disordered breathing exclusion) fail. Two first line active therapies are enuresis alarm (highest sustained cure rate but 8 to 12 weeks to work) and desmopressin (rapid response, useful for camps or sleepovers, but relapse on cessation is common). A specific short deadline favours desmopressin cover with a plan for the alarm afterwards. Anticholinergics are reserved for detrusor overactivity or combined therapy after first line failure.
key_points: Enuresis alarm is the highest sustained cure rate therapy but needs 8 to 12 weeks to work.
Desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer (or 200 microg tablet) at bedtime is preferred for short term cover such as camps.
Anticholinergics are reserved for detrusor overactivity or combination therapy after first line failure.
explanation.pearls: For a 6 week camp deadline: desmopressin 120 microg sublingual wafer at bedtime with strict evening fluid restriction; plan an enuresis alarm as durable therapy after the camp.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline on Enuresis
International Children's Continence Society standardisation on monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis

subtopic_detail: Neonatal testicular torsion presenting on day 2 of life with a firm hemiscrotal mass
stem: A term boy is reviewed on day 2 of life. The left hemiscrotum has been firm, bluish and non-tender since birth, and the testis cannot be distinguished from the surrounding oedema. The right testis is normal.

data_table.Investigations: Scrotal ultrasound shows an enlarged heterogeneous left testis with absent intratesticular Doppler flow and a normal right testis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative plan?

options.text: Manual detorsion at the cotside now under nitrous oxide analgesia
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is not appropriate in the neonate; the neonatal scrotum requires operative exploration. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Warm compresses with repeat scrotal ultrasound in 24 hours
options.rationale: Observation risks loss of the contralateral testis if bell clapper anatomy is present; contralateral fixation is prioritised. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Urgent exploration with left orchidectomy and contralateral orchidopexy
options.rationale: Neonatal torsion presenting at birth with a firm discoloured testis and absent Doppler flow is almost always non salvageable prenatal or perinatal torsion. Contralateral orchidopexy at the same operation is essential because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral, risking metachronous torsion of the only remaining testis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Semi-urgent exploration in a few days for left orchidectomy alone
options.rationale: Contralateral orchidopexy is essential because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral; failing to fix the right testis risks metachronous torsion. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

options.text: Repeat Doppler at 6 and 12 hours before any operative decision
options.rationale: Serial imaging delays care; the plan is defined by the clinical finding of a firm, discoloured neonatal testis and absent Doppler flow. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline

explanation.summary: Neonatal testicular torsion often occurs prenatally or perinatally; the testis at birth is typically necrotic and non salvageable. The critical clinical decision is not testicular salvage but protection of the contralateral testis by fixation at the same operation. Bell clapper anatomy predisposes to bilateral torsion and metachronous loss. Ultrasound with Doppler helps confirm loss of flow but does not delay operative planning. Post operatively, parents require counselling about fertility, testosterone monitoring at puberty and consideration of testicular prosthesis at adolescence.
key_points: Neonatal torsion at birth is almost always non salvageable prenatal torsion.
Contralateral orchidopexy at the same operation is the critical intervention because bell clapper anatomy is often bilateral.
Repeat imaging delays care and does not change the plan of urgent exploration and fixation.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal firm blue hemiscrotum with absent Doppler flow: urgent scrotal exploration; left orchidectomy plus right orchidopexy to protect the contralateral testis from metachronous torsion.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Neonatal Surgical Guideline
American Urological Association guideline on testicular torsion in the neonate

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa in a swimmer with intact tympanic membrane
stem: A 12-year-old competitive swimmer has 4 days of increasing left ear pain and itching, worse on chewing and on pulling the pinna. She is afebrile, with no vertigo and no facial weakness.

data_table.Examination: Tender tragus, oedematous erythematous left ear canal with debris, tympanic membrane intact after clearance

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line therapy?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Systemic antibiotics are not first line for uncomplicated otitis externa; topical therapy achieves higher local concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

options.text: Aural toilet and topical ciprofloxacin with dexamethasone drops
options.rationale: First line therapy for acute otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines is aural toilet (wick or microsuction) plus topical ciprofloxacin 0.3 percent plus dexamethasone 0.1 percent 5 drops twice daily for 7 days, with pool avoidance until symptoms resolve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

options.text: Aluminium acetate ear drops alone for 5 days, then review
options.rationale: Aluminium acetate has some effect but topical antimicrobial therapy is more effective; it is not first line monotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

options.text: Warm saline bulb syringe irrigation twice daily at home
options.rationale: Irrigation risks worsening the canal maceration; aural toilet by trained personnel plus topical antibiotic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin is reserved for otitis externa with cellulitis extending beyond the canal, malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, or refractory disease; it is not first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Otitis externa)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis externa is diagnosed clinically by canal inflammation and tragal or pinna tenderness. First line therapy in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines is aural toilet plus a topical antimicrobial with a corticosteroid such as ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops, with pool avoidance until symptoms resolve. Systemic antibiotics are added for cellulitis spread beyond the canal. Necrotising otitis externa is suspected in diabetics or immunocompromised patients with severe pain, granulation tissue at the bony cartilaginous junction, or cranial nerve palsy; it needs urgent ear nose throat specialist review, imaging and intravenous ciprofloxacin. If the tympanic membrane is perforated or grommets are present, an aminoglycoside containing drop is avoided.
key_points: First line: aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone ear drops for 7 days.
Oral antibiotics only if cellulitis extends beyond the canal or in immunocompromise.
Avoid aminoglycoside drops with perforated tympanic membrane or grommets.
explanation.pearls: Uncomplicated acute otitis externa with intact tympanic membrane: aural toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin plus dexamethasone 5 drops twice daily for 7 days, plus pool avoidance until symptoms resolve.

sources.label: American Academy of Otolaryngology Clinical Practice Guideline on Acute Otitis Externa

subtopic_detail: Metformin candidacy in adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation
stem: A 14-year-old girl has a body mass index of 34 kg/m^2 (above the 99.5th centile) and acanthosis nigricans. Six months of a structured dietitian and exercise program produced no metabolic improvement.
