data_table.Investigations: Blood pressure 132/82 mmHg (above the 95th centile), fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.1%, 2-hour glucose 9.4 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy should be added to intensified lifestyle intervention?

options.text: Referral for bariatric surgery with sleeve gastrectomy
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is considered after failure of intensified pharmacological and lifestyle programs and typically at body mass index >=40 or >=35 with severe comorbidity; not first line here. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Orlistat 120 mg with each meal as first line therapy
options.rationale: Orlistat is not first line pharmacotherapy for adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation; metformin is preferred when dysglycaemia is present. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Liraglutide 3 mg subcutaneously daily as first line
options.rationale: Liraglutide 3 mg is TGA registered for adolescent obesity from age 12 but is not first line for impaired glucose regulation and access via the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme is limited. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously at bedtime
options.rationale: Insulin is inappropriate for impaired glucose regulation without established diabetes; metformin is the recommended first line pharmacotherapy. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Metformin 500 mg daily, titrated to 2 g over four weeks
options.rationale: Metformin is a recommended adjunct to lifestyle intervention in adolescents 10 years and older with obesity and impaired glucose regulation (impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, or haemoglobin A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent) when lifestyle alone is inadequate. Titration from 500 mg daily to 2 g daily over 4 weeks is standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Metformin is a recommended adjunct to intensified lifestyle intervention in adolescents (10 years or older) with obesity and impaired glucose regulation, defined as impaired fasting glucose 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L, impaired glucose tolerance (2 hour 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L), or haemoglobin A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent, when lifestyle alone is inadequate. Standard titration is extended release 500 mg daily up to 2 g daily over 4 weeks. Liraglutide 3 mg is TGA registered from age 12 for adolescent obesity but is not first line for dysglycaemia. Bariatric surgery is reserved for body mass index over 40 or over 35 with severe comorbidity after failed intensive therapy. Screen for polycystic ovary syndrome, non alcoholic fatty liver disease and obstructive sleep apnoea.
key_points: Metformin is first line pharmacotherapy in adolescent obesity with impaired glucose regulation after failed lifestyle intervention.
Titrate extended release 500 mg daily up to 2 g daily over 4 weeks.
Bariatric surgery: body mass index >=40 or >=35 with severe comorbidity after failed intensive medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: Adolescent obesity with impaired glucose tolerance after failed 6 month lifestyle program: add metformin extended release 500 mg daily titrated to 2 g daily over 4 weeks alongside continued lifestyle intervention.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Paediatric Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Obesity in Children Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome first relapse definition and next line therapy after multiple relapses
stem: A 5-year-old boy with steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome diagnosed 8 months ago presents with his fourth relapse. Each previous relapse responded to prednisolone within 10 days. He now has a weight z score 3 SD above baseline, striae and cushingoid facies.

data_table.Examination: Periorbital oedema, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol, albumin 22 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 intravenously as a single dose
options.rationale: Rituximab is reserved for complicated frequently relapsing or steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome that has failed a conventional steroid sparing oral agent; it is not first line here. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Prednisolone 60 mg/m^2 daily with a 12 week wean
options.rationale: Continued repeated steroid courses without a sparing agent worsen the established steroid toxicity; a steroid sparing agent is indicated. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Urgent percutaneous renal biopsy before any agent
options.rationale: Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome with prompt response does not require biopsy before a steroid sparing trial; biopsy is considered if steroid resistant or atypical features are present. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg daily with prednisolone induction
options.rationale: Frequently relapsing (>=2 relapses in 6 months or >=4 in 12 months) or steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome with steroid toxicity is an indication for a steroid sparing agent alongside a fresh steroid induction. Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg) is a standard KDIGO first line steroid sparing option; levamisole (where available), calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil are alternatives. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

options.text: Lisinopril 5 mg daily alone in place of steroids
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are antiproteinuric adjuncts, not induction therapy for active nephrotic relapse; induction plus steroid sparing is required. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases)
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

explanation.summary: Frequently relapsing steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome is defined as at least 2 relapses in 6 months or at least 4 in 12 months, and steroid dependent as relapse during steroid taper or within 2 weeks of stopping. Both are indications for a steroid sparing agent alongside a fresh steroid induction, particularly if steroid toxicity is established. First line steroid sparing options in KDIGO are oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg), levamisole where available, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil. Rituximab is reserved for complicated cases after failure of a conventional steroid sparing agent. Renal biopsy is not required before a steroid sparing trial in typical steroid sensitive disease.
key_points: Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome: >=2 relapses in 6 months or >=4 in 12 months.
Steroid sparing options include cyclophosphamide, levamisole, calcineurin inhibitors and mycophenolate mofetil.
Rituximab reserved for complicated disease after conventional agents fail.
explanation.pearls: Fourth relapse with steroid toxicity: prednisolone induction and taper alongside cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day for 8 to 12 weeks (cumulative dose limit 168 mg/kg) as the steroid sparing agent.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Nephrotic Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Differentiating multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children from Kawasaki disease at initial workup
stem: An 8-year-old girl has five days of fever, non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a maculopapular rash, extremity oedema and cervical lymphadenopathy. She has abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Household SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed five weeks ago.

data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 45 ng/L (less than 15), lymphocytes 0.7 x10^9/L, platelets 128 x10^9/L, ejection fraction 48% with no coronary aneurysm

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children over Kawasaki disease?

options.text: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis with cracked, fissured lips
options.rationale: Bilateral non purulent conjunctivitis is a classic feature of both conditions and does not discriminate. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Older age, abdominal symptoms, lymphopenia and raised troponin
options.rationale: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children typically presents in older children (median 8 to 10 years), with prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia early, myocardial dysfunction with elevated troponin, and a recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or seropositivity. Classic Kawasaki disease is a disease of children under 5 with a normal or elevated platelet count and coronary artery aneurysm rather than global left ventricular dysfunction as the cardiac lesion. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Five days of unremitting fever with a truncal maculopapular rash
options.rationale: Fever and rash are shared features; they do not discriminate. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy measuring more than 1.5 cm
options.rationale: Cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm and mucous membrane changes are shared features of both conditions; not discriminatory. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

options.text: Extremity oedema with a polymorphous rash over the trunk
options.rationale: Extremity oedema and rash are classic Kawasaki disease features and do not discriminate multisystem inflammatory syndrome. (Source: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
source_refs: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

explanation.summary: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children is defined by fever, laboratory evidence of inflammation, evidence of multiorgan involvement (cardiac, renal, respiratory, haematological, gastrointestinal, dermatological or neurological), recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or seropositivity, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses. It typically presents in older children (median 8 to 10 years) with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, lymphopenia, elevated ferritin and troponin, and myocardial dysfunction. Kawasaki disease occurs mainly in children under 5, with normal or elevated platelet count and coronary artery aneurysm as the classic cardiac lesion. Initial management shares intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg but multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children also uses methylprednisolone and consideration of anakinra or infliximab in refractory cases.
key_points: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children: older age, prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, elevated troponin, myocardial dysfunction.
Kawasaki disease: median age under 5, normal or elevated platelets, coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiogram.
Both treated with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg; multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children adds methylprednisolone.
explanation.pearls: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children differentiators: older age (median 8 to 10 years), prominent gastrointestinal features, lymphopenia, elevated troponin, myocardial dysfunction rather than coronary aneurysm, plus recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure or IgG positivity.

sources.label: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children
American College of Rheumatology Clinical Guidance for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

subtopic_detail: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia recognition with severe thrombocytopenia at birth
stem: A term boy has widespread petechiae and a small subgaleal haematoma at 6 hours of age. His mother is well, with a booking platelet count of 285 x10^9/L and no antiplatelet medication.

data_table.Investigations: Platelets 15 x10^9/L (150-450), haemoglobin 168 g/L, coagulation profile normal, cranial ultrasound no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate transfusion strategy?

options.text: Antigen matched platelets, HPA-1a negative if unknown, with immunoglobulin 1 g/kg
options.rationale: Suspected neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia with severe thrombocytopenia (<30 x10^9/L) is treated with human platelet antigen matched platelet transfusion (HPA-1a negative if the antigen is unknown, since HPA-1a is the most common alloantigen in Caucasian populations), plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg to reduce further platelet destruction and prolong response duration. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Random donor platelets 10 mL/kg immediately, without any immunoglobulin cover
options.rationale: Random donor platelets are consumed by the maternal antibody within hours; the response is transient and poor. Human platelet antigen matched platelets are preferred. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Maternal washed apheresis platelets with oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Maternal platelets require apheresis, washing to remove antibody and irradiation to prevent graft versus host disease; they take time and are used if human platelet antigen matched platelets are unavailable. Corticosteroids have limited evidence in the neonate. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Serial platelet counts six-hourly, transfusing only below 5 x10^9/L or if bleeding
options.rationale: Severe thrombocytopenia in a neonate with intracranial haemorrhage risk requires urgent transfusion regardless of clinical bleeding; the intracranial haemorrhage risk (10 to 20 percent, often in utero) mandates prompt correction. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg over 30 minutes as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma does not correct platelet count and is not appropriate treatment for immune thrombocytopenia. (Source: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia)
source_refs: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia presents with severe isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well neonate of a mother with a normal platelet count, most commonly due to maternal antibody against fetal HPA-1a inherited from the father. Intracranial haemorrhage risk is 10 to 20 percent, often in utero, and can occur despite in utero intravenous immunoglobulin. Treatment of severe thrombocytopenia (<30 x10^9/L) is human platelet antigen matched (HPA-1a negative) platelet transfusion plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg. Maternal washed and irradiated apheresis platelets are a backup. Antenatal management of subsequent pregnancies with weekly maternal intravenous immunoglobulin from 20 to 26 weeks is standard.
key_points: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: severe isolated thrombocytopenia in a well neonate with a maternal normal platelet count.
Treatment: HPA-1a negative platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg.
Intracranial haemorrhage risk is 10 to 20 percent, often in utero, mandating urgent transfusion at platelets below 30 x10^9/L.
explanation.pearls: Severe neonatal thrombocytopenia (platelets 15) with a well mother and no maternal platelet drop is neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: HPA-1a negative platelets plus intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg immediately.

sources.label: British Society for Haematology Guideline on Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia
International Collaboration on Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia recommendations

subtopic_detail: Severe combined immunodeficiency unmasked by live rotavirus vaccine complication after routine immunisation
stem: A 5-month-old boy has 6 weeks of watery diarrhoea, weight fallen from the 25th to below the 3rd centile, and oral candidiasis. A sibling died at 8 months of infection.

data_table.Investigations: Lymphocytes 0.6 x10^9/L, CD3 0.02 x10^9/L, T cell receptor excision circles absent
data_table.Microbiology: Lavage: Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus; stool vaccine strain rotavirus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ganciclovir, deferring immunology
options.rationale: Treating opportunistic infections alone without immediate immunology and transplant referral misses the diagnosis window; severe combined immunodeficiency mortality without haematopoietic stem cell transplant is 100 percent by 2 years. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Discharge on home oxygen with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and monthly review
options.rationale: Home discharge is unsafe with severe combined immunodeficiency and active Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus and vaccine strain rotavirus enteritis; specialist inpatient management with isolation is essential. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Protective isolation, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative products, urgent transplant referral
options.rationale: Severe combined immunodeficiency confirmed by absent T cell receptor excision circles and profoundly low CD3, CD19 and natural killer cells requires immediate protective isolation, use of irradiated cytomegalovirus negative cellular blood products (to prevent transfusion associated graft versus host disease), Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, avoidance of all live vaccines and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant workup because untreated mortality is close to 100 percent by 2 years. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Continue the schedule with rotavirus and measles-mumps-rubella at 12 months
options.rationale: Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe combined immunodeficiency; live rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella and measles-mumps-rubella vaccines can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

options.text: Trial oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for presumed eosinophilic enteropathy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids in undiagnosed severe combined immunodeficiency will worsen opportunistic infections; the priority is diagnosis and transplant referral. (Source: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline)
source_refs: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline

explanation.summary: Severe combined immunodeficiency is a paediatric emergency with mortality close to 100 percent by age 2 without haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Live vaccines including rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella and measles-mumps-rubella can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease and must be avoided. Diagnosis is confirmed by absent T cell receptor excision circles and profoundly low CD3 (and often CD19 and natural killer) counts. Management is immediate protective isolation, Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, intravenous immunoglobulin replacement, treatment of opportunistic infections, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative cellular blood products, and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Family counselling is essential for future pregnancies; T cell receptor excision circle newborn screening is now standard in several AU jurisdictions.
key_points: Severe combined immunodeficiency requires urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant; untreated mortality is close to 100 percent by 2 years.
All cellular blood products must be irradiated and cytomegalovirus negative.
All live vaccines (rotavirus, bacillus Calmette-Guerin, oral polio, varicella, measles-mumps-rubella) are contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: Severe combined immunodeficiency (absent T cell receptor excision circles, CD3 <0.05, and vaccine strain rotavirus enteritis): protective isolation, irradiated cytomegalovirus negative blood products, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and urgent haematopoietic stem cell transplant workup.

sources.label: European Society for Immunodeficiencies SCID Guideline
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Primary Immunodeficiency Guideline

subtopic_detail: Escalation of respiratory support in an infant with bronchiolitis on general paediatric ward
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the general ward at 2 am. A 4 month old term infant was admitted 6 hours ago with a 3 day history of coryza, cough and increasing work of breathing. His mother says he took only 30 percent of his usual feeds today and has had 2 wet nappies in 24 hours. His weight is 6.4 kg and he is fully immunised.

On examination he is alert but tachypnoeic with moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze and fine crackles. His nappy is dry. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Feeding: 30% of baseline oral intake in past 12 hours, 2 wet nappies in 24 hours
data_table.Chest: Bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, no tracheal tug

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate respiratory intervention?

options.text: Start low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min via a humidified circuit, titrate to keep SpO2 at or above 90 percent, and reassess work of breathing in one hour
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis with SpO2 below 90 percent and moderate work of breathing needs low flow nasal oxygen first line, titrated to a target SpO2 of at least 90 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min via humidified circuit and admit to the high dependency unit for close monitoring now
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants who fail a trial of low flow oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min after at least 1 to 2 hours; it is not the first respiratory step in ward level bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000, and repeat if the work of breathing persists
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol and adrenaline are not recommended in viral bronchiolitis under 12 months; they do not change length of stay or oxygen requirement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, review in one hour, and start oxygen only if the SpO2 drops further overnight
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in acute viral bronchiolitis; delaying oxygen when SpO2 is already 89 percent is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now with pressure support because his respiratory rate and recession predict imminent respiratory failure requiring definitive airway
options.rationale: He is alert with only moderate recession and no apnoea; escalation should begin with the least invasive effective option, which is low flow oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is managed supportively with feeding support and oxygen. Low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min is the first line respiratory support, titrated to SpO2 of at least 90 percent. High flow nasal cannula is a second line intervention for infants failing low flow after 1 to 2 hours, not a first choice. Bronchodilators, adrenaline, corticosteroids and antibiotics have no routine role.
key_points: Low flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min is first line; target SpO2 at or above 90 percent.
High flow nasal cannula is second line after failure of low flow.
Bronchodilators, nebulised adrenaline and corticosteroids do not change outcomes in viral bronchiolitis.
explanation.pearls: SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent on room air; start low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min and reassess before escalating to high flow.

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid selection and disposition in moderate viral croup in an emergency department
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 22 month old girl is brought in at midnight with a 12 hour history of barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing that started after a 2 day coryzal illness. She is settled on her mother's lap and pink. She has stridor audible only when she becomes upset and moderate intercostal recession at rest. Her chest is otherwise clear.

She has no drooling, no toxic appearance and no history of intubation, asthma or immunodeficiency. She is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Airway: Barking cough, hoarse voice, stridor only on agitation, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Work of breathing: Moderate intercostal recession at rest, no tracheal tug, no fatigue

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 now, and admit to a monitored bed for at least 4 hours
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone plus nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession or exhaustion, not moderate croup that settles when calm. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and observe in the emergency short stay area for 4 hours before deciding disposition
options.rationale: Moderate croup is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; observation for a few hours is appropriate if there was no nebulised adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days at home, arrange general practice review the following morning and discharge the child now
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg is an alternative if dexamethasone is not available, but a single dose is used, not a 3 day course; observation before discharge is still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give humidified air by face mask alone and reassess in one hour, avoiding any corticosteroid because of the risk of secondary bacterial tracheitis
options.rationale: Humidified air alone does not improve viral croup and there is no evidence that dexamethasone increases bacterial tracheitis; steroid is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg immediately and arrange urgent ear nose and throat review for consideration of nasoendoscopy to exclude epiglottitis
options.rationale: There is no drooling, tripod posture or toxic appearance; empirical ceftriaxone and nasoendoscopy are not indicated for classic viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Viral croup severity is graded by stridor and recession at rest. Mild and moderate croup are both treated with a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. The higher dose of 0.6 mg/kg with nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, defined by stridor and marked recession at rest with agitation or exhaustion. Observation for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline is required before discharge; a shorter period is acceptable after oral steroid alone.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
Observe for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline before considering discharge.
explanation.pearls: Stridor only on agitation with moderate recession is moderate croup: give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and observe for a few hours before discharge.

subtopic_detail: Investigation of a febrile well appearing infant under three months in emergency
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 5 week old boy is brought in by his parents because of a rectal temperature of 38.4 degC at home an hour ago. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery, is exclusively breast fed and has been feeding normally. He looks pink, alert and content in his father's arms in the cubicle. He has no rash, no bulging fontanelle and no focal signs of infection.

His mother had negative group B streptococcus screening in pregnancy. He has had no contact with anyone with known infection and has not travelled overseas. He is not on any medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 76/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.General: Alert, well perfused, no rash, anterior fontanelle soft and flat
data_table.Focus of infection: Ears, throat and skin unremarkable; no cough, no vomiting, no diarrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, give paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally and discharge home with advice to return if the fever exceeds 39 degC or the infant becomes unwell
options.rationale: Well appearance in an infant under 3 months does not exclude serious bacterial infection; discharging without workup is unsafe at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take a bag urine specimen only, discharge home once the sample is sent and arrange telephone follow up with the general practitioner in 24 hours
options.rationale: Under 3 months of age with fever, the required investigations include blood culture and lumbar puncture as well as urine; bag urine is unreliable and cannot be sent as the only investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Full septic screen including blood culture, urine catheter specimen, lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin now
options.rationale: A rectal temperature of 38 degC or higher in an infant less than 3 months is a full septic workup indication irrespective of appearance, with empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take blood cultures and inflammatory markers only and start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily, deferring lumbar puncture until results are back
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture should not be deferred pending markers in an infant less than 6 weeks with fever unless there is a contraindication; ceftriaxone monotherapy is also not the preferred neonatal regimen. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Admit for 48 hours of observation without any investigations or antibiotics, and perform investigations only if the fever recurs above 38 degC on the ward
options.rationale: Watchful waiting without investigation in an infant under 3 months with documented fever is unsafe and misses early treatable bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

explanation.summary: Any infant less than 3 months old with a documented temperature of at least 38 degC needs a full septic workup regardless of general appearance because the risk of serious bacterial infection is high and clinical assessment is unreliable at this age. Investigations include blood culture, urine by catheter or suprapubic aspirate and lumbar puncture, with empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin in Australia. Bag urine is not sent as a definitive specimen. Watching without investigation is unsafe.
key_points: Infant under 3 months with fever at or above 38 degC: full septic workup regardless of appearance.
Catheter or suprapubic urine, blood culture and lumbar puncture are all needed.
Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the standard neonatal regimen.
explanation.pearls: A well looking infant under 3 months with fever still needs a full septic screen and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; do not send bag urine alone or defer the lumbar puncture.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in Neonates

subtopic_detail: First hour management of severe acute asthma in a school aged child in emergency
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 6 year old girl is brought in by ambulance with a 12 hour history of worsening wheeze and cough after a viral upper respiratory illness. She is on inhaled salbutamol as needed and fluticasone 100 mcg twice daily. She has needed her reliever every hour at home overnight.

On arrival she is anxious, sits forwards and can only speak in single words. She has widespread wheeze with markedly reduced air entry at the bases, subcostal and tracheal tug and moderate use of accessory muscles. She is not obviously exhausted and there is no cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 /min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Respiratory: Widespread wheeze, reduced air entry at bases, subcostal and tracheal tug, single word sentences
data_table.Peak flow: Unable to perform because of dyspnoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first hour management?

options.text: Give intravenous salbutamol infusion 5 mcg/kg/min immediately as a bolus and continuous infusion in preference to inhaled bronchodilator via spacer therapy
options.rationale: Intravenous salbutamol is reserved for life threatening asthma failing inhaled therapy; inhaled salbutamol via spacer is first line even in severe cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg immediately as first line therapy and start non invasive ventilation while awaiting paediatric intensive care review
options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is second line, reserved for severe or life threatening asthma not responding to initial salbutamol, prednisolone and ipratropium in the first hour. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give a single dose of nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000, oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and start empirical amoxicillin for likely bacterial pneumonia today
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not first line in asthma; dexamethasone is not the preferred oral corticosteroid; empirical antibiotics are not indicated for asthma exacerbations without pneumonia. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give salbutamol 12 puffs via metered dose inhaler and spacer every 20 minutes for one hour, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and titrated oxygen to SpO2 above 94 percent
options.rationale: In severe childhood asthma, first hour treatment is back to back salbutamol via spacer (or nebulised if unable), oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg and titrated oxygen; ipratropium is added if response is poor. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give inhaled fluticasone 500 mcg via spacer every hour and defer systemic corticosteroid until the child has failed 4 hours of inhaled controller escalation
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids are not effective for acute exacerbations; systemic corticosteroid is given in the first hour to reduce admission and relapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

explanation.summary: Severe acute asthma in a child needs immediate salbutamol delivered by spacer (12 puffs for over 6 years) every 20 minutes for the first hour, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg or intravenous methylprednisolone if oral not tolerated) and titrated oxygen to SpO2 above 94 percent. Ipratropium 8 puffs is added by spacer if the response is inadequate. Second line therapy is intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes for life threatening or non responding exacerbations, then intravenous salbutamol or aminophylline. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is pneumonia.
key_points: First hour: 12 puffs salbutamol via spacer every 20 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, titrated oxygen.
Add ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer if inadequate response in the first hour.
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg is second line for severe or non responding cases.
explanation.pearls: Severe childhood asthma first hour: back to back inhaled salbutamol 12 puffs every 20 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, titrated oxygen and add ipratropium for poor response.

subtopic_detail: Choice of reduction versus surgical exploration in confirmed ileocolic intussusception with equivocal peritonism
stem: A 9-month-old boy has 8 hours of episodes of drawing his knees up and crying, settling between episodes but becoming progressively lethargic. He has vomited twice, once bile stained, and passed blood stained mucus per rectum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, central capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Abdomen: Soft, right upper quadrant fullness, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Target sign with preserved Doppler perfusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Barium enema now, without resuscitation or antibiotics
options.rationale: Barium is not used in AU centres because of chemical peritonitis risk if perforation occurs; pre procedure resuscitation and cross match are standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Immediate laparotomy and manual reduction, bypassing enema
options.rationale: Bile stained vomiting alone is not a contraindication to air enema; without peritonism, perforation or shock, enema reduction is attempted first with surgical backup. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Nasogastric polyethylene glycol and repeat ultrasound in 4 hours
options.rationale: Osmotic laxatives are not used to reduce intussusception; observation alone risks progression to ischaemia and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Intravenous ondansetron and discharge once vomiting settles
options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception on ultrasound requires urgent reduction and admission; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Resuscitate, cross match, give antibiotics, then air enema reduction
options.rationale: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonism, perforation or shock is managed by air enema reduction after resuscitation, cross match and antibiotic cover, with surgery on standby. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in infants presents with paroxysmal crying, drawing up the legs, vomiting and blood stained mucus in the nappy. Ultrasound target sign is diagnostic. Provided there is no peritonism, perforation on imaging, or refractory shock, first line treatment in Australia is air (pneumatic) enema reduction in interventional radiology after intravenous fluid resuscitation, blood cross match and antibiotic cover, with paediatric surgery on standby. Barium is avoided because of chemical peritonitis risk if perforation occurs. Surgery is reserved for peritonism, perforation, failed enema or a lead point.
key_points: Diagnosis by ultrasound target sign; look for signs of ischaemia and perforation before deciding.
Air enema is first line if no peritonism, perforation or refractory shock; resuscitate and give antibiotics first.
Surgery indications: peritonism, perforation, failed enema reduction or identified lead point.
explanation.pearls: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonism goes to air enema reduction after fluids, cross match and antibiotics; barium is not used because of chemical peritonitis risk.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Journal of Surgery Intussusception Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Choosing intensive phototherapy versus exchange transfusion in a term neonate with rising bilirubin
stem: A term 3.4 kg boy is 60 hours old. His mother is blood group A rhesus positive and he is O rhesus positive. He is alert and feeding well.

data_table.Bilirubin trend: 380 micromol/L at 52 hours, 405 micromol/L at 60 hours on single surface phototherapy
data_table.Laboratory: Haemoglobin 145 g/L (145-225), direct antiglobulin test positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to exchange transfusion now without escalating phototherapy
options.rationale: Intensive multiple surface phototherapy is escalated first; exchange is reserved for failure to respond, or bilirubin above the exchange line, or acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Escalate to intensive phototherapy, recheck bilirubin in 4 hours, cross match
options.rationale: Bilirubin rising above the phototherapy line with a positive direct antiglobulin test in a haemolytic pattern needs intensive phototherapy and blood cross match while awaiting the response; exchange is not yet mandatory. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Stop phototherapy for 6 hours and repeat the bilirubin off treatment
options.rationale: Stopping phototherapy in a haemolytic pattern with rising bilirubin above threshold risks progression to acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and defer further phototherapy
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered in rhesus or ABO haemolytic disease not responding to intensive phototherapy, not before intensive phototherapy has been tried. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Continue single surface phototherapy and recheck in 12 hours
options.rationale: Single surface phototherapy has already failed to control the rise; delaying escalation for 12 hours risks bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management is guided by hour specific bilirubin nomograms with separate phototherapy and exchange transfusion thresholds and by risk factors including haemolytic pattern, prematurity and clinical instability. A positive direct antiglobulin test suggests ABO or rhesus haemolysis and lowers the treatment threshold. When bilirubin rises despite single surface phototherapy, the next step is intensive multiple surface phototherapy plus attention to hydration and feeding, with blood cross match in preparation for exchange. Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered if intensive phototherapy fails in immune haemolytic disease. Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin exceeds the exchange line or acute bilirubin encephalopathy develops.
key_points: Escalate to intensive phototherapy before considering exchange when bilirubin rises above threshold.
Positive direct antiglobulin test lowers thresholds and warrants cross match early.
Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg is second line after intensive phototherapy in immune haemolysis.
explanation.pearls: Rising serum bilirubin above threshold on single phototherapy with positive direct antiglobulin test: escalate to intensive multiple surface phototherapy, cross match blood and consider intravenous immunoglobulin before exchange.

subtopic_detail: Secondary prophylaxis regimen in a first episode of acute rheumatic fever without carditis in a high risk community
stem: An 11-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote Northern Territory community had a first episode of acute rheumatic fever 6 weeks ago with polyarthritis and a positive antistreptolysin O titre.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography at the index episode and today shows no valvular abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate secondary prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg once weekly for 3 years, then repeat echocardiography
options.rationale: Azithromycin is not the preferred agent in AU; duration is not 3 years and echocardiography is not used to decide when to stop. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily for 5 years, then stop
options.rationale: Oral penicillin is second line only if intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin cannot be given; a 5 year fixed duration is not the AU standard. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units intramuscularly every 28 days until age 21
options.rationale: In Australia, secondary prophylaxis for acute rheumatic fever without carditis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer, especially in a high risk community. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: No prophylaxis, with aspirin only if arthritis recurs in the next year
options.rationale: Absence of carditis does not remove the need for prophylaxis; recurrent episodes are common and cause carditis on subsequent presentations. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units intramuscularly every 12 weeks
options.rationale: The correct dosing interval is 28 days (or 21 days in special situations), not 12 weeks; prednisolone is not used for prevention. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

explanation.summary: Secondary prophylaxis after acute rheumatic fever prevents recurrent group A streptococcal infection and progression to rheumatic heart disease. In Australia the first line agent is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days. Duration is stratified by the episode and outcome: at least 10 years after the last episode or until age 21 (whichever is longer) for acute rheumatic fever without carditis; longer in the presence of persistent or worsening rheumatic heart disease. Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin twice daily is reserved for patients who cannot receive intramuscular therapy. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from high risk communities have a high recurrence risk that justifies the longer duration.
key_points: First line: intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days.
Duration for acute rheumatic fever without carditis: at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin twice daily is second line for those unable to have intramuscular therapy.
explanation.pearls: Australian secondary prophylaxis for acute rheumatic fever is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer; longer if carditis or rheumatic heart disease is present.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Rheumatic Fever

subtopic_detail: Emergency management of suspected cerebral oedema during treatment for paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis with borderline neurology
stem: A 9-year-old boy is 4 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis with a 10 mL/kg saline bolus, deficit fluids and insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour. He now has a new headache.

data_table.Neurology: Glasgow Coma Score 15 to 13, pupils reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and CT brain before osmotherapy
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is not first line for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA; imaging must not delay osmotherapy when clinical criteria are met. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Bolus 20 mL/kg saline and run 1.5 times maintenance fluid
options.rationale: The clinical picture is Cushing response with intracranial hypertension, not hypovolaemia; further crystalloid bolus and higher rates worsen cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Increase insulin to 0.1 units/kg/hour and give bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is a recognised risk factor for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA and is not recommended; higher insulin does not treat cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give 3% saline 3 mL/kg, cut fluids a third, call retrieval
options.rationale: Falling Glasgow Coma Score, new headache and rising blood pressure with bradycardia meet AU paediatric DKA criteria for cerebral oedema; hypertonic saline (or 20 percent mannitol), fluid reduction and neurosurgical retrieval are first line. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Continue fluids, give paracetamol and reassess in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Observation without acting on falling Glasgow Coma Score and Cushing response allows brainstem herniation; osmotherapy must not be delayed. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis and often develops during the first 4 to 12 hours of treatment. Diagnostic clues include a falling Glasgow Coma Score, new headache, incontinence, bradycardia with rising blood pressure (Cushing response) and cranial nerve palsies. Australian paediatric guidelines require immediate osmotherapy with 3 percent hypertonic saline 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes or 20 percent mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg, reduction of intravenous fluid rate by around a third, head up positioning and urgent neurosurgical retrieval. Bicarbonate, further fluid boluses and rapid glucose falls are risk factors and should be avoided. Imaging must not delay osmotherapy when clinical criteria are met.
key_points: Cushing response and falling Glasgow Coma Score in DKA meet clinical criteria for cerebral oedema.
Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 2 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg immediately and reduce fluid rate.
Bicarbonate use, aggressive volume and rapid glucose fall are recognised risk factors.
explanation.pearls: New headache with falling Glasgow Coma Score and bradycardia and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment is cerebral oedema: give hypertonic 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 g/kg immediately, cut the fluid rate by a third and call retrieval.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and Hyperglycaemic Hyperosmolar State

subtopic_detail: Admission threshold for bronchiolitis in a well-perfused infant with borderline saturations and adequate feeding
stem: A 4-month-old term infant has 3 days of coryza and 1 day of cough. He is taking 60% of his usual feeds and has had no apnoeas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 /min, RR 55 /min, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild subcostal recession, bilateral crackles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with low flow oxygen targeting saturation above 92%
options.rationale: Persistent SpO2 below 92 percent on room air in a bronchiolitis infant meets AU admission criteria; feeding below 50 to 75 percent of normal is a further indication and low flow oxygen with feed review is standard ward care. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and admit if there is no response
options.rationale: Salbutamol trials are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and response is not a validated admission criterion in the AU pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days and reassess
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated in acute viral bronchiolitis under 12 months and do not alter disposition. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home on room air with general practice review tomorrow
options.rationale: Discharge is not safe with SpO2 below 92 percent and reduced feeding under 75 percent; both are AU admission triggers regardless of proximity to hospital. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high flow humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg per minute now
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants failing standard low flow oxygen or with moderate to severe work of breathing; escalation before a trial of low flow is not the AU first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is managed with supportive care alone; bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated in the Australian guideline. Admission criteria in AU tertiary paediatric emergency departments include persistent room air SpO2 below 92 percent, feeding less than 50 to 75 percent of normal, moderate to severe work of breathing, apnoeas, dehydration, or clinician concern in a family without safe follow up. Low flow nasal cannula oxygen (up to 2 L per minute) is the first line respiratory support; high flow is reserved for those failing low flow, and continuous positive airway pressure or transfer to a paediatric intensive care unit is considered next. Feeding is often the earliest and most sensitive marker of severity.
key_points: AU admission triggers: SpO2 below 92% persistently, feeds less than 50 to 75% of normal, moderate to severe work of breathing.
Low flow nasal cannula oxygen is the first line respiratory support before high flow.
Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: Feeding under 50 to 75 percent of normal intake in a bronchiolitis infant is an admission trigger in its own right in the AU pathway even if the SpO2 is 92 percent or above.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic versus observation decision in uncomplicated acute otitis media in a well 18 month old with bilateral disease
stem: An 18-month-old girl has 2 days of ear tugging, fever and disturbed sleep, and had acute otitis media 6 months ago. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.ENT: Both tympanic membranes bulging, opaque and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days with analgesia
options.rationale: Cephalosporins are not first line for uncomplicated acute otitis media in AU and add resistance risk without benefit over amoxicillin. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days with analgesia
options.rationale: Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years or with fever above 38 degC is a specific AU indication for immediate amoxicillin rather than a delayed script or observation. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Analgesia with a delayed amoxicillin script if no better at 48 hours
options.rationale: Delayed prescription is offered for unilateral acute otitis media without fever in a well older child; bilateral disease under 2 years with fever needs immediate treatment. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 22.5 mg/kg twice daily, 7 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48 to 72 hours of amoxicillin, not first line for a second episode months apart. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Refer for tympanocentesis and culture directed antibiotic choice
options.rationale: Tympanocentesis is reserved for treatment failure, immunocompromise or suppurative complications; it is not needed in an uncomplicated first presentation. (Source: eTG: Acute Otitis Media)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in Australian non-Aboriginal children under 2 years with bilateral disease or associated fever above 38 degC is a specific indication for immediate amoxicillin rather than observation with a delayed script. Unilateral disease in an older well child without fever can be managed with analgesia and a delayed prescription filled at 48 hours if symptoms persist. Amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days is first line; amoxicillin plus clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have a lower threshold for immediate antibiotics and longer courses because of higher rates of chronic suppurative otitis media.
key_points: Bilateral acute otitis media under 2 years or fever above 38 degC: immediate amoxicillin.
Unilateral acute otitis media in a well child over 2 years: delayed script at 48 hours is reasonable.
Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is second line for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours, not first line.
explanation.pearls: Immediate amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days is the AU first line for any child with bilateral acute otitis media under 2 years, not the delayed script offered in older well children.

subtopic_detail: Combined oral contraceptive request in a Gillick competent 15 year old without parental involvement
stem: A 15-year-old girl requests the combined oral contraceptive pill. She attends alone with one sexual partner aged 15 and declines to involve her parents. She explains correctly how to take the pill and manage a missed pill, and there are no safeguarding concerns.

data_table.Medical: BP 112/68 mmHg, BMI 22 kg/m2, no migraine, non-smoker

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline until a parent attends to give consent, as she is 15
options.rationale: Australian law recognises Gillick competence for consent to health care in minors; a 15 year old assessed competent may consent without parental involvement. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Prescribe and telephone her parents once the script is dispensed
options.rationale: Breaching confidentiality without her consent is not lawful and undermines therapeutic engagement; disclosure is only mandated for a mandatory reporting risk. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Prescribe and discuss long acting reversible contraception options
options.rationale: She meets Gillick competence with no contraindications; AU guidance actively promotes discussion of long acting reversible contraception alongside prescribing the requested method. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Offer condoms only until she turns 16, avoiding any prescription
options.rationale: Condoms alone give inferior pregnancy protection and denying hormonal contraception to a competent adolescent is neither guideline concordant nor legally required. (Source: RACGP: Adolescent Contraception)

options.text: Report the sexual activity to child protection before prescribing
options.rationale: Consensual sexual activity between similarly aged 15 year olds without exploitation is not a mandatory report in Victoria; a report here would breach confidentiality without cause. (Source: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework)
source_refs: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework

explanation.summary: Australian law and Royal Australian College of General Practitioners guidance recognise Gillick competence for adolescents consenting to health care. A minor under 16 years assessed as understanding the nature, purpose and consequences of a treatment may consent without parental involvement. Mandatory reporting is triggered by exploitation, coercion, a significant age gap or a partner in a position of power, not by consensual activity between similarly aged 15 year olds. Long acting reversible contraception is the most effective option and should be offered at the same visit even when a specific method is requested. Confidentiality is central to adolescent engagement; disclosure without consent is only justified for a safeguarding risk.
key_points: Gillick competence allows minors under 16 to consent to their own health care in Australia.
Consensual sexual activity between similarly aged 15 year olds is not automatically a mandatory report.
Offer long acting reversible contraception at the same visit even when a specific method is requested.
explanation.pearls: A Gillick competent 15 year old with no contraindications may be prescribed combined oral contraception confidentially in Australia; mandatory reporting only follows exploitation or a significant age gap, not similarly aged consensual sex.

sources.label: Victorian Child Wellbeing and Safety Framework

subtopic_detail: Follow up plan for a 40 hour old term breastfed newborn with a serum bilirubin just below the phototherapy line on the AU nomogram
stem: A 40-hour-old term girl is breastfeeding 2 to 3 hourly with five wet nappies in 24 hours and 5% weight loss. Her direct antiglobulin test is negative.

data_table.Investigations: Serum total bilirubin 240 micromol/L; Australian phototherapy line at this age 280 micromol/L
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, normal tone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start intensive phototherapy now and prepare for exchange transfusion
options.rationale: Her serum bilirubin sits below the phototherapy line and there is no evidence of severe or rapidly rising haemolytic jaundice to warrant intensive phototherapy or exchange preparation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Give a 60 mL formula top up now and plan no repeat measurement
options.rationale: Formula top ups are not first line in a well established breastfed baby with normal weight loss and normal urine output; repeat bilirubin remains needed to check trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Discharge today with general practitioner review at two weeks of age
options.rationale: A bilirubin within 40 to 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy line at under 48 hours needs repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours; discharge without follow up risks missing a crossing trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Continue breastfeeding with support and repeat serum bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours
options.rationale: AU practice for a bilirubin within about 50 micromol/L of the line under 48 hours is to continue feeding, support breastfeeding and repeat in 12 to 24 hours to track the trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Perform a full septic screen and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: There are no clinical features of sepsis in this well feeding afebrile baby; a septic screen and empiric antibiotics are not indicated for isolated jaundice within the safe zone. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice in the first week is common; the Australian consensus phototherapy nomogram plots total serum bilirubin against age in hours and gestation. Values below the phototherapy line but within about 50 micromol/L of it, especially in the first 48 hours, warrant repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours because bilirubin can continue to rise. Direct antiglobulin negativity and maternal group compatibility make isolated ABO or rhesus haemolytic disease unlikely, but ongoing tracking is still required until levels plateau. Breastfeeding support, adequate hydration and follow up review are the mainstays; formula top ups are not first line in a well feeding baby with normal weight loss and urine output. Early discharge without a repeat bilirubin risks missing a crossing trajectory.
key_points: Values within about 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy line under 48 hours need repeat measurement in 12 to 24 hours.
The AU consensus nomogram is plotted by age in hours and gestation.
Support breastfeeding; formula top ups are not first line in a well feeding baby with normal weight loss.
explanation.pearls: A term breastfed newborn with a bilirubin within 50 micromol/L of the AU phototherapy line under 48 hours needs a repeat serum bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours to plot the trajectory, not immediate phototherapy or discharge.

reference_ranges.value: phototherapy line ~280 micromol/L at 40 hours (AU consensus nomogram)

subtopic_detail: Approach to a 3 year old with 6 days of fever and only 2 clinical criteria but supportive laboratory features suggestive of incomplete Kawasaki disease
stem: A 3-year-old boy has 6 days of fever to 39.6 degrees C unresponsive to antipyretics. He is irritable, with bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection and a peeling perineal rash, but no adenopathy or lip changes.

data_table.Bloods: CRP 128 mg/L, ESR 82 mm/hr, platelets 512 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 68 U/L
data_table.Other: Sterile pyuria; blood and respiratory virus cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care and observe for further clinical criteria
options.rationale: Waiting for the classical 5 criteria misses the treatment window; supportive laboratory features with 2 criteria and fever above 5 days meet AU incomplete Kawasaki pathway thresholds. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and benzylpenicillin for occult infection
options.rationale: Cultures are negative, viral panel negative and the picture (perineal desquamation, sterile pyuria, hepatitis, hyponatraemia, thrombocytosis) fits incomplete Kawasaki rather than a bacterial focus. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Give intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg alone and reassess on day 8
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin is first line in Kawasaki disease and should not be replaced by pulse steroid alone; steroid is added to high risk patients or given as rescue. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Arrange outpatient rheumatology review in one week before treatment
options.rationale: Delaying decision by a week risks coronary artery aneurysm; the syndrome fits incomplete Kawasaki now and IVIG is time critical within 10 days of fever onset. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin and echocardiography
options.rationale: Fever 5 or more days with 2 clinical criteria plus supportive labs (CRP above 30, ESR above 40, plus 3 or more of albumin low, anaemia, ALT elevated, platelets high, WCC high, sterile pyuria) meets AU incomplete Kawasaki criteria for IVIG and low dose aspirin with baseline echocardiography. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child with 5 or more days of fever and 2 or 3 principal clinical criteria plus supporting laboratory features because 15 to 20 percent of cases present incompletely. Supporting labs include C reactive protein above 30 mg/L or erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/hr, and 3 or more of hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase, thrombocytosis after day 7, leucocytosis and sterile pyuria. Baseline echocardiography looks for coronary artery abnormalities, but treatment should not wait for it if the diagnosis is otherwise clear. Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin (3 to 5 mg per kg daily until markers normalise and echocardiography is clear at 6 to 8 weeks) is first line. High risk patients may receive adjunctive corticosteroid.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: 5 or more days of fever, 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory features.
Supportive labs: CRP above 30, ESR above 40, plus 3 or more of low albumin, anaemia, ALT high, platelets high, WCC high, sterile pyuria.
First line: intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg plus low dose aspirin with baseline echocardiography.
explanation.pearls: Perineal desquamation and sterile pyuria are two supportive features that often clinch an incomplete Kawasaki diagnosis when the mucocutaneous criteria are incomplete; treat within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk.

subtopic_detail: Nephrology referral criteria in a child with new IgA vasculitis and unexpected proteinuria on urinalysis
stem: A 6-year-old boy has a palpable purpuric rash over his buttocks and lower legs for 5 days with migratory ankle pain, 10 days after an upper respiratory illness.

data_table.Urine: 3+ protein, 2+ blood, red cell casts; protein:creatinine 320 mg/mmol (normal below 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric nephrologist today for biopsy consideration
options.rationale: Protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol (nephrotic range) or persistent above 100 for 4 or more weeks in IgA vasculitis is an AU trigger for urgent nephrology referral and biopsy consideration. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks and review
options.rationale: Corticosteroids reduce arthralgia and abdominal pain but do not prevent renal disease; commencing empirically without nephrology input in nephrotic range proteinuria is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

options.text: Reassure and repeat urinalysis at general practice in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Nephrotic range proteinuria with red cell casts is not benign and needs urgent specialist review; the standard weekly then monthly surveillance schedule assumes normal or trace urine findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

options.text: Start oral ramipril 2.5 mg daily and defer specialist input
options.rationale: Angiotensin blockade is not first line in acute paediatric nephrotic range proteinuria without a diagnosis; nephrology guides use and biopsy comes first. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

options.text: Give intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg and discharge home
options.rationale: Pulse steroid is a nephrology decision after biopsy in crescentic disease; discharge without nephrology input for nephrotic range proteinuria is unsafe. (Source: KHA-CARI: Paediatric Nephrotic Range Proteinuria)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schoenlein purpura) is the commonest paediatric small vessel vasculitis and usually self limits. Renal involvement affects around a third of children in the first 6 months and is the main determinant of long term prognosis. All children with IgA vasculitis should have weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, fortnightly for 2 months, then monthly to 6 months. Persistent proteinuria above 100 mg per mmol for 4 or more weeks or any nephrotic range proteinuria (above 250 mg per mmol) triggers urgent nephrology referral and consideration of renal biopsy. Corticosteroids reduce joint and abdominal symptoms but do not prevent nephritis.
key_points: All IgA vasculitis children need urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for at least 6 months.
Protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol or persistent above 100 for 4 weeks triggers urgent nephrology referral.
Corticosteroids do not prevent nephritis; they reduce joint and abdominal symptoms only.
explanation.pearls: Nephrotic range proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol) with red cell casts in new IgA vasculitis is an AU trigger for urgent paediatric nephrology referral, not for empirical prednisolone alone.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic pathway in a stable 22 month old with witnessed aspiration event and normal early chest radiograph
stem: A 22-month-old boy choked on peanuts 4 hours ago. He coughed forcefully, went red in the face, then settled, and has coughed intermittently since.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108 /min, RR 26 /min, SpO2 97% on room air
data_table.Clinical: Alert; mild expiratory wheeze right lower zone, bilateral air entry
data_table.Imaging: Inspiratory chest radiograph normal, no foreign body or hyperinflation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with advice to return if breathing or cough worsens
options.rationale: A witnessed peanut aspiration with a focal wheeze is a strong clinical indication for bronchoscopy regardless of a normal saturation and an initially normal radiograph; early chest films are normal in around 20 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Refer today for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: A history of witnessed choking with any of persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry meets AU indications for rigid bronchoscopy even with a normal radiograph. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Obtain expiratory and lateral decubitus films before considering bronchoscopy
options.rationale: Expiratory or decubitus views can support the diagnosis but a normal series does not exclude foreign body; clinical history plus focal signs still mandates bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol and oral prednisolone for viral wheeze
options.rationale: A witnessed choke and focal wheeze is not viral wheeze; bronchodilators and steroids risk masking the picture and delay definitive bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Request a contrast computed tomography scan of the chest today
options.rationale: Radiation is not first line when the pretest probability is high; bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and does not need to await computed tomography. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

explanation.summary: Paediatric foreign body aspiration classically presents in a toddler with a witnessed choking episode followed by cough, wheeze or stridor. Peanuts, seeds and small toys are the commonest culprits. A normal supine inspiratory chest radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis; 20 percent of early films are normal. Expiratory films or lateral decubitus views may show unilateral air trapping. When history plus any of persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry are present, rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic and should not wait for advanced imaging. Delayed diagnosis risks obstructive pneumonia, atelectasis and bronchiectasis.
key_points: Witnessed choking with persistent cough, focal wheeze or asymmetric air entry mandates rigid bronchoscopy.
A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude foreign body aspiration.
Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic and comes before computed tomography.
explanation.pearls: In a toddler with a witnessed choke and a focal wheeze, rigid bronchoscopy is indicated even with a normal chest radiograph; up to 20 percent of early films are read normal in confirmed foreign body aspiration.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial stabilisation of critical coarctation of the aorta presenting as circulatory collapse in a 3 week old missed at the neonatal check
stem: A 3-week-old term boy has 24 hours of poor feeding, greyness with feeds and mottling. The newborn check was normal. The nearest cardiac centre is 3 hours away by retrieval team.

data_table.Perfusion: Right arm BP 96/58, right leg BP 58/34 mmHg, femoral pulses weak

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus and reassess
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid boluses can precipitate pulmonary oedema in duct dependent systemic circulation; small measured boluses (5 to 10 mL per kg) with reassessment are preferred and prostaglandin is the priority. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Intubate and start adrenaline 0.1 microgram/kg/min
options.rationale: Intubation may drop the arterial CO2 and worsen the left to right shunt and pulmonary steal; ventilation targets must protect ductal flow; inotrope alone without prostaglandin is not first line. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Prostaglandin E1 10 nanogram/kg/min, watching for apnoea
options.rationale: Prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute reopens the arterial duct and restores lower body perfusion in duct dependent systemic circulation; apnoea and hypotension are the two main early adverse effects. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Oral propranolol 0.5 mg/kg for outflow obstruction
options.rationale: The picture is upper to lower limb pressure gradient with weak femorals and post ductal desaturation, not hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; beta blockade will worsen shock. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

options.text: Face mask oxygen 10 L/min to a pre-ductal saturation of 100%
options.rationale: High inspired oxygen closes the arterial duct and worsens duct dependent systemic perfusion; target saturations are 75 to 85 percent in single ventricle physiology and around 85 to 92 percent in coarctation while duct is preserved. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease

explanation.summary: Critical coarctation of the aorta presents in the first weeks of life with shock as the arterial duct closes and lower body perfusion collapses. An upper to lower limb blood pressure gradient of 20 mmHg or greater, weak or absent femoral pulses and a pre to post ductal saturation gradient (arm minus foot) of 3 percent or more are the pathognomonic triad. Initial management is intravenous prostaglandin E1 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute to reopen the duct, cautious fluid resuscitation (5 to 10 mL per kg boluses reassessed), preservation of spontaneous ventilation and avoidance of high inspired oxygen which closes the duct and worsens the left to right pulmonary steal. Complications of prostaglandin include apnoea, fever, flushing and hypotension; be ready to intubate. Definitive treatment is surgical or catheter based repair after transfer to a paediatric cardiac centre.
key_points: Pre to post ductal saturation gradient of 3% or more (upper minus lower) is pathognomonic for duct dependent systemic obstruction.
