Prostaglandin E1 5 to 20 nanograms per kg per minute reopens the arterial duct and restores lower body perfusion.
Avoid high FiO2 (closes duct) and large fluid boluses (worsens pulmonary oedema in duct dependent systemic circulation).
explanation.pearls: In a shocked neonate with a pre to post ductal saturation gap and weak femorals, start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms per kg per minute before any large fluid bolus or high FiO2 and prepare for apnoea within 60 minutes of commencement.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Critical Congenital Heart Disease
RCH CPG: Duct Dependent Congenital Heart Disease

subtopic_detail: Assessment and initial management of a paediatric iron overdose from prenatal multivitamins
stem: A 22-month-old boy weighing 12 kg presents 90 minutes after being found with his mother's ferrous sulfate tablets, 65 mg elemental iron each; about 20 are missing. He has vomited twice with dark material in the emesis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, BP 92/54 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert but pale, mild epigastric tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Abdominal radiograph and serum iron 4 to 6 hours after ingestion
options.rationale: Ingested elemental iron above 60 mg/kg is potentially toxic; abdominal radiograph may show radiopaque tablets and a 4 to 6 hour post ingestion serum iron guides chelation. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Gastric lavage now with activated charcoal 1 g/kg by orogastric tube
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron and gastric lavage is not routinely recommended; whole bowel irrigation is considered if radiopaque tablets are visible. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Empirical intravenous deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour before any iron level
options.rationale: Empirical deferoxamine is reserved for severe symptoms or shock; peak level at 4 to 6 hours guides use rather than routine empirical therapy. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Discharge after an hour of observation with review tomorrow
options.rationale: Symptomatic ingestion with tachycardia, pallor and vomiting requires observation and iron level; discharge at 1 hour misses the delayed toxic phase. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Oral acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg over an hour, repeated 4-hourly twice
options.rationale: N acetylcysteine is used for paracetamol not iron toxicity; there is no role in acute iron overdose beyond compassionate use. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Paediatric iron overdose progresses in five phases starting with gastrointestinal irritation within 6 hours, then a latent phase, followed by shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity and finally gastric outlet obstruction. Ingested elemental iron above 20 mg/kg produces symptoms, above 60 mg/kg is potentially toxic, and above 150 mg/kg is potentially lethal. Assessment includes abdominal radiograph looking for radiopaque tablets and a serum iron level at 4 to 6 hours post ingestion. Deferoxamine 15 mg per kg per hour is indicated for serum iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, acidosis or altered conscious state. Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol is considered if the radiograph shows visible tablets.
key_points: Assessment: abdominal radiograph and serum iron level 4 to 6 hours after ingestion.
Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/h for shock, coma, acidosis or iron level above 90 micromol/L.
Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron; consider whole bowel irrigation if tablets are visible on abdominal radiograph.
explanation.pearls: Paediatric iron ingestion above 60 mg/kg elemental requires abdominal radiograph and serum iron at 4 to 6 hours; deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour intravenous if level above 90 micromol/L or shock.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and first line management of paediatric anaphylaxis to peanut in a school aged child
stem: A 7-year-old girl weighing 24 kg arrives 20 minutes after one bite of a peanut butter sandwich. Within 5 minutes she developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling and cough.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 34 /min, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Examination: Short phrases, periorbital angioedema, bilateral wheeze, no stridor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and nebulised salbutamol, deferring adrenaline
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and bronchodilators do not treat anaphylaxis; delaying intramuscular adrenaline increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram into the mid anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: Adrenaline intramuscular by ASCIA banded weight table is first line; 20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (EpiPen), repeat every 5 min if needed. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 10 microgram/kg as a slow bolus over 5 minutes
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis in a monitored setting; first line is intramuscular for a child not in arrest. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Oral cetirizine 10 mg with intravenous fluid and 4 hours of observation
options.rationale: Oral antihistamine treats urticaria but not airway compromise or hypotension; anaphylaxis mandates intramuscular adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram into the deltoid, repeated at 10 minutes
options.rationale: 150 microgram dose is for 10 to 20 kg; a 24 kg child receives 300 microgram, and thigh (vastus lateralis) is preferred over deltoid. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction defined by acute onset of skin or mucosal involvement plus either respiratory compromise or hypotension. Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the single first line intervention and delaying it increases mortality. The ASCIA banded weight table sets dose by weight class: 7.5 to 10 kg receives 150 microgram, 10 to 20 kg receives 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr), 20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (EpiPen), above 50 kg receives 300 to 500 microgram. Adjuncts include supine positioning, high flow oxygen, intravenous fluid bolus 20 mL/kg for hypotension and nebulised salbutamol for wheeze. Antihistamines and corticosteroids treat associated urticaria but neither prevents nor treats anaphylaxis.
key_points: IM adrenaline anterolateral thigh is first line; ASCIA banded weight table dosing.
20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) IM; repeat every 5 minutes if needed.
Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjuncts and never replace adrenaline in anaphylaxis.
explanation.pearls: For paediatric anaphylaxis 20 to 50 kg give intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation in an 8 month old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on the general ward. An 8 month old girl weighing 9 kg was admitted 6 hours ago with her first episode of wheeze after 3 days of coryza and a barking cough that has now settled. She is exclusively formula fed and had a term birth.

On assessment she has a wet cough, moderate subcostal recession, and widespread fine crackles with expiratory wheeze. Her vital signs are pulse 168, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 88 percent on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius. She has taken 30 mL of her normal 180 mL feed in the last 4 hours but her nappies remain wet. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for RSV; a chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with no focal consolidation.

Her capillary refill is 2 seconds and her mucous membranes are moist. She has had no apnoeas witnessed on continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 62, SpO2 88% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: NPA positive for RSV; CXR shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation
data_table.Feeding: 30 mL of 180 mL feed in last 4 hours; nappies remain wet

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her respiratory support?

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to SpO2 at least 90 percent
options.rationale: First-line respiratory support in RCH bronchiolitis pathways is low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min titrated to SpO2 at least 90 percent; HFNC is only escalated to if low-flow fails after 2 hours (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with a target SpO2 above 94 percent
options.rationale: HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after a trial of 1 to 2 hours in RCH bronchiolitis pathways; jumping to HFNC first is not the initial step and an SpO2 above 94 percent is above the RCH target of at least 90 percent (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with oxygen and reassess in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months; wheeze is due to airway plugging rather than smooth muscle constriction and trials show no benefit (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg with humidified room air by facemask
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids have no role in acute bronchiolitis outside of trial settings; a barking cough that settled does not indicate active croup requiring steroid (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Intubate for mechanical ventilation and transfer to the paediatric intensive care unit
options.rationale: There is respiratory distress but no impending apnoea, no exhaustion and no failure of first-line oxygen; intubation is disproportionate before a trial of graded non-invasive support (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest lower respiratory infection in infants under 12 months and RSV accounts for the majority of admissions in Australia. RCH pathways sit oxygen at the centre of supportive care and place low-flow nasal prong oxygen (1 to 2 L/min) as the first-line escalation once SpO2 falls below 90 percent on room air. HFNC is a second-line step reserved for infants failing low-flow after around 2 hours or with worsening work of breathing; jumping straight to HFNC is a common protocol drift. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely useful and salbutamol may transiently drop SpO2.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is at least 90 percent, not 92 to 94 percent
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min is the first oxygen step
HFNC (2 L/kg/min) is escalation for low-flow failure at around 2 hours
Salbutamol, steroids and antibiotics are not routine
Assess feeding and hydration alongside work of breathing
explanation.pearls: The RCH bronchiolitis SpO2 target of 90 percent reflects PARIS trial data showing similar outcomes with permissive hypoxaemia; higher targets drive avoidable HFNC escalation.

subtopic_detail: Peanut anaphylaxis banded IM adrenaline in a 4 year old
stem:
You are the emergency department paediatric registrar. A 4 year old boy weighing 17 kg is brought in by ambulance 25 minutes after biting a chocolate bar containing peanut. He has known egg allergy but no prior peanut exposure.

His parents describe rapid onset facial swelling, a widespread bumpy red rash, and a barking noise on breathing in with progressive difficulty getting his words out. On arrival he is sitting upright, drooling, and pale. Vital signs are pulse 172, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 90 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. His parents report he uses a preventer inhaler daily for asthma but is well between attacks.

He has audible inspiratory stridor and marked intercostal recession; auscultation reveals bilateral expiratory wheeze. He has never had an EpiPen prescribed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 44, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Facial angioedema, widespread urticaria, inspiratory stridor with drooling, bilateral expiratory wheeze

lead_in: What is the single best initial dose and route of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 micrograms IV bolus over 1 minute through peripheral access
options.rationale: IV bolus adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis and arrest under critical care supervision; first-line remains IM into the thigh and IV bolus risks fatal arrhythmia (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 300 micrograms IM into the mid outer thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: The 300 mcg EpiPen band starts at 20 kg; his weight of 17 kg puts him in the 150 mcg band and 300 mcg risks tachyarrhythmia (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 170 micrograms IM calculated as 10 micrograms per kilogram of body weight
options.rationale: The ASCIA AU standard for prescribing anaphylaxis adrenaline uses a banded weight table rather than 10 mcg/kg arithmetic; per-kg dosing is not the AU field practice (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 150 micrograms IM into the mid outer thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: ASCIA bands EpiPen Jr 150 mcg IM for a child 10 to 20 kg; his 17 kg falls in this band and the correct route is IM into the anterolateral thigh with repeat at 5 minutes (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with high-flow oxygen at 6 L/min
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically but is not systemic anaphylaxis therapy; IM adrenaline is the first-line for anaphylaxis with hypotension (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis).

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is defined by acute onset with skin or mucosal involvement plus airway compromise or hypotension. ASCIA is the Australian authority for acute management and specifies IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh using a banded weight table rather than mg/kg arithmetic. Second-line therapies include IV fluids for hypotension, nebulised adrenaline for stridor, and salbutamol for bronchospasm; steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only and never delay adrenaline. Observation for 4 hours after resolution is required because of biphasic reactions.
key_points: Adrenaline 150 mcg IM (EpiPen Jr band) for 10 to 20 kg
Adrenaline 300 mcg IM (EpiPen band) for 20 kg or more
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if no response
IV bolus adrenaline is a critical care rescue only
Observe 4 hours after resolution for biphasic reaction
explanation.pearls: For a child under 10 kg the ASCIA table gives adrenaline 0.1 mg (100 mcg) IM; below infants there is no branded autoinjector and 0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000 drawn from an ampoule is used.

subtopic_detail: Moderate croup steroid dose selection in a 2 year old
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 2 year old boy weighing 13 kg is brought in at 2 am with a barking cough and a hoarse voice. He was well the day before with only coryza; his mother says the noisy breathing woke him. He is fully immunised and has no other medical history.

On assessment he has a barking cough on triage, and stridor is audible only when he becomes upset. His chest wall shows mild suprasternal indrawing at rest with no substernal recession. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. He is alert, playing intermittently with a toy, and drinks small sips of water on request.

His parents report no drooling, no cyanosis and no previous croup admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Barking cough; stridor when agitated only; mild suprasternal indrawing at rest; alert and interacting

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days with no scheduled observation
options.rationale: Prednisolone is inferior to single-dose dexamethasone in croup because its shorter half-life increases relapse; a 3 day course is not standard (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose with observation for 4 hours
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup at RCH; using it here overtreats a moderate presentation and observation after single-dose steroid without adrenaline is 3 hours (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with 3 hour observation after last neb
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession; using it here is escalation beyond the presentation and does not replace steroid (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg with 3 hour observation and discharge if stable
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is an alternative only when the child cannot tolerate oral steroid; oral dexamethasone is preferred in AU because of ease, better absorption and lower cost (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose with observation for 3 hours
options.rationale: RCH gives dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild to moderate croup as a single dose; the higher 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis, usually parainfluenza, that peaks between 6 months and 3 years. RCH grades it as mild (stridor with agitation only), moderate (stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession), or severe (stridor at rest with marked recession, agitation or lethargy). Steroids reduce need for adrenaline and admission; oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is standard for mild to moderate, with 0.6 mg/kg reserved for severe. Nebulised adrenaline (a flat 5 mL of 1:1000) buys hours in severe cases and mandates a 3 hour observation after the last dose because of rebound.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is standard for mild or moderate croup
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally is reserved for severe croup
Nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1:1000) is severe-only
Observation for 3 hours after last adrenaline is required
Do not perform pharyngeal examination in suspected epiglottitis
explanation.pearls: In AU practice single-dose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg PO reaches peak effect at 2 to 4 hours with duration up to 72 hours, covering the typical resolution window.

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months without a source in a 5 week old
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 5 week old boy weighing 4.2 kg is brought in by his parents because he has felt hot and has been feeding poorly for 6 hours. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth. His mother had a group B streptococcus swab that was not returned before delivery and she received no intrapartum antibiotics.

On examination he is drowsy but rouseable. His fontanelle is flat and there is no rash. Vital signs are pulse 178, blood pressure 68/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius rectally. His capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and his peripheries feel cool. A rapid capillary blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0). His father, a paediatric intensive care nurse, asks whether the workup can be limited to blood and urine given his uncomplicated antenatal history.

A bedside ultrasound of the bladder shows adequate volume for catheter sampling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 68/44 mmHg, RR 62, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rouseable, flat fontanelle, CRT 3 seconds centrally, cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 3.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his investigation and management?

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin with next day paediatric outpatient review by the GP
options.rationale: Any unwell infant under 3 months with fever requires admission with parenteral empirical antibiotics after septic workup; discharge on oral therapy is unsafe (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood cultures and urine culture only with IV ceftriaxone and a 4 hour observation
options.rationale: Omitting LP under 3 months misses meningitis which cannot be excluded clinically at this age; ceftriaxone is also relatively contraindicated in the neonatal period because of hyperbilirubinaemia risk (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Full septic workup including lumbar puncture with empirical IV cefotaxime and IV benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: In infants under 3 months with fever without source and features of sepsis, RCH mandates a full septic workup including LP plus empirical cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin to cover group B streptococcus and Listeria; his mother had no intrapartum prophylaxis (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Blood cultures alone with IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy and paediatric review
options.rationale: Monotherapy does not cover the gram negative and Listeria spectrum required under 3 months and blood cultures alone miss urinary tract and CNS sources (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: CRP and procalcitonin, defer LP until markers return, then decide on antibiotics
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics for biomarkers in an unwell infant under 3 months breaches the sepsis hour and normal inflammatory markers do not exclude meningitis in the neonate (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: Serious bacterial infection in infants under 3 months cannot be reliably excluded clinically; the risk is highest under 28 days and remains substantial from 4 to 12 weeks. RCH pathways require a full septic workup (blood culture, urine catheter, LP) and empirical parenteral antibiotics whenever the infant is unwell or under 4 weeks. The AU empirical combination is cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover early gram negatives, group B streptococcus and Listeria; ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonate because of biliary sludging and displacement of bilirubin. Blood culture and urine alone miss meningitis which shifts management from days of treatment to weeks.
key_points: Unwell infant under 3 months with fever requires full septic workup
AU empirical antibiotics: cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
Avoid ceftriaxone in the neonate because of bilirubin displacement
LP is not optional even with normal inflammatory markers
Group B streptococcus and Listeria coverage is age-specific
explanation.pearls: Group B streptococcus late-onset disease presents at 7 days to 3 months, most often as meningitis; early-onset disease presents in the first 6 days and is largely septicaemia. Benzylpenicillin covers both windows.

subtopic_detail: New onset paediatric DKA fluid rate in a 9 year old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 9 year old girl weighing 30 kg presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 4 kg weight loss and 8 hours of vomiting. She is drowsy but rouseable. There is no history of diabetes.

On examination her respirations are deep and rapid and her breath smells of nail polish remover. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Her capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and her tongue is dry. Point of care testing shows glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), venous pH 7.10 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-32), ketones 5.6 mmol/L (<0.6). Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (30-70).

A nurse asks whether to start a 20 mL/kg saline bolus given the delayed capillary refill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 108/70 mmHg, RR 34, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), venous pH 7.10 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-32), ketones 5.6 mmol/L (<0.6), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (30-70)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial fluid management?

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 20 minutes then reassess before further fluid
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is standard paediatric shock volume but in DKA it is now avoided as first-line because of higher cerebral oedema risk shown in observational data (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes then reassess before further fluid
options.rationale: Australasian paediatric DKA protocols use 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 30 minutes for shock or poor perfusion rather than 20 mL/kg to minimise cerebral oedema risk; reassessment before further fluid is required (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline; RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Immediate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h with no crystalloid until glucose is under 15 mmol/L
options.rationale: Fluid should precede insulin by at least an hour to reduce cerebral oedema and rebound hypoglycaemia risk; insulin without fluid is not APEG standard (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV bolus over 30 minutes to reverse the acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA and is associated with worse neurologic outcomes and paradoxical CNS acidosis (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

options.text: Hartmann's solution 20 mL/kg over 20 minutes then insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h
options.rationale: Balanced crystalloid can be used later but the first-line resuscitation in AU paediatric DKA is a 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus and insulin is started at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h after 1 hour of fluid (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline).

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA carries a risk of cerebral oedema that is uncommon in adults and drives most morbidity. APEG and RCH pathways use a smaller resuscitation bolus (10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride) than the general paediatric shock volume, reassess before repeating, and delay insulin for at least 60 minutes after fluid is started. Insulin is 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h and is never bolused. Bicarbonate is not used because it worsens neurologic outcomes. Recognise the high-risk features: age under 5 years, new onset, pH under 7.1, initial urea rise, and rapid osmolar shifts.
key_points: AU paediatric DKA bolus is 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride, not 20
Delay insulin for at least 60 minutes after fluid is started
Insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, never bolus
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA
Watch for cerebral oedema in the first 12 to 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Suspect cerebral oedema at any deterioration in Glasgow Coma Scale, bradycardia with hypertension (Cushing's response), or new headache; give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3 percent 5 mL/kg while imaging.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease diagnosis and IVIG timing in a 2 year old
stem: A 2-year-old girl has had 6 days of fever to 40 degrees C despite two courses of amoxicillin, with 3 days of rash, cracked bleeding lips and a strawberry tongue. No conjunctivitis or lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Examination: Irritable, oedematous dorsum of both hands and feet
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L, platelets 620 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, albumin 24 g/L, sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Lumbar puncture with intravenous vancomycin and cefotaxime
options.rationale: No meningitic signs are present and CSF cell counts are not part of Kawasaki work-up; broad-spectrum antibiotics do not treat the underlying vasculitis (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease).

options.text: Continue amoxicillin and add roxithromycin for atypical cover
options.rationale: Prolonged fever unresponsive to antibiotics with mucocutaneous features and inflammatory markers is not treated by broader antibiotics; missing Kawasaki risks coronary aneurysm (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease).

options.text: Paracetamol for symptom control, reassessing after 48 hours
options.rationale: Symptomatic management alone in Kawasaki disease allows the coronary artery aneurysm window to close beyond 10 days when IVIG efficacy falls sharply (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement).

options.text: Echocardiography with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin
options.rationale: She meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria (fever 5 days plus 2 of 5 principal features with supportive labs: CRP high, platelets high, albumin low, ALT high, sterile pyuria and anaemia); IVIG plus aspirin is indicated and echocardiogram baselines coronary artery status (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement; RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease).

options.text: High dose oral prednisolone monotherapy for 14 days
options.rationale: Oral steroids are used as an adjunct in high risk patients such as the Kobayashi score high risk group or IVIG resistant disease; steroid monotherapy is not first-line in AU (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement).

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium vessel vasculitis of childhood whose only preventable morbidity is coronary artery aneurysm; IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent. Complete criteria require fever at least 5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features (conjunctivitis, rash, lips or oral mucosal changes, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete disease is diagnosed with fever plus fewer principal features when supportive laboratory features are present, and treatment is unchanged. High dose aspirin is anti-inflammatory during the acute phase then low-dose aspirin continues for coronary risk.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 to under 5 percent
Incomplete Kawasaki meets criteria with fewer features plus lab support
High dose aspirin for anti-inflammatory effect, then low-dose
Baseline echocardiogram documents coronary status
Efficacy of IVIG falls sharply beyond 10 days of fever
explanation.pearls: The Kobayashi score identifies IVIG-resistant Japanese children; it is not calibrated in Australian populations but a high score triggers steroid coprescription with IVIG in high risk cases.

subtopic_detail: Therapeutic hypothermia eligibility in HIE in a term neonate
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar. A term male neonate is delivered by category 1 caesarean at 39+2 weeks for prolonged fetal bradycardia following a cord prolapse. Time from decision to delivery was 22 minutes. His Apgar scores are 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes and 4 at 10 minutes. He required positive pressure ventilation with intubation at 3 minutes and one dose of adrenaline.

Cord arterial pH is 6.92 with base deficit 17 mmol/L. At 40 minutes of age he is intubated on synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation. He has spontaneous breathing between mechanical breaths, no seizures, but marked hypotonia and absent gag. His pupils are equal and reactive. Blood glucose is 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-6.0). His weight is 3450 grams.

At 55 minutes of age he opens his eyes to painful stimuli only, has no spontaneous movements, and demonstrates absent primitive reflexes. The retrieval team is 90 minutes away. The consultant neonatologist by phone asks you to decide the next intervention.

data_table.Apgar scores: 1 at 1 minute, 3 at 5 minutes, 4 at 10 minutes
data_table.Neurological examination at 55 minutes: Marked hypotonia, absent gag, opens eyes to pain only, no spontaneous movement, absent primitive reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-6.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Warm to 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius with radiant warmer until the retrieval team arrives
options.rationale: Active warming above 37 degrees Celsius in HIE worsens neurologic outcomes; missing the 6 hour cooling window forfeits therapeutic hypothermia neuroprotection (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement).

options.text: Initiate passive cooling to target rectal temperature 33.5 degrees Celsius while awaiting retrieval
options.rationale: He meets AU therapeutic hypothermia criteria (term, cord pH under 7.0 with base deficit at least 12, moderate to severe encephalopathy on modified Sarnat) and the 6 hour therapeutic window requires cooling to begin now with passive cooling during transfer (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement; RCH CPG: Neonatal encephalopathy).

options.text: Give phenobarbital 20 mg/kg intravenous loading dose for seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Prophylactic phenobarbital does not improve outcomes in HIE and is reserved for observed or amplitude-EEG confirmed seizures; the immediate priority is cooling (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement).

options.text: Bolus 10 mL/kg of 10 percent glucose intravenously to correct hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: His glucose is within normal range and glucose bolus in HIE can worsen neurologic outcomes through cerebral hyperperfusion (Source: ANZNN Therapeutic Hypothermia Consensus Statement).

options.text: Give a further dose of intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg to support blood pressure
options.rationale: There is no blood pressure or ongoing arrest indication documented and further adrenaline risks tachyarrhythmia and cerebral hyperperfusion; the therapeutic priority is cooling (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation).

explanation.summary: Therapeutic hypothermia is the only proven neuroprotective intervention for moderate to severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy and must start within 6 hours of birth to be effective. Australian eligibility requires gestational age at least 35 weeks, evidence of intrapartum asphyxia (Apgar under 5 at 10 min, ongoing resuscitation at 10 min, cord pH under 7.0, or base deficit at least 12), and moderate or severe encephalopathy on modified Sarnat. Passive cooling during retrieval is acceptable when servo controlled cooling is not immediately available; target core temperature is 33.5 degrees Celsius for 72 hours followed by slow rewarming. Antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated but continuous amplitude EEG guides treatment.
key_points: Therapeutic hypothermia window closes at 6 hours from birth
Target core temperature 33.5 degrees Celsius for 72 hours
Eligibility needs asphyxia evidence plus moderate to severe encephalopathy
Passive cooling acceptable during retrieval
Never actively warm above 37 degrees Celsius in HIE
explanation.pearls: Modified Sarnat encephalopathy grading combines level of consciousness, spontaneous activity, posture, tone, primitive reflexes, and autonomic system; two features in moderate or severe columns qualify for cooling.

subtopic_detail: Suspected urea cycle disorder in a 4 day old neonate
stem: A 4-day-old boy weighing 3.6 kg is transferred with 12 hours of vomiting after feeding well from birth. He is deeply drowsy, hypotonic and hypothermic, with deep sighing respirations.

data_table.Investigations: Glucose 4.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.48, pCO2 24 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L, ammonia 480 micromol/L (under 100), urine ketones negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Start high protein nasogastric feeds to prevent catabolism
options.rationale: Protein must be withheld until the diagnosis is confirmed and ammonia is controlled; further nitrogen load worsens hyperammonaemia in a urea cycle defect (Source: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin for sepsis
options.rationale: Cultures are pending but the absent acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, normal CRP and profound hyperammonaemia point to metabolic disease; sepsis rarely produces ammonia over 400 (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus).

options.text: Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg intravenously as a loading dose
options.rationale: Phenobarbital treats seizures but does not lower ammonia; hyperammonaemia over 200 micromol/L directly injures the brain and requires urgent ammonia removal (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus).

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg intravenously over 30 minutes
options.rationale: The blood gas shows alkalosis rather than acidosis; bicarbonate worsens the alkalaemia and does nothing for the hyperammonaemia (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus).

options.text: Stop protein, give 10 per cent dextrose at 8 mg/kg/min, dialyse
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis with absent acidosis, absent ketones and ammonia over 400 micromol/L in a term neonate suggests a urea cycle disorder; RACP metabolic guidance advises stopping protein, giving anabolic glucose and starting haemodialysis for ammonia over 400 (Source: RACP Metabolic Consensus; Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

explanation.summary: Neonatal urea cycle disorders classically present after an initial well period as feeding declines, with vomiting, hypothermia, tachypnoea and encephalopathy; the tachypnoea produces a distinctive respiratory alkalosis. Ammonia over 200 micromol/L is neurotoxic and over 400 mandates extracorporeal removal (haemodialysis is more efficient than exchange transfusion). Protein must be stopped and endogenous catabolism reversed with high-rate glucose (with insulin as needed) to reduce ongoing nitrogen liberation. Definitive diagnosis needs plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid and organic acids; ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate) are added under metabolic team guidance.
key_points: Well after birth then decompensates with vomiting suggests IEM
Respiratory alkalosis with high ammonia is the urea cycle pattern
Ammonia over 400 micromol/L needs haemodialysis
Stop protein and give anabolic glucose immediately
Send plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid and organic acids
explanation.pearls: Organic acidaemias also decompensate in the neonate but produce metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap and positive ketones; the biochemical fingerprint separates them from urea cycle disorders.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Inborn Errors of Metabolism

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen therapy escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the ward. A 5 month old previously well infant was admitted 6 hours ago with a 3 day coryzal illness, cough, and increasing work of breathing. He is feeding at half his usual volumes and has had no apnoeas.

On assessment now he is alert and consolable in his father's arms. Chest auscultation reveals widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. He has moderate subcostal recession, tracheal tug, and nasal flaring. He is not grunting.

Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 58, SpO2 88% in room air, temperature 37.8. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. Nasopharyngeal swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 92/58, RR 58, SpO2 88% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and consolable; widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze; moderate subcostal recession, tracheal tug, nasal flaring; no grunting
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg (35-45), HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-32); NPA positive RSV
data_table.Feeding: 50% of usual volumes over past 12 hours; no apnoeas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to keep SpO2 at or above 90%
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance escalates in a stepwise fashion beginning with low flow nasal prong oxygen when SpO2 persistently drops below 90%; titration to a target of 90% avoids the harms of over oxygenation and prolonged admission (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and reassess in 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow oxygen after an adequate trial or for infants with severe work of breathing; PARIS 1 showed no benefit as first line over standard oxygen (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back three times and reassess bronchodilator response
options.rationale: Nebulised bronchodilators are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months because there is no sustained clinical benefit and they can worsen ventilation perfusion mismatch (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Escalate to bilevel non invasive ventilation because SpO2 remains below 90% in room air
options.rationale: Non invasive ventilation is a PICU level intervention considered after low flow and high flow trials fail with rising pCO2 or exhaustion; his gas and mental state do not yet warrant it (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Continue room air observation with hourly work of breathing scoring and no supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: SpO2 persistently at 88% in room air with moderate recession meets the RCH threshold to commence supplemental oxygen; watchful waiting risks prolonged hypoxia (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: Typical RSV bronchiolitis with hypoxia below 90% and moderate work of breathing. Australian practice starts low flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to a 90% target. HFNC and non invasive ventilation are reserved for failure of low flow. Bronchodilators are not routine in this age group.
key_points: RCH threshold to start oxygen is SpO2 persistently below 90%.
Low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min is first line, not HFNC.
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: For under 12 month bronchiolitis at RCH, low flow oxygen to a SpO2 target of 90% precedes any HFNC trial.

subtopic_detail: Croup severity based dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 2 year old is brought in at 2200 by his mother with a barking cough and hoarse voice that woke him. He is normally well and fully immunised.

In the cubicle he is settled on his mother's knee, drinking a small amount of water, with an audible barking cough between sentences. There is mild inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when he is quiet. Chest wall recession is limited to mild suprasternal indrawing. He is alert with normal colour.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.9. His mother declines nasal prong oxygen because it distresses him and reports no drooling or difficulty swallowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 34, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Barking cough with hoarse voice; mild inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when quiet; mild suprasternal indrawing only; alert with normal colour
data_table.Feeding and swallow: Drinking water in cubicle; no drooling; no dysphagia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen?

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally once with disposition review at 30 minutes
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with marked recession, hypoxia, agitation, or exhaustion; using it routinely in mild to moderate croup adds no efficacy and needless steroid exposure (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally once with disposition review at 30 minutes
options.rationale: RCH classifies stridor at rest with only mild recession as mild to moderate croup, for which 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone as a single dose is the recommended regimen (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once with disposition review at 30 minutes
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children who cannot tolerate the oral route; an alert 2 year old drinking water in the cubicle should receive oral dexamethasone (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily for 3 days with review before further doses
options.rationale: RCH and the CDC croup evidence base favour a single dose of dexamethasone over a prednisolone course because relapse rates are higher and duration of steroid exposure is longer (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Withhold corticosteroids and observe for 4 hours before making a treatment decision
options.rationale: Stridor at rest is the threshold to give dexamethasone; delaying treatment prolongs symptoms and extends emergency length of stay (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: Stridor at rest with only mild recession fits the RCH mild to moderate croup band. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is standard; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe cases. Nebulised budesonide is a route substitute, not a preferred first agent. Prednisolone courses are inferior to single dose dexamethasone.
key_points: Dose 0.15 mg/kg for mild to moderate croup at RCH.
Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup (marked recession, hypoxia, agitation).
Oral dexamethasone is preferred over nebulised budesonide when tolerated.
explanation.pearls: The RCH severity to dose rule is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild to moderate croup and 0.6 mg/kg only for severe.

sources.label: Bjornson et al. Cochrane review: Nebulised epinephrine for croup

subtopic_detail: UTI imaging after first typical episode
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 14 month old girl in outpatients 2 weeks after her first admission with pyelonephritis. She was fully immunised, was born at term after uncomplicated antenatal ultrasounds, and has had no prior infections.

During admission urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. She defervesced within 24 hours of intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and completed oral cefalexin at home. Renal function and electrolytes on discharge were within normal limits.

Today she is thriving on the paediatric growth centiles. Her parents ask what imaging she needs. Antenatal renal ultrasounds at 20 and 32 weeks were reported as normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 50th centile
data_table.Illness course: Defervesced within 24 hours of IV antibiotics; oral course completed
data_table.Renal function: Discharge creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What imaging is most appropriate now?

options.text: Arrange a DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to look for renal cortical scarring in this child
options.rationale: DMSA scanning is not part of the RCH cascade for a first typical UTI and adds radiation without changing management for a well thriving child (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange an outpatient renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks to exclude an anatomical abnormality
options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine ultrasound after a first typical UTI in a child older than 6 months with normal antenatal imaging; this is a NICE style pathway not adopted by RCH (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Reassure the family that no routine renal tract imaging is required after this first typical UTI
options.rationale: RCH restricts routine ultrasound to atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without documented normal antenatal scans; a typical single UTI in a well infant older than 6 months does not require imaging (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram to grade reflux before considering long term prophylaxis
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive and is not first line for a single typical UTI in an older infant; RCH reserves it for selected atypical or recurrent cases after ultrasound findings (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Commence long term oral trimethoprim prophylaxis until an outpatient specialist review takes place
options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis after a first typical UTI has minimal benefit in preventing scarring and RCH does not recommend it routinely for a well child (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

explanation.summary: A well thriving 14 month old with a first typical UTI, normal antenatal scans, and prompt defervescence needs no routine imaging under the RCH cascade. Imaging is reserved for atypical or recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not part of the RCH pathway.
key_points: RCH does not recommend routine ultrasound after a single typical UTI over 6 months old.
Atypical features (poor response after 48 hours, non E coli, sepsis, mass, raised creatinine) trigger imaging.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH first UTI cascade.
explanation.pearls: Under RCH, a single typical UTI in a well child over 6 months of age with normal antenatal scans requires no routine imaging.

subtopic_detail: Rehydration route after failed oral rehydration
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. An 18 month old boy has had 2 days of loose watery bowel motions and vomiting. His mother has been offering oral rehydration solution at home but he continues to vomit small amounts within 10 minutes of every offer.

In the department he is alert but tired, with sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and skin turgor is reduced. Peripheries are warm. He weighs 11 kg, previously 12 kg.

Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.6. He has just received a single oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg and again vomited a 30 mL sip of oral rehydration solution 15 minutes later.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 92/54, RR 28, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Weight: 11 kg today; 12 kg at well child check 3 weeks ago (approximately 8% loss)
data_table.Examination: Alert but tired; sunken eyes; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally; reduced skin turgor; warm peripheries
data_table.Interventions so far: Ondansetron 2 mg oral 15 minutes ago; 30 mL oral rehydration solution vomited again

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Admit for observation and offer clear fluids ad libitum without a structured rehydration plan
options.rationale: Ad libitum sipping in a child who repeatedly vomits does not correct the estimated 8% deficit in a defined time and lengthens admission (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Cannulate and give a 20 mL/kg intravenous saline bolus followed by intravenous maintenance fluids
options.rationale: Intravenous rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or failure of nasogastric rehydration; this child is not shocked and has not yet had an NGT trial (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Give a further oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg and continue small volume oral rehydration solution sips
options.rationale: A single ondansetron dose is the RCH recommended maximum; repeat oral dosing has no evidence and delays effective rehydration in a child already failing the oral route (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and rehydrate at 25 mL/kg/hour of oral rehydration solution for 4 hours with electrolyte review
options.rationale: For mild to moderate dehydration where oral rehydration has failed, RCH prefers nasogastric rehydration ahead of intravenous fluids because it corrects deficit safely and avoids cannulation morbidity (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Give an intramuscular metoclopramide 0.15 mg/kg dose to control vomiting before further oral trials
options.rationale: Metoclopramide is not first line for paediatric gastroenteritis vomiting in Australia because of extrapyramidal risk; ondansetron is preferred but NGT is the escalation when it fails (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

explanation.summary: This child has mild to moderate dehydration with failed oral rehydration despite a single dose of ondansetron. RCH prefers nasogastric rehydration next, at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours, before intravenous fluids. IV therapy is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line after failed oral rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration.
Ondansetron dose in this age group is a single dose only.
IV rehydration is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.
explanation.pearls: For mild to moderate paediatric dehydration that fails oral rehydration, the RCH next step is nasogastric rehydration at 25 mL/kg/hour, not intravenous fluids.

subtopic_detail: Fever workup under 3 months
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 5 week old term boy is brought in by his parents for feeding poorly for the past 6 hours and one episode of vomiting.

He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery. His mother was group B streptococcus positive on antenatal screening but received two doses of intrapartum benzylpenicillin. Antenatal serology, including hepatitis and syphilis, was within normal limits.

On examination he is pale, mottled to the knees, and only briefly responsive to handling. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no rash. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally. Peripheries are cool.

Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 68/38, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 38.4. Point of care glucose is 3.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 68/38, RR 62, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled to knees, only briefly responsive; anterior fontanelle soft; no rash; capillary refill 3 seconds; cool peripheries
data_table.Antenatal: Term normal vaginal delivery; mother GBS positive with 2 doses intrapartum benzylpenicillin; hepatitis and syphilis serology within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial workup and empirical antibiotic plan?

options.text: Observation on the paediatric ward for 24 hours without immediate empirical antibiotics or lumbar puncture
options.rationale: An unwell appearing febrile infant under 3 months requires empirical antibiotics within the first hour after cultures; observation alone would delay life saving treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood culture, urine, and oral amoxicillin as an outpatient with 24 hour paediatric review
options.rationale: Outpatient oral antibiotics are inappropriate for a febrile infant under 3 months, and an unwell appearance mandates admission with intravenous therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood culture and urine only, deferring lumbar puncture until CRP and procalcitonin results
options.rationale: Under 3 months, biomarker guided deferral of lumbar puncture is not recommended by RCH; occult meningitis has been missed with a strategy that waits for inflammatory markers (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood culture, urine, chest x ray, and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone with lumbar puncture only if unwell
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonatal period because of ceftriaxone calcium precipitation and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia risks; cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin is preferred (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Full septic workup including blood culture, urine, and lumbar puncture, then intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: For a febrile infant under 3 months, particularly one who is unwell appearing, RCH mandates full septic screening including CSF and empirical intravenous cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: An unwell febrile infant under 3 months needs a full septic workup, including lumbar puncture, and empirical intravenous cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria in the neonatal age band. Ceftriaxone is avoided at this age because of bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation risk. Outpatient oral antibiotics, biomarker guided deferral of the CSF sample, and pure observation all delay definitive treatment in a window where mortality rises hour by hour.
key_points: Under 3 months: full septic screen including CSF for any unwell appearance.
Cover Listeria with benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime under 4 to 6 weeks.
Avoid ceftriaxone in the neonatal period.
explanation.pearls: For an unwell febrile infant under 3 months, RCH gives cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin, not ceftriaxone, alongside a full septic screen including lumbar puncture.

subtopic_detail: Adrenaline dosing in paediatric anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the paediatric consultant on for the emergency department. A 4 year old girl weighing 16 kg develops generalised urticaria, lip swelling, and a hoarse cough 5 minutes after her first taste of a cashew.

She has a personal history of eczema and known egg allergy managed by an accredited paediatric allergist. There is an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan in her school bag. No adrenaline autoinjector has yet been used tonight.

On assessment she is anxious and pale with audible inspiratory stridor and mild subcostal recession. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral wheeze. Peripheries are warm.

Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 84/48, respiratory rate 38, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.8. Intravenous access has not yet been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 84/48, RR 38, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Anxious, pale; audible inspiratory stridor; mild subcostal recession; bilateral wheeze; warm peripheries
data_table.Background: Eczema; known egg allergy; ASCIA action plan in bag; no autoinjector given yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adrenaline dose and route to give immediately?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram from an EpiPen Junior into the mid anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: ASCIA and the RCH anaphylaxis guideline use banded weight based intramuscular dosing; EpiPen Junior 150 microgram is the correct autoinjector for a child in the 10 to 20 kg band (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram from an EpiPen into the mid anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: The 300 microgram EpiPen is reserved for children 20 kg and above; giving it to a 16 kg child overshoots the ASCIA banded dose (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 160 microgram (10 microgram/kg) undiluted through a peripheral cannula
options.rationale: ASCIA reserves intravenous adrenaline infusions for refractory anaphylaxis in a monitored setting and does not use bolus 10 microgram/kg IV as first line; IM is the correct starting route (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow oxygen for the airway compromise
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline may be considered adjunctively for upper airway oedema but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in a child with anaphylaxis (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 160 microgram (10 microgram/kg) into the upper arm
options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline is not recommended in anaphylaxis because peripheral vasoconstriction delays absorption; the intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the standard site (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis).
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: This child meets anaphylaxis criteria with airway involvement, wheeze, and borderline blood pressure. ASCIA uses banded weight based intramuscular adrenaline dosing; 150 microgram is the correct dose for the 10 to 20 kg band. The 300 microgram dose is reserved for 20 kg and above. IV bolus adrenaline is not first line.
key_points: ASCIA bands: EpiPen Junior 150 microgram for 10 to 20 kg; EpiPen 300 microgram for 20 kg and above.
IM anterolateral thigh is the correct route; subcutaneous is inadequate.
IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases in a monitored setting.
explanation.pearls: Weight 16 kg puts a child in the 10 to 20 kg ASCIA band, which is EpiPen Junior 150 microgram IM.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: DKA initial fluid choice
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the resuscitation cubicle. A 9 year old girl weighing 30 kg presents with a 3 week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and 3 kg weight loss, and 24 hours of vomiting.

She is alert but exhausted. She has deep sighing respirations. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Mucous membranes are dry.

Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.4. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.08, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L. Sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine within normal limits. She has an intravenous cannula sited.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 96/58, RR 34, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Alert but exhausted; deep sighing respirations; capillary refill 3 seconds; dry mucous membranes; cool peripheries
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.08, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, urea 8 mmol/L, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid regimen?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 600 mL (20 mL/kg) over 15 minutes as an urgent resuscitation bolus for shock
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is reserved for genuine shock in paediatric DKA and rapid resuscitation increases the risk of cerebral oedema in the alert child (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 300 mL (10 mL/kg) over 30 to 60 minutes then reassess before deficit fluid
options.rationale: Australian ISPAD aligned protocols give a cautious 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes in the alert dehydrated child, then reassess before deficit rehydration to avoid cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline 300 mL over 30 minutes as the initial fluid to prevent hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Dextrose containing fluid is not used in the initial resuscitation bolus; dextrose is added once serum glucose falls to about 14 to 17 mmol/L during ongoing insulin (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann) 300 mL over 30 minutes to correct the metabolic acidosis directly
options.rationale: Hartmann is not a substitute for 0.9% saline in the initial DKA bolus in Australian paediatric practice; the lactate is not the reason to change the first fluid and adds no acidosis correction advantage (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

options.text: Commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour before any fluid is given to shut down ketogenesis
options.rationale: Insulin is deliberately started after the initial fluid, at least 1 hour later in most Australian protocols, because early insulin worsens the fluid shift risk of cerebral oedema (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis).

explanation.summary: This is severe DKA with an intact conscious state and modest hypovolaemia rather than frank shock. Australian ISPAD aligned practice gives a cautious 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, reassesses, then plans deficit fluid over 48 hours. Insulin infusion is delayed by at least an hour and dextrose is added only when serum glucose falls to about 14 to 17 mmol/L to minimise cerebral oedema risk.
key_points: Initial fluid in paediatric DKA is 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 30 to 60 minutes unless shocked.
Insulin is delayed by at least 1 hour to reduce cerebral oedema risk.
Dextrose is added when glucose falls to 14 to 17 mmol/L, not upfront.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA at RCH, the first fluid is 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 30 to 60 minutes; insulin waits at least 1 hour.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and HHS

subtopic_detail: Order of hour one interventions
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 4 year old with a 2 day febrile illness is triaged looking mottled, drowsy, and cool to the elbows. There is a petechial rash over the ankles that does not blanch.

Vital signs on arrival: pulse 172, blood pressure 74/38, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 39.8. Capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally.

You have called for senior support and a resuscitation trolley is at the bedside. Intraosseous access is available if peripheral cannulation fails. Blood culture bottles and intravenous cefotaxime are drawn up and ready. A 20 mL/kg saline bolus is prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172, BP 74/38, RR 40, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 39.8
data_table.Examination: Mottled, drowsy, cool to elbows; non blanching petechial rash over ankles; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Available: IO kit ready, cefotaxime drawn up, 20 mL/kg saline bolus prepared, blood culture bottles at bedside

lead_in: What is the most appropriate order of interventions in the first hour?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus then defer antibiotics until formal blood cultures return in the laboratory in 6 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics must not be delayed for definitive culture results; the first empirical dose is given within the first hour after the culture is drawn (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min immediately, then attempt IV access for antibiotics
options.rationale: Adrenaline follows fluid resuscitation up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in Australian paediatric sepsis pathways; giving it first delays antibiotics and cultures without addressing hypovolaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Obtain IV or IO access, draw blood cultures, give IV cefotaxime within the hour, then a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway prioritises timely access, cultures, and antibiotics inside 60 minutes, with rapid 20 mL/kg boluses; inotropes come after fluids not before (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Arrange urgent CT brain first to exclude raised intracranial pressure before any antibiotic, fluid, or vasoactive drug
options.rationale: CT brain is not required before empirical antibiotics or fluid in a child with clinical sepsis and no focal neurology; imaging must not delay antibiotics (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Give oral paracetamol only and rescreen vital signs at 30 minutes before deciding on further intervention
options.rationale: A child with mottling, drowsiness, tachycardia, hypotension for age, and a non blanching rash needs immediate resuscitation, not antipyresis alone (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

explanation.summary: This is meningococcal type paediatric sepsis with cold shock. The RCH pathway is IV or IO access, blood cultures, antibiotic within the hour, then rapid crystalloid boluses of 20 mL/kg titrated up to 40 to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes come after fluid resuscitation, not before.
key_points: Access, cultures, antibiotic within 60 minutes.
20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes; repeat to 40 to 60 mL/kg.
Inotropes come after fluid not before.
explanation.pearls: At RCH the paediatric sepsis order is access, cultures, antibiotic within the hour, then 20 mL/kg saline boluses; inotropes follow the fluids.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
ANZICS Paediatric Study Group sepsis pathway

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizures with disconfirming metabolic profile
stem: A term girl born 60 hours ago, with normal Apgars and cord pH 7.28, has recurrent 30-second episodes of rhythmic jerking of the right arm and leg. She is alert between events.

data_table.Cranial ultrasound: Left middle cerebral artery territory hyperechoic lesion
data_table.Pending: Septic screen, ammonia and lactate pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start therapeutic whole body cooling to 33.5 degrees C for 72 hours
options.rationale: Therapeutic hypothermia is only supported for moderate to severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy meeting entry criteria within 6 hours; it is not indicated for perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke and this baby is well perfused (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal cooling guideline).

options.text: Load intravenous levetiracetam 40 mg/kg, with fewer adverse effects
options.rationale: The NEOLEV2 trial showed levetiracetam is inferior to phenobarbital at controlling neonatal seizures, and phenobarbital remains the first line antiepileptic in Australian neonatal practice (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

options.text: Give intravenous 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg and calcium gluconate 1 mL/kg
options.rationale: Glucose and ionised calcium are both within the neonatal reference range so metabolic replacement is not the mechanism; the stroke on cranial ultrasound is the discriminator that redirects therapy to antiepileptic loading (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

options.text: Load intravenous phenobarbital 20 mg/kg and transfer for aEEG
options.rationale: In neonatal seizures with corrected metabolic causes, the first line antiepileptic in Australian NICUs is intravenous phenobarbital 20 mg/kg, alongside continuous aEEG monitoring at a tertiary centre to guide further therapy and treat electrographic only seizures (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

options.text: Await the lactate and ammonia before starting any antiepileptic
options.rationale: Delaying antiepileptic loading in ongoing neonatal seizures risks secondary brain injury; treat the seizures now and pursue metabolic screen in parallel (Source: Australasian NETS Neonatal seizures guideline).

explanation.summary: This is a term baby with focal motor seizures, normal glucose and ionised calcium, and a cranial ultrasound consistent with perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke. Metabolic causes are effectively excluded so antiepileptic loading with phenobarbital is next, alongside urgent transfer for aEEG and MRI. Levetiracetam is inferior in the neonatal window and cooling is not indicated outside HIE criteria.
key_points: First line neonatal antiepileptic in Australia is phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV, not levetiracetam.
Normal glucose and ionised calcium exclude common reversible causes.
Cooling is only for HIE meeting entry criteria within 6 hours.
explanation.pearls: In focal neonatal seizures with normal glucose and calcium and stroke on cranial ultrasound, load phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV and transfer for aEEG rather than trialling levetiracetam.

subtopic_detail: Sudden refusal to use an arm after a longitudinal pull in a toddler
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 2 year old girl brought in by her father an hour after he lifted her by one hand to stop her stepping off a kerb. She cried briefly and has not used the arm since.

She is settled on her father's lap with the right arm held loosely at her side, forearm turned inwards. She reaches confidently for a sticker with her left hand and ignores it when you offer it on the right. There is no swelling, no bruising and no deformity, and she does not cry when you palpate the clavicle, humerus, forearm or wrist. She cries only when you attempt to turn the palm upwards. She is fully immunised, has no previous presentations and was born at term.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling or bruising, no bony tenderness along clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna or wrist, distal pulses present, capillary refill under 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a hyperpronation manoeuvre at the elbow and observe for return of arm use
options.rationale: A history of axial traction with the arm held pronated, no bony tenderness and pain only on supination is a bedside diagnosis, and reduction is attempted without imaging. Hyperpronation succeeds more often than supination flexion and is less painful, with arm use typically returning within thirty minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

options.text: Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm before attempting any reduction manoeuvre
options.rationale: Radiographs are reserved for an atypical history, focal bony tenderness, swelling or deformity, or failure of two reduction attempts, none of which are present. Films in this setting are usually normal and delay a manoeuvre that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and arrange fracture clinic review within the following week
options.rationale: Immobilisation treats a fracture, and this presentation has no bony tenderness, swelling or deformity to support one. A week in a sling leaves a readily reducible annular ligament entrapment untreated and prolongs the disuse. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection given the injury mechanism described
options.rationale: The mechanism given accounts fully for the presentation and matches the child's stage of development, so this is not an unexplained injury. Traction on an extended arm is the ordinary cause and a survey exposes the child to radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Give oral ibuprofen and review in four hours to see whether arm use returns spontaneously
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution does occur but is unpredictable and leaves the child in pain and functionally one handed meanwhile. Analgesia is reasonable adjunctive care yet it is not the treatment when a simple manoeuvre resolves the problem in minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Radial head subluxation)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation follows sudden longitudinal traction on a pronated extended arm and results from the annular ligament slipping over the radial head. The child holds the limb pronated and slightly flexed, refuses to use it, and is characteristically comfortable at rest with no swelling, no bruising and no bony tenderness anywhere along the limb. Pain reproduced only on attempted supination is the discriminating finding and separates it from a fracture. Reduction is attempted on clinical grounds alone, with hyperpronation preferred over supination flexion because it succeeds more often and hurts less. Radiographs belong to children with focal tenderness, swelling, deformity, an inconsistent history, or failure of two reduction attempts.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated arm is the mechanism, most often between one and four years
Absence of swelling, bruising and bony tenderness argues strongly against fracture
Hyperpronation has a higher success rate and causes less pain than supination flexion
Arm use usually returns within thirty minutes of successful reduction
Image only for atypical history, focal bony signs, or two failed attempts
explanation.pearls: Distract the child with a sticker or toy held at the midline after the manoeuvre, because spontaneous reach across with the affected hand within thirty minutes is the most reliable confirmation of success, and warn parents that recurrence happens in about a quarter of children before the annular ligament strengthens at around five years.

subtopic_detail: Persistent moist umbilical lesion after cord separation in a well infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 week old boy whose mother reports the belly button has stayed wet since the cord came away at day twelve. She has been dabbing it with cooled boiled water and finds a small yellow stain on his singlet each day.

He is breastfeeding well, has regained above birth weight and is tracking along the 50th centile. At the umbilicus there is a pink moist stalk about 4 mm across sitting within the umbilical ring, with no surrounding redness or induration of the abdominal wall and no discharge that smells of urine or faeces. Pressing gently around the umbilicus does not cause him to cry.

data_table.Examination: Pink moist stalk 4 mm at the umbilicus within the ring, scant serous discharge, no periumbilical erythema, no induration, abdomen soft, no palpable mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise salt application by the parents twice daily and reassess the umbilicus after four weeks
options.rationale: Topical salt has been described and is sometimes used, but it is slower and less reliable than cautery performed in the clinic and depends heavily on parental technique. It is a reasonable fallback where cautery is unavailable rather than the first choice. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Apply silver nitrate to the lesion with protection of the surrounding skin and review in one week
options.rationale: A small pink moist stalk of granulation tissue persisting after cord separation in an otherwise well infant responds to chemical cautery, and one or two applications are usually sufficient. Surrounding skin is protected with a barrier because silver nitrate causes chemical burns to normal epidermis. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Take a swab and start oral flucloxacillin for presumed umbilical infection of the cord stump
options.rationale: Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, induration, tenderness and systemic upset, none of which are present here. Treating a bloodless granulation stalk with antibiotics exposes the infant to adverse effects without addressing the tissue that is weeping. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound scan to define the anatomy before any local treatment is given
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the discharge is urinary or faecal, when the lesion is large or firm and bright red, or when granulation fails to settle after cautery, since those suggest a patent urachus or vitellointestinal remnant. Scanning every moist umbilicus adds cost and delay without altering the usual outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)
