options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for elective excision of the lesion under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgical excision is held back for lesions that persist after adequate chemical cautery or that prove to be an umbilical polyp of intestinal or urothelial mucosa. Committing a well 5 week old to general anaesthesia ahead of a bedside treatment is disproportionate. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

explanation.summary: Granulation tissue at the umbilicus is common after cord separation and presents as a small pink moist stalk that weeps serous fluid onto clothing. The critical distinction is from an umbilical polyp, which is a remnant of the vitellointestinal duct or urachus lined by intestinal or urothelial mucosa, and from a patent urachus or vitelline duct, which discharge urine or faecal material. A polyp is typically firmer, brighter red and does not shrink with cautery, and it needs surgical referral and imaging. Omphalitis is a separate and urgent diagnosis marked by periumbilical erythema, induration and systemic illness in a neonate. Simple granulation tissue is treated with silver nitrate applied to the lesion with the surrounding skin protected, usually with resolution after one or two applications.
key_points: Granulation tissue is soft, pink and shrinks with silver nitrate; a polyp is firm, bright red and does not
Urine or faecal discharge points to a patent urachus or vitellointestinal duct and needs imaging
Periumbilical erythema and induration in a neonate indicates omphalitis and warrants urgent assessment
Protect surrounding skin during cautery because silver nitrate burns normal epidermis
Persistent lesion after adequate cautery earns a surgical opinion
explanation.pearls: Failure of a supposed granuloma to shrink after two silver nitrate applications is the practical trigger to refer, because an umbilical polyp of retained vitellointestinal mucosa will not respond to cautery and may sit above a persistent duct that requires excision.

subtopic_detail: Persistent head turn preference with a neck lump in a young infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8 week old girl referred by her maternal child health nurse because she always turns her head one way. She was born at term by vacuum extraction after a prolonged second stage.

Her mother says she feels a firm oval lump about the size of an olive low in the right side of the neck. The head rests tilted towards the right shoulder with the chin pointing left, and you can passively rotate the chin to the right only about halfway before firm resistance. The right sternocleidomastoid is thickened and firm without warmth or overlying redness. She fixes and follows across the midline with both eyes, and her hips abduct fully and symmetrically with no clunk.

data_table.Examination: Head tilt to the right with chin rotation to the left, firm 2 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid, passive chin rotation to the right restricted to approximately 45 degrees, no lymphadenopathy, red reflex present bilaterally, hips stable with full symmetrical abduction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a magnetic resonance scan of the brain and cervical cord to exclude a posterior fossa lesion
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for torticollis with neurological signs, abnormal tone, vomiting or a tilt appearing after a period of normal head control. This infant has an identifiable muscular cause and a normal neurological examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Reassure the mother that the posture resolves spontaneously and review at the twelve month check
options.rationale: Watchful waiting without stretching risks progressive muscle shortening, secondary skull asymmetry and facial deformity, and children referred late have worse outcomes. Reassurance alone is appropriate only for positional preference without restriction or a mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer for physiotherapy with a home stretching and positioning program and arrange clinical review
options.rationale: Restricted passive rotation with a firm mass within the sternocleidomastoid after an instrumental birth is the typical picture, and early physiotherapy with stretching and positioning resolves the great majority when started in the first months. Earlier referral gives better outcomes, so the program begins now rather than after further investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange urgent ultrasound of the neck mass and cervical spine radiographs before any treatment
options.rationale: Ultrasound is used when the mass has atypical features or the diagnosis is unclear, and radiographs when a bony anomaly of the cervical spine is suspected. A firm mass confined to the sternocleidomastoid with the classic tilt and rotation pattern needs neither before starting stretches. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to ophthalmology for assessment of an ocular cause of the persistent head posture
options.rationale: Ocular torticollis from a superior oblique palsy is a genuine cause of head tilt but produces no neck mass and no restriction of passive rotation. It also tends to appear once fixation matures rather than in the first weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis is the commonest cause of a fixed head tilt in early infancy and is associated with difficult or instrumental delivery and intrauterine crowding. The head tilts towards the affected sternocleidomastoid and the chin rotates away from it, and a firm fusiform mass within the muscle is present in a proportion of infants. Restriction of passive rotation is what separates it from a simple positional preference and from ocular torticollis, in which passive range is full. Management is physiotherapy with a stretching and positioning program, and outcomes are best when this starts within the first few months. Imaging and specialist referral are for atypical features, neurological signs, failure to improve, or a tilt of later onset.
key_points: Head tilts towards the affected muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Restricted passive rotation distinguishes muscular from positional or ocular torticollis
Early physiotherapy resolves the large majority; late referral has poorer outcomes
Examine the hips, since developmental dysplasia coexists in a meaningful minority
Later onset tilt, vomiting or abnormal tone shifts the differential towards neuroimaging
explanation.pearls: Always examine the hips in an infant with congenital muscular torticollis, because developmental dysplasia of the hip coexists in roughly one in five and both conditions share the crowded intrauterine mechanism, so a normal neonatal hip check does not remove the need to reassess.

subtopic_detail: Progressive asymmetry of the infant skull noticed by parents at four months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4 month old boy whose parents are worried that the back of his head looks lopsided. They noticed it at about eight weeks and think it has become more obvious.

He sleeps on his back and spends much of the day in a car capsule that they carry between the house and the car. Viewed from above, the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits forward of the left, and the right side of the forehead is slightly fuller than the left. The sutures feel open with no palpable ridge, and the anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. He smiles socially, follows across the midline and lifts his head well when placed on his tummy. Head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with ipsilateral anterior ear displacement and ipsilateral frontal bossing, sutures palpably open with no ridging, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, full passive neck rotation both directions, head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for consideration of early suture release and cranial vault surgery
options.rationale: Surgery addresses true craniosynostosis, in which the fused suture ridges and the head shape is trapezoid with the ear pulled backwards on the affected side. The pattern here is the opposite and open sutures exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange fitting of a cranial orthotic helmet now to correct the asymmetry before growth slows further
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is considered for moderate to severe deformity that fails to improve with repositioning, usually from around six months. Fitting one before a trial of conservative measures commits the family to cost and daily wear that most infants never need. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Recommend side lying and prone sleep positions overnight to take pressure off the flattened occiput
options.rationale: Non supine sleep raises the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy and is never advised to manage head shape. Pressure relief is achieved during waking hours and by alternating the head position within supine sleep. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Advise repositioning with increased supervised tummy time and arrange review in six to eight weeks
options.rationale: A parallelogram head shape with the ear and forehead displaced forwards on the flattened side, open sutures and normal head growth is positional in origin and responds to repositioning and increased time off the occiput. Review confirms improvement and identifies the minority who need a helmet or further assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction of the sutures
options.rationale: Skull imaging is directed at suspected premature suture fusion, signalled by a palpable ridge, a trapezoid rather than parallelogram shape or abnormal head growth. Scanning a typical positional deformity delivers ionising radiation to an infant brain for no change in management. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Positional plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was adopted and is compounded by prolonged time in capsules and rockers. The characteristic shape is a parallelogram: occipital flattening with the ipsilateral ear displaced forwards and ipsilateral frontal bossing, with open sutures and normal head growth. Lambdoid craniosynostosis, the important mimic, produces a trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced backwards, a palpable ridge over the fused suture and often a compensatory mastoid bulge. Management of the positional form is repositioning, supervised tummy time while awake, and treatment of any coexisting torticollis, with review to confirm improvement. Helmet therapy is reserved for moderate or severe deformity that has not improved with these measures, and safe supine sleep is never traded away for head shape.
key_points: Parallelogram shape with the ear forwards on the flat side indicates a positional cause
Trapezoid shape with the ear backwards and a palpable ridge suggests lambdoid synostosis
Repositioning and supervised tummy time are first line and are effective in most infants
Helmets are for moderate to severe deformity persisting despite repositioning
Supine sleep is maintained regardless of head shape concerns
explanation.pearls: Check passive neck rotation in every infant with occipital flattening, because untreated congenital muscular torticollis keeps the head resting on the same point and repositioning advice will fail until the tight sternocleidomastoid is being stretched by a physiotherapy program.

subtopic_detail: Painless fluctuating scrotal swelling present since birth in an infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 11 month old boy whose parents report that one side of his scrotum has been puffy since he was born. They say it looks bigger in the evening and smaller when he wakes.

He is thriving and has had no vomiting, no irritability and no change in his bowel habit. The right hemiscrotum is enlarged and non tender, the swelling transilluminates, and you can get above it with your fingers so that the cord above is normal. Both testes are palpable within the scrotum and are of equal size. The swelling does not reduce with gentle pressure and there is no palpable thickening at the external ring.

data_table.Examination: Right hemiscrotal swelling that transilluminates, non tender, upper border palpable with normal cord above, both testes descended and equal, no palpable inguinal component, abdomen soft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for surgical repair within the next few weeks given the risk of bowel becoming trapped
options.rationale: Incarceration risk belongs to an inguinal hernia, which presents as a reducible inguinal swelling that does not transilluminate and in which the upper border cannot be defined. Early operation is the rule for hernia and the exception for hydrocele. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Arrange scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to characterise the swelling and assess testicular blood flow
options.rationale: Ultrasound is used when the testis cannot be palpated, when the swelling is solid or does not transilluminate, or when torsion or a tumour is a concern. Here both testes are palpable and normal and the physical signs already define the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.text: Aspirate the fluid in clinic to relieve the swelling and to confirm the nature of the contents
options.rationale: Aspiration of a paediatric hydrocele is not performed because the fluid reaccumulates through the patent processus and the needle risks injuring bowel within a coexisting hernia. Definitive treatment when needed is ligation of the processus vaginalis. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.text: Refer urgently to the emergency department for exploration given the possibility of testicular torsion
options.rationale: Torsion presents with sudden severe pain, a tender high riding testis and an unwell child, and has a course of hours rather than eleven months. A painless swelling of this duration does not fit and urgent exploration is not warranted. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

options.text: Reassure the parents and review at two years of age, referring if the swelling persists then
options.rationale: A transilluminating scrotal swelling with a normal cord above it and no inguinal component is a communicating hydrocele, and the processus vaginalis closes spontaneously in most boys during the first two years. Referral is made if it persists beyond that age, enlarges progressively, or an inguinal component appears. (Source: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

explanation.summary: A hydrocele in an infant reflects fluid tracking down a patent processus vaginalis and characteristically transilluminates, is painless and varies in size across the day. The critical bedside distinction from an inguinal hernia is whether the upper border can be defined with a normal cord above and whether the swelling reduces, since a hernia extends into the inguinal canal, does not transilluminate reliably and can be reduced. Most communicating hydroceles resolve as the processus closes during the first two years, so observation is standard. Surgical referral follows persistence beyond two years, progressive enlargement, or the appearance of an inguinal component. Aspiration has no role in children because fluid simply reaccumulates and bowel may be injured.
key_points: Transillumination and a palpable upper border with normal cord identify a hydrocele
Failure to get above the swelling or a reducible mass indicates an inguinal hernia
Most communicating hydroceles resolve spontaneously by two years of age
Hernia in infancy is repaired promptly because of incarceration risk
Aspiration is not used in children; ligation of the processus is the operation when needed
explanation.pearls: A hydrocele that appears for the first time after infancy, or one that becomes tense and tender in an older boy, should prompt scrotal ultrasound rather than reassurance, since a reactive hydrocele can be the presenting sign of an underlying testicular tumour or of torsion of an appendix testis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Scrotal pain and swelling

subtopic_detail: Red swollen foreskin with dysuria in an uncircumcised boy
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 4 year old uncircumcised boy brought in by his father with a sore penis for two days. He has been crying when he passes urine and holding on, and his father noticed the end of the penis looks red and puffy.

His father has been retracting the foreskin daily at bath time because he read it should be pulled back to keep it clean. On examination the distal foreskin and glans are erythematous and oedematous with a small amount of thick discharge at the preputial opening. The foreskin is not retracted and returns easily to its resting position when you release it. He is passing urine in a normal stream and the abdomen is soft with no loin tenderness. He is afebrile and drinking normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Erythema and oedema of the distal prepuce and glans, thick discharge at the preputial opening, foreskin lies in normal position and is not trapped behind the glans, no cellulitis of the shaft, no inguinal lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise saline bathing with topical treatment and stop the daily forcible retraction of the foreskin
options.rationale: Localised balanoposthitis in an afebrile boy with a normal urinary stream is treated with saline baths and a topical agent, and the forced retraction that caused the microtrauma is stopped. Physiological adhesions separate on their own and forcible retraction is the usual precipitant. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

options.text: Attempt manual reduction of the foreskin now with ice and sustained compression of the glans
options.rationale: Reduction manoeuvres treat paraphimosis, in which a retracted foreskin traps behind the corona and constricts the glans. This foreskin sits in its normal position and returns freely, so there is nothing to reduce. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

options.text: Collect a clean catch urine sample and commence oral trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Urinary infection is suggested by fever, systemic upset, loin tenderness or an abnormal stream, none of which are present, and local inflammation readily explains the pain on voiding. Contamination from the inflamed prepuce also makes a sample unreliable at this moment. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Refer for circumcision to prevent recurrent episodes and to allow easier hygiene in the future
options.rationale: Circumcision is considered for recurrent balanoposthitis or for pathological scarring of the prepuce, not for a first uncomplicated episode. Most boys have no further trouble once retraction stops and the physiological adhesions are left alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin because of the risk of ascending infection of the urinary tract
options.rationale: Parenteral antibiotics are for a child who is febrile or systemically unwell or who has spreading cellulitis of the shaft. An afebrile boy with localised preputial inflammation is managed at home with local measures. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

explanation.summary: Balanoposthitis is inflammation of the glans and prepuce and is common in uncircumcised boys, frequently precipitated by forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin. Presentation is with local redness, swelling, discharge and pain on voiding, and the child is usually afebrile and systemically well. The essential differential is paraphimosis, where a retracted foreskin has become trapped behind the corona and constricts the glans, which is a urological emergency requiring reduction. Treatment of uncomplicated balanoposthitis is saline bathing and a topical agent, together with the crucial advice to stop forcible retraction, since the prepuce separates spontaneously over childhood. Systemic antibiotics and referral are reserved for spreading cellulitis, systemic illness, or recurrent disease with pathological scarring.
key_points: Forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin is the usual precipitant
Paraphimosis is the emergency mimic and is identified by a foreskin trapped behind the corona
Saline bathing plus a topical agent treats most first episodes at home
Fever, systemic upset or spreading cellulitis moves treatment to systemic antibiotics
Circumcision is for recurrent disease or pathological scarring, not a single episode
explanation.pearls: Distinguish physiological non retractility, which is normal in most boys until well into school age, from true pathological phimosis with a pale scarred fibrous ring at the tip, because only the latter is an indication for topical corticosteroid or surgical referral.

subtopic_detail: Crops of umbilicated papules with surrounding dermatitis in a school aged child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6 year old girl whose mother has noticed small bumps spreading across her daughter's trunk and armpit over three months. Two of them have become red and itchy in the past week and the mother is worried the school will exclude her.

There are around twenty firm dome shaped papules 2 to 4 mm across, several with a central dimple, clustered in the right axilla and scattered on the adjacent trunk. Two lesions are surrounded by a patch of dry itchy dermatitis. There is no honey coloured crust, no pustule, no surrounding warmth and no lymphadenopathy. She has mild atopic dermatitis controlled with an emollient and swims twice weekly at the local pool. She is otherwise well and fully immunised.

data_table.Examination: Approximately twenty firm umbilicated papules 2 to 4 mm on right axilla and trunk, two with surrounding eczematous change, no crusting or pustulation, no regional lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange immunological assessment including lymphocyte subsets given the number of lesions present
options.rationale: Immune workup is considered for very extensive or unusually persistent disease, especially with other infections or failure to thrive. Around twenty lesions over three months in a thriving child with mild atopic dermatitis is ordinary. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Explain that the lesions resolve without treatment and treat the surrounding dermatitis topically
options.rationale: Molluscum contagiosum in a well immunocompetent child is self limiting over months to a couple of years, and no exclusion from school or swimming is required. The itchy eczematous halo around individual lesions responds to a topical corticosteroid and emollient, which also reduces scratching and spread. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to treat secondary bacterial infection of the lesions
options.rationale: Bacterial superinfection is suggested by honey coloured crust, pustulation, warmth and tenderness rather than by a dry itchy halo. The inflammation described is eczematous and antibiotics would not address it. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Refer for cryotherapy to all lesions and exclude her from swimming until the skin has cleared
options.rationale: Physical destruction is painful, risks scarring and dyspigmentation, and is generally avoided in young children given spontaneous resolution. Exclusion from school and swimming is not recommended and adds social cost without controlling transmission. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Prescribe topical permethrin to the whole body and treat all household contacts on the same day
options.rationale: Scabies is treated this way and presents with intensely itchy burrows in web spaces, wrists and axillae with affected household members, not with discrete umbilicated papules. The morphology described does not fit a mite infestation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection producing firm dome shaped umbilicated papules, most often in preschool and primary school children and frequently spread by direct contact and shared towels. Lesions are self limiting, usually clearing over six to eighteen months, and treatment is not required in immunocompetent children. Two phenomena worry families unnecessarily: an eczematous halo around lesions, which is an immune response and is treated with a topical corticosteroid, and the so called beginning of the end inflammation, in which lesions become red and angry shortly before resolving. Children are not excluded from school or swimming, though covering lesions and avoiding shared towels is sensible. Destructive treatments are painful and risk scarring and are reserved for selected situations.
key_points: Central umbilication of firm dome shaped papules is the diagnostic morphology
Spontaneous resolution over six to eighteen months is the natural history
An eczematous halo is an immune reaction and is treated with topical corticosteroid
No exclusion from school or swimming; cover lesions and avoid sharing towels
Very extensive or persistent disease prompts consideration of underlying immunodeficiency
explanation.pearls: Warn parents in advance that individual lesions often turn red, swollen and tender in the weeks before they disappear, because this beginning of the end reaction is regularly mistaken for bacterial infection and leads to unnecessary courses of oral antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: Parental concern about inward pointing feet in a walking toddler
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 2 year old boy whose grandmother insists his feet point inwards and that he needs special boots. His parents say he trips a little more than his older sister did but plays happily at the park all afternoon.

He walks with both feet turned inwards to a similar degree and runs without difficulty. With him lying prone and the knees flexed, the foot points inwards relative to the thigh on both sides. Passive hip rotation is symmetrical with internal rotation of about 50 degrees and external rotation of about 45 degrees on each side. The lateral border of each foot is straight and there is no crease at the midfoot. There is no pain, no limp and no asymmetry, and he has met all developmental milestones.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bilateral in-toeing gait, thigh foot angle inwardly directed and equal bilaterally, hip internal rotation 50 degrees and external rotation 45 degrees bilaterally, straight lateral foot borders, no pain or limp, normal neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for serial casting of both feet to correct the inward deviation of the forefoot
options.rationale: Serial casting treats metatarsus adductus, in which the forefoot deviates inwards giving a curved lateral border and a medial midfoot crease, and only when it is rigid. The foot borders are straight here so the deformity is not in the foot. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Arrange physiotherapy for a supervised program of hip external rotation strengthening exercises
options.rationale: Rotational alignment of the tibia is determined by bone shape rather than muscle balance, so strengthening does not change it. Physiotherapy has a role where there is genuine neuromuscular abnormality, which the normal examination excludes. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Reassure the family that the gait corrects with growth and review if pain or asymmetry develops
options.rationale: Symmetrical in-toeing from internal tibial torsion in a painless child with symmetrical hip rotation and straight foot borders is a normal stage of lower limb development that remodels through early childhood. Referral is triggered by pain, asymmetry, limp, regression of gait or an abnormal neurological examination. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Prescribe corrective boots with a torsion bar to be worn overnight until the gait has normalised
options.rationale: Night braces and torsion bars do not alter the natural history and burden the child and family with equipment. They persist in family lore because spontaneous remodelling occurs regardless of what is worn. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Arrange radiographs of both hips and lower limbs to measure the degree of femoral anteversion
options.rationale: Imaging is not used to assess rotational profile in a well child, since the diagnosis is made from the prone rotational examination at the bedside. Excess femoral anteversion also gives internal rotation far exceeding external rotation, which is not the pattern here. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

explanation.summary: In-toeing has three levels of origin and the prone rotational examination localises which one applies. Metatarsus adductus lies in the foot and gives a curved lateral border with a medial midfoot crease, internal tibial torsion lies in the leg and gives an inwardly directed thigh foot angle, and excess femoral anteversion lies in the hip and gives internal rotation greatly exceeding external rotation with a W sitting preference. Internal tibial torsion typically appears when walking begins and remodels through the preschool years, while femoral anteversion peaks around age five and also improves. Reassurance is the treatment, since braces, special footwear and exercises do not change the natural history. Referral is prompted by pain, asymmetry, limp, functional limitation, deterioration or neurological abnormality.
key_points: Prone rotational examination localises in-toeing to foot, tibia or femur
Straight lateral foot border excludes metatarsus adductus as the cause
Symmetrical hip rotation argues against excess femoral anteversion
Internal tibial torsion appears with early walking and remodels spontaneously
Pain, asymmetry, limp or neurological signs are the referral triggers
explanation.pearls: Asymmetrical in-toeing deserves a different level of attention from symmetrical in-toeing, because unilateral rotational change with a subtle limp can be the presenting sign of a spastic hemiplegia or of hip pathology, and both are missed if the finding is filed as normal variation.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear after a low energy twist with normal initial radiographs
stem: A 20-month-old boy has refused to walk since yesterday, after catching his foot and twisting as he came off a slide. He cried briefly, then played on until bath time. He is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Crawls readily, full painless hip, knee and ankle range, pain on gentle torsion of the mid tibia
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L, tibia and fibula radiographs show no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound and joint aspiration
options.rationale: Septic arthritis presents with fever, systemic upset, raised inflammatory markers and pain through passive hip movement, and this child is afebrile with a normal C-reactive protein and painless hip movement. Aspiration is invasive and the clinical picture points to bone rather than joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Acutely limping child)

options.text: Refer to child protection for a skeletal survey
options.rationale: The mechanism was witnessed, is developmentally plausible for a walking toddler and matches the injury pattern, so this is not an unexplained fracture. Concern would rise sharply if the same injury were found in a child not yet walking. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange a same-day technetium bone scan of the leg
options.rationale: Bone scanning is sensitive but delivers a significant radiation dose and is reserved for a limping child in whom the site of pathology genuinely cannot be localised. Here the pain localises to the tibia and empirical immobilisation achieves the same end. (Source: RCH CPG: Acutely limping child)

options.text: Immobilise in an above-knee backslab, review in one week
options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft in a toddler is frequently invisible on initial films and is a clinical diagnosis based on refusal to weight bear with focal pain on tibial torsion after a low energy twist. Immobilisation and review is standard, and repeat films at one to two weeks show periosteal reaction if confirmation is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler fracture)

options.text: Discharge with analgesia since radiographs are normal
options.rationale: Initial radiographs miss a substantial proportion of these fractures because the spiral lucency is undisplaced and may be visible in only one plane. Treating a normal film as an exclusion sends home a child with a genuine fracture and no protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler fracture)

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral or oblique fracture of the tibial shaft in a child roughly between nine months and three years, produced by a low energy twisting force with the foot fixed. The classic trap is that initial radiographs are normal or show only a subtle lucency in one plane, so a negative film does not exclude the injury and the diagnosis rests on the history and on focal pain reproduced by gentle torsion of the tibia. Management is immobilisation with orthopaedic review, and periosteal reaction on films at one to two weeks confirms the diagnosis retrospectively when needed. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis are the important alternatives and are suggested by fever, systemic upset, raised inflammatory markers and pain on passive joint movement. A fracture of this kind in a child who is not yet independently mobile carries an entirely different significance and requires child protection assessment.
key_points: Low energy twist with a fixed foot in a toddler is the classic mechanism
Normal initial radiographs do not exclude the fracture; up to a third are occult
Focal pain on gentle tibial torsion with painless joint movement localises to bone
Immobilise and review; repeat films at one to two weeks show periosteal reaction
The same fracture in a pre-ambulant infant demands child protection assessment
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child has been walking independently before accepting a toddler fracture as innocent, because a spiral tibial fracture in a child who has never cruised or walked has no plausible self generated mechanism and moves the presentation directly into a child protection pathway.

subtopic_detail: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent athlete with night pain and a thigh mass
stem: A 13-year-old basketballer has had anterior right knee pain for ten weeks, worse despite six weeks of rest and now waking him at night. He has lost 3 kg over four months.

data_table.Examination: Firm deep swelling over the distal femur, tibial tuberosity not tender, small knee effusion
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-170), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (100-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Graded quadriceps loading with activity modification
options.rationale: This is the management of traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity, where tenderness sits over the bony prominence below the kneecap and pain settles with relative rest. Tenderness above the kneecap and deterioration despite six weeks off sport contradict that diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee as initial imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is essential for local staging but follows the plain radiograph, which characterises the aggressive periosteal reaction and matrix that establish suspicion. Ordering a scan limited to the knee also risks missing a lesion centred in the femoral metaphysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

options.text: Empirical oral antibiotics for subacute osteomyelitis
options.rationale: Subacute osteomyelitis can mimic bone tumour and cause night pain, but a firm palpable soft tissue mass with weight loss is not explained by it, and treating blind delays a time critical diagnosis. Antibiotics before imaging and tissue diagnosis also confound interpretation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

options.text: Open biopsy of the thigh mass at the local hospital
options.rationale: Biopsy of a suspected primary bone sarcoma is planned and performed by the unit that will carry out the definitive resection, because a poorly placed tract contaminates compartments and can convert a limb sparing operation into an amputation. Speed matters but so does who holds the scalpel. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

options.text: Plain radiographs with prompt paediatric orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Night pain, pain persisting despite rest, weight loss and a firm deep mass over the distal femur are red flags for primary bone malignancy, and plain radiography is the first imaging test and is highly informative in osteosarcoma. Referral runs in parallel because biopsy must be planned by the treating sarcoma unit rather than performed locally. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

explanation.summary: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent athlete is usually benign and most often traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity or patellofemoral pain, both of which improve with relative rest and loading programs. The features that break this pattern are pain that wakes the child at night, pain that worsens despite rest, systemic features such as weight loss, and any palpable deep mass, and osteosarcoma has a peak incidence in the adolescent growth spurt with the distal femur the commonest site. A raised alkaline phosphatase in this setting is supportive but not diagnostic and is not required to act. Plain radiography is the correct first investigation and typically demonstrates an aggressive periosteal reaction and abnormal matrix, after which magnetic resonance imaging stages the lesion locally. The biopsy must be arranged by the sarcoma service, since an inappropriately placed tract can compromise limb salvage.
key_points: Night pain and pain worsening despite rest are the cardinal red flags in adolescent bone pain
Tenderness above rather than at the tibial tuberosity moves the diagnosis away from apophysitis
Distal femur is the commonest osteosarcoma site and the peak is the adolescent growth spurt
Plain radiograph is the first imaging test; magnetic resonance imaging then stages locally
Biopsy is planned and performed by the sarcoma unit, never locally
explanation.pearls: A previous benign label such as growing pain or apophysitis is one of the strongest contributors to delayed sarcoma diagnosis, so treat failure to improve after six weeks of genuine rest as an indication to image rather than as a reason to reinforce the original advice.

subtopic_detail: Abrupt pallor and lethargy after a facial rash illness in a child with a known red cell disorder
stem: A 7-year-old girl with hereditary spherocytosis is pale and lethargic. A week ago she had a red rash on both cheeks and a lacy rash on her arms.

data_table.Examination: Marked pallor, spleen 3 cm below the costal margin, unchanged
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 54 g/L (baseline 108), reticulocytes 6 x10^9/L (baseline 210), bilirubin 14 micromol/L, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the single most important investigation?

options.text: Parvovirus B19 serology with polymerase chain reaction testing
options.rationale: A slapped cheek illness followed by profound anaemia with a suppressed reticulocyte count in a child with chronic haemolysis is transient aplastic crisis, in which parvovirus B19 arrests erythroid precursors for about a week. Serology plus nucleic acid testing confirms it, and testing matters because it identifies the household infection risk to pregnant contacts and to other children with haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Repeat direct antiglobulin testing with a red cell eluate
options.rationale: Autoimmune haemolysis raises the reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates and typically gives a positive antiglobulin test with rising bilirubin. Here the reticulocytes are suppressed, bilirubin is low and the antiglobulin test is already negative. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for infiltration
options.rationale: Marrow infiltration usually depresses more than one lineage and is accompanied by bruising, bone pain, lymphadenopathy or an abnormal white cell picture. A normal white cell and platelet count with an isolated red cell arrest after a viral exanthem does not warrant an invasive marrow test. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound measuring the spleen for sequestration
options.rationale: Splenic sequestration causes a rapidly enlarging spleen with a falling haemoglobin and a high reticulocyte count as the marrow responds. This spleen is unchanged from the clinic record and the reticulocyte count has collapsed. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

options.text: Iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation
options.rationale: Iron deficiency develops over months with microcytosis and does not produce a fall to this level within a week. Chronic haemolysis also tends towards iron loading rather than depletion once transfusions begin. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors and halts red cell production for roughly a week, which is clinically silent in a child with a normal red cell lifespan but catastrophic when the lifespan is already shortened by hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia or sickle cell disease. The signature is severe anaemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, and bilirubin often falls rather than rises because haemolysis is not increased. This inverted pattern is the key discriminator from a haemolytic crisis, splenic sequestration or autoimmune haemolysis, all of which drive reticulocytosis. Treatment is supportive with transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, and marrow recovery follows within one to two weeks. Confirming parvovirus also triggers contact advice, since infection in pregnancy risks fetal hydrops and infection in other children with haemolytic disorders risks the same crisis.
key_points: Anaemia with a suppressed reticulocyte count after a viral exanthem indicates red cell aplasia
Bilirubin falls in aplastic crisis because haemolysis is not increased
Rising reticulocytes point instead to haemolysis, sequestration or bleeding
Management is supportive with transfusion; the marrow recovers in one to two weeks
Confirmation drives contact tracing for pregnant women and other haemolytic patients
explanation.pearls: The child is most infectious in the week before the facial rash appears and is generally no longer infectious once the rash is visible, so exclusion at rash onset achieves little, while a pregnant household contact who was exposed in the preceding week needs parvovirus serology and fetal surveillance arranged.

subtopic_detail: Worsening bow legs in a heavy toddler beyond the age of expected remodelling
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3 year old boy referred because his legs bow outwards. His mother says other people have started commenting and that it looks worse now than when he began walking at eleven months.

He weighs above the 97th centile for age and his height is on the 50th centile. Standing with the medial malleoli together, the gap between the knees measures 7 cm, and the bowing is more pronounced on the left than the right. As he walks you notice the left knee thrusts outwards during stance. He has no bone pain, no fractures and no dental problems, and he drinks around 600 mL of full cream cow milk daily alongside a varied diet with fish and eggs.

data_table.Examination: Intercondylar distance 7 cm with asymmetry left greater than right, lateral thrust of the left knee during stance phase, no wrist or costochondral widening, no frontal bossing, weight above 97th centile, height 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.55 mmol/L (1.10-1.95), alkaline phosphatase 260 U/L (children 100-400), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe night splints for both legs and arrange physiotherapy to correct the walking pattern
options.rationale: Night splinting has no role in either physiological varus or in a progressive physeal deformity, and the abnormal gait is a consequence of the bony alignment rather than a learned pattern. Bracing that is used for infantile tibia vara is a specific daytime knee ankle foot orthosis prescribed after imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Arrange standing long leg alignment radiographs and refer to paediatric orthopaedics for review
options.rationale: Bowing that is asymmetrical, worsening after the age at which physiological varus should be correcting, and accompanied by a lateral thrust in a heavy child points to a growth disturbance of the proximal tibial physis rather than a normal variant. Standing alignment films quantify the deformity and allow the metaphyseal diaphyseal angle to be measured, and orthopaedic input is needed because bracing or osteotomy may be required. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Reassure the family that the alignment corrects spontaneously and arrange review in twelve months
options.rationale: Physiological varus is symmetrical and is correcting by around two years towards neutral and then valgus, so worsening asymmetrical bowing at three years falls outside that pattern. Waiting a further year allows a progressive physeal deformity to become harder to correct. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Commence high dose oral colecalciferol with elemental calcium supplementation and repeat bloods
options.rationale: Nutritional rickets is excluded by a normal corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D level together with the absence of wrist widening or costochondral swelling. Supplementing a replete child treats no deficiency and delays the correct assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Refer for a skeletal survey and genetic assessment to investigate a possible underlying bone dysplasia
options.rationale: A skeletal dysplasia is suggested by short stature with a height well below the expected range for the family and by disproportionate limb segments. This child's height is on the 50th centile, which makes a generalised dysplasia unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Lower limb alignment follows a predictable arc, with physiological varus at the start of walking correcting towards neutral by about two years and passing through a valgus phase before settling near adult alignment by about seven years. Departures from that arc are what matter, and the concerning features are asymmetry, progression rather than improvement, an intercondylar distance beyond about 6 cm, short stature, bone pain and a lateral thrust of the knee during stance. Infantile tibia vara affects the medial proximal tibial physis, is strongly associated with high body mass and early walking, and produces exactly this asymmetrical progressive picture. Nutritional rickets is the main metabolic alternative and is screened for with calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D, which are normal here. Standing long leg radiographs with orthopaedic referral is the correct pathway once the presentation leaves the physiological arc.
key_points: Physiological varus corrects by around two years and is symmetrical and painless
Asymmetry, progression and a lateral knee thrust indicate a physeal growth disturbance
High body mass and early walking are the recognised associations of infantile tibia vara
Normal calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D exclude nutritional rickets
Standing long leg alignment films are the imaging of choice, not knee views alone
explanation.pearls: Measure the intercondylar distance with the medial malleoli touching and record it in the notes at each visit, because a gap that is widening across two visits after the second birthday is a more reliable trigger for radiographs than any single measurement, and the metaphyseal diaphyseal angle can then be calculated from a standing film to separate tibia vara from persistent physiological varus.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

subtopic_detail: Nipple pain and poor weight gain attributed to a restrictive lingual frenulum
stem: A 12-day-old girl feeds every two hours for fifty minutes with audible clicking. Her mother has cracked nipples and shooting pain each feed, unchanged after two days of lactation support.

data_table.Examination: Frenulum inserts near the tongue tip; tongue cannot lift above mid mouth or past the lower gum
data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3420 g, 3140 g day four, 3180 g today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical antifungal for mother and infant for thrush
options.rationale: Candidal nipple pain classically begins after a period of comfortable feeding and is burning pain persisting between feeds, often with a shiny areola. Pain present from the outset with clicking and poor transfer points to a mechanical problem instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Division of the upper lip frenulum with oral motor therapy
options.rationale: Evidence for division of the upper lip frenulum to improve breastfeeding is weak and the practice is not recommended in Australian paediatric guidance. Adding an unproven procedure and a therapy program delays the intervention with the best evidence. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

options.text: Frenotomy with continued lactation support and weight review
options.rationale: Frenotomy is offered when an anatomically restrictive frenulum is coupled with a demonstrated feeding problem that has not responded to skilled lactation support, which is exactly this pair after two days of hands on work. The procedure is quick and low risk in a young infant, and continued lactation support afterwards is what converts the anatomical change into improved transfer. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

options.text: Continue lactation support alone and reassess in two weeks
options.rationale: Skilled support is the correct first step and has already been delivered across two days without change, while the infant remains below birth weight at twelve days. Repeating an intervention that has failed risks established low supply and early weaning. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

options.text: Transfer to expressed milk by bottle to heal the nipples
options.rationale: Full transfer to expressed feeding is a reasonable temporary rescue for severe damage but does not address the restriction and commonly ends direct breastfeeding altogether. It also adds a substantial expressing burden without treating the cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Tongue tie)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia is common and most infants with a visible frenulum feed perfectly well, so the decision to divide rests on function rather than appearance. The threshold combines an anatomically restrictive frenulum, demonstrated by limited tongue elevation and extension with notching of the tip, and a feeding problem such as persistent nipple pain and damage, clicking, prolonged feeds and inadequate weight gain. Crucially, skilled lactation assessment must come first, since positioning and attachment correction resolves the majority of nipple pain without any procedure. Where support has been delivered and the problem persists, frenotomy is a quick low risk office procedure that improves maternal nipple pain most consistently, and lactation follow up afterwards is essential. Division of the upper lip frenulum is not supported and posterior tongue tie remains a contested entity.
key_points: Appearance alone never justifies frenotomy; function plus anatomy does
Skilled lactation support must be delivered and shown to fail first
Restricted elevation and extension with tip notching define an anatomical restriction
Maternal nipple pain is the outcome that improves most consistently after division
Upper lip frenulum division is not recommended for breastfeeding difficulty
explanation.pearls: Weight against birth weight is the objective anchor in these consultations: an infant who has not regained birth weight by day fourteen has a feeding problem requiring action regardless of the frenulum, while a thriving infant with an obvious tongue tie and comfortable feeding needs no procedure at all.

subtopic_detail: Widespread itchy eruption with palmar involvement in an infant under two months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 7 week old boy whose parents report he has been scratching and unsettled for two weeks and that a rash has spread over him. His mother has an intensely itchy rash on her wrists and between her fingers that is worse at night.

He has erythematous papules and pustules on the palms and soles, scattered papules over the trunk, and several nodules in the axillae and groin. There are burrows visible on the instep of the left foot. He has a low grade eczema history but this eruption looks different to his parents and has not responded to emollient and one percent hydrocortisone. He is feeding well and weight is tracking on the 25th centile. There is no fever and no honey coloured crusting.

data_table.Examination: Papules and pustules on palms and soles, burrows on the left instep, nodules in axillae and groin, scattered truncal papules, scalp spared of nodules, no crusting or cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Weight on the 25th centile, no laboratory tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for the infant?

options.text: Topical benzyl benzoate 25 percent applied to the body below the neck on three consecutive nights
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is an alternative scabicide but causes marked stinging and irritant dermatitis and requires dilution in young children, so it is not the preferred first agent in infancy. Restricting application to below the neck also misses the scalp and face, which are involved at this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Escalation to a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily for the whole eruption
options.rationale: Corticosteroid suppresses the itch and the inflammatory response while the mites continue to multiply, producing the modified and often widespread picture sometimes called incognito scabies. It has a place only after scabicidal treatment for the residual post scabetic itch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Oral cefalexin suspension for seven days to treat presumed bacterial infection of the pustular lesions
options.rationale: Pustules in infantile scabies are usually sterile and part of the infestation rather than bacterial superinfection, which would show honey coloured crusting, warmth or cellulitis. Antibiotics are added only when those secondary features are present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Topical permethrin 5 percent applied to the whole body including scalp, with all contacts treated
options.rationale: Palmoplantar pustules, burrows and axillary nodules with an itchy household contact is scabies, and permethrin 5 percent is the preferred agent in Australia and may be used from the neonatal period under medical supervision. Infants differ from adults in that the scalp, face, neck, palms and soles must all be treated, and simultaneous treatment of every household contact prevents immediate reinfestation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Oral ivermectin given as a single weight based dose with a repeat dose after seven days elapse
options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is not used in infants below 15 kg because safety at low body weight has not been established, and it is reserved for crusted scabies, outbreaks and treatment failure. The weight here is far below that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult presentation in both distribution and treatment. Infants characteristically have palmar and plantar involvement with pustules, nodules in the axillae and groin, and involvement of the scalp, face and neck, all sites that are typically spared in adults. Diagnosis is clinical, strongly supported by an intensely itchy household contact with the classic nocturnal itch, and burrows are the pathognomonic lesion. Permethrin 5 percent is the Australian first line agent and can be used in young infants under medical supervision, applied to the entire body surface including the scalp and face in this age group, with all household and close contacts treated on the same day regardless of symptoms. Itch persists for two to four weeks after successful eradication, and this post scabetic itch should be treated symptomatically rather than being read as treatment failure.
key_points: Infantile scabies involves palms, soles, scalp and face, unlike the adult distribution
Permethrin 5 percent is first line and covers the whole body including the scalp in infants
All household and close contacts are treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms
Oral ivermectin is avoided below 15 kg and is reserved for crusted disease or failure
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and is not evidence of treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Reserve a second permethrin application for seven days after the first, since the agent is not fully ovicidal and a repeat treatment kills mites hatching from surviving eggs, while treating persistent itch at three weeks with repeated scabicide instead of an emollient and a short corticosteroid course causes irritant dermatitis that is then mistaken for continuing infestation.

subtopic_detail: Sharply marginated perioral and perineal erosions with diarrhoea in a breastfed preterm infant
stem: A 4-month-old girl born at 30 weeks, exclusively breastfed, has a nappy rash unresponsive to two weeks of topical antifungal. She has had loose stools for a month and has lost the ability to roll.

data_table.Examination: Sharply marginated erosive plaques periorally, perineally, on fingertips and heels; no satellite lesions; sparse lightened hair
data_table.Growth: Weight has fallen from the 25th to the 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 28 g/L (35-50), alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L (100-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to nystatin with hydrocortisone cream
options.rationale: Candidal nappy rash involves the skin folds with satellite pustules and responds to antifungal treatment, neither of which fits a rash that has failed two weeks of therapy and extends to the mouth, fingertips and heels. Adding a corticosteroid treats inflammation without correcting the underlying deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Nappy rash)

options.text: Refer for skin biopsy with immunofluorescence
options.rationale: Immunobullous disease in infancy is rare and presents with tense blisters and erosions in a distribution not confined to periorificial and acral sites, without the systemic triad seen here. Biopsy delays a treatment that would produce a visible response within days. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

options.text: Trial an extensively hydrolysed formula
options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy in an exclusively breastfed infant is managed by maternal dietary exclusion rather than formula, and it does not produce sharply marginated acral erosions or hair depigmentation. The rash distribution is the finding that does not fit an allergic enteropathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.text: Arrange sweat chloride and faecal elastase testing
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis can present with a zinc responsive rash through malabsorption and deserves consideration, but newborn screening covers the great majority of Australian infants and the rash still requires zinc replacement whatever the cause. Testing without treating leaves a rapidly correctable deficiency unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

options.text: Measure serum zinc and start zinc supplementation
options.rationale: An acral and periorificial erosive eruption resistant to antifungals, with diarrhoea, sparse lightening hair, developmental regression and faltering growth, is the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and hair change that defines zinc deficiency, and the low alkaline phosphatase is a supportive clue because that enzyme is zinc dependent. Treatment is started before the level returns because the clinical response within days is itself confirmatory and the deficiency is rapidly reversible. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutritional deficiencies)

explanation.summary: Zinc deficiency in an exclusively breastfed infant arises either from an inherited defect of intestinal zinc absorption or, distinctively, from a maternal defect in the mammary zinc transporter that produces breast milk of abnormally low zinc content in an entirely well mother. Preterm infants are at particular risk because most zinc is accrued in the third trimester and their requirements per kilogram are high. The clinical signature is a sharply marginated erosive eruption in periorificial and acral distribution that fails antifungal and barrier treatment, together with diarrhoea, irritability, developmental regression, faltering growth and sparse depigmenting hair. A low serum alkaline phosphatase is a useful supporting clue because the enzyme requires zinc, and serum zinc should be interpreted alongside albumin since zinc is largely protein bound and hypoalbuminaemia lowers the measured value. Supplementation is started empirically because the dermatological response within days is both therapeutic and diagnostic.
key_points: Periorificial plus acral erosions failing antifungal therapy is the pattern to recognise
Preterm infants have low zinc stores because accrual is a third trimester event
A well mother can produce zinc deficient milk through a mammary transporter defect
Low alkaline phosphatase supports the diagnosis because the enzyme is zinc dependent
Interpret serum zinc alongside albumin and treat empirically rather than waiting
explanation.pearls: Measure zinc in the mother's breast milk rather than her serum when an exclusively breastfed infant responds to supplementation, because a maternal SLC30A2 mammary transporter defect leaves her own serum zinc and her health entirely normal, and identifying it changes counselling for any subsequent infant she breastfeeds.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis versus transient synovitis in the acutely limping preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy in the emergency department. For two days he has refused to put any weight on his right leg, and his mother says he was off his food and hot to touch overnight. He had a runny nose that settled a fortnight ago.

He lies with the right hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and cries with any attempt at internal rotation. There is no rash and no other joint is involved. Ultrasound of the right hip shows a moderate effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.9 C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.9 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 56 mm/h (<15), blood culture collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for hip joint aspiration before antibiotics are started
options.rationale: He meets four of the four predictors used in Australian practice: non-weight bearing, temperature above 38.5 C, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L. Aspiration of the effusion under orthopaedic care secures the microbiological diagnosis, and taking it before antibiotics preserves culture yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any invasive intervention
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging answers a different question: it is used when osteomyelitis is suspected alongside or instead of joint infection, or when the effusion is not accessible. Here ultrasound has already shown drainable fluid and imaging only delays the diagnostic tap. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin now and repeat the inflammatory markers in 24 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration reduce the chance of isolating an organism from joint fluid, which matters because treatment runs for weeks and may need narrowing. Give the first dose immediately after the sample is taken, not before it. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Admit for observation on regular paracetamol and repeat the hip ultrasound tomorrow
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound cannot distinguish infected from reactive fluid, so a repeat scan will not change the decision it is being used to defer. Observation is reasonable only when the predictor count is low and the child is afebrile. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

options.text: Oral ibuprofen with orthopaedic review in 48 hours if he is still not weight bearing
options.rationale: This is the pathway for transient synovitis, which is afebrile with normal or near-normal inflammatory markers. A temperature of 38.9 C with a C-reactive protein of 78 mg/L places him in the high-probability band and a 48 hour delay risks irreversible cartilage damage. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

explanation.summary: A hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation is the position of maximum capsular volume and is the joint's way of minimising pressure from an effusion. The Kocher predictors were derived to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis, and the probability of infection climbs steeply as predictors accumulate rather than at any single cut-off. Ultrasound reliably detects an effusion but cannot characterise it, so the fluid must be sampled. Untreated septic arthritis of the hip destroys articular cartilage within days and can infarct the femoral head, which is why this sits alongside testicular torsion as a same-day surgical problem.
key_points: The four predictors are non-weight bearing, fever above 38.5 C, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L
Ultrasound confirms an effusion but never tells you whether it is infected
Blood cultures and joint fluid go before the first antibiotic dose wherever the delay is minutes rather than hours
Transient synovitis follows a viral illness, the child is afebrile and inflammatory markers are normal or marginal
Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism beyond the neonatal period in Australia
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is the leading cause of septic arthritis between 6 months and 4 years and grows poorly on solid media, so joint fluid should be inoculated directly into a paediatric blood culture bottle at the bedside rather than sent dry.

subtopic_detail: Choosing hip ultrasound or radiograph by age in late-presenting developmental dysplasia
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 6-month-old girl brought in by her father, who has noticed that her nappy is harder to fasten on one side and that one leg looks shorter when she lies on her back. She was born at term in the breech position and her newborn hip examination was recorded as normal.

On examination there is asymmetry of the thigh skin creases and limited abduction of the left hip to 50 degrees. The Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative.

data_table.Examination: Left hip abduction limited to 50 degrees, asymmetric thigh creases, apparent left femoral shortening, Ortolani and Barlow negative, spine and lower limb neurology normal

lead_in: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Static and dynamic ultrasound of both hips performed by a paediatric sonographer
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the correct modality under 4.5 months, when the femoral head is still cartilaginous and acoustically transparent. At 6 months the ossific nucleus casts an acoustic shadow over the medial acetabulum and the study becomes unreliable. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Computed tomography of the pelvis with three-dimensional acetabular reconstruction
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantial gonadal radiation dose to an infant and adds nothing to a plain film at the diagnostic stage. It has a narrow role in complex revision surgical planning. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under general anaesthesia within two weeks
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for assessing reduction after closed or open surgical treatment, not for making the initial diagnosis. It requires sedation or anaesthesia in this age group for no diagnostic gain over a plain film. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis with the hips in the neutral position
options.rationale: Beyond about 4.5 months the femoral head ossifies and the cartilaginous landmarks that ultrasound depends on are obscured, so the plain radiograph becomes the investigation of choice. Acetabular index and the relationship of the ossific nucleus to Perkin's and Hilgenreiner's lines are assessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Repeat clinical hip examination by the child health nurse at the 12-month check
options.rationale: Limited abduction with apparent femoral shortening after 3 months is the presentation of an established dislocation, and Ortolani and Barlow become negative precisely because the hip is no longer reducible. Waiting six months converts a closed reduction into an open one. (Source: RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a spectrum from mild acetabular shallowness to fixed dislocation, and the physical signs change as the child grows. In the newborn the unstable hip can be provoked in and out of the socket, which is what the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres detect; once the hip sits dislocated and the soft tissues contract, those tests fall silent and asymmetric abduction becomes the most sensitive sign. Breech presentation, female sex and a positive family history are the three risk factors that trigger imaging in Australia even when the examination is normal. A normal newborn check never excludes the diagnosis, because dysplasia can develop after birth.
key_points: Ultrasound is the modality under 4.5 months; the plain pelvic radiograph takes over after that
Limited abduction and apparent femoral shortening are the signs of an established dislocation
Negative Ortolani and Barlow in an older infant is reassuring only if abduction is full and symmetric
Breech presentation at or after 36 weeks, female sex and a first-degree family history warrant imaging regardless of examination
Later diagnosis means a higher chance of open reduction, femoral osteotomy and early degenerative disease
explanation.pearls: A Pavlik harness is effective up to about 6 months of age and carries a failure rate above 50% once the hip is dislocated and irreducible, which is why the Australian newborn risk-factor ultrasound is booked at 6 weeks rather than left to the routine checks.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

subtopic_detail: Topical versus oral antibiotic threshold in childhood impetigo
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-year-old girl whose mother reports three crusty yellow patches around her right nostril and upper lip that appeared four days ago and are slowly spreading outwards. Her older brother had something similar last month.

She is systemically well, eating normally and has been at school throughout. Examination shows three discrete lesions, the largest 15 mm across, with honey-coloured crust and no surrounding spreading erythema, warmth or induration. There is no lymphadenopathy and no other body site is affected.

data_table.Examination: Three crusted lesions on the right perinasal skin and upper lip, largest 15 mm, no cellulitic margin, no regional lymphadenopathy, remainder of skin clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Topical fusidic acid twice daily with school exclusion until all crusts have gone
options.rationale: Fusidic acid resistance in Australian Staphylococcus aureus isolates is high enough that it is no longer preferred, and exclusion runs only until 24 hours of treatment with lesions covered, not until healing. Both halves of this option are wrong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical mupirocin 2% applied three times daily for five days after crust removal
options.rationale: Australian guidance reserves oral antibiotics for widespread or multiple-site disease, systemic symptoms or outbreak settings, and treats localised impetigo topically. Soaking and removing crust first is part of the treatment because it lets the ointment reach the colonised skin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole twice daily for a three-day short course
options.rationale: This is the regimen used in remote Australian communities where impetigo is often extensive and where methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common, and it is an oral agent for the same reason that oral cefalexin is wrong here. The near-pair distinction is the burden of disease, not the organism. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

options.text: Oral cefalexin given four times daily for a seven-day course starting today
options.rationale: Oral therapy is indicated when lesions are numerous, spread across multiple body regions, or the child is systemically unwell, none of which applies here. Using it for three localised lesions adds gastrointestinal side effects and selection pressure without improving cure rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical hydrogen peroxide 1% cream applied twice daily until the crusting settles
options.rationale: Antiseptic creams are an option in some overseas guidance for very limited disease but are not the Australian recommendation, and evidence for cure is weaker than for topical antibiotics. They have a role in decolonisation adjuncts rather than as primary treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and less commonly Streptococcus pyogenes, and the two cannot be separated clinically. The management decision is driven almost entirely by extent rather than by organism, because topical therapy cannot reliably cover widespread disease and oral therapy is unnecessary for a few lesions. Crust is a reservoir of organisms and a barrier to topical penetration, so soaking it off with a warm damp cloth before each application materially improves cure. The public health dimension matters in Australian practice because untreated streptococcal skin infection is a driver of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and contributes to the rheumatic heart disease burden in some communities.
key_points: Localised disease is treated topically; oral antibiotics are for multiple sites, extensive lesions or systemic symptoms
Remove crust by soaking before each topical application
Fusidic acid is avoided in Australia because of resistance rates
Children may return to school 24 hours after treatment starts if lesions are covered
Recurrent or extensive impetigo warrants a scabies examination and household screening
explanation.pearls: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows skin infection by 3 to 6 weeks rather than the 1 to 2 weeks that follows pharyngitis, so a child with cola-coloured urine one month after impetigo needs a blood pressure and urinalysis, not a throat swab.

subtopic_detail: Timing of diagnostic audiology after a refer result on newborn hearing screening
stem:
You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 3-week-old boy in the newborn follow-up clinic. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and went home on day two. The state newborn hearing screening program recorded a refer result in the left ear on both the initial automated screen and the repeat screen before discharge, with a pass in the right ear.

He is feeding and growing well, and his mother says he startles to the dog barking. Examination including the external ears and a search for craniofacial or neck anomalies is unremarkable, and there is no family history of childhood deafness.

data_table.Examination: Normal pinnae and patent canals bilaterally, no preauricular pits or tags, no neck sinuses, no dysmorphic features, weight on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat surgery for tympanometry and microsuction of the left ear
options.rationale: Tympanometry is unreliable in the first few months because the infant ear canal is compliant, and there is no otoscopic abnormality to suction. Surgical referral follows the audiological diagnosis rather than preceding it. (Source: RCH CPG: Hearing Loss)

options.text: Reassure the parents and rescreen with automated testing at the 6-week immunisations
options.rationale: Rescreening has already been done and failed, so repeating the same test answers nothing and consumes the diagnostic window. A behavioural startle to a loud noise is a brainstem reflex that is preserved in unilateral and in moderate bilateral loss. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)
