A persistent head tilt in a child is an ominous sign that may reflect a fourth nerve palsy or tonsillar herniation rather than a musculoskeletal problem. Papilloedema is a late sign, so its absence never excludes the diagnosis.
key_points: Morning headache relieved by vomiting, plus any new neurological sign, mandates urgent intracranial imaging
A new persistent head tilt in a child is a posterior fossa red flag, not torticollis
Magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred modality for the posterior fossa; computed tomography is the rapid substitute
Lumbar puncture before imaging in a child with papilloedema risks herniation
Absent papilloedema does not exclude a tumour, since it appears late in the course
explanation.pearls: Migraine essentially never begins with headaches that consistently wake a child before dawn; a fixed early morning pattern over more than 4 weeks should trigger imaging rather than prophylaxis.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Signs and symptoms of brain cancer in children

subtopic_detail: Acting on a migration percentage threshold during cerebral palsy hip surveillance
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community child development clinic. A 6-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System level V, attends for his annual review with his mother.

He is fully dependent for transfers and uses a supportive seating system. He takes baclofen and had botulinum toxin injections to both adductors 18 months ago. His mother reports no change in his comfort, and he shows no distress on handling or during nappy changes.

On examination hip abduction is 30 degrees on the right and 45 degrees on the left, with no fixed flexion contracture. The annual anteroposterior pelvis radiograph performed last week is reported with a migration percentage of 42 per cent on the right and 18 per cent on the left, compared with 26 per cent and 16 per cent a year ago.

data_table.Examination: Hip abduction 30 degrees right and 45 degrees left, no fixed flexion contracture, no pain on handling
data_table.Imaging: Anteroposterior pelvis radiograph migration percentage 42 per cent right and 18 per cent left; previous year 26 per cent right and 16 per cent left
data_table.Medications: Baclofen; botulinum toxin to adductors 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pelvis radiograph in 6 months and continue the current surveillance schedule
options.rationale: Six-monthly radiographs are the surveillance interval for a level V child whose migration percentage sits below 30 per cent; once the threshold is crossed, surveillance is no longer the answer and referral is. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for assessment for hip reconstructive surgery
options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral under the Australian hip surveillance guidelines, and a value of 42 per cent rising 16 points in a year indicates progressive displacement that usually needs bony reconstruction rather than soft tissue measures alone. Absence of pain is expected at this stage and is not a reason to wait, because the aim of surveillance is to intervene before the hip becomes painful and dislocated. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Repeat botulinum toxin injections to both adductors and reassess him in 6 months
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin reduces adductor tone and may improve seating comfort, but it does not reverse established displacement and there is no evidence it prevents progression once the migration percentage exceeds 30 per cent. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Fit a night-time hip abduction brace and reassess him clinically in 6 months
options.rationale: Abduction bracing has not been shown to prevent progressive hip displacement in cerebral palsy and is frequently poorly tolerated; it is a comfort and positioning measure, not a structural one. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Increase the baclofen dose and arrange physiotherapy review of his standing program
options.rationale: Higher baclofen doses reduce tone and may help care and comfort but do not alter the mechanical course of hip displacement, and a level V child has no independent standing program to modify. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

explanation.summary: Hip displacement affects around a third of children with cerebral palsy and the risk rises steeply with Gross Motor Function Classification System level, reaching about 90 per cent at level V. Australian hip surveillance programs were built on this relationship: they set radiograph frequency by motor level and age, and use the migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to Perkin's line, as the trigger for action. Referral is indicated at a migration percentage above 30 per cent or with progression of more than 10 percentage points per year. A dislocated hip in a non-ambulant child causes pain, difficulty with perineal care, seating problems and scoliosis, and salvage surgery at that stage is far less satisfactory than earlier reconstruction. Pain is a late and unreliable marker, which is exactly why radiographic surveillance exists.
key_points: Migration percentage above 30 per cent, or progression over 10 points in a year, triggers orthopaedic referral
Surveillance frequency is set by Gross Motor Function Classification System level; level V children need annual or six-monthly radiographs from 2 years of age
Absence of hip pain does not justify delay, since pain appears once displacement is advanced
Botulinum toxin, baclofen and bracing address tone and comfort but do not prevent progressive displacement
Late salvage surgery for a dislocated hip gives poorer outcomes than timely reconstruction
explanation.pearls: Migration percentage is measured from a standardised anteroposterior pelvis film with the legs in neutral rotation; a rotated film falsely alters the value, so check positioning before acting on a borderline reading around 30 per cent.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

subtopic_detail: Referred knee pain with obligate external rotation in an adolescent
stem: A 13-year-old boy has five weeks of dull left knee ache after sport, with no injury. He has limped for a fortnight. His body mass index is on the 97th centile.

data_table.Examination: Left knee full painless range with no effusion; the left leg rolls into obligate external rotation on hip flexion
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Outpatient magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee
options.rationale: The knee examination is entirely normal, so imaging it will be unrevealing; this is the referred-pain anti-pattern in which the symptomatic joint rather than the affected joint is investigated. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Ultrasound of the left hip looking for an effusion
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the right first test for suspected transient synovitis or septic arthritis in a younger child, but a normal C-reactive protein and afebrile state make infection unlikely and ultrasound cannot show the bony slip. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Physiotherapy for a graded quadriceps loading program
options.rationale: Treating this as a soft tissue overuse problem allows continued weight bearing, and further slip during that period converts a stable presentation into an unstable one with a markedly higher risk of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Blood cultures and urgent hip aspiration under imaging
options.rationale: Aspiration is the investigation for suspected septic arthritis, which a 5-week history, normal temperature, normal white cell count and normal C-reactive protein together make very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Non-weight-bearing, pelvic radiographs, orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with weeks of knee pain and a limp is the classic presentation of a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and radiographs must include a frog-leg lateral because early slips are missed on the anteroposterior view alone. Immediate non-weight-bearing and orthopaedic referral prevent progression to an unstable slip. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis typically presents between 10 and 16 years, is more common in boys and strongly associated with obesity, and around a quarter of cases present with knee or thigh pain alone because of referral through the obturator nerve. Delay is the single biggest determinant of outcome: a stable slip, in which the child can still weight bear, has a low risk of avascular necrosis, whereas an unstable slip carries a risk in the order of 20 to 50 per cent. Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most reliable bedside sign. Around 20 per cent of cases are bilateral at presentation and more become so later, so both hips are imaged and the contralateral hip is monitored. Endocrine screening is considered where the child is younger than 10, underweight or unusually short, since hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and renal osteodystrophy are recognised associations.
key_points: Any adolescent with knee pain and a limp needs the hip examined and imaged
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the key bedside discriminator
Request anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvis views; early slips are invisible on the anteroposterior view alone
Make the child non-weight-bearing immediately, since progression to an unstable slip sharply raises the risk of avascular necrosis
Image both hips, as around 20 per cent are bilateral at presentation
explanation.pearls: On the anteroposterior film, draw Klein's line along the superior femoral neck: in a normal hip it intersects part of the femoral head, and failure to do so indicates a slip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Immediate airway and pouch management in a newborn who cannot pass a nasogastric tube
stem: A term girl born 2 hours ago has needed repeated suctioning for frothy oral secretions and went dusky at her first feed. A size 8 French nasogastric tube meets resistance at 11 cm from the gums. Surgical transfer is 2 hours away.

data_table.Antenatal: 20-week scan: polyhydramnios with a non-visualised stomach bubble
data_table.Examination: Pink in air, no respiratory distress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wide bore replogle tube on continuous low suction, nil by mouth
options.rationale: A double lumen replogle tube on continuous low suction empties the blind upper pouch and is the single measure that prevents ongoing aspiration of pooled saliva during the hours before transfer and surgery. Keeping the baby nil by mouth and nursing head-up completes the holding management. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network clinical practice resources

options.text: Contrast swallow to define the obstruction before transfer
options.rationale: Contrast in a blind upper pouch spills into the airway and causes chemical pneumonitis; a plain chest and abdominal radiograph with a firm tube in situ answers the anatomical question safely. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

options.text: Elective intubation and ventilation for the road transfer
options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation can preferentially inflate the stomach through a distal fistula, causing gastric distension, splinting of the diaphragm and even perforation; intubation is reserved for babies who genuinely need it for respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin for presumed sepsis
options.rationale: The baby is afebrile with normal perfusion and the secretions have a mechanical explanation, so empirical sepsis therapy addresses the wrong problem; antibiotics may be started later if aspiration pneumonitis develops. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal sepsis)

options.text: Slow continuous nasogastric feeds until retrieval arrives
options.rationale: Feeding cannot be delivered through a tube that will not pass, and nursing flat increases the risk of reflux of gastric contents up through a distal fistula into the trachea. Head-up positioning is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

explanation.summary: Oesophageal atresia occurs in about 1 in 3500 births and is frequently signalled antenatally by polyhydramnios with a small or absent stomach bubble, although these findings have low positive predictive value on their own. The postnatal hallmark is excessive frothy oral secretions with choking on the first feed, and the bedside test is the inability to pass a firm tube beyond about 10 cm. Holding management aims entirely at protecting the airway from two sources of soiling: saliva pooling in the blind upper pouch, and gastric acid refluxing up a distal fistula. Associated anomalies occur in around half of cases, so echocardiography, renal ultrasound and careful examination of the anus and limbs are performed before or soon after surgery. Definitive repair is undertaken at a paediatric surgical centre.
key_points: Frothy secretions with choking on the first feed plus a tube that will not pass beyond about 10 cm is the clinical diagnosis
A replogle tube on continuous low suction with head-up nursing and nil by mouth is the holding management
Contrast studies risk aspiration pneumonitis; a plain radiograph with the tube in situ is the safe confirmatory image
Avoid elective positive pressure ventilation where a distal fistula may be present, because of gastric distension
Screen for associated cardiac, renal, vertebral, anorectal and limb anomalies before repair
explanation.pearls: Gas in the stomach and bowel on the plain film means a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula is present, whereas a gasless abdomen indicates pure atresia and predicts a long gap needing delayed repair.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network clinical practice resources

subtopic_detail: First line genetic testing for global developmental delay with a suggestive maternal pedigree
stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred to your developmental paediatrics clinic because he has no single words and does not point to share interest. He flaps both hands when excited and becomes distressed by the hand dryer in public toilets.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a normal newborn bloodspot screen and a normal newborn hearing screen. Formal audiology at age 3 confirmed normal hearing thresholds bilaterally.

His mother mentions that her brother lives in supported accommodation and has never worked because of an intellectual disability that was never explained. Her own mother stopped having periods at 38 and developed a tremor and unsteadiness in her early sixties that has been attributed to ageing.

On examination his head circumference is on the 90th centile, he has a long face with prominent ears, and his joints are hypermobile. He makes poor eye contact throughout the consultation.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 90th centile, long face with prominent ears, generalised joint hypermobility, hand flapping, poor eye contact
data_table.Investigations: Normal newborn bloodspot screen; audiology at age 3 with normal thresholds bilaterally
data_table.Family history: Maternal uncle with unexplained intellectual disability; maternal grandmother with cessation of periods at 38 and a late-onset tremor with unsteadiness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial genetic investigation?

options.text: Standard karyotype with fluorescence in situ hybridisation for common microdeletions
options.rationale: Karyotype resolves only rearrangements larger than about 5 to 10 megabases and has been superseded as a first line test by microarray, which detects far smaller copy number changes across the whole genome. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Methylation studies of chromosome 15 for Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes
options.rationale: Targeted methylation testing is appropriate when the phenotype fits, which would require neonatal hypotonia and hyperphagia, or the ataxic gait with a happy demeanour and severe speech absence of Angelman syndrome; neither matches this boy. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Chromosomal microarray in parallel with FMR1 CGG trinucleotide repeat analysis
options.rationale: Australian practice pairs chromosomal microarray with FMR1 repeat analysis as the first line for unexplained global developmental delay, and the pedigree here of an affected maternal uncle, premature ovarian insufficiency in the grandmother and her late-onset tremor with ataxia is the recognisable X-linked signature of an expanding FMR1 repeat across generations. Microarray is still done in parallel because copy number variants remain the commonest single yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

options.text: MECP2 sequencing and deletion or duplication analysis for a Rett spectrum disorder
options.rationale: Classic Rett syndrome affects girls and features developmental regression with loss of purposeful hand use and acquired microcephaly, none of which fits a boy with a head circumference on the 90th centile. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Whole exome sequencing of the child with both parents sequenced as a trio
options.rationale: Exome sequencing has a real place in Australian practice but sits at the second tier, undertaken through a clinical genetics service after microarray and FMR1 testing are non-diagnostic. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

explanation.summary: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and results from expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Because a maternal premutation expands to a full mutation when transmitted, the family history often shows affected males in the maternal line alongside premutation carriers with their own distinct phenotypes. Two of those carrier phenotypes are diagnostically valuable: fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency in women, and fragile X-associated tremor and ataxia syndrome in older carriers of either sex. The physical features in the child, a long face, prominent ears, macrocephaly and joint hypermobility, are supportive but often subtle before puberty. A diagnosis has direct implications for reproductive counselling across the extended family, which is why cascade testing through a clinical genetics service follows confirmation.
key_points: Chromosomal microarray plus FMR1 repeat analysis is the first line pair for unexplained global developmental delay in Australia
Premature ovarian insufficiency and late-onset tremor with ataxia in the maternal line are premutation carrier signatures
Repeat expansion occurs on maternal transmission, so affected males cluster in the maternal line
Exome sequencing is a second tier test arranged through clinical genetics after first line testing is negative
A confirmed diagnosis triggers cascade testing and reproductive counselling for the wider family
explanation.pearls: FMR1 repeat sizes matter: under 45 is normal, 45 to 54 is intermediate, 55 to 200 is a premutation carrying ovarian insufficiency and tremor-ataxia risk, and over 200 is the full mutation causing fragile X syndrome.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

subtopic_detail: Sequencing imaging before tissue sampling of an abdominal mass in a preschool child
stem: A 3-year-old girl has a smooth firm left upper abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. She is well, with no bruising or weight loss. Her general practitioner has booked computed tomography and core biopsy for next week.

data_table.Investigations: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg (above the 95th centile), haemoglobin 118 g/L, urine dipstick blood one plus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with the planned computed tomography and core biopsy
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a renal tumour spills tumour cells into the retroperitoneum and upstages the disease to stage III under Children's Oncology Group criteria, committing the child to abdominal radiotherapy she might otherwise avoid. The scheduling outside a paediatric oncology centre compounds the error. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.text: Request a bone marrow aspirate and urinary catecholamine measurement
options.rationale: Marrow sampling and catecholamines are the right workup for a neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and is accompanied by bone pain, periorbital bruising or marrow failure; none of those is present and a mass confined to one flank points elsewhere. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.text: Start an antihypertensive and review the abdomen in two weeks
options.rationale: Treating the hypertension in isolation ignores its cause, which in a child with a renal mass is usually renin secretion by the tumour or renal artery compression, and a 2-week delay is unjustifiable for an undiagnosed abdominal mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)

options.text: Urgent abdominal ultrasound with renal vein and caval Doppler
options.rationale: Ultrasound with Doppler is the correct first imaging step because it establishes the renal origin of the mass and, critically, looks for tumour thrombus extending into the renal vein and inferior vena cava, which changes the surgical approach and must be known before any operation. Referral to a paediatric oncology centre follows immediately, and tissue diagnosis is made by the treating surgical team rather than by percutaneous biopsy. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.text: Contrast computed tomography of chest and abdomen as first imaging
options.rationale: Cross-sectional chest and abdominal imaging is needed for staging, but it follows ultrasound rather than replacing it, and it neither answers the venous thrombus question as reliably nor avoids the radiation burden in a preschool child when the first question is simply whether the mass is renal. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

explanation.summary: An abdominal mass in a preschool child is a malignancy until proven otherwise, and the two dominant diagnoses are nephroblastoma and neuroblastoma. Distinguishing them at the bedside rests on whether the mass crosses the midline, whether the child looks systemically well, and whether there are marrow or bone features. Hypertension and haematuria point towards a renal origin. The management pathway diverges sharply from adult oncology practice in one respect: percutaneous biopsy of a suspected nephroblastoma is avoided because tumour spill upstages the disease and adds radiotherapy to the treatment. North American and European protocols differ, with upfront nephrectomy favoured in one and preoperative chemotherapy in the other, and Australian centres follow a defined protocol, which is another reason the child must reach a paediatric oncology centre before anyone takes tissue.
key_points: Ultrasound with Doppler of the renal vein and inferior vena cava is the first imaging study for a suspected renal tumour
Percutaneous biopsy upstages nephroblastoma through tumour spill and should not be arranged outside a paediatric oncology centre
A mass that crosses the midline in an unwell child with bone pain or periorbital bruising suggests neuroblastoma instead
Hypertension with haematuria in a child with a flank mass points to a renal origin
Refer immediately to a paediatric oncology centre, which coordinates staging imaging and definitive tissue diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Tumour thrombus reaches the inferior vena cava in around 4 to 10 per cent of nephroblastomas and occasionally extends to the right atrium; finding it before surgery is what changes the operative plan and the need for cardiac bypass.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

subtopic_detail: Escalating airway management when prone positioning fails in a newborn with a cleft soft palate
stem: A term boy of 36 hours has a cleft of the soft palate and a receding chin. He is nursed prone for noisy breathing when supine. Overnight he had three sleep desaturations to 78% and one during a feed.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO2 96% in air awake and prone, comfortable at rest
data_table.Investigations: Capillary gas pH 7.30, carbon dioxide 58 mmHg, bicarbonate 27 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue prone nursing and review after a further 24 hours
options.rationale: Prone positioning is the correct first measure but it has now been tried and has failed, as shown by repeated sleep desaturations and a rising carbon dioxide while already prone; continuing it accepts ongoing intermittent hypoxaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)

options.text: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and arrange craniofacial review
options.rationale: A nasopharyngeal airway stents the airway past the tongue base and is the standard next step in the Australian escalation ladder when positioning alone fails, and it can be managed in a special care nursery and maintained during transfer. The mildly raised carbon dioxide with a normal bicarbonate indicates obstruction that is real but not yet chronic, which is the window in which a nasopharyngeal airway works well. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)
source_refs: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

options.text: Intubate electively and transfer him ventilated to intensive care
options.rationale: Intubation in this anatomy is technically difficult and commits an otherwise stable baby to sedation, ventilation and its complications, when a less invasive measure has not yet been tried. It becomes the right answer only if a nasopharyngeal airway fails or the baby develops respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)

options.text: Start nasogastric feeds and continue nursing him prone
options.rationale: Nasogastric feeding addresses the feeding-related events and the weight loss, and will very likely be needed, but it leaves the sleep obstruction untreated and is therefore an incomplete answer to a problem that is primarily one of airway patency. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)

options.text: Refer for mandibular distraction osteogenesis as definitive management
options.rationale: Mandibular distraction is a surgical option for babies who fail non-surgical airway measures, so it sits several rungs further up the ladder and is decided by the craniofacial team after a sleep study, not selected at 36 hours of age. (Source: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

explanation.summary: A receding chin with a cleft of the soft palate in a newborn with airway obstruction describes Pierre Robin sequence, in which a small mandible displaces the tongue base backwards and obstructs the pharynx. Management follows a stepwise ladder: prone or side positioning first, then a nasopharyngeal airway, then continuous positive airway pressure or tongue-lip adhesion, then mandibular distraction osteogenesis, with tracheostomy reserved for failure of all of these. Feeding difficulty runs alongside the airway problem because the cleft prevents an effective seal, and specialised soft compressible bottles with assisted delivery, or nasogastric supplementation, are commonly required. Objective assessment with overnight oximetry or polysomnography guides escalation better than daytime observation, since obstruction is worst during sleep. About half of affected babies have an associated syndrome, most often Stickler syndrome, so genetic and ophthalmological review is arranged.
key_points: The escalation ladder runs positioning, then nasopharyngeal airway, then continuous positive airway pressure or tongue-lip adhesion, then mandibular distraction, with tracheostomy last
Failure of positioning is defined by ongoing sleep desaturation or rising carbon dioxide while already prone
Sleep is when obstruction is worst, so overnight oximetry or polysomnography guides escalation, not daytime observation
Feeding support with specialised teats or nasogastric supplementation addresses the separate problem of poor seal across the cleft
Around half have an associated syndrome, most commonly Stickler syndrome, warranting genetics and ophthalmology review
explanation.pearls: Size the nasopharyngeal airway to reach from the nostril to the tragus and pass it about 1 cm beyond the tongue base; too short a tube fails to relieve the obstruction and is a common reason for apparent treatment failure.

sources.label: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

subtopic_detail: Frenotomy decision for ankyloglossia when the feeding problem is positional
stem: A 9-day-old girl's mother has severe nipple pain at every feed; the baby slips off the breast and clicks.

data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3400 g, nadir 3100 g, today 3250 g; six heavy nappies
data_table.Examination: Tongue elevates to mid-mouth and lateralises fully; thin membrane behind the lower gum ridge
data_table.Feeding assessment: Shallow latch, head held away from the breast; pain settles on repositioning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Structured lactation support for attachment and positioning
options.rationale: Tongue elevation to mid-mouth with bilateral lateralisation and a membrane inserting behind the gum ridge is a mild restriction, and the observed pain resolved with repositioning, so the feeding problem is attachment rather than the frenulum. Weight has been regained above the nadir with adequate output, which buys time for hands-on lactation review before any procedure. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

options.text: Frenotomy of the lingual frenulum within a week
options.rationale: Frenotomy is reserved for restriction that demonstrably impairs feeding after skilled lactation assessment, and here the assessment identified a positional cause that responded to repositioning. Frenotomy would be correct if pain and transfer failed to improve with optimised attachment. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

options.text: Formula top-up after each breastfeed, review in a week
options.rationale: Weight is tracking up from the nadir with six heavy nappies daily, so intake is adequate and routine top-ups risk reducing maternal supply. Top-ups would be correct if weight were still falling or below the birth weight by day 14. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding problems)

options.text: Topical nystatin to the nipples and the baby's mouth
options.rationale: Nipple and oral candidiasis causes persistent burning pain that does not change with repositioning, and there is no oral plaque or nipple appearance described here. Antifungal treatment would be correct if pain persisted after attachment was optimised and typical signs were present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Division of the upper labial frenulum under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Upper lip tie division has no established feeding benefit and the restriction described here is lingual, not labial. General anaesthesia is never the default route for a neonatal frenulum in any case, since frenotomy is an awake bedside procedure. (Source: RACGP: Tongue tie and breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Nipple pain in the early weeks is far more often a problem of attachment and positioning than of anatomy, and the two are commonly conflated because a visible frenulum invites a mechanical explanation. Assessment of ankyloglossia is functional rather than anatomical: what matters is whether the tongue can elevate and lateralise enough to draw the nipple deep into the mouth, not whether a membrane is visible. A structured feed observation by a skilled practitioner is the investigation, and it frequently identifies a correctable hold. Frenotomy rates have risen internationally well beyond what the evidence supports, and an unnecessary procedure exposes a neonate to bleeding and to the false reassurance that the feeding problem has been addressed. Adequate output and a weight tracking up from the physiological nadir mean there is time to do this properly.
key_points: Tongue elevation to mid-mouth with bilateral lateralisation indicates mild restriction unlikely to be the cause of feeding failure
A full feed observed by a lactation practitioner is the assessment that decides whether a frenulum is functionally significant
Pain that settles with repositioning points to attachment rather than anatomy
Weight regained above the day-4 nadir with six or more heavy nappies daily indicates adequate transfer
Upper labial frenulum division has no established breastfeeding benefit
explanation.pearls: Physiological weight loss bottoms out around day 4 at up to 10 per cent of birth weight and birth weight should be regained by day 14; a baby already climbing from the nadir does not need top-ups while attachment is being corrected.

subtopic_detail: Radial head subluxation where the mechanism reported does not fit the classic pull
stem:
You are the resident in a suburban emergency department. A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her father because she will not use her left arm. He says she was swinging between him and her older sister by the hands when she suddenly cried out, and she has held the arm still against her body since.

She settled quickly and is now playing with a sticker using her right hand. She has no bruising anywhere and no previous fractures. Her father reports no fall and no direct blow.

On examination she holds the left arm slightly flexed at the elbow with the forearm turned palm-down. She resists turning the palm upward. There is no swelling, no deformity and no point tenderness over the clavicle, the humerus, the olecranon or the distal radius. She moves the fingers, wrist and shoulder normally and the radial pulse is present.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held flexed with forearm pronated, resists supination, no swelling or deformity, no point tenderness over clavicle, humerus, olecranon or distal radius, normal finger, wrist and shoulder movement, radial pulse present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the elbow before attempting any manipulation
options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in radial head subluxation and delay a manoeuvre that restores function within minutes. Imaging would be correct if there were swelling, deformity, bony point tenderness or a mechanism involving a fall or direct blow. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Perform a supination and flexion reduction manoeuvre at the bedside without prior imaging
options.rationale: A longitudinal traction mechanism with a pronated arm, absent swelling and no point tenderness over any bony landmark is a clinical diagnosis of radial head subluxation, and the management is immediate bedside reduction. Imaging before reduction is not required when the history and examination are typical and there is no localised bony tenderness. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply an above-elbow backslab and arrange fracture clinic review within the following week
options.rationale: Immobilisation treats a fracture that has not been demonstrated and leaves a reducible subluxation unreduced for days. A backslab would be correct for a confirmed undisplaced supracondylar or forearm fracture, which would show swelling or focal tenderness. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Perform a skeletal survey and notify the child protection team before any elbow manipulation
options.rationale: The mechanism is consistent, developmentally plausible and matches the injury, and there is no bruising or injury pattern raising concern. A skeletal survey would be correct where the history is absent, changes, or does not fit the injury, particularly in a child under 2 years. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the elbow joint to exclude an effusion before attempting manipulation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is not part of the assessment pathway for a pulled elbow and an effusion is not the lesion in radial head subluxation. Ultrasound would be correct in suspected septic arthritis of the hip, where an effusion guides aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation happens when the annular ligament slips over the radial head during axial traction on an extended, pronated arm, and it is one of the few paediatric musculoskeletal presentations diagnosed and cured within a single consultation. The classic picture is a child under 5 who simply stops using the arm rather than complaining of a specific painful point, which is why the absence of swelling and focal tenderness is as important as the mechanism. Reduction by supination with elbow flexion, or by hyperpronation, restores use within minutes and often produces a palpable click. Failure to regain use after two attempts is the trigger to image, because an undisplaced fracture can mimic the presentation. Recurrence is common until about age 5 and parents should be warned against lifting the child by the hands.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated, extended arm is the mechanism; a fall or direct blow points elsewhere
The child refuses to use the arm rather than localising pain, and the arm is held pronated and slightly flexed
Absence of swelling, deformity and bony point tenderness makes imaging unnecessary before reduction
Supination with flexion or hyperpronation both work and often produce a palpable click
Image after two failed reduction attempts, because an occult fracture can present identically
explanation.pearls: Return of spontaneous arm use within about 15 minutes of a single supination and flexion manoeuvre confirms the diagnosis retrospectively; if the child is still not using the arm after two attempts, radiograph rather than repeat the manoeuvre a third time.

subtopic_detail: Referral threshold for persistent middle ear effusion with documented language delay
stem: A 4-year-old boy does not respond when called across the room and turns the television up loud. He uses short phrases rather than sentences, with no ear discharge or pain.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes retracted and dull with fluid levels
data_table.Investigations: Flat tympanograms bilaterally; audiogram conductive loss averaging 35 dB; same findings 4 months ago; expressive language below the third centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Watchful waiting with repeat audiogram in 3 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is the correct approach for the first 3 months because most effusions resolve spontaneously, but that window has already passed and language is now measurably affected. Further observation would be correct if hearing were better than 25 dB and language were age-appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Four-week course of oral amoxicillin, review at completion
options.rationale: Prolonged antibiotics do not produce durable resolution of a sterile middle ear effusion and expose the child to resistance and adverse effects. Amoxicillin would be correct for acute otitis media with a bulging erythematous drum and systemic symptoms, which are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Ear, nose and throat referral for ventilation tubes
options.rationale: Bilateral effusion persisting beyond 3 months with a hearing loss of this degree and a documented language impact meets the threshold for surgical referral rather than further observation. The 4-month-old note establishes persistence, which is the element that converts watchful waiting into referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Intranasal corticosteroid for 8 weeks, then tympanometry
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroids have not been shown to clear middle ear effusion or improve hearing outcomes in children. They would be correct for allergic rhinitis causing nasal obstruction, which is a separate problem and is not described here. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

options.text: Nasal balloon autoinflation three times daily for 3 months
options.rationale: Autoinflation offers a small short-term benefit and is a reasonable adjunct during the observation window, but it does not substitute for referral once persistence and language impact are established. It would be correct as an interim measure in the first 3 months of a newly detected effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion

explanation.summary: Middle ear effusion after acute otitis media is extremely common and the great majority clears without intervention within 3 months, which is why the default is observation rather than treatment. The decision to operate turns on three things together: bilateral persistence beyond that window, the degree of hearing loss, and whether that loss is translating into a developmental or educational cost. A child with a 35 dB bilateral loss is missing conversational speech at a distance, and the speech pathology report converts an audiological number into a functional argument for intervention. Ventilation tubes restore hearing promptly and are usually extruded within 9 to 15 months. Antibiotics, steroids and decongestants have all been studied and none produces durable clearance, so offering them mainly delays the referral.
key_points: Observe for 3 months first: most effusions resolve spontaneously after acute otitis media
Refer when bilateral effusion persists beyond 3 months with hearing loss and a functional impact
A flat tympanogram with a retracted dull drum and fluid level confirms effusion rather than acute infection
Antibiotics, intranasal steroids and decongestants do not durably clear middle ear effusion
Document the developmental cost, since it is what converts an audiogram into an operative indication
explanation.pearls: A bilateral conductive loss averaging 25 dB or worse persisting past 3 months is the audiological trigger for ear, nose and throat referral; below that threshold, hearing is usually adequate for language acquisition and observation continues.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis media with effusion
NICE: Otitis media with effusion in under 12s

subtopic_detail: Formula selection after a non-IgE cow milk reaction that recurred on an extensively hydrolysed feed
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric outpatient clinic. A 10-week-old boy is brought in by his mother with 4 weeks of loose, mucousy stools streaked with blood and increasing irritability after feeds.

He has been formula fed since birth. Four weeks ago his general practitioner changed him from a standard cow milk formula to an extensively hydrolysed formula, which he has taken exclusively since. His mother reports the stools improved for about a week and then returned to being loose and blood-streaked.

He has never had hives, facial swelling, wheeze or vomiting within minutes of a feed. His weight has dropped from the 50th centile at birth to the 15th centile today. On examination he is alert and well perfused, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no perianal fissure, no skin rash and no organomegaly.

data_table.Growth: Birth weight 50th centile, today 15th centile
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, abdomen soft and non-tender, no perianal fissure, no rash, no organomegaly
data_table.Feeding: Extensively hydrolysed formula exclusively for 4 weeks after standard cow milk formula; initial improvement then relapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a soy based formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: A substantial proportion of infants with non-IgE cow milk proteinopathy react to soy as well, so soy is not a reliable next step under 6 months of age. Soy formula would be reasonable in an older infant with isolated IgE-mediated cow milk allergy and confirmed soy tolerance. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Request skin prick testing to cow milk protein and withhold any formula change pending results
options.rationale: Skin prick testing detects IgE sensitisation and is negative in the non-IgE delayed pattern described here, so a normal result would wrongly reassure. Testing would be correct if reactions occurred within minutes with urticaria, angioedema or wheeze. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Change to a lactose free cow milk formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: The reaction is to intact or partly hydrolysed cow milk protein, and a lactose free formula retains that protein while removing a sugar that is not the problem. Lactose free formula would be correct for transient secondary lactose intolerance after a proven gastroenteritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

options.text: Change to an amino acid based formula and arrange paediatric dietetic review within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Persistent blood-streaked stools and centile fall despite 4 weeks of an extensively hydrolysed formula identify the minority of infants whose residual peptide load still drives the reaction, and the next step up the ladder is an amino acid based formula. Dietetic involvement is needed because faltering growth on an elimination diet requires energy and nutrient adequacy to be checked. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Request faecal calprotectin and colonoscopy and withhold any formula change pending results
options.rationale: Endoscopy is not required to diagnose food protein induced proctocolitis in a well infant, where response to elimination is the diagnostic test. Colonoscopy would be correct if bleeding persisted on an amino acid formula or if there were systemic features suggesting inflammatory bowel disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

explanation.summary: Food protein induced allergic proctocolitis presents in the first months of life as blood-streaked mucousy stools in an otherwise well infant, and it is a delayed, non-IgE process, so allergy testing has no role in diagnosis. Management is a stepped elimination: an extensively hydrolysed formula first, which resolves the problem in roughly 90 per cent of cases, and an amino acid formula for the remainder who still react to residual peptides. The pattern of partial improvement followed by relapse on a hydrolysate is characteristic of that residual peptide load rather than of treatment failure through non-adherence. Faltering growth changes the urgency because it signals that intake and absorption are both being affected. Most infants tolerate cow milk protein again by 12 months, so a planned reintroduction under supervision belongs in the longer term plan.
key_points: Blood-streaked mucousy stools in a well infant suggest non-IgE food protein induced proctocolitis
Skin prick and specific IgE testing are negative in non-IgE disease and do not exclude it
Extensively hydrolysed formula is first-line and resolves about 90 per cent of cases
Amino acid formula is the next step when symptoms persist or relapse on a hydrolysate
Soy formula is unsuitable under 6 months because of frequent co-reactivity
explanation.pearls: Expect symptoms to settle within 2 to 4 weeks of starting an appropriate elimination formula; relapse after an initial week of improvement on an extensively hydrolysed feed is the signal to escalate to amino acid based formula rather than to question adherence.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention
RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing positional head flattening from suture fusion in an infant with a ridged head shape
stem:
You are the resident in a community child health clinic. A 5-month-old boy is brought in by his father because the back of his head looks flat and one ear looks pushed forward.

He was born at term and sleeps on his back. His father says he has always preferred to turn his head to the right and that he spends most of his waking time in a bouncer. Head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile since birth.

On examination the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits anterior to the left and the right forehead is more prominent than the left, so that the head viewed from above is a parallelogram. The anterior fontanelle is open and soft. There is no palpable ridge over any suture. Passive neck rotation is restricted to the left with a firm thickening palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid.

data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with right ear anterior and right frontal bossing, parallelogram head shape from above, anterior fontanelle open and soft, no palpable sutural ridge
data_table.Neck: Passive rotation restricted to the left, firm thickening palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a craniofacial surgeon for assessment of premature fusion of the lambdoid suture
options.rationale: Lambdoid synostosis produces a trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly and a palpable ridge, which is the opposite ear displacement to the parallelogram described here. Referral would be correct if the ear sat posteriorly, a ridge were palpable, or head circumference were crossing centiles. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Request a computed tomography scan of the skull with three-dimensional reconstruction of the sutures
options.rationale: Positional plagiocephaly is a clinical diagnosis and computed tomography delivers ionising radiation to an infant brain for no management gain. It would be correct where examination genuinely suggests synostosis and a craniofacial service requests it to plan surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange fitting of a moulding helmet orthosis now and review the head shape in 3 months
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is a second-line option considered from around 6 months when conservative measures have failed, and it does nothing for the underlying neck restriction. It would be correct for severe persisting asymmetry after an adequate trial of physiotherapy and repositioning. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Advise front sleeping overnight to offload the flattened occiput and review the head shape in 3 months
options.rationale: Prone sleeping is a major modifiable risk factor for sudden unexpected death in infancy and must never be advised to improve head shape. Repositioning is achieved by alternating head orientation while supine and by waking tummy time under supervision. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretching and advise repositioning and supervised tummy time
options.rationale: A parallelogram head shape with the ipsilateral ear displaced anteriorly, a normal head circumference and no sutural ridge is positional deformity driven by a restricted sternocleidomastoid, and the treatment is physiotherapy for the torticollis plus repositioning. Treating the neck restriction is the element that prevents recurrence, because the head shape follows the preferred head position. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Positional plagiocephaly became substantially more common after supine sleeping was adopted to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy, and it is benign, but it is frequently confused with craniosynostosis. The discriminator is geometry rather than severity: positional flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, producing a parallelogram viewed from above, while lambdoid synostosis restricts growth and pulls the ipsilateral ear backward into a trapezoid with a palpable ridge. Congenital muscular torticollis underlies a large share of positional cases and is the reason the deformity recurs if only repositioning is advised. Head circumference crossing centiles or a ridged suture are the findings that should prompt craniofacial referral. Most positional asymmetry improves substantially once the infant becomes mobile and spends less time lying against a surface.
key_points: Parallelogram head with the ipsilateral ear displaced anteriorly indicates positional deformity
Trapezoid head with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly plus a palpable ridge indicates lambdoid synostosis
Normal head circumference tracking along a centile argues against synostosis
Treat the associated sternocleidomastoid restriction or the head shape will recur
Never advise prone sleeping to offload a flattened occiput
explanation.pearls: Check passive neck rotation in every infant with an asymmetric head: congenital muscular torticollis drives the positional preference, and physiotherapy started before 6 months resolves the great majority without a helmet.

subtopic_detail: Timing of propranolol for a segmental facial haemangioma still in proliferative phase
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric dermatology clinic. A 7-week-old girl is brought in by her mother, who says a faint pink patch on the left cheek noticed in the first fortnight has become a raised red lesion that is enlarging weekly.

She was born at 34 weeks and weighed 1900 g. Her mother says the lesion bleeds slightly when rubbed against a bunny rug but is not painful and the baby feeds and sleeps normally.

On examination there is a bright red plaque measuring 45 mm across the left cheek, extending to the lateral upper lip and the left lower eyelid margin. The lid lesion does not currently obstruct the visual axis. There is no ulceration. There is a second 6 mm red papule on the left shoulder. Cardiovascular examination is normal and there is no lumbosacral lesion. A recent ophthalmology review documented normal fundi and no astigmatism.

data_table.Examination: Bright red plaque 45 mm across the left cheek extending to the lateral upper lip and left lower eyelid margin, visual axis clear, no ulceration, second 6 mm papule on the left shoulder
data_table.Investigations: Ophthalmology review: normal fundi, no astigmatism; cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral propranolol with dose escalation and monitoring under specialist supervision
options.rationale: A large segmental facial lesion involving the eyelid margin and lip that is still proliferating at 7 weeks carries a high risk of functional and cosmetic complication, and systemic propranolol is first-line treatment. The proliferative phase runs to roughly 5 months, so starting now captures the window in which treatment alters the trajectory rather than merely accelerating involution. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Observe with serial photographs and review in 3 months, expecting spontaneous involution
options.rationale: Most small truncal lesions can be observed safely, but a periocular and perioral segmental lesion can cause deprivation amblyopia and permanent lip distortion before involution begins. Observation would be correct for the 6 mm shoulder papule, which threatens no structure. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Start topical timolol maleate gel applied twice daily and review the lesion in 3 months
options.rationale: Topical beta blockade has useful effect only on thin superficial lesions of limited size and would not control a 45 mm segmental plaque. Timolol would be correct for the small flat shoulder papule or a superficial lesion under about 10 mm. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment of the cheek lesion and review the lesion in 3 months
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser penetrates only the superficial dermis and is used mainly for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulcerated lesions. It would be correct once the lesion has involuted and left surface vessels, not as proliferative-phase control. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone with a weaning schedule and monitoring under specialist supervision
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid was the former first-line agent but propranolol is more effective and better tolerated, so steroid is now reserved for propranolol failure or contraindication. Prednisolone would be correct where beta blockade is contraindicated, such as in significant reactive airways disease. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas follow a predictable course: a herald patch in the first weeks, rapid proliferation to about 5 months, then slow involution over years. Because the natural history is benign for most lesions, the clinical skill lies in recognising the minority that need treatment, which are those threatening vision, the airway, feeding or permanent disfigurement, and those that ulcerate. Periocular lesions can induce astigmatism and deprivation amblyopia even without covering the pupil, so ophthalmology review is part of the assessment rather than a substitute for treatment. A large segmental facial lesion also raises the question of PHACE association, which warrants cerebrovascular and cardiac imaging before beta blockade lowers perfusion pressure. Timing matters more here than in most paediatric dermatology, because a lesion allowed to complete proliferation leaves fibrofatty residue that no drug reverses.
key_points: Proliferation runs to roughly 5 months, so treatment decisions cannot wait for a routine review interval
Treat lesions threatening vision, airway, feeding, or causing ulceration or permanent disfigurement
Oral propranolol is first-line; corticosteroid is now second-line for failure or contraindication
Topical timolol is limited to thin superficial lesions of small size
Large segmental facial lesions raise the possibility of PHACE association warranting imaging
explanation.pearls: A periocular haemangioma can cause amblyopia through astigmatism from lid pressure without ever covering the pupil, so a clear visual axis does not make observation safe.

subtopic_detail: Management of a limping toddler with a normal radiograph and a low-energy twisting mechanism
stem: An 18-month-old boy has refused to bear weight on his right leg since yesterday, after catching his foot in trampoline netting and twisting as he fell. He is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Crawls readily, full painless hip and knee movement, swelling over the distal shin, pain on gentle tibial torsion
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L, tibia and fibula radiographs show no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with analgesia and general practitioner review
options.rationale: A normal radiograph does not exclude this fracture, and leaving an unstable tibia unsupported causes ongoing pain and refusal to weight bear. Discharge without immobilisation would be correct if tibial torsion were painless and the refusal to weight bear were unexplained by a focal sign. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Apply an above-knee backslab with orthopaedic review
options.rationale: A low-energy twisting injury in a newly walking toddler with focal distal tibial tenderness and a normal radiograph is an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture, which is radiographically occult in a substantial proportion of cases at presentation. Immobilisation on clinical grounds is the standard approach, with review when periosteal reaction makes the fracture visible. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Urgent hip ultrasound to look for a joint effusion
options.rationale: Hip movements are full and painless and the tenderness is over the distal tibia, so the hip is not the source and an effusion is not expected. Hip ultrasound would be correct for a limping child with restricted or painful hip rotation where septic arthritis or transient synovitis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Technetium bone scan of both lower limbs, then review
options.rationale: Bone scanning delivers a significant radiation dose and is reserved for a limping child with no localising sign after clinical and radiographic assessment. It would be correct where the site of pathology genuinely cannot be localised, which is not the case with focal tibial torsional pain. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and tibial MRI
options.rationale: Osteomyelitis is the important alternative but requires fever or elevated inflammatory markers, both of which are normal here, and a clear traumatic mechanism argues against it. Antibiotics and magnetic resonance imaging would be correct if the child were febrile with a raised C-reactive protein and no convincing injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: The toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft produced by a low-energy twisting force in a child in the first years of independent walking, and its defining feature is that the initial radiograph is often normal. The periosteum is thick and intact in this age group, so the fracture is stable and the injury is far less dramatic than the refusal to weight bear suggests. The diagnostic task is really one of exclusion: a normal hip examination, normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever separate it from septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, which are the diagnoses that cannot be missed. Treating on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for radiographic proof is the accepted approach, and a repeat film at 10 to 14 days shows periosteal new bone that confirms it retrospectively. Healing is reliable and long-term sequelae are rare.
key_points: Low-energy twisting in a child aged roughly 9 months to 3 years is the characteristic mechanism
Initial radiographs are frequently normal because the fracture is undisplaced and spiral
Focal pain on gentle tibial torsion localises the injury and separates it from hip pathology
Normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever argue against osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
Immobilise on clinical suspicion; periosteal reaction confirms the diagnosis on later imaging
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone appears on repeat radiographs at about 10 to 14 days, so a film taken at the 1 to 2 week orthopaedic review confirms the fracture that the presentation film missed.

subtopic_detail: First-line antiseizure choice for childhood absence epilepsy in a girl of childbearing potential
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric neurology clinic. A 7-year-old girl is brought in by her father after her teacher reported that she blanks out in class up to 20 times a day, each time for a few seconds, and then carries on mid-sentence.

Her father has noticed the same at home and says she does not fall or shake, and there is no confusion afterwards. Development and school performance were previously normal, though her reading has slipped this term.

In clinic she is asked to blow on a paper windmill for 3 minutes. Twice she stops blowing, stares, and her eyelids flutter, then she resumes without any awareness of the pause. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. An electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background, with no photoparoxysmal response and no polyspike bursts. She has never had a myoclonic jerk or a generalised convulsion.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal; hyperventilation for 3 minutes provoked two episodes of behavioural arrest with eyelid flutter and no postictal confusion
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram: generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background, no photoparoxysmal response, no polyspike bursts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Sodium valproate, titrated to response with monitoring for weight gain and tremor
options.rationale: Valproate controls absence seizures effectively but carries dose-related teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harm, so it is avoided in females of childbearing potential when an equally effective alternative exists. It would be the choice if generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexisted, since ethosuximide does not protect against them. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Lamotrigine, titrated slowly to response with monitoring for rash and hypersensitivity
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is less effective than either ethosuximide or valproate for absence seizures and its mandatory slow titration delays control in a child having 20 events daily. It would be reasonable as third-line therapy or where both first-line agents have failed or are not tolerated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ethosuximide, titrated to response with monitoring for gastrointestinal upset
options.rationale: In typical childhood absence epilepsy without generalised convulsions, ethosuximide gives seizure freedom rates equal to valproate with significantly less attentional impairment, which matters directly given the reported decline in reading. It is preferred over valproate in a girl because it avoids the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks that accompany long-term valproate exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Carbamazepine, titrated to response with monitoring for rash and hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Sodium channel blockers aggravate generalised absence and myoclonic seizures and can precipitate absence status, so carbamazepine is contraindicated here. It would be appropriate for focal epilepsy, where the discharge is localised rather than generalised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Levetiracetam, titrated to response with monitoring for irritability and behavioural change
options.rationale: Levetiracetam has weaker evidence in absence epilepsy than the established first-line agents and was inferior in comparative trials. It is widely used in other generalised epilepsies and would be considered where first-line options have failed or behavioural monitoring is acceptable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between 4 and 10 years and is confirmed by the combination of brief behavioural arrest without postictal confusion, ready provocation by hyperventilation, and generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background. The clinical trap is that frequent brief absences are often mistaken for inattention or daydreaming, and a slipping school performance is commonly the presenting complaint rather than the seizures themselves. The comparative trial evidence is unusually clear for a paediatric epilepsy: ethosuximide and valproate control seizures equally, but valproate impairs attention more, and ethosuximide therefore wins on the outcome that matters to a child in the classroom. The important caveat is that ethosuximide has no efficacy against generalised tonic-clonic seizures, so a history of any convulsion changes the choice. Prognosis is good, with most children entering remission by adolescence.
key_points: Hyperventilation for 3 minutes provokes an absence in most untreated children and is a bedside diagnostic test
Generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background is the electroencephalographic signature
Ethosuximide and valproate are equally effective, but ethosuximide preserves attention better
Ethosuximide does not protect against generalised tonic-clonic seizures
Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine aggravate generalised absence seizures
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about any lifetime generalised convulsion before choosing ethosuximide: it has no efficacy against tonic-clonic seizures, and their presence moves the choice to valproate or lamotrigine despite the attentional and teratogenic trade-offs.

sources.label: Epilepsy Action Australia: Childhood absence epilepsy

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic and wound decision for a facial dog bite presenting outside the primary closure window
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 5-year-old girl is brought in 14 hours after the family dog bit her cheek when she leaned over its food bowl.

Her mother washed the wound with soap and water at home and did not seek care overnight because the child settled and slept. The dog is fully vaccinated, lives at home and has never left Australia.

Her immunisations are documented as up to date including four doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine. On examination there are two puncture wounds and a 20 mm curved laceration over the right cheek, 15 mm below the lower eyelid. The wound edges are moderately swollen with surrounding erythema extending 10 mm, and there is a small amount of serous discharge. She is afebrile, eating normally, and there is no facial nerve weakness and no bony step.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Two puncture wounds and a 20 mm curved cheek laceration 15 mm below the right lower eyelid, moderate oedema with 10 mm surrounding erythema and serous discharge, no facial nerve weakness, no bony step
data_table.Immunisation: Four doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral amoxicillin with clavulanate, with immediate primary suture closure in the department
options.rationale: Primary closure of a bite presenting at 14 hours with established local inflammation traps inoculated organisms and raises the risk of deep infection. Primary closure would be correct for a clean facial bite irrigated and closed within roughly 8 hours with no signs of inflammation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral cefalexin monotherapy, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Cefalexin has unreliable activity against Pasteurella multocida and no anaerobic cover, so it is not adequate for a bite wound despite being a standard skin infection agent. It would be appropriate for uncomplicated non-bite cellulitis caused by streptococci and staphylococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Copious irrigation and a tetanus immunoglobulin injection, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is reserved for tetanus-prone wounds in people who are incompletely immunised or whose status is unknown, and this child has four documented vaccine doses. Immunoglobulin would be correct if fewer than three doses were documented or the history were unavailable. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral amoxicillin with clavulanate, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanate covers Pasteurella multocida and the oral anaerobes that make dog bites infect, and prophylaxis is indicated for facial bites regardless of appearance. Beyond about 8 hours with established oedema and erythema the wound is left open for delayed closure or revision rather than sutured primarily. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Copious irrigation and rabies immunoglobulin with vaccine, and plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Australia is free of classical rabies and the only local lyssavirus reservoir is bats, so a domestic dog with no overseas travel poses no lyssavirus risk. Post-exposure prophylaxis would be correct after a bat bite or scratch in Australia, or a dog bite acquired overseas. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Dog bites deliver a mixed inoculum of aerobes and anaerobes deep into tissue, and the two management decisions that matter are which antibiotic and whether to close. Amoxicillin with clavulanate is the Australian agent of choice because it is the only widely used oral option covering Pasteurella multocida alongside staphylococci, streptococci and anaerobes. Facial bites occupy a special position: the cosmetic stakes push toward early closure and the excellent facial blood supply makes it safer than elsewhere, but that latitude closes once the wound is several hours old and inflamed. Australia's rabies-free status means lyssavirus prophylaxis turns on bat contact or overseas acquisition rather than on the bite itself, which is a frequent source of unnecessary anxiety. Bites near the eyelid margin, over joints, or involving the hand warrant a lower threshold for specialist involvement.
key_points: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is first-line because it covers Pasteurella multocida plus anaerobes
Prophylaxis is indicated for bites to the face, hands, feet, over joints, and in immunocompromised children
Primary closure is limited to early, clean, well-irrigated wounds; inflamed or late wounds are left open
Australian domestic dogs pose no classical rabies risk; bats are the local lyssavirus reservoir
Tetanus immunoglobulin is for incomplete or unknown immunisation, not for every bite
explanation.pearls: In penicillin-allergic children the Australian bite alternative is trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole plus metronidazole, because cefalexin and clindamycin each leave Pasteurella multocida uncovered.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a markedly raised creatine kinase found during investigation of speech delay in a boy
stem:
You are the resident in a general paediatric clinic. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his mother because he is difficult to understand and is not keeping up with his kindergarten group.

His mother says he walked at 19 months, struggles with stairs and asks to be carried after short walks. He has never lost a skill he had acquired. There is no family history of neuromuscular disease.

On examination he rises from the floor by turning prone and pushing his hands up his thighs. His calves are firm and bulky. Power is 4/5 at the hip girdle and 5/5 distally, reflexes are present and symmetrical and plantar responses are flexor. There is no ptosis, no facial weakness and no fasciculation. Blood taken to investigate the developmental concern shows alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (<40), bilirubin 8 micromol/L (<20) and creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60-300).

data_table.Examination: Gowers manoeuvre positive, calf hypertrophy, proximal power 4/5 with distal power 5/5, reflexes present and symmetrical, plantar responses flexor, no ptosis or facial weakness
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (<40), bilirubin 8 micromol/L (<20), creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request liver ultrasound and a viral hepatitis screen and refer to a paediatric hepatology service
options.rationale: The raised aminotransferases originate from muscle rather than liver, which the normal bilirubin and grossly elevated creatine kinase indicate, so a hepatic workup pursues an artefact. Hepatology referral would be correct if gamma-glutamyl transferase were also raised and creatine kinase were normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer to a paediatric neurodisability service
options.rationale: Central imaging does not explain a creatine kinase of this magnitude, which is a muscle-specific finding, and reflexes and plantar responses are normal. Brain imaging would be correct for global delay with upper motor neuron signs, microcephaly or regression. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Request an open muscle biopsy for dystrophin immunostaining and refer to a neuromuscular service
options.rationale: Biopsy is invasive and is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative but clinical suspicion persists. It would be correct after deletion, duplication and sequence analysis all return negative in a boy with this phenotype. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Request nerve conduction studies with electromyography and refer to a neuromuscular service
