options.rationale: Electrophysiology confirms a myopathic pattern but does not identify the cause and adds a distressing procedure when a blood test gives the diagnosis. It would be useful where a neuropathy or a neuromuscular junction disorder is suspected and creatine kinase is normal or only mildly raised. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Request dystrophin gene deletion and duplication analysis and refer to a neuromuscular service
options.rationale: Proximal weakness with a Gowers manoeuvre, calf hypertrophy and a creatine kinase in the thousands in a boy of this age is dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and genetic testing has replaced muscle biopsy as the first-line confirmatory test. Deletion and duplication analysis detects around 70 per cent of causative variants, with sequencing for the remainder. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is frequently diagnosed late because the earliest presentation is developmental rather than obviously neuromuscular, with speech delay and difficulty keeping up being common first complaints. A creatine kinase discovered incidentally is often the moment the diagnosis becomes apparent, and the characteristic value is in the thousands to tens of thousands rather than the modest elevation seen with exercise or trauma. Raised aminotransferases are a well-recognised trap, because alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are both released from damaged muscle and boys are not uncommonly investigated for liver disease before anyone measures a creatine kinase. Early molecular diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started before substantial function is lost prolongs ambulation, and because exon-skipping therapies depend on knowing the precise variant. Genetic confirmation also enables carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the mother and wider family.
key_points: Speech and global developmental delay are common presenting complaints before weakness is recognised
Gowers manoeuvre plus calf hypertrophy plus creatine kinase in the thousands is the diagnostic triad
Raised alanine and aspartate aminotransferase come from muscle; a normal bilirubin points away from liver
Deletion and duplication analysis is first-line and detects roughly 70 per cent of variants
Muscle biopsy is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative
explanation.pearls: Measure creatine kinase in any boy with unexplained developmental delay who is not yet walking by 18 months or who has isolated aminotransferase elevation with a normal bilirubin and gamma-glutamyl transferase.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Choosing between alkalinisation and dialysis in adolescent salicylate poisoning with a falling pH
stem: A 15-year-old girl took an unknown quantity of aspirin 6 hours ago. Her ears are ringing; she is agitated but oriented and passing urine freely.

data_table.Investigations: Salicylate 640 mg/L at 4 hours and 810 mg/L at 6 hours; arrival gas pH 7.47, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L; repeat pH 7.29, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L
data_table.Treatment so far: 2 L intravenous sodium bicarbonate over 2 hours; urine pH 7.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis with continued bicarbonate infusion
options.rationale: A rising concentration above 700 mg/L together with a falling arterial pH despite adequate urinary alkalinisation meets the criteria for extracorporeal removal, and each feature independently would justify it. The fall in pH is the critical change, because acidaemia shifts salicylate into the non-ionised form that crosses into the brain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Continue bicarbonate alone and repeat the concentration
options.rationale: Alkalinisation has already been delivered to a urine pH of 7.6 and the concentration is still climbing while the arterial pH falls, so persisting without escalation allows deterioration. Continued alkalinisation alone would be correct if the concentration were falling and the arterial pH were stable or rising. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Repeated activated charcoal every 4 hours by nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Multiple dose charcoal can limit ongoing absorption from a concretion but does not remove salicylate already distributed to tissue, and it carries aspiration risk in a vomiting, agitated patient. It would be a useful adjunct earlier in a protected, non-vomiting patient with a rising concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with controlled ventilation
options.rationale: Intubation in salicylate poisoning is hazardous because any drop in minute ventilation during the apnoeic period worsens acidaemia and can precipitate cardiac arrest. It would be necessary only for airway failure or exhaustion, and then with ventilation matched to the pre-intubation respiratory rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Intravenous acetylcysteine by the standard regimen
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity by replenishing glutathione and has no role against salicylate, which causes oxidative phosphorylation uncoupling rather than a reactive metabolite injury. It would be indicated if a co-ingested paracetamol concentration sat above the treatment line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Salicylate poisoning produces a characteristic mixed picture of respiratory alkalosis from direct respiratory centre stimulation superimposed on a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The initial gas here shows the alkalotic phase, and the transition to acidaemia marks the point at which the patient is decompensating rather than improving. That transition is dangerous out of proportion to the numbers, because salicylate is a weak acid whose non-ionised fraction rises as pH falls, allowing it to cross the blood-brain barrier and cause cerebral oedema, seizures and death. Urinary alkalinisation works by trapping ionised salicylate in the tubule and is the mainstay of moderate poisoning, but once it has been optimised and concentrations still rise, only extracorporeal removal will clear the drug. Salicylate concentrations should be repeated every 2 hours until falling, because delayed and erratic absorption from tablet concretions means a single value never excludes serious toxicity.
key_points: Expect mixed respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap metabolic acidosis; a falling pH signals decompensation
Acidaemia increases the non-ionised fraction that crosses into the brain, so pH matters more than concentration alone
Haemodialysis is indicated for concentrations above roughly 700 mg/L, acidaemia, altered mental state, or renal failure
Intubation is high risk because loss of compensatory hyperventilation can precipitate arrest
Repeat concentrations every 2 hours until clearly falling, because absorption is delayed and erratic
explanation.pearls: If intubation becomes unavoidable in salicylate poisoning, match the ventilator to the patient's own pre-intubation minute ventilation, often above 30 breaths per minute, rather than to conventional lung-protective settings.

subtopic_detail: Chelation threshold and source control for an asymptomatic child with an elevated blood lead level
stem: A 3-year-old boy is referred after community screening found an elevated blood lead level. He is asymptomatic and frequently mouths dirt and paint flakes. The family lives in a 1950 weatherboard house with peeling paint; his father works at the smelter and changes clothes at home.

data_table.Investigations: Venous blood lead 28 micrograms/dL, haemoglobin 104 g/L, mean cell volume 68 fL, ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150), abdominal radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous sodium calcium edetate chelation
options.rationale: Parenteral chelation is reserved for encephalopathy or levels at or above 70 micrograms/dL, and this child is asymptomatic at 28 micrograms/dL. It would be correct for a child with seizures, altered consciousness or a level in that range. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Notify public health for environmental assessment
options.rationale: Below the chelation threshold the interventions that lower a blood lead level are removal of the source and correction of iron deficiency, because iron deficiency upregulates the divalent metal transporter that absorbs lead from the gut. A level of 5 micrograms/dL or above is notifiable in Australian jurisdictions and triggers the environmental investigation that addresses both the paint and the take-home occupational exposure. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Commence oral succimer chelation as an outpatient
options.rationale: Oral chelation is generally considered from about 45 micrograms/dL, and trials at lower levels showed no cognitive benefit while the level rebounded once the drug stopped. Succimer would be appropriate for a symptomatic child or one in that higher band with the source already removed. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Give calcium and vitamin D supplementation daily
options.rationale: Adequate dietary calcium modestly reduces lead absorption and is part of general advice, but supplementation alone does not lower an established level while exposure continues. It would be a reasonable adjunct once the environmental source had been identified and controlled. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Arrange whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol
options.rationale: Bowel irrigation is used to clear ingested radio-opaque lead objects or paint chips seen on imaging, and this radiograph shows none. It would be correct where a retained lead foreign body such as a swallowed sinker or fragment were visible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Childhood lead exposure in Australia clusters around older housing with deteriorating pre-1970 paint, mining and smelting communities, and take-home contamination on parental work clothing, all three of which are present in this family. There is no threshold below which lead is known to be safe, and the cognitive effects are subclinical at the levels most children present with, so the absence of symptoms is expected rather than reassuring. The counterintuitive part of management is that chelation is not the answer for most elevated levels: it lowers the measured blood concentration without demonstrated cognitive benefit at moderate levels, and the level rebounds from bone stores once treatment stops. Source removal is the only intervention that changes long-term body burden, which is why notification and an environmental health assessment do more than any drug. Iron deficiency deserves specific attention because it both increases gastrointestinal lead absorption and independently harms development, so the two problems compound each other.
key_points: Blood lead of 5 micrograms/dL or above is notifiable in Australia and triggers environmental investigation
Source removal and correction of iron deficiency are the interventions that lower body burden at moderate levels
Oral chelation is generally considered from about 45 micrograms/dL; parenteral therapy for encephalopathy or 70 micrograms/dL and above
Chelation at moderate levels lowers the blood concentration without demonstrated cognitive benefit and is followed by rebound from bone
Take-home exposure on parental work clothing is a recognised route in smelting and mining communities
explanation.pearls: Iron deficiency increases lead absorption through the shared divalent metal transporter 1 in the duodenum, so replacing iron in a lead-exposed child lowers the level independently of any chelating agent.

sources.label: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

subtopic_detail: Whether to continue antibiotic prophylaxis after a second febrile urinary infection with high grade reflux
stem: A 14-month-old girl is reviewed after her second febrile Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, treated 4 months and 5 weeks ago. She is thriving, has no constipation and is taking no medication.

data_table.Investigations: Renal ultrasound: bilateral hydronephrosis with dilated ureters, normal cortical thickness. Micturating cystourethrogram: grade IV reflux on the left, grade III on the right, no posterior urethral valve. Creatinine 26 micromol/L (15-35). Post-treatment urine culture sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: No prophylaxis, with prompt treatment of future infections
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is supported for low grade reflux and for a single infection, but this child has had two febrile infections with grade IV reflux, where recurrence risk and renal scarring risk are both substantially higher. No prophylaxis would be appropriate for grade I or II reflux after a single infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Referral for ureteric reimplantation surgery now
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for breakthrough febrile infection on prophylaxis, progressive scarring, or reflux persisting beyond early childhood, because most reflux resolves as the intravesical ureteric tunnel lengthens with growth. Reimplantation would be correct after failure of medical management. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Nightly low dose oral trimethoprim prophylaxis
options.rationale: Recurrent febrile infection combined with high grade dilating reflux is the subgroup in which prophylaxis reduces recurrence, even though trials show no benefit for low grade reflux or a single infection. Trimethoprim is the standard Australian agent at a quarter of the treatment dose, given nightly while the reflux is expected to resolve spontaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Nightly low dose oral amoxicillin prophylaxis
options.rationale: Amoxicillin achieves poor urinary concentrations relative to resistance rates in Escherichia coli and rapidly selects resistant organisms, so it is not used for urinary prophylaxis beyond the neonatal period. It is the preferred prophylactic agent only in infants under about 6 weeks, where trimethoprim is avoided. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Dimercaptosuccinic acid scan before any decision
options.rationale: A cortical scan documents established scarring but does not alter the decision to start prophylaxis in a child who already has proven high grade reflux and recurrent febrile infection. It would be useful later to establish a baseline of renal parenchymal damage for long-term follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Vesicoureteric reflux was historically treated aggressively on the assumption that reflux caused scarring and that preventing infection would prevent renal failure, but randomised trials substantially narrowed the indications for both prophylaxis and surgery. The current position is that prophylaxis provides a modest absolute reduction in recurrence concentrated in children with dilating grades III to V reflux and recurrent febrile infection, while conferring little benefit at lower grades and selecting for resistant organisms in everyone. This child sits squarely in the group where the evidence still supports treatment. Australian practice reserves the micturating cystourethrogram for atypical or recurrent infection rather than performing it routinely, and its findings here directly determine management. Most reflux resolves spontaneously as the child grows and the intravesical ureteric tunnel lengthens, so prophylaxis is a holding measure rather than a permanent commitment, and bladder and bowel dysfunction should be addressed once the child is toilet trained.
key_points: Prophylaxis benefit concentrates in dilating grade III to V reflux with recurrent febrile infection
Trimethoprim at a quarter of the treatment dose nightly is the standard Australian prophylactic agent
Amoxicillin is unsuitable for prophylaxis beyond the neonatal period because of resistance selection
Surgery follows breakthrough febrile infection on prophylaxis or progressive scarring, not initial diagnosis
Most reflux resolves spontaneously with growth, so prophylaxis is an interim measure
explanation.pearls: Breakthrough febrile urinary infection while adherent to nightly trimethoprim is the specific trigger that converts medical management into a surgical referral, so document adherence before attributing a recurrence to prophylaxis failure.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing structural clubfoot from positional foot deformity in the newborn and the timing of Ponseti casting
stem:
You are the resident reviewing a 3-day-old boy on the postnatal ward before discharge. His mother says both of his feet 'turn in and point down' and that they have looked this way since birth.

He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy with normal liquor volume. Birth weight was 3300 g and he is feeding well.

On examination both forefeet are adducted and both heels are held in varus and equinus. Neither foot can be brought up past 20 degrees of plantarflexion despite firm pressure, and there is a deep transverse crease across each medial arch. Both calves are visibly thinner than expected for his size. Hip abduction is full and symmetrical with no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral forefoot adduction with hindfoot varus and equinus; neither foot correctable past 20 degrees of plantarflexion
data_table.Skin and soft tissue: Deep transverse medial arch crease bilaterally; bilateral calf wasting
data_table.Hips: Full symmetrical abduction, Ortolani and Barlow negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for Ponseti serial casting to start this week
options.rationale: Rigid equinovarus that will not correct past plantarflexion, with a deep medial crease and calf wasting, is structural talipes equinovarus rather than a positional deformity. Ponseti casting is most effective when started in the first weeks of life while the ligaments are still highly responsive to maternal relaxin, so referral is made before discharge rather than deferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Teach the parents passive stretching exercises and review the feet at six weeks
options.rationale: Passive stretching is the treatment for positional talipes, which is soft and fully correctable to a neutral dorsiflexed position at the cot side. These feet are fixed in equinus with skin creases and calf wasting, and six weeks of stretching would waste the window in which casting works best. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Arrange a foot and ankle ultrasound before deciding on orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Talipes equinovarus is a clinical diagnosis made on rigidity and the classic crease and calf findings, and imaging of the foot does not change the decision to cast. Imaging is reserved for atypical or syndromic feet being planned for surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Apply overnight below-knee splints and refer to orthopaedics at three months
options.rationale: Bracing has a role only after the deformity has been corrected by casting, as the Ponseti maintenance phase with a foot abduction orthosis. Splinting an uncorrected rigid foot achieves nothing and a three month delay materially worsens the number of casts needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound at six weeks and refer if the feet remain deformed
options.rationale: Hip imaging is the right reflex when a foot deformity coexists with risk factors or an abnormal hip examination, but abduction here is full and symmetrical with negative Ortolani and Barlow testing. Deferring the foot referral to the hip scan appointment delays the time-critical intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Foot deformity in the newborn splits into positional deformity, which is supple and self-correcting, and structural talipes equinovarus, which is rigid and needs treatment. The three findings that mark the structural form are failure to correct the equinus passively, deep medial and posterior skin creases, and wasting of the calf, all of which reflect a genuinely short and abnormal posteromedial soft tissue complex. The Ponseti method uses weekly manipulation and above-knee casting, usually followed by a percutaneous tendo-Achilles tenotomy, and then a foot abduction orthosis worn for several years. Treatment started in the first weeks of life needs fewer casts and achieves better long-term function than treatment deferred to later infancy. Untreated clubfoot leads to weight bearing on the lateral border of the foot with callus, pain and disability.
key_points: Rigidity, creases and calf wasting separate structural talipes from positional deformity
Ponseti casting should begin in the first weeks of life, not after a period of observation
Imaging of the foot does not guide the decision to cast
Bracing belongs to the maintenance phase after casting has corrected the deformity
Examine the hips in every infant with a foot deformity, but a normal hip examination does not delay foot referral
explanation.pearls: The Ponseti maintenance orthosis is worn 23 hours a day for the first 3 months after casting and then at night until about age 4; non-adherence to the brace is the single largest driver of recurrence.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
BMJ Best Practice: Congenital talipes equinovarus

subtopic_detail: Minimum interval between two parenteral live vaccines when catching up an incompletely vaccinated child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15-month-old girl who arrived in Australia six weeks ago. Her mother brings a handwritten card from their previous country listing three doses of a diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis containing vaccine and two doses of polio vaccine, with no record of any measles containing vaccine.

Ten days ago the family attended a different practice, where she was given a measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. The mother now wants 'everything else she has missed' done today so the child can start childcare.

The girl is well, afebrile and thriving, with no immunosuppressive conditions and no medications. She has had no blood products or immunoglobulin. You determine that she still requires varicella vaccine and a Haemophilus influenzae type b containing vaccine.

data_table.Vaccines documented: Three doses diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine, two doses polio vaccine
data_table.Recent vaccine: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine given 10 days ago at another practice
data_table.Still required today: Varicella vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b containing vaccine
data_table.Examination: Well and afebrile, growth on the 50th centile, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the varicella vaccine?

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine today at a separate injection site
options.rationale: Two parenteral live vaccines must be given either on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart, and 10 days falls inside that window. Giving it today risks interferon mediated blunting of the varicella response, which would then require a repeat dose. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine at least four weeks after the measles vaccine
options.rationale: Where two parenteral live vaccines are not given on the same day, the minimum interval is 4 weeks, so the varicella dose is scheduled for at least 28 days after the measles containing vaccine. The Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine is inactivated and can be given today without waiting. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Check varicella and measles serology first and vaccinate only if she is not immune
options.rationale: Serological testing is not required before catch-up vaccination in a well child with no documented disease, and vaccinating a person who is already immune is safe. Pre-vaccination serology is reserved for specific groups such as some hepatitis B and varicella exposures in adults. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine one week from now with paracetamol cover
options.rationale: One week still falls short of the 4 week minimum interval between two parenteral live vaccines. Routine prophylactic paracetamol is also not recommended because it can reduce antibody responses and is reserved for specific meningococcal B schedules. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Repeat the measles vaccine today and give the varicella vaccine in three months
options.rationale: The measles containing dose 10 days ago was valid and counts towards her schedule, so repeating it adds no benefit. Three months is the interval used after an immunoglobulin or blood product exposure, which she has not had. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Catch-up schedules turn on a small number of interval rules rather than on the individual vaccine. Inactivated vaccines can be co-administered with anything and have no minimum spacing from other vaccines, so the Haemophilus influenzae type b dose proceeds today. Two parenteral live vaccines interact through a transient interferon response, so they are given on the same day or separated by at least 4 weeks; if the interval is breached the second dose is invalid and must be repeated. Live oral vaccines such as rotavirus are exempt from this rule. Children under 10 years presenting for catch-up can complete a full schedule relatively quickly because most remaining antigens are inactivated.
key_points: Two parenteral live vaccines: same day, or at least 4 weeks apart
A dose given inside the 4 week window is invalid and must be repeated
Inactivated vaccines have no minimum interval from other vaccines
Pre-vaccination serology is not routine in catch-up of a well child
Live oral vaccines are not subject to the 4 week parenteral live vaccine rule
explanation.pearls: Tuberculin skin testing is suppressed by measles containing vaccine: do the skin test on the same day as the vaccine or wait at least 4 weeks, otherwise a false negative is likely.

subtopic_detail: Choice of scabicide in an infant below the minimum age for topical permethrin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 6-week-old boy whose mother says he has become 'covered in angry spots' over the past fortnight and cries and squirms most of the night.

He was born at term and is breastfed and thriving. His mother has had an intensely itchy rash on her wrists and between her fingers for about six weeks, and his 4-year-old sister has a similar itchy rash.

On examination there are erythematous papules and pustules scattered over the trunk, and vesicles and burrows involving both palms and both soles as well as the scalp. Skin scrapings taken in clinic show a mite and several ova on light microscopy.

data_table.Examination: Papules and pustules on trunk; vesicles and burrows on palms, soles and scalp
data_table.Investigations: Skin scraping microscopy shows a mite and ova
data_table.Household: Mother and 4-year-old sister both have an itchy rash of about six weeks duration
data_table.Growth and feeding: Exclusively breastfed, weight tracking on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Apply permethrin 5 per cent cream to the infant and treat all household contacts
options.rationale: Permethrin 5 per cent is the standard Australian first-line scabicide but is not recommended below 2 months of age, and this infant is 6 weeks old. It is the right agent for the mother and sister, who should be treated on the same day. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

options.text: Apply benzyl benzoate 25 per cent lotion to the infant and all household contacts
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is highly irritant on infant skin and at full strength risks a severe chemical dermatitis, so it is not used in this age group. It is a second-line agent for older children and adults when permethrin has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply sulfur 5 per cent ointment to the infant and treat all household contacts
options.rationale: Sulfur in white soft paraffin is the preferred scabicide below 2 months of age, applied to the whole body including scalp, face, palms and soles for three consecutive nights. Simultaneous treatment of every household member on the same day is what prevents the cycle of reinfestation from the untreated mother and sister. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral ivermectin to the infant and all household contacts
options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is not used under 15 kg because safety data in small infants are lacking, and it is reserved for crusted scabies, outbreaks or treatment failure. It would be a reasonable adjunct for adult contacts in a crusted scabies scenario, which this is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply hydrocortisone 1 per cent to the infant and treat the contacts with permethrin
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats the eczematous reaction but leaves the mite alive, and used alone it can produce the poorly inflamed, widely disseminated picture of scabies incognito. Steroid has a place only alongside a scabicide for persistent post-scabetic itch. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult disease in both distribution and treatment. Infants characteristically involve the scalp, face, palms and soles, sites that are deliberately spared when treating adults, so the application instructions change with age. Permethrin 5 per cent is the Australian first-line agent from 2 months onward, and sulfur preparations fill the gap below that age. Treatment fails far more often because contacts were not treated simultaneously than because the drug was wrong, so every household member and any regular carer is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms. Itch persists for 2 to 4 weeks after successful treatment and is not by itself evidence of failure.
key_points: Permethrin 5 per cent is first line from 2 months of age; below that use sulfur in white soft paraffin
In infants apply the scabicide to scalp, face, palms and soles as well as the body
Treat every household member on the same day, symptomatic or not
Oral ivermectin is avoided under 15 kg and is reserved for crusted scabies or failure
Post-scabetic itch lasting 2 to 4 weeks does not mean treatment failed
explanation.pearls: Wash bedding and clothing in hot water on the day of treatment; items that cannot be washed are sealed in a plastic bag for 72 hours, which exceeds the time a mite survives off human skin.

subtopic_detail: Management of cyanotic breath-holding spells when iron studies are abnormal
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric assessment unit reviewing an 18-month-old boy brought in after an episode at home. His mother says he was told he could not have a biscuit, cried hard for about fifteen seconds, then 'went silent, turned blue around the lips and flopped'. He was limp for roughly ten seconds, then took a breath and was crying and reaching for her within half a minute.

There have been six such episodes in four months, every one of them beginning with a period of prolonged crying after frustration or a minor injury. He has never had an episode during sleep, at rest or during exercise, and there has been no jerking of the limbs and no incontinence.

He is developmentally normal and drinks about a litre of cow milk daily. Cardiovascular examination is normal with equal volume femoral pulses. Blood tests are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 120/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 68 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 microgram/L (15-150), electrolytes and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal tone and development, normal heart sounds, equal volume femoral pulses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Every episode has been preceded by a prolonged cry with an identifiable provocation, which is the hallmark of a breath-holding spell rather than a seizure. Electroencephalography would be indicated if events occurred without a trigger, during sleep, or with a prolonged postictal phase, none of which applies here. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for an echocardiogram and exercise testing
options.rationale: Structural heart disease is suggested by events at rest or on exertion, a murmur or abnormal pulses, and cardiovascular examination and femoral pulses are normal. Echocardiography is the wrong test for a child whose episodes are reliably provoked by crying. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Commence oral sodium valproate and review the frequency of episodes in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antiseizure medication has no role in breath-holding spells because the events are reflex in origin rather than epileptic. Valproate would additionally be a poor first choice in any young child given its hepatic and metabolic risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral iron supplementation and review the frequency of episodes in eight weeks
options.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with a ferritin of 7 microgram/L confirms iron deficiency, driven here by an intake of about a litre of cow milk daily, and treating it reduces both the frequency and severity of breath-holding spells. Iron is given for at least 3 months to refill stores, with parental reassurance about the benign natural history and first aid positioning. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Arrange a 12 lead electrocardiogram and withhold treatment until the result is available
options.rationale: An electrocardiogram is a reasonable screen when spells are of the pallid type, occur without a preceding cry, or there is a family history of sudden death, and it can be done in parallel rather than as a reason to withhold iron. Here the cyanotic phenotype with a consistent crying trigger makes a primary arrhythmia a remote possibility. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

explanation.summary: Breath-holding spells affect up to 5 per cent of young children and divide into a cyanotic type, provoked by anger or frustration, and a pallid type, provoked by pain or fright and mediated by vagal asystole. The diagnosis rests on the stereotyped sequence of provocation, cry, colour change and brief loss of tone with rapid recovery, and investigations are directed at the two things that genuinely change management: iron deficiency and, in atypical or pallid cases, a cardiac conduction abnormality. Iron deficiency is present in a large proportion of affected children and correcting it reduces spell frequency, which is the only pharmacological intervention with a reasonable evidence base. Parents are taught to lay the child flat on their side and let the event end on its own, avoiding shaking, mouth-to-mouth or cold water. The condition resolves spontaneously by school age and does not increase the risk of epilepsy.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical: a provocation, a prolonged cry, then colour change and loss of tone with rapid recovery
Check a full blood count and ferritin in every child with breath-holding spells
Iron replacement reduces spell frequency and is the only drug treatment with useful evidence
Reserve electroencephalography for events without a trigger, during sleep, or with prolonged recovery
Consider an electrocardiogram for pallid spells or a family history of sudden death
explanation.pearls: Cow milk intake above 500 mL per day in a toddler is itself a cause of iron deficiency through occult gut blood loss and calcium mediated inhibition of iron absorption; capping milk at 500 mL is part of the treatment, not an afterthought.

subtopic_detail: Threshold for specialist assessment of an asymptomatic murmur first heard in early infancy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar performing a 6-week health check on a 5-week-old girl. Her mother has no concerns and says she feeds for about twenty minutes on each side without stopping to rest, and has never gone sweaty or dusky during a feed.

She was born at 38 weeks by elective caesarean section for breech presentation. Birth weight was 3200 g and she now weighs 4100 g. Her newborn examination at 12 hours of age was documented as normal with no murmur heard.

On examination she is pink and alert. There is a grade 2/6 systolic murmur heard at the left sternal edge with no radiation and no thrill. Heart sounds are normal with a single second sound. Femoral pulses are equal in volume to the brachial pulses. Pre-ductal and post-ductal oxygen saturations are both 99 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99 per cent pre-ductal and post-ductal, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Cardiovascular examination: Grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, no thrill, no radiation, normal single second heart sound
data_table.Pulses: Femoral pulses equal in volume to brachial pulses
data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3200 g, current weight 4100 g, tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the murmur at the twelve month health check
options.rationale: The features that allow a murmur to be called innocent at the bedside, such as a vibratory Still murmur that softens on standing, are not reliably assessable in early infancy. A murmur appearing after a documented normal newborn examination is exactly the pattern seen when a ventricular septal defect becomes audible as pulmonary vascular resistance falls. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and an electrocardiogram before deciding on referral
options.rationale: Chest radiography and electrocardiography are insensitive for the defects that present this way and a normal pair of tests does not exclude a significant lesion. Echocardiography has superseded both as the investigation that settles the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Measure four limb blood pressures and reassure the parents if the readings are equal
options.rationale: Four limb pressures screen for coarctation, and the equal volume femoral pulses already make that diagnosis unlikely, so a normal result would not explain the murmur. Excluding one lesion is not the same as characterising the murmur. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Review her in the practice in three months and refer only if the murmur persists
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate for an asymptomatic murmur with clearly innocent characteristics in an older child, not for a new murmur under 1 year of age. A left-to-right shunt can drive heart failure and faltering growth well within a three month window. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Refer for paediatric cardiology review with echocardiography within the next few weeks
options.rationale: Any murmur first detected under 1 year of age warrants specialist assessment with echocardiography, because a substantial proportion represent structural disease and bedside criteria for innocence do not perform well at this age. She is well and growing, so the referral is timely rather than emergency, and the family can be told that many such murmurs prove to be small defects or normal flow. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

explanation.summary: Murmurs are heard in a large minority of children at some point, and most are innocent, but the prior probability of structural disease is far higher in the first year of life than later in childhood. The newborn examination misses lesions whose murmur depends on a pressure gradient that only develops as pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first weeks, so a ventricular septal defect or an atrioventricular septal defect commonly declares itself at the 6 week check rather than at birth. Features that would prompt urgent rather than routine referral include poor feeding with sweating or tachypnoea, faltering growth, a diastolic murmur, a thrill, absent or delayed femoral pulses, cyanosis or an abnormal second heart sound. Echocardiography is the investigation of choice; chest radiography and electrocardiography lack the sensitivity to exclude significant disease. In an older child with a classic Still murmur, normal pulses and no symptoms, reassurance without imaging is entirely reasonable.
key_points: A murmur first heard under 1 year of age warrants specialist assessment with echocardiography
A normal newborn check does not exclude a shunt lesion that becomes audible weeks later
Chest radiography and electrocardiography are not sensitive enough to exclude structural disease
Red flags for urgent referral include feeding difficulty, faltering growth, diastolic murmur, thrill, weak femoral pulses or cyanosis
Bedside criteria for an innocent murmur are reliable in older children, not in infants
explanation.pearls: A ventricular septal defect murmur is loudest when the defect is small: as the defect gets larger the gradient falls, so a quiet murmur with a loud pulmonary second sound and tachypnoea is more worrying than a loud isolated murmur.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of paediatric heart murmurs

subtopic_detail: Adolescent knee pain with obligate external rotation on hip flexion and the weight bearing decision
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy who has had a dull ache in his left knee for about seven weeks. His mother says he has been walking 'with his foot turned out' and no longer plays soccer at lunchtime.

He recalls no injury. The pain is worse after activity and settles with rest. He has not been febrile and has not been unwell in any other way. His weight is above the 97th centile and his height is on the 25th centile.

On examination the left knee is not warm, has no effusion and moves through a full painless range. The tibial tuberosity is not tender. When you flex the left hip the thigh rolls into external rotation and you cannot flex it in the neutral plane, and internal rotation of the left hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right.

data_table.Knee examination: No effusion, no warmth, full painless range of movement, tibial tuberosity not tender
data_table.Hip examination: Obligate external rotation of the left thigh on hip flexion; left internal rotation 10 degrees, right 40 degrees
data_table.Growth: Weight above the 97th centile, height on the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange knee radiographs and refer to physiotherapy for quadriceps strengthening
options.rationale: Imaging the knee answers the wrong question, because the knee examination is entirely normal and the pain is referred along the obturator nerve from the hip. Loading the joint through a strengthening program before the hip is imaged risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Advise activity modification with simple analgesia and review him again in six weeks
options.rationale: Activity modification is the treatment for Osgood-Schlatter disease, which produces tenderness localised to the tibial tuberosity that is absent here. A six week delay in a slipped upper femoral epiphysis substantially increases the risk of slip progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Keep him non-weight bearing and arrange urgent orthopaedic review with pelvic films
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation in an overweight adolescent is the classic sign of a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which needs anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs and surgical fixation. Non-weight bearing from the moment of suspicion is the intervention that protects the epiphyseal blood supply while transfer is arranged. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Arrange an urgent knee ultrasound and aspirate any joint effusion that is identified
options.rationale: Aspiration is the right move for a suspected septic joint, which presents with fever, an effusion and pain through a restricted arc, none of which is present over a seven week history. Ultrasound of a clinically normal knee will not identify the proximal femoral pathology. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and review him once the report arrives
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging of the knee would be reasonable for mechanical knee symptoms such as locking or giving way with a normal radiograph, but the knee here is normal on examination. The delay inherent in outpatient magnetic resonance imaging is also unacceptable when the hip is the problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp

explanation.summary: A slipped upper femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and is missed most often because roughly a quarter of children present with knee or distal thigh pain and no hip complaint at all. The peak age is 10 to 16 years, obesity is the dominant risk factor, and bilateral disease eventually occurs in about a fifth of cases. The single most useful bedside sign is obligate external rotation: as the hip is flexed the thigh rotates outward because the metaphysis has displaced anteriorly relative to the epiphysis. Radiographs must include a frog-leg lateral view, since an early slip can look normal on the anteroposterior film alone. Management is in situ screw fixation, and the key determinant of outcome is whether the slip remains stable, so any child with a suspected slip is made non-weight bearing immediately.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain and a normal knee
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with loss of internal rotation is the hallmark sign
Order anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvic radiographs, not knee films
Make the child non-weight bearing from the moment the diagnosis is suspected
Obesity is the leading risk factor and about 20 per cent eventually slip on the other side
explanation.pearls: On the anteroposterior pelvis, Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck should intersect part of the epiphysis; if it passes entirely above the epiphysis the slip is present even when the femoral head still looks round.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute hip pain and limp
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Frequency of slit lamp screening in antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular juvenile arthritis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a rheumatology clinic. A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen, warm left knee for four months and a swollen right ankle for six weeks. Her mother says she is stiff and clingy in the mornings and loosens up by mid-morning, and that she has not been febrile at any point.

There is no rash and no lymphadenopathy. Both eyes look white and quiet and she has never complained that they hurt or that light bothers her, and she does not rub them.

Investigations show an antinuclear antibody titre of 1:320 with a negative rheumatoid factor. Inflammatory markers are mildly raised. A diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is made and intra-articular corticosteroid injection is planned.

data_table.Joints: Left knee and right ankle swollen and warm; morning stiffness easing by mid-morning
data_table.Eyes: White and quiet on external inspection; no pain, photophobia or eye rubbing reported
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody 1:320, rheumatoid factor negative, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 15)
data_table.Systemic features: No fever, no rash, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ophthalmic surveillance plan?

options.text: Arrange ophthalmology review only if she develops a red or a painful eye
options.rationale: The uveitis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is characteristically chronic, anterior and completely asymptomatic, so waiting for a red or sore eye means waiting for a complication. Symptom-triggered review is appropriate in the acute anterior uveitis of an older human leucocyte antigen B27 positive child, which is painful and photophobic. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange annual visual acuity testing by an optometrist from the time of school entry
options.rationale: Visual acuity is preserved until posterior synechiae, band keratopathy or cataract have already formed, so acuity testing detects the disease too late. The eye also needs magnified examination of the anterior chamber, which an acuity chart cannot provide. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange slit lamp examination now and then repeat it every twelve months
options.rationale: Twelve monthly screening is the interval used for the lowest risk groups, such as older children with rheumatoid factor positive polyarticular disease or systemic onset disease. Applying it to a young antinuclear antibody positive girl leaves a year in which silent inflammation can scar the anterior chamber. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange fundoscopy at each rheumatology visit and refer her if it looks abnormal
options.rationale: Fundoscopy examines the posterior segment, whereas this disease inflames the anterior chamber, where cells and flare are only visible on slit lamp examination. A normal fundus therefore provides false reassurance. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

options.text: Arrange slit lamp examination now and then repeat it every three months
options.rationale: Onset under 7 years with oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody defines the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, and three monthly slit lamp screening is the recommended interval for the first several years. Screening continues on this schedule even when the arthritis is in remission, because eye and joint activity are not correlated. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis complicates up to a fifth of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and is the main cause of preventable visual loss in this population. Risk is stratified by three variables: subtype, age at onset and antinuclear antibody status, with young antinuclear antibody positive girls with oligoarticular disease at the top of the risk table and screened three monthly. The inflammation is silent, so the child gives no warning and the first sign may be an irregular pupil from posterior synechiae or a reduced red reflex from cataract. Screening intervals lengthen with time since diagnosis and with increasing age, but surveillance continues for years and is not stopped when the joints settle. Established uveitis is treated with topical corticosteroid and mydriatics, escalating to methotrexate and then adalimumab if control is not achieved.
key_points: Risk stratification uses subtype, age at onset and antinuclear antibody status
Antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular disease with onset under 7 years is screened three monthly
The uveitis is asymptomatic, so symptom-triggered review is unsafe
Slit lamp examination is required; acuity testing and fundoscopy both miss it
Eye and joint disease activity are independent, so screening continues in joint remission
explanation.pearls: Adalimumab combined with methotrexate outperforms methotrexate alone for refractory juvenile idiopathic arthritis associated uveitis; etanercept is the anti-tumour necrosis factor agent that does not work for the eye disease despite controlling the joints.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

subtopic_detail: Urgency of referral for a unilateral white pupillary reflex noticed on family photographs
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 14-month-old girl whose father shows you four photographs taken over the past two months. In each one her right pupil looks white while the left shows the usual red glow of a camera flash.

Her mother adds that over the last three weeks the right eye 'drifts in towards her nose' when she is tired, and that she seems to bump into things on that side. The girl was born at term, has no relevant family history and her development is on track.

On examination visual behaviour is asymmetric: she objects when you occlude the left eye but not when you occlude the right. The right red reflex is dull and pale compared with a bright red reflex on the left. The cornea is clear and the eye is white and not watering, and there is no proptosis. Cover testing reveals an inward shift of the right eye.

data_table.Ocular examination: Right red reflex dull and pale, left bright red; cornea clear, conjunctiva white, no watering, no proptosis
data_table.Visual behaviour: Objects to occlusion of the left eye but not the right
data_table.Cover test: Inward shift of the right eye on cover testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ophthalmology for examination under anaesthesia within this week
options.rationale: An asymmetric white reflex with a new squint in a toddler demands dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia at a tertiary centre within days, because retinoblastoma is the diagnosis that must be excluded first and survival and eye salvage both fall sharply with delay. Squint developing in the second year is a recognised second presentation of the same disease once central vision has been lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer to orthoptics for a squint assessment at the next available clinic appointment
options.rationale: Treating this as an isolated squint ignores the abnormal red reflex, which is the finding that changes the differential entirely. Routine orthoptic referral would be right for a comitant squint with symmetrical bright red reflexes and normal visual behaviour. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Arrange an outpatient orbital ultrasound and review her with the result in a month
options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate an intraocular mass with calcification but it neither excludes small tumours nor stages the eye, and a month of waiting is unacceptable. Imaging is arranged by the ophthalmology service alongside examination under anaesthesia, not instead of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Reassure the parents that the appearance is a camera flash artefact and review as needed
options.rationale: A pseudoleukocoria from off-axis flash is symmetrical or varies between photographs, whereas this is reproducibly unilateral across four images and is confirmed by a dull red reflex on examination. Reassurance in this setting is the commonest route to a delayed diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Prescribe patching of the left eye and refer to ophthalmology within the next three months
options.rationale: Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once a structural cause of reduced vision has been excluded, and patching the better eye here would leave a child functionally blind while a tumour goes untreated. Amblyopia therapy follows the fundus examination, never precedes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

explanation.summary: Leukocoria is an abnormal white pupillary reflex and is the presenting sign in roughly 60 per cent of retinoblastomas, with squint accounting for a further 20 per cent. Other causes include congenital cataract, persistent fetal vasculature, Coats disease, toxocariasis and retinopathy of prematurity, and all of them warrant prompt ophthalmological assessment because visual development is time critical. Parents commonly notice the abnormality in photographs before any clinician does, and a parental report of a white reflex should be believed even if the reflex looks normal in a brightly lit consulting room. Examination under anaesthesia with full mydriasis and scleral indentation is the definitive assessment, since a struggling toddler cannot be adequately examined awake. Retinoblastoma is heritable in about 40 per cent of cases, so genetic counselling and examination of siblings follow the diagnosis.
key_points: Compare the red reflexes of both eyes in the same view; asymmetry is the abnormal finding
Leukocoria and new squint are the two commonest presentations of retinoblastoma
Believe a parental report of a white reflex in photographs even if your examination looks normal
Definitive assessment is dilated examination under anaesthesia at a tertiary centre within days
Never patch an eye for presumed amblyopia before a structural cause has been excluded
explanation.pearls: Around 40 per cent of retinoblastoma is heritable through a germline RB1 mutation, and those children need lifelong surveillance for second primary cancers, particularly osteosarcoma, which is why genetic testing is arranged at diagnosis rather than later.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

subtopic_detail: Score threshold for starting pharmacological treatment of neonatal abstinence and the feeding decision
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward caring for a 4-day-old boy born at 38 weeks to a mother who has been on supervised methadone 60 mg daily for two years through an opioid treatment program. Urine drug screening at booking and at delivery detected methadone only.

He was born by normal vaginal delivery weighing 2900 g. He is rooming in with his mother in a quiet, dimly lit single room, is being swaddled and held skin to skin, and is breastfeeding every two to three hours.

Over the last twelve hours the midwife has recorded modified Finnegan scores of 9, 10 and 9 on three consecutive four hourly assessments. He is tremulous when disturbed, has a high pitched cry that settles with holding, sleeps less than an hour after feeds and has had three loose stools. Glucose, electrolytes and temperature are all within normal limits and there are no seizures.

data_table.Scores: Modified Finnegan scores 9, 10 and 9 on three consecutive four hourly assessments
data_table.Clinical features: Tremor on handling, high pitched cry settling with holding, sleep less than one hour after feeds, three loose stools
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose, electrolytes and temperature within normal limits; no seizure activity
data_table.Care to date: Rooming in, quiet dim environment, swaddling, skin to skin, breastfeeding two to three hourly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral phenobarbital, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is the agent of choice when the withdrawal is from a non-opioid sedative or when polysubstance exposure is documented, and it is added as a second agent if morphine alone fails. Using it first for pure methadone withdrawal treats the wrong receptor and brings unnecessary sedation. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Commence oral morphine, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Three consecutive modified Finnegan scores of 8 or more is the trigger for pharmacological treatment, and oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal because it replaces the same receptor activity and is weaned predictably. Breastfeeding continues because methadone transfers into milk in very small quantities and reduces both the severity and duration of withdrawal. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Continue non-pharmacological care alone and rescore him on four hourly cycles
options.rationale: Optimised non-pharmacological care is the foundation of management and is already in place, but it has not held the scores below threshold across three consecutive assessments. Persisting with it alone risks poor feeding, weight loss and seizures. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Commence oral clonidine, continue rooming in and support continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Clonidine is an adjunct used to reduce total opioid exposure or when morphine weaning stalls, not a first-line single agent. Its hypotensive and bradycardic effects also require closer monitoring than a postnatal ward usually provides. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

options.text: Advise formula feeding, transfer him to the nursery and commence oral morphine
options.rationale: Separating mother and baby worsens withdrawal scores and removes the single most effective non-pharmacological intervention, and stopping breastfeeding removes the small protective opioid transfer through milk. Formula feeding is advised for maternal human immunodeficiency virus infection or ongoing unsanctioned drug use, neither of which applies here. (Source: NSW Health: Neonatal abstinence syndrome)

explanation.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome follows in utero exposure to opioids and presents with central nervous system irritability, autonomic overactivity and gastrointestinal dysfunction, typically within 24 to 72 hours for heroin and later, up to 5 to 7 days, for methadone because of its longer half-life. Scoring systems such as the modified Finnegan tool exist to make the decision to treat reproducible rather than impressionistic, and the standard triggers are three consecutive scores of 8 or more or two consecutive scores of 12 or more. Non-pharmacological care, meaning rooming in, minimal handling, a quiet dim environment, swaddling and frequent small feeds, reduces the proportion of babies who need drug treatment and is never abandoned when medication starts. Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal, weaned by protocol once scores have been controlled for 24 to 48 hours. Breastfeeding is actively encouraged for mothers stable on methadone or buprenorphine, and babies exposed to methadone need observation for at least 5 days before discharge.
key_points: Treat when three consecutive modified Finnegan scores are 8 or more, or two are 12 or more
Oral morphine is first line for opioid withdrawal; phenobarbital is for sedative or polysubstance exposure
Non-pharmacological care continues alongside drug treatment, it is not replaced by it
Breastfeeding is encouraged on stable methadone or buprenorphine and shortens withdrawal
Methadone exposed babies are observed for at least 5 days because onset is delayed
explanation.pearls: Naloxone is contraindicated at the birth of an opioid exposed baby even when the baby is apnoeic, because it precipitates acute withdrawal and seizures; ventilate instead and let the exposure wear off.

subtopic_detail: Imaging and drainage decision in parapneumonic collection failing 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl who was admitted 48 hours ago with right sided pneumonia and started on intravenous benzylpenicillin. Her mother says she is 'no better at all' and is still hot and breathing fast.

She remains febrile to 39.2°C with ongoing tachypnoea and now lies curled towards her right side and cries when moved. Her oxygen requirement has risen from room air to 2 L/min by nasal prongs to keep saturations at 94 per cent.

On examination there is stony dullness to percussion over the right lower zone with absent breath sounds and reduced chest wall movement on that side. A repeat chest radiograph shows opacification of the right hemithorax to the level of the hilum with a meniscus. Blood cultures taken on admission remain negative and inflammatory markers have risen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 94 per cent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 39.2°C
data_table.Examination: Stony dullness and absent breath sounds over the right lower zone with reduced chest wall movement
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows right hemithorax opacification to hilar level with a meniscus
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 218 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 24.6 x10^9/L (4.0-12.0), blood cultures negative at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the intravenous antibiotics for a further 48 hours and repeat the chest film
options.rationale: Persistent fever, rising inflammatory markers and a rising oxygen requirement at 48 hours define antibiotic failure, and a loculated collection will not resolve with more of the same therapy. Continued observation alone is reasonable only for a small free-flowing effusion in a child who is improving. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Arrange contrast computed tomography of the chest and refer her to cardiothoracic surgery
options.rationale: Computed tomography adds radiation without changing the initial drainage decision and is reserved for suspected necrotising pneumonia, bronchopleural fistula or failure of chest drainage. Ultrasound answers the question of loculation better and with no ionising radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Perform a diagnostic pleural tap and discharge her home on oral antibiotics afterwards
options.rationale: A diagnostic tap without a drain leaves the collection in place, and a child on supplemental oxygen with a rising C-reactive protein is not dischargeable. Simple aspiration alone is an option only for a small, free-flowing, non-purulent effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Arrange chest ultrasound then insert a chest drain with an intrapleural fibrinolytic agent
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the imaging of choice to size the collection and demonstrate septations, and a large loculated empyema in a child failing antibiotics is drained with a small bore catheter plus intrapleural urokinase or alteplase. This combination shortens hospital stay and has outcomes equivalent to primary video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery at lower cost. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Change to intravenous vancomycin and meropenem and repeat the blood cultures every day
options.rationale: Broadening antibiotic cover does not address the mechanical problem of a loculated collection that antibiotics penetrate poorly, though cover is usually widened to include Staphylococcus aureus at the time of drainage. Blood cultures are positive in only a minority of paediatric empyema and repeating them daily will not guide management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: A parapneumonic effusion complicates a significant minority of childhood bacterial pneumonias and progresses through an exudative phase, a fibrinopurulent phase with septation, and finally an organising phase with a fibrous peel. The decision point is not the presence of fluid but whether the child is failing treatment, judged by persistent fever beyond 48 hours, rising inflammatory markers, an increasing oxygen requirement or a rising respiratory rate. Ultrasound is the first imaging test because it distinguishes free fluid from septated collections, estimates volume and marks a safe drainage site, all without radiation. Small bore pigtail drainage with intrapleural fibrinolysis is the standard first intervention in Australian paediatric centres, with video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery reserved for failure. Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the commonest organism but Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are over-represented in empyema, so antibiotic cover is broadened at the time of drainage.
key_points: Failure at 48 hours means persistent fever, rising markers or a rising oxygen requirement
Ultrasound is the imaging of choice; computed tomography is reserved for complications
Small bore drain plus intrapleural fibrinolytic is the standard first intervention
Broadening antibiotics alone does not treat a loculated collection
Cover Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes once empyema is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Long-term lung function after paediatric empyema is essentially normal even when the radiograph remains abnormal for months, so persistent opacification at discharge is not a reason to extend antibiotics or re-drain.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parapneumonic effusion and empyema

subtopic_detail: Isolated breast development in a toddler with normal growth velocity and unadvanced bone age
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 2-year-old girl referred because of breast development. Her mother noticed 'small lumps under both nipples' at around 18 months and says they have waxed and waned since, being more obvious some weeks than others.

There has been no change in body odour, no acne, no pubic or axillary hair and no vaginal bleeding. She takes no medications and there are no creams, gels or supplements in the house.

On examination she has Tanner stage 2 breast tissue bilaterally with no areolar enlargement or pigmentation, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair and no clitoromegaly. Her height has tracked steadily along the 60th centile across four measurements since 12 months of age, giving a growth velocity of 8 cm per year. A bone age radiograph reports a skeletal age of 2 years 1 month against a chronological age of 2 years 2 months.

data_table.Pubertal staging: Tanner stage 2 breast bilaterally without areolar enlargement, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, no clitoromegaly
data_table.Growth: Height tracking along the 60th centile across four measurements; growth velocity 8 cm per year
data_table.Imaging: Bone age 2 years 1 month against chronological age 2 years 2 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test and repeat the bone age film
options.rationale: Stimulation testing is used to confirm central activation when the clinical picture already suggests true precocious puberty, meaning progressive staging with accelerated growth and an advanced bone age. Testing a child whose skeletal age matches her chronological age generates cost, distress and false positives without altering management. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary within the next month
options.rationale: Central nervous system imaging is indicated once central precocious puberty has been biochemically confirmed, and the yield is highest in girls under 6 years and in all boys. Imaging a child with no evidence of gonadotrophin activation would require sedation for no diagnostic gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist and refer her to endocrinology
options.rationale: Agonist therapy is reserved for confirmed central precocious puberty where rapid progression threatens final adult height or causes psychosocial harm. Suppressing an axis that has not been activated exposes the child to injections and side effects with no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and measure serum oestradiol and the adrenal androgens
options.rationale: Ultrasound and androgen measurement search for a peripheral oestrogen or androgen source such as an ovarian cyst, a McCune-Albright lesion or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, all of which produce virilisation, rapid progression or bleeding. The absence of pubic hair, clitoromegaly, acne and growth acceleration argues strongly against a peripheral source. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her growth and pubertal staging again in six months
options.rationale: Isolated waxing and waning breast tissue in a toddler with no other secondary sexual characteristics, a normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age is premature thelarche, a benign self-limiting variant. Serial review of height velocity and staging is the investigation, because progression over 6 months is what separates thelarche from true precocity. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

explanation.summary: Premature thelarche is isolated breast development, usually appearing between 6 months and 3 years, driven by transient follicular activity in a minipubertal ovary rather than by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. It is distinguished from true precocious puberty by what is absent as much as by what is present: no pubic or axillary hair, no acne or adult body odour, no growth acceleration and no bone age advance. Bone age is the single most informative investigation because oestrogen exposure sufficient to develop breast tissue over months would also advance the skeleton. Serial observation over 6 months is diagnostic, since thelarche stays static or regresses while true precocity progresses through the Tanner stages. Referral thresholds are breast development before 8 years in girls or testicular enlargement before 9 years in boys when accompanied by growth acceleration or bone age advance.
key_points: Premature thelarche is isolated breast tissue with no other secondary sexual characteristics
Normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age are the reassuring findings
Serial staging and height velocity over 6 months is the diagnostic test
Investigate when there is pubic hair, acne, growth acceleration, bleeding or virilisation
Brain imaging follows biochemical confirmation of central activation, not clinical suspicion alone
explanation.pearls: Areolar enlargement and pigmentation, rather than the size of the breast bud itself, is the physical sign that most reliably marks genuine oestrogen exposure and should prompt investigation even when the bone age is only mildly advanced.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Puberty disorders

subtopic_detail: Setting for influenza vaccination in a child with previous anaphylaxis to egg
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy in early autumn whose parents want him vaccinated against influenza before a family trip.

At 11 months of age he developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting and audible wheeze within ten minutes of his first taste of scrambled egg, and was treated with intramuscular adrenaline in an emergency department. Skin prick testing was subsequently positive to egg white and he carries an adrenaline autoinjector.

He has received his measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at 12 months without any reaction. He is well today, has no asthma and has had no recent febrile illness. Your practice has an adrenaline autoinjector, oxygen and a resuscitation trolley, and a second staff member is on site.

data_table.Allergy history: Anaphylaxis to egg at 11 months treated with intramuscular adrenaline; skin prick test positive to egg white
data_table.Vaccine history: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at 12 months tolerated without reaction
data_table.Practice resources: Adrenaline autoinjector, oxygen, resuscitation trolley and a second staff member available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer the influenza vaccine in the practice with 15 minutes of observation
options.rationale: Egg allergy of any severity, including previous anaphylaxis, is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in Australia, because the ovalbumin content of registered vaccines is below the threshold that triggers reactions. Vaccination proceeds in any setting equipped to manage anaphylaxis, with the same standard 15 minute observation applied to every vaccinee. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Refer him to a specialist immunisation clinic for the influenza vaccine in hospital
options.rationale: Specialist immunisation clinic referral is reserved for a documented anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the vaccine itself or to one of its other components such as gelatin or neomycin. Referring for egg allergy alone creates a delay in which the child may miss the season altogether. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the influenza vaccine in two divided doses 30 minutes apart in the practice
options.rationale: Graded or split dosing was historical practice abandoned once studies showed no excess reactions with full single doses in egg allergic children. Splitting the dose risks giving an incomplete antigen load and is not a licensed method of administration. (Source: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child)
source_refs: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

options.text: Withhold the influenza vaccine and rely on vaccination of his household contacts
options.rationale: Cocooning through household vaccination is an adjunct for infants under 6 months who cannot be vaccinated, not a substitute for a child who is eligible. Withholding leaves a preschool child, a group with high influenza hospitalisation rates, unprotected on the basis of a contraindication that does not exist. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Perform skin prick testing to the influenza vaccine before administering the dose
