The pattern here is the mirror image, with evening pain and a normal morning. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

options.text: Start a six week trial of ibuprofen each evening and repeat the examination
options.rationale: Regular scheduled anti-inflammatory for six weeks medicalises a self-limiting condition and exposes the child to gastric and renal risk for episodic pain that responds to rubbing. Simple analgesia as needed is all that is warranted. (Source: RACGP: Growing pains in children)

options.text: Arrange a full blood count, film and inflammatory markers before reassuring
options.rationale: Blood tests are indicated when a red flag is present, such as a limp, unilateral or persistent daytime pain, fever, weight loss, bruising or organomegaly. Investigating a textbook benign pattern generates incidental abnormalities and prolongs parental anxiety rather than resolving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

options.text: Explain the benign pattern, advise massage and simple analgesia, and review
options.rationale: Bilateral pain confined to the evening or night, in the muscles rather than the joints, in a thriving child who is entirely well and running normally by day, is benign nocturnal limb pain and needs no investigation. Explanation, massage, heat and simple analgesia with planned review is the complete management. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pain, still widely called growing pains, affects up to a third of primary school aged children and is a clinical diagnosis made on pattern rather than on tests. The defining features are pain that is bilateral, muscular rather than articular, confined to the evening or night, and completely absent by morning in a child whose growth, examination and activity are normal. The conditions that must not be missed all break that pattern in a specific way, with leukaemia producing bone pain, bruising, pallor or organomegaly, osteoid osteoma producing focal unilateral night pain, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis producing morning stiffness with joint signs. Because the diagnosis rests on the absence of red flags rather than on a normal test, safety-netting and planned review carry the clinical weight. A child whose pain migrates into the day, becomes unilateral, or is accompanied by a limp is re-examined and investigated.
key_points: Bilateral, muscular, evening or night pain with a completely normal morning is the pattern.
A limp, unilateral pain, fever, weight loss, bruising or organomegaly are the red flags.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes morning stiffness, the reverse of this timing.
No investigation is required when the pattern is typical and the examination is normal.
explanation.pearls: Pain that wakes a child from sleep is not by itself alarming in benign limb pain, but pain that persists into the following morning or produces a limp has left the benign pattern and warrants a full blood count, film and radiograph of the symptomatic site.

subtopic_detail: symmetrical bow legs in an eighteen month old of normal stature walking without pain
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18-month-old girl whose grandmother has told the family her legs are bending outwards and that she needs braces. She started walking at 13 months, runs after her brother, and has never complained of leg pain or refused to weight bear.

On examination she stands with the medial malleoli together and there is a gap of about 5 cm between the medial femoral condyles, which is symmetrical on the two sides. The bowing is centred at the knees, the tibiae are not sharply angulated, and there is no lateral thrust of either knee as she walks. There is no tenderness, no swelling and no restriction of hip or knee movement. Her height and weight are both on the 50th centile and have tracked there since birth. She has a varied diet including dairy, plays outdoors daily, and takes no medications. Her wrists and costochondral junctions feel normal.

data_table.Lower limb examination: Symmetrical intercondylar distance of 5 cm with the malleoli together, bowing centred at the knees
data_table.Gait: Walks and runs without a limp and with no lateral thrust at either knee
data_table.Growth: Height and weight both on the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Other findings: No wrist or costochondral widening, full hip and knee range of movement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, record the intercondylar distance and review the gait in six months
options.rationale: Symmetrical genu varum centred at the knees in a child of normal stature who walks without pain is the physiological pattern, which peaks around 18 months and corrects spontaneously. Documenting the intercondylar distance gives an objective measure to compare against at review. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Request standing long leg alignment radiographs of both lower limbs today
options.rationale: Alignment films are reserved for bowing that is asymmetrical, progressive after the age of two, sharply angulated, painful, or accompanied by short stature. None of those applies, and radiographing physiological varus exposes a toddler to radiation for a normal result. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Check serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D level
options.rationale: Nutritional rickets is the metabolic near pair and it is suggested by short stature or faltering growth, wrist and costochondral widening, delayed dentition or a restricted diet with little sun exposure. A child on the 50th centile with normal wrists and a varied diet does not warrant the panel. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for consideration of bracing this year
options.rationale: Bracing has no role in physiological varus, which corrects without intervention, and orthopaedic referral is reserved for the patterns that do not correct. Offering a brace treats the grandmother's concern rather than the child's leg. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey to look for an underlying skeletal dysplasia
options.rationale: A skeletal dysplasia declares itself with short stature, disproportion between limb and trunk length, or a family history, and normal centile tracking argues strongly against one. A skeletal survey is a substantial radiation exposure that this presentation does not justify. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Lower limb alignment follows a predictable developmental arc, with physiological varus maximal at around 18 months, a neutral axis at about two years, physiological valgus peaking near three to four years, and adult alignment reached by about seven. Parents and grandparents commonly present a toddler at the varus peak, so recognising the normal trajectory prevents a cascade of imaging and referral. The findings that take a child off the physiological pathway are asymmetry, progression after age two, sharp angulation at the proximal tibia, pain, a lateral thrust at the knee during stance, and short stature. Blount disease and nutritional rickets are the two diagnoses that account for most pathological varus, and each is suggested clinically before any test is ordered. Measuring and recording the intercondylar distance converts a subjective impression into a number that can be compared at the next visit.
key_points: Physiological varus peaks near 18 months and neutralises by about two years.
Symmetry, normal stature and a painless gait define the physiological pattern.
Asymmetry, progression after age two, or a lateral knee thrust suggests Blount disease.
Short stature with wrist or costochondral widening points instead to rickets.
explanation.pearls: Record the intercondylar distance in centimetres with the medial malleoli touching: a physiological varus shrinks at the six month review, whereas a measurement that is unchanged or larger after the second birthday is the trigger for standing alignment radiographs.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

subtopic_detail: boggy scalp swelling crossing the suture lines with tachycardia and pallor hours after a ventouse delivery
stem: A 4-hour-old term boy delivered by ventouse is pale and sleepy; the midwife says his head feels soft and squelchy all over.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse fluctuant scalp swelling crossing the sagittal suture to the nape; central capillary refill four seconds
data_table.Serial measurement: Head circumference up 2.5 cm since birth
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (145-225)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Measure head circumference hourly and observe on the ward
options.rationale: Serial head circumference is the right monitoring tool but it is not a treatment, and this infant has already declared himself with tachycardia, hypotension, pallor and a falling haemoglobin. Observation on a postnatal ward without venous access is how these babies exsanguinate into the scalp. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Transfer to the neonatal unit for volume replacement and transfusion
options.rationale: A swelling that crosses suture lines and shifts with position in a shocked infant after instrumental delivery is bleeding into the subaponeurotic space, which can hold the entire circulating volume. Immediate transfer with volume replacement and early red cell transfusion, alongside correction of coagulopathy, is the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the head before transfer
options.rationale: This is a clinical diagnosis made at the cot side, and taking a shocked neonate to a scanner before restoring circulating volume delays the only intervention that changes the outcome. Imaging has a place later for a suspected coexisting intracranial bleed or skull fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Give intramuscular phytomenadione and repeat coagulation
options.rationale: Vitamin K should certainly be confirmed as given and a coagulopathy corrected, but neither addresses the acute hypovolaemia and neither works fast enough to matter in the next fifteen minutes. This is an adjunct to resuscitation, not a substitute for it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Apply a compression bandage and recheck the haemoglobin
options.rationale: Head wrapping does not tamponade the subaponeurotic space, which communicates widely from orbit to nape, and a tight bandage obscures the serial head circumference that is being used to track ongoing bleeding. It substitutes a mechanical gesture for circulatory support. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal resuscitation)

explanation.summary: Subgaleal haemorrhage is bleeding into the loose areolar plane between the epicranial aponeurosis and the periosteum, a potential space that extends from the orbital ridges to the nape of the neck and can accommodate the whole neonatal blood volume. It complicates roughly 4 per 10000 spontaneous births and rises sharply with vacuum extraction, particularly after multiple pulls or a failed attempt followed by forceps. The bedside discriminator from the two benign mimics is anatomical, since caput succedaneum is superficial and pits while cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal and therefore stops at the suture lines, whereas subgaleal blood crosses them and shifts with gravity. Each centimetre of head circumference increase corresponds to roughly 38 mL of blood, so serial measurement is the monitoring tool while volume replacement is the treatment. Mortality approaches one in five once shock develops, which is why any infant delivered by vacuum has scalp and observation checks scheduled rather than left to chance.
key_points: Blood crossing the suture lines and shifting with position distinguishes it from cephalhaematoma.
Vacuum extraction, particularly multiple pulls or sequential instruments, is the main risk factor.
Tachycardia, pallor and a rising head circumference indicate ongoing loss into the scalp.
Treatment is volume resuscitation and transfusion in a neonatal unit, not imaging first.
explanation.pearls: Each 1 cm rise in head circumference in a subgaleal haemorrhage represents roughly 38 mL of blood, which in a 3.5 kg newborn is about 13 per cent of the circulating volume, so a 2 cm increase over a few hours is a haemorrhagic emergency however well the baby looked at birth.

subtopic_detail: firm bright red umbilical lesion unchanged after two courses of topical treatment in a five week old
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 5-week-old girl whose umbilical stump separated at day nine. Her parents were shown how to apply table salt to a small red lump at the navel three weeks ago, and when that made no difference your colleague cauterised it with silver nitrate a fortnight later. The lump is unchanged and the parents describe a clear sticky discharge that keeps staining her singlets.

On examination there is an 8 mm bright red firm lesion protruding from the umbilicus with a smooth glistening surface that looks like the inside of a lip. It does not blanch on pressure, it feels solid rather than soft, and it did not shrink or whiten with either treatment. The surrounding skin is normal in colour with no induration, no warmth and no tenderness. She is afebrile and thriving with a weight gain of 240 grams in the past week. There is no cough on handling and no leakage of urine or intestinal content from the lesion.

data_table.Umbilical examination: 8 mm firm bright red protruding lesion with a smooth glistening non-blanching surface
data_table.Surrounding skin: Normal colour without induration, warmth or tenderness
data_table.Treatment response: No change after three weeks of topical salt and one silver nitrate cauterisation
data_table.Growth: Weight gain of 240 grams over the past week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a further course of topical salt therapy for seven more days
options.rationale: Salt desiccates the friable granulation tissue of an umbilical granuloma, which is dull pink, soft and blanching, and a lesion that has already failed salt is by definition not behaving like one. Repeating a treatment that has twice failed delays the diagnosis rather than testing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Cauterise the lesion with silver nitrate again at this consultation
options.rationale: Silver nitrate works on granulation tissue and does nothing to epithelialised intestinal or urothelial mucosa, and repeated application risks chemical burns to the surrounding abdominal skin. Two failed treatments are the signal to reconsider the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for excision and histological examination
options.rationale: A firm bright red non-blanching lesion with a mucosal appearance that has resisted both salt and silver nitrate is an umbilical polyp, a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric or urachal duct lined by intestinal or urothelial mucosa. It requires surgical excision with histology and assessment for a deeper persistent tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Swab the umbilicus and start oral cefalexin for suspected omphalitis
options.rationale: Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, induration, tenderness and a systemically unwell infant, and it is a paediatric emergency in the neonatal period rather than a five week outpatient problem. The skin around this lesion is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Omphalitis)

options.text: Request an abdominal ultrasound to look for a patent urachal remnant
options.rationale: Ultrasound is a reasonable adjunct where a urachal sinus is suspected, particularly with urinary leakage, but it does not distinguish granuloma from polyp at the surface and it does not remove the lesion. Imaging is arranged by the surgical team alongside excision rather than instead of referral. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Umbilical anomalies)

explanation.summary: Most red umbilical lesions after cord separation are granulomas, which are soft, dull pink, friable, blanching masses of granulation tissue that respond to desiccation with salt or to silver nitrate cautery. An umbilical polyp is the important mimic and it is a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct or urachus lined by heterotopic intestinal or bladder mucosa, which is why it appears bright red, firm, glistening and mucosal and why it is entirely unresponsive to chemical treatment. The practical rule is that failure of adequate topical therapy reclassifies the lesion rather than earning another course. Excision is required both to remove the polyp and to exclude a deeper patent tract to the ileum or bladder, which can present later with faecal or urinary discharge, infection or volvulus around a persistent band. Histology of the excised specimen confirms the mucosal lining and directs any further imaging.
key_points: Granuloma is soft, dull pink and blanching; polyp is firm, bright red and mucosal.
Failure of salt or silver nitrate reclassifies the lesion rather than warranting repeat treatment.
A polyp is a vitellointestinal or urachal duct remnant and requires surgical excision.
A persistent deep tract can later cause discharge, infection or volvulus around a band.
explanation.pearls: Two failed treatments is the decision point: an umbilical lesion that has not shrunk after an adequate course of salt and one silver nitrate application is referred for excision rather than treated a third time, because a polyp has no granulation tissue for either agent to act on.

subtopic_detail: anterior chest wall depression in a tall adolescent with arachnodactyly and a high arched palate
stem: A 14-year-old boy asks about surgery for the dip in his chest, which deepened over two years of rapid growth. A maternal uncle died suddenly at 41.

data_table.Anthropometry: Height 97th centile, parents of average height, arm span exceeding height by 6 cm, positive thumb and wrist signs
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical lower sternal depression, high narrow palate, early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Reassure and review after the pubertal growth spurt
options.rationale: Waiting is reasonable for an isolated chest wall depression in an otherwise unremarkable adolescent, but it is not reasonable when a diastolic murmur and a family history of unexplained sudden death in a young adult are present. Aortic root dilatation progresses silently during exactly the growth phase he is in. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

options.text: Chest radiograph to calculate the Haller index before referral
options.rationale: The Haller index is derived from cross-sectional imaging rather than a plain film and it grades the severity of the chest wall deformity only. It is the near pair to the correct answer in that both are imaging, but it measures the cosmetic problem rather than the lethal one. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pectus excavatum)

options.text: Referral to paediatric surgery for minimally invasive repair
options.rationale: A chest wall repair addresses the deformity the boy has asked about while leaving the systemic condition it is a marker of entirely unassessed. Surgical planning in a connective tissue disorder also requires the aortic dimensions to be known beforehand. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography with aortic root measurement
options.rationale: Tall stature with disproportionate arm span, positive thumb and wrist signs, a high arched palate, chest wall deformity and an early diastolic murmur point to a heritable connective tissue disorder, and the murmur suggests aortic regurgitation from root dilatation. Echocardiography with root measurement indexed to body surface area is the investigation that determines both diagnosis and immediate risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

options.text: Spirometry with a formal cardiopulmonary exercise test
options.rationale: Lung function quantifies the restriction some deep chest wall deformities cause and is used when surgery is being planned for functional reasons, but it does not assess the aorta. A boy who swims twice a week without breathlessness is unlikely to have physiology that changes management. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pectus excavatum)

explanation.summary: Pectus excavatum is common and usually isolated, but it is also a systemic feature in the revised Ghent criteria for Marfan syndrome, so its presence obliges a look for the other systemic features rather than a straight referral for repair. The systemic score counts findings such as wrist and thumb signs, reduced upper to lower segment ratio with increased arm span to height ratio, scoliosis, pes planus, a high arched palate and characteristic facial features. Aortic root dilatation at the sinuses of Valsalva is the feature that determines prognosis, since dissection and rupture account for most premature deaths, and it is measured by echocardiography and indexed as a Z score for body surface area. An early diastolic murmur in this setting represents aortic regurgitation from a dilated root and moves the assessment from elective to prompt. Management once confirmed includes beta blockade or an angiotensin receptor blocker, serial imaging, avoidance of isometric and contact sport, and family screening, all of which are unavailable until the echocardiogram is done.
key_points: Pectus excavatum is a systemic feature of Marfan syndrome, not only a cosmetic issue.
Arm span to height ratio, thumb and wrist signs and palate shape build the systemic score.
An early diastolic murmur suggests aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Echocardiography with a body surface area indexed root Z score drives all further management.
explanation.pearls: An aortic root Z score of 2 or more at the sinuses of Valsalva satisfies the aortic criterion in the revised Ghent nosology, and a root diameter approaching 45 mm in an adolescent with Marfan syndrome is the usual threshold for referral to consider prophylactic root replacement.

subtopic_detail: irreducible tender groin lump in a vomiting four month old with a previously intermittent swelling
stem: A 4-month-old boy born at 32 weeks has screamed for five hours and vomited bile three times. A right groin lump that came and went has stayed up.

data_table.Examination: Firm tender 3 cm right groin swelling to the scrotum, no upper border; testes normal; abdomen distended, bowel sounds high-pitched

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Book an elective herniotomy on the next operating list
options.rationale: Elective repair is what should have happened when the reducible lump was first noticed, and it is the correct pathway for a hernia that reduces easily. Once incarceration with obstruction has occurred the timeframe is hours, not weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed strangulated bowel
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given as part of preparation for theatre when strangulation is suspected, but they are an adjunct and do not relieve the obstruction. The near pair to keep in mind is an infected or necrotic segment already perforated, which would show peritonism, fever and shock rather than this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply ice and review the swelling in the morning if he settles
options.rationale: Delay is the single most dangerous choice here because incarcerated bowel becomes ischaemic within hours and the testicular vessels sharing the inguinal canal are compressed at the same time. Bilious vomiting with a distended abdomen indicates obstruction that is already established. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Arrange an urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler first
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the right test when the diagnosis is in doubt between a hydrocele, a torted testis and a hernia, but here both testes are normal and separately palpable and there is no upper border to the swelling. Waiting for imaging in an obstructed infant costs the bowel time it does not have. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Give analgesia, attempt gentle reduction, involve surgeons urgently
options.rationale: An irreducible groin swelling with no upper border, bilious vomiting and abdominal distension in an ex-premature infant is an incarcerated inguinal hernia, and adequate analgesia with gentle sustained taxis succeeds in the majority. Surgical involvement is contemporaneous because failure of reduction mandates immediate operation and successful reduction still requires repair on the same admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

explanation.summary: Indirect inguinal hernia in infancy results from a patent processus vaginalis and carries a far higher incarceration risk than in adults, concentrated in the first year and highest in ex-premature infants, which is why repair is arranged promptly rather than deferred. The bedside discriminators are that a hernia has no palpable upper border because it extends through the external ring into the abdomen, while a hydrocele transilluminates, has an upper border and does not obstruct, and a torted testis presents with an abnormal tender testis rather than a separate groin mass. Incarceration announces itself with irreducibility, pain, and then bilious vomiting and distension as bowel obstruction develops. Adequate opioid analgesia and sedation allow gentle sustained taxis to succeed in most cases, after which repair proceeds on the same admission once oedema settles, typically within 24 to 48 hours. Failed reduction, peritonism or systemic compromise means immediate operation, and the ipsilateral testis is at risk throughout because the cord structures are compressed at the external ring.
key_points: Inability to define an upper border distinguishes a hernia from a hydrocele or testicular problem.
Prematurity markedly increases the risk of incarceration in the first year of life.
Analgesia with gentle sustained taxis reduces most incarcerated infant hernias.
Repair follows on the same admission, and failed reduction means immediate operation.
explanation.pearls: In an incarcerated infant inguinal hernia the ipsilateral testis is at risk from cord compression as well as the bowel, so the operation note and the discharge examination both record testicular size, and a testis that is smaller at six week review prompts surgical re-referral.

subtopic_detail: unilateral in-toeing with a painless limp and reduced hip abduction in a three year old
stem: A 3-year-old girl who started walking at 15 months has always dipped to the right as she walks, painlessly, and her right foot turns in when she runs.

data_table.Hip examination: Abduction in flexion 70 degrees left and 40 degrees right, increased right internal rotation
data_table.Leg length: Right knee lower than left with hips and knees flexed
data_table.Distal examination: Normal thigh-foot axis and foot border bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis and both hips
options.rationale: Unilateral in-toeing with a painless Trendelenburg gait, restricted abduction in flexion and a positive Galeazzi sign is late-presenting developmental dysplasia, in which the femur internally rotates to keep the head in a shallow acetabulum. After the femoral head has ossified a plain pelvic radiograph is the diagnostic test. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Night time derotation brace with review in twelve months
options.rationale: Derotation devices and twister cables have no evidence of benefit even for the benign rotational variants they were designed for, and they treat the visible foot position rather than the hip driving it. Bracing an undiagnosed dysplastic hip wastes a year of growth. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Gait analysis and in-shoe orthotics through podiatry
options.rationale: Orthotics address the foot and would be considered for a metatarsus adductus, which is excluded here by the normal lateral foot border. They cannot influence acetabular development and the referral delays the radiograph. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips to assess the acetabular angle
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the imaging of choice for developmental dysplasia but only while the femoral head is still cartilaginous, conventionally under about four to six months of age. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinguishing point is that after the ossific nucleus appears the head casts an acoustic shadow and a plain radiograph becomes the accurate study. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Reassurance that rotational profiles correct with growth
options.rationale: Benign rotational variants are symmetrical, involve no limp and leave hip abduction and leg length untouched, whereas this child has unilateral findings with restricted abduction and apparent shortening. Reassurance here would allow a treatable hip to deteriorate through the years when treatment works best. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

explanation.summary: In-toeing in a toddler is usually one of three benign rotational variants, namely metatarsus adductus in infancy, internal tibial torsion in the second year and increased femoral anteversion from around three years, all of which are symmetrical, painless and self-correcting. The clinical value of a rotational profile is that it localises the level of the problem, with the lateral foot border assessing the forefoot, the thigh-foot axis assessing the tibia, and hip rotation assessing the femur. A unilateral pattern is the finding that takes a child off that pathway, because a dysplastic hip produces compensatory femoral internal rotation along with a Trendelenburg gait, reduced abduction in flexion and apparent femoral shortening. Late-presenting developmental dysplasia is missed by newborn examination and neonatal ultrasound in a meaningful minority, and it presents exactly like this once walking is established. Treatment after walking age generally requires closed or open reduction with femoral or pelvic osteotomy rather than a harness, and outcomes deteriorate with every year of delay.
key_points: Benign rotational variants are symmetrical, painless and leave hip examination normal.
Unilateral in-toeing with a Trendelenburg gait points to the hip, not the foot or tibia.
Restricted abduction in flexion plus a positive Galeazzi sign is dysplasia until excluded.
Ultrasound is accurate only before the femoral ossific nucleus appears; then use radiography.
explanation.pearls: Hip ultrasound loses accuracy once the femoral ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months, so a walking child with suspected developmental dysplasia is imaged with an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph rather than the ultrasound used in the newborn period.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: postauricular swelling pushing the ear outwards five days into oral treatment for an ear infection
stem: A 4-year-old girl started oral amoxicillin five days ago for right ear pain. The pain settled, then returned worse, with swelling behind the ear since yesterday.

data_table.Examination: Tender fluctuant postauricular swelling, loss of the crease, pinna displaced down and out, bulging tympanic membrane
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 128 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to oral cefalexin and review her again in two days
options.rationale: Swapping one oral agent for another concedes that the first has failed while leaving the child on a route that cannot achieve adequate concentrations in infected bone. Cefalexin also has poorer activity against the pneumococcus and Streptococcus pyogenes that predominate here. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics with urgent otolaryngology review
options.rationale: Postauricular swelling with loss of the crease and a displaced pinna in a febrile child with a bulging drum is acute mastoiditis, a suppurative complication of otitis media involving the mastoid air cells. Admission for high dose intravenous antibiotics with same-day otolaryngology involvement for possible myringotomy or cortical mastoidectomy is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin drops and continue the oral course
options.rationale: Topical quinolone drops treat otitis externa and discharging grommets, and otitis externa is the near pair because it also causes canal changes and postauricular tenderness. The distinction is that otitis externa spares the middle ear, gives pain on tragal pressure with a normal drum, and does not displace the pinna or obliterate the postauricular crease. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient computed tomography of the temporal bones
options.rationale: Imaging has a definite role in suspected intracranial extension, subperiosteal abscess or a poor response to treatment, but this is a clinical diagnosis and an outpatient appointment introduces a delay of days. Antibiotics are started first and imaging arranged from the ward if needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Aspirate the swelling in clinic and send fluid for culture
options.rationale: Needle aspiration of a postauricular collection without imaging or surgical support risks injuring the facial nerve and the sigmoid sinus, both of which lie in the operative field. Drainage, where required, is a theatre procedure performed by an otolaryngologist. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

explanation.summary: Acute mastoiditis is the commonest suppurative complication of acute otitis media and follows spread of infection from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells, which communicate with it directly through the aditus ad antrum. Incidence has fallen in the antibiotic era but the diagnosis persists and is now often seen in children who have been on oral therapy, so recent antibiotic treatment is no reassurance at all. The clinical triad is postauricular erythema, tenderness and swelling with loss of the postauricular crease, protrusion of the pinna inferiorly and laterally, and signs of middle ear infection such as a bulging drum or sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus are the usual organisms, and treatment is intravenous antibiotics with otolaryngology involvement, proceeding to myringotomy with or without grommet insertion, or cortical mastoidectomy, where there is a subperiosteal abscess or failure to improve. The complications that make this a same-day problem are facial nerve palsy, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, subperiosteal or Bezold abscess, labyrinthitis, meningitis and intracranial abscess, so any new focal neurological sign, altered conscious state or neck stiffness prompts urgent contrast imaging.
key_points: Loss of the postauricular crease with a displaced pinna is the defining physical sign.
Recent or current oral antibiotic treatment does not exclude the diagnosis.
Otitis externa spares the middle ear and does not displace the pinna.
Facial palsy, neck stiffness or altered conscious state signal intracranial extension.
explanation.pearls: Compare the two ears from behind and above with the child sitting up: the loss of the postauricular crease and the forward and downward displacement of the pinna are far more obvious from that angle than from the front, and they are what separate mastoiditis from simple postauricular lymphadenitis.

subtopic_detail: limping toddler with a normal initial tibial radiograph after a low height twisting fall
stem:
You are the registrar in a suburban emergency department. An 18-month-old boy is brought in because he has refused to walk since yesterday afternoon, when he slid off the bottom step of a play fort and his foot caught under him. His mother says he screamed briefly, settled with a cuddle, and has been his usual cheerful self since, but he now crawls everywhere and cries if she stands him up.

He is afebrile and has been eating and drinking normally, with no rash and no recent illness. On examination he lies happily on the trolley and moves both hips and knees through full range without complaint. There is no swelling, warmth or bruising of either leg. He cries reproducibly when you gently rotate the right foot relative to the shin, and settles as soon as you stop. Radiographs of the right tibia and fibula in two planes are reported as showing no fracture.

data_table.Examination: Full painless range at both hips and knees, no joint swelling, warmth or effusion
data_table.Palpation: Distress on gentle torsion of the right tibia, no focal bony tenderness elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Right tibia and fibula radiographs, two views: no fracture identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Request an urgent magnetic resonance scan of the right leg under sedation today
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance would show the fracture line, but it needs sedation at this age and does not change a management plan that is immobilisation either way. It is reserved for the child whose symptoms persist despite immobilisation or whose picture suggests infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Arrange an urgent hip ultrasound to look for a joint effusion before discharge
options.rationale: Hip ultrasound is the move when the hip is the painful joint, but this boy moves both hips through full range without complaint and localises to tibial torsion. The near pair is transient synovitis, which restricts internal rotation of the hip and does not reproduce pain on rotating the foot against the shin. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and advice to mobilise as tolerated at home
options.rationale: Analgesia alone is reasonable when the examination is genuinely normal, but reproducible pain on tibial torsion is a positive finding and unprotected weight bearing on an occult spiral fracture prolongs the limp. A normal first radiograph does not exclude the injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Apply an above ankle walking boot and review clinically in seven to ten days
options.rationale: A well child with a torsional mechanism, pain on tibial rotation and no bony tenderness elsewhere has an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture until proven otherwise, and this pattern is invisible on up to half of first films. Immobilisation with clinical review, rather than repeat imaging, is the management whether or not a fracture is later confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Send blood cultures with inflammatory markers and admit for intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A septic workup belongs to the febrile or systemically unwell limping child, and this boy is afebrile, feeding normally and settles the moment the leg is left alone. Treating him as infected commits him to a cannula and admission for a mechanical injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: The toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft caused by a low energy twisting force in a newly ambulant child, typically between nine months and three years. Because the periosteum is thick and the fracture line is often hairline and oblique, initial radiographs miss a large proportion of cases and the diagnosis is made clinically. The differential that matters is infection, so the afebrile, systemically well child with a clear mechanism can be immobilised and reviewed rather than investigated further. Persistent refusal to weight bear at review, fever, or a rising inflammatory response should redirect towards osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. Non-accidental injury deserves consideration when the child is not yet walking independently, because the mechanism requires an ambulant child.
key_points: Low energy torsional mechanism in a newly walking child with refusal to weight bear.
Pain reproduced by rotating the foot against the shin, with no focal bony tenderness.
Up to half of initial radiographs are normal; a normal film does not exclude it.
Immobilise and review clinically; reserve advanced imaging for atypical or persistent cases.
A spiral tibial fracture in a child who cannot yet walk should raise safeguarding concern.
explanation.pearls: Healing periosteal new bone appears on radiographs at about 10 to 14 days, so a repeat film a fortnight later confirms the diagnosis retrospectively if it is ever needed, which is why the plaster goes on before the imaging is conclusive.

subtopic_detail: infant with a persistently watering eye and crusted lashes since the first weeks of life
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-month-old boy whose mother says his left eye has watered constantly since he was about two weeks old. Tears spill down the cheek even when he is content, and most mornings the lashes are stuck together with a yellowish crust that wipes away easily with a warm washer. She has been given two courses of antibiotic drops by a colleague, each of which cleared the crusting for a few days before it returned.

He was born at term and is growing along the 50th centile. On examination he fixes and follows your face with each eye covered in turn, and the left conjunctiva is white and quiet with no injection. Pressing over the area between the inner corner of the eye and the nose produces a bead of mucoid material at the lid margin. The corneas are clear and of equal size, and the red reflex is present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Left epiphora with quiet white conjunctiva, no lid or periorbital swelling, no photophobia
data_table.Eye assessment: Red reflex present and symmetrical, corneal diameters equal and corneas clear, fixes and follows with either eye
data_table.Provocation: Mucoid reflux at the punctum on pressure over the lacrimal sac

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management at this visit?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin and arrange paediatric review within forty eight hours
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are for acute dacryocystitis, in which the sac becomes red, tense and tender with surrounding cellulitis and the infant is often febrile. Expressible mucoid material from a soft non-tender sac is not infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent ophthalmology review the same day for measurement of intraocular pressure
options.rationale: Same day review is for infantile glaucoma, the important near pair, which also waters but adds photophobia, blepharospasm, corneal clouding and an enlarged corneal diameter. Clear corneas of equal size and a comfortable child make it very unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

options.text: Teach lacrimal sac massage with lid hygiene and review him at twelve months of age
options.rationale: Epiphora from birth with mucoid reflux, a quiet conjunctiva and a normal red reflex is congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and around 90 per cent resolve spontaneously during the first year. Massage and lid hygiene with planned review is the correct conservative course. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

options.text: Refer for probing of the nasolacrimal duct under general anaesthesia within the month
options.rationale: Probing is the correct step, but the timing is wrong: intervention before twelve months treats obstructions that would have resolved on their own and adds an anaesthetic. Probing is reserved for persistence beyond a year or for recurrent dacryocystitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction)

options.text: Prescribe a further week of chloramphenicol eye drops four times daily and reassess
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic treats bacterial conjunctivitis, which injects the conjunctiva and does not persist for months against a white quiet eye. Repeated courses explain the transient improvement without addressing an anatomical blockage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction affects up to one in five infants and arises from a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner at the distal end of the duct. It presents with epiphora and mattering from the first weeks of life, with a white conjunctiva between episodes, and mucoid material that can be expressed from the sac. Two conditions must be excluded before reassurance: infantile glaucoma, which adds photophobia, corneal clouding and enlargement, and acute dacryocystitis, which makes the sac red, tense and tender. Spontaneous resolution occurs in about 90 per cent by twelve months, so probing is deferred until then in the uncomplicated child. Persistent obstruction beyond a year, or recurrent infection of the sac, warrants ophthalmology referral for probing with or without intubation.
key_points: Watering from the first weeks of life with a quiet white conjunctiva suggests duct obstruction.
Expressible mucoid reflux at the punctum supports the diagnosis.
Exclude infantile glaucoma: photophobia, corneal clouding, enlarged corneal diameter.
About 90 per cent resolve by twelve months; massage and hygiene in the interim.
Refer earlier for recurrent dacryocystitis or if signs of glaucoma appear.
explanation.pearls: Crigler massage works by raising hydrostatic pressure in the sac: press firmly over the sac just medial to the inner canthus and stroke downward towards the nose about ten times, twice daily, rather than rubbing the eyelid itself.

subtopic_detail: day one newborn not moving one arm fully after a delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia
stem:
You are the paediatric resident asked to review a term baby boy on the postnatal ward at 18 hours of age. His birth weight was 4320 g and the delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia relieved with the McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure. The midwife has noticed he is not moving his right arm as freely as his left during cares and cries when she dresses him.

On examination he is pink, alert and feeding well at the breast. He grips your finger firmly with both hands and flexes and extends both elbows and wrists spontaneously when he is unwrapped. The right Moro reflex is reduced in amplitude compared with the left. You feel a step and crepitus over the middle of the right collarbone and he grimaces as you do so. The overlying skin is intact with no bruising, and there is no swelling of the arm or forearm.

data_table.Examination: Palpable step and crepitus over the mid right clavicle, intact overlying skin, no arm swelling
data_table.Neurological: Symmetrical palmar grasp, spontaneous elbow and wrist movement bilaterally, asymmetrical Moro
data_table.Feeding: Breastfeeding established, alert and pink between feeds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Pin the sleeve to the body for three weeks and arrange orthopaedic review in clinic
options.rationale: Strapping the limb is an adult and older child strategy and offers nothing in a neonate whose clavicle remodels completely within weeks. It also restricts the arm movement that keeps the shoulder supple. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

options.text: Reassure the parents, give regular paracetamol and handle the arm gently for two weeks
options.rationale: A mid clavicular fracture after shoulder dystocia with an intact palmar grasp and preserved elbow and wrist movement is a bony injury alone, and these unite rapidly without any intervention. Analgesia and careful handling are all that is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

options.text: Request a skeletal survey and notify the child protection team before discharge home
options.rationale: A skeletal survey investigates unexplained fractures, and this one has a documented obstetric mechanism in a macrosomic baby delivered with shoulder dystocia. Escalating to safeguarding for an explained birth injury exposes the family to unwarranted investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the shoulder joint to exclude a proximal humeral separation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is useful when the shoulder itself is swollen and the humeral epiphysis may have separated, which produces a pseudoparalysis with swelling and no palpable clavicular step. The palpable crepitus over the collarbone already localises the injury. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Birth injuries)

options.text: Refer urgently to the brachial plexus clinic for nerve conduction studies within the week
options.rationale: Urgent plexus referral belongs to the baby with a true palsy, the key near pair. Obstetric brachial plexus injury abolishes the palmar grasp in lower root lesions or holds the arm adducted and internally rotated in upper root lesions, whereas this baby grips and moves the elbow and wrist. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth injury)

explanation.summary: Clavicular fracture is the commonest fracture of birth, occurring in around one to two per cent of vaginal deliveries and far more often when the birth weight exceeds 4000 g or shoulder dystocia occurs. The critical examination task is to separate the bony injury from an accompanying brachial plexus palsy, because the two often coexist and the management differs entirely. Preserved palmar grasp with spontaneous elbow and wrist movement against an asymmetrical Moro points to pain-limited movement rather than denervation. Uncomplicated clavicular fractures need no imaging, no immobilisation and no orthopaedic follow-up, and parents should be warned that a palpable lump of callus will appear within a week or two. Any baby with a genuine plexus lesion needs early referral because the window for surgical assessment is measured in months.
key_points: Macrosomia and shoulder dystocia are the dominant risk factors.
Grip and distal movement distinguish a painful clavicle from a plexus palsy.
No immobilisation, no imaging and no orthopaedic follow-up are needed.
Warn parents about the callus lump appearing at one to two weeks.
Refer early if grip is absent or the arm is held adducted and internally rotated.
explanation.pearls: An asymmetrical Moro reflex on its own does not distinguish fracture from plexus injury, because pain inhibits the reflex; it is the palmar grasp, which is spared in Erb palsy and absent in Klumpke palsy, that tells you which nerve roots are involved.

subtopic_detail: school aged child with nasal symptoms that worsened again after an initial improvement at day seven
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old girl brought back by her father. She started with a blocked nose and a cough twelve days ago, was clearly getting better by about day six, and then over the last three days has become worse again with thick discoloured nasal discharge, a daytime cough and a temperature her father measured at home at 38.6 degrees.

She has missed two days of school and complains that her face aches when she leans forward to put on her shoes. She has had no previous sinus problems and takes no regular medications. On examination she is alert and well perfused with moist mucous membranes. There is mucopurulent discharge in both nasal passages and tenderness over both cheeks. The tympanic membranes are pearly and mobile, the pharynx is mildly injected without exudate, and the chest is clear on auscultation. There is no periorbital swelling, no proptosis and eye movements are full and painless.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Examination: Bilateral mucopurulent nasal discharge with maxillary tenderness, clear chest, pearly mobile tympanic membranes
data_table.Eye assessment: No periorbital swelling or proptosis, full painless eye movements, normal visual acuity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide intranasal saline with analgesia and advise review if not settling in a week
options.rationale: Saline and analgesia alone are correct for the uncomplicated viral illness that is steadily improving, or for symptoms under ten days without double sickening. A documented second deterioration with fever changes the probability enough to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start intranasal mometasone with an oral decongestant for a seven day course
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid is an adjunct in chronic and allergic rhinosinusitis rather than a treatment for an acute bacterial episode, and oral decongestants are not recommended in this age group. Neither addresses the bacterial infection. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin and arrange clinical review in forty eight to seventy two hours
options.rationale: Double sickening, a clear improvement then deterioration after day five with fever and purulent discharge, is the pattern that identifies acute bacterial sinusitis rather than a prolonged viral illness. Amoxicillin is the first line agent in Australia and review at 48 to 72 hours catches non-response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone with urgent ophthalmology and otolaryngology review
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy and urgent specialist review are the correct response to orbital or intracranial extension, the complication to fear. Full painless eye movements with no periorbital swelling or proptosis exclude that here. (Source: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Refer for a computed tomography scan of the sinuses before deciding on treatment
options.rationale: Sinus imaging is reserved for suspected complications or for surgical planning in recurrent disease, because mucosal thickening is common in well children and does not confirm infection. It would add radiation without changing this plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Most paediatric rhinosinusitis is viral and resolves within ten days, so the diagnostic problem is deciding which child has a bacterial infection worth treating. Three patterns justify antibiotics: persistent symptoms beyond ten days without improvement, severe symptoms with fever above 39 degrees and purulent discharge for three or more consecutive days, or double sickening in which a clearly improving illness worsens again. Australian guidance makes amoxicillin the first line, with amoxicillin and clavulanate reserved for treatment failure or recent antibiotic exposure. The complications that drive urgent referral are orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess and intracranial extension, so eye signs and neurological status must be documented at every assessment. Failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours of starting antibiotics should prompt reassessment rather than a simple repeat script.
key_points: Double sickening after day five is a recognised trigger for antibiotic treatment.
Amoxicillin is first line in Australia; escalate only for failure or recent antibiotic use.
Imaging is for suspected complications or surgical planning, not for diagnosis.
Document eye movements, proptosis and visual acuity to exclude orbital spread.
Reassess rather than repeat the script if there is no response by 72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Orbital cellulitis in a child almost always originates from the ethmoid sinuses through the thin lamina papyracea, so painful or restricted eye movement in a child with sinusitis is a surgical emergency rather than a reason to change oral antibiotic.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

subtopic_detail: toddler whose thumb has become fixed in a bent position at the end joint over several months
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 2-year-old girl whose mother has noticed over the past four months that the end of her right thumb stays bent. It was intermittent at first and would click straight when her mother pulled on it, but for the last six weeks it has stayed bent all the time.

There was no injury that anyone recalls. She uses the hand normally for feeding herself and building towers, and does not appear to be in pain. On examination the right thumb is held flexed at the joint nearest the nail and you cannot passively straighten it fully. There is a firm mobile nodule on the palmar surface at the base of the thumb that moves with the tendon. The thumb is warm, pink and not tender, and the skin creases are normal. The left thumb extends fully and there is no nodule. All other digits move normally and she has no joint swelling elsewhere.

data_table.Examination: Fixed flexion at the right interphalangeal joint of the thumb, full passive range at all other digits
data_table.Palpation: Firm mobile nodule over the palmar aspect of the first metacarpophalangeal joint, non-tender
data_table.Systemic: No joint swelling, warmth or effusion elsewhere, normal skin creases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inject the flexor sheath with corticosteroid and review the thumb again in four weeks
options.rationale: Sheath injection is an adult treatment for trigger digit and is not used in young children, in whom the pathology is a size mismatch between a thickened tendon and the pulley rather than inflammation. It also requires sedation at this age. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Trigger finger)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric hand surgeon for consideration of release of the tendon sheath
options.rationale: A fixed flexion deformity at the thumb interphalangeal joint with a palpable nodule over the flexor tendon is paediatric trigger thumb, and a contracture that has been fixed for weeks is unlikely to resolve without surgical release of the A1 pulley. Referral avoids a permanent deformity. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this resolves spontaneously and review her in twelve months
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution does occur, but rates fall sharply once the deformity is fixed rather than intermittently triggering, and this one has been fixed for six weeks. Waiting a further year risks a stiff joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

options.text: Arrange hand therapy for a night extension splint and passive stretching for six months
options.rationale: Splinting and stretching have a role in the intermittently triggering thumb that still extends passively, but they do not reliably correct an established fixed contracture. Six months of therapy delays a definitive procedure without changing the outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Trigger thumb)

options.text: Request inflammatory markers with an antinuclear antibody and refer to rheumatology
options.rationale: This workup targets juvenile idiopathic arthritis, the near pair when a child holds a digit flexed. Arthritis produces a swollen warm tender joint with morning stiffness rather than a painless nodule that glides with the flexor tendon. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric trigger thumb is a mechanical mismatch between a nodular thickening of the flexor pollicis longus tendon, called Notta's node, and the A1 pulley at the base of the thumb. Unlike adult trigger finger it is not an inflammatory condition and is only rarely associated with systemic disease, so it presents painlessly and is usually noticed by a parent rather than the child. Most children present with the thumb already fixed in flexion because the earlier intermittent triggering phase passes unnoticed. Spontaneous resolution is reported in a proportion of cases, particularly under one year of age and when the thumb still extends passively, which is why observation is reasonable early and surgery is preferred once the contracture is fixed. Release of the A1 pulley is a short day procedure with a high success rate and low recurrence.
key_points: Painless fixed flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint in a toddler.
A firm nodule gliding with the flexor tendon at the metacarpophalangeal level.
It is mechanical rather than inflammatory, so corticosteroid injection is not used.
Observation suits the young infant or the passively correctable thumb.
Refer for A1 pulley release once the deformity is fixed.
explanation.pearls: The nodule of paediatric trigger thumb sits at the metacarpophalangeal level rather than at the joint that is bent, so palpating the base of the thumb while passively flexing and extending the tip is what confirms the diagnosis without any imaging.

subtopic_detail: toddler with brief stiffening and jerking after a minor knock, going pale before losing consciousness
stem: A 20-month-old girl knocked her forehead lightly on a table, opened her mouth to cry but made no sound, went white around the lips and limp within seconds. Her limbs then stiffened and jerked for 15 seconds before she came round. Two similar episodes have followed minor bumps.

data_table.Examination: Afebrile, small forehead bruise, symmetrical tone and reflexes, dual heart sounds with no murmur

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain
options.rationale: Head imaging is driven by the severity of the head injury and by focal neurological signs, and a light knock in a child who is now alert and neurologically normal meets no imaging criterion. The bump was the trigger, not the cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Head injury)

options.text: Sleep deprived electroencephalogram within four weeks
options.rationale: Electroencephalography addresses epilepsy, but the sequence here starts with a trigger and pallor and ends with rapid recovery, which is circulatory rather than epileptic. An incidental abnormality on the trace risks anticonvulsants for a benign condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

options.text: Twelve lead electrocardiogram with corrected QT
options.rationale: The pallor preceding collapse and the trivial provoking stimulus identify this as a reflex anoxic seizure, in which the convulsive movements are secondary to cerebral hypoperfusion. The one condition that mimics it and kills is a long QT syndrome, so an electrocardiogram is the single essential test. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

options.text: Full blood count with ferritin and iron studies
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is genuinely associated with these episodes and treating it reduces their frequency, so this is a reasonable adjunct. It is not the priority investigation because it cannot exclude the arrhythmic mimic that would be fatal to miss. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding attacks)

options.text: Venous blood gas with glucose and electrolytes
options.rationale: Metabolic testing helps when recovery is prolonged or the child is unwell between episodes, neither of which applies to a toddler back to baseline in five minutes. A normal result would not change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Reflex anoxic seizure, sometimes called a pallid breath holding attack, is a vagally mediated asystolic pause of several seconds triggered by pain, surprise or a minor knock in a young child. The child goes pale first, loses consciousness, and only then develops tonic stiffening or a few clonic jerks, which distinguishes the sequence from a primary generalised seizure where the convulsion comes first and colour change follows. Recovery is rapid with a short period of floppiness rather than the prolonged drowsiness of a true postictal state. The essential investigation is an electrocardiogram, because long QT syndrome and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia can present identically after a fright and carry a risk of sudden death. Iron deficiency is a common associated factor and treatment reduces attack frequency, so ferritin is worth checking once the cardiac assessment is clear.
key_points: Trigger then pallor then collapse then convulsion is the reflex anoxic sequence.
A primary seizure convulses first and changes colour afterwards.
Recovery is within minutes without a prolonged postictal phase.
An electrocardiogram with the corrected QT interval is mandatory in every case.
Treat coexisting iron deficiency, which reduces attack frequency.
explanation.pearls: Ask the witness which came first, the colour change or the jerking, because pallor preceding the convulsion points to a circulatory cause while a convulsion preceding the colour change points to epilepsy, and that single question separates them more reliably than any description of the movements.

subtopic_detail: toddler refusing all fluids with painful mouth ulcers and swollen bleeding gums on day two
stem: A 22-month-old boy has refused all drinks since yesterday and is drooling constantly. Fever and irritability began two days ago.

data_table.Mouth: Shallow ulcers on tongue, buccal mucosa and hard palate; gingivae swollen and bleeding on contact
data_table.Skin: No vesicles on hands, feet or buttocks
data_table.Hydration: Dry lips, moist tongue, capillary refill under two seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluids with intravenous aciclovir
options.rationale: Intravenous aciclovir is for the immunocompromised child or for disseminated disease, and this boy has moist mucous membranes, normal perfusion and wet nappies. Cannulating before an adequately analgesed oral trial converts a ward avoidable presentation into an admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis)

options.text: Give intranasal fentanyl, offer oral fluids, start oral aciclovir
options.rationale: Gingivostomatitis with bleeding swollen gums and palatal involvement is herpes simplex rather than an enteroviral exanthem, and aciclovir started within 72 to 96 hours of onset shortens the illness and the period of poor intake. Effective analgesia first is what allows a trial of oral fluids to succeed. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis)

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone and arrange paediatric review tomorrow
options.rationale: Corticosteroid has no role in herpetic gingivostomatitis and may prolong viral shedding, in contrast to its use in croup and some autoimmune oral ulceration. It also does not address the immediate barrier to drinking, which is pain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with metronidazole and dental review
options.rationale: This combination treats acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, the near pair, which produces punched out interdental ulceration with grey slough and halitosis in older children and adolescents. Diffuse shallow ulcers across the tongue and palate in a toddler are viral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Oral and Dental)

options.text: Give oral paracetamol and discharge with topical lidocaine gel
options.rationale: Paracetamol alone rarely provides enough analgesia for this degree of mucosal pain, and viscous lidocaine is avoided in young children because of systemic absorption and the risk of impairing the swallow. Discharge without a documented drinking trial risks representation with dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis)

explanation.summary: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is the commonest symptomatic first infection with herpes simplex virus type one and peaks between six months and five years. The feature that separates it from hand, foot and mouth disease is the gingivitis: red, swollen gums that bleed on contact, with ulcers extending onto the anterior tongue, buccal mucosa and hard palate, and no peripheral rash. The illness is self limiting over ten to fourteen days but the pain regularly causes enough reduction in oral intake to require hospital assessment. Aciclovir gives a modest benefit in symptom duration and oral intake when started within the first three to four days, and after that window it is not worth commencing. Adequate analgesia is the intervention that most often prevents admission, because many children who refuse fluids at triage will drink once the pain is controlled.
key_points: Bleeding swollen gingivae with palatal ulcers and no peripheral rash indicates herpes simplex.
Hand, foot and mouth disease spares the gingivae and adds a rash on hands, feet and buttocks.
Analgesia before a supervised drinking trial is the step that avoids admission.
Oral aciclovir helps only if started within about 72 to 96 hours of symptom onset.
Intravenous therapy is for failed oral intake, immunocompromise or dissemination.
explanation.pearls: Herpetic whitlow on a sucked thumb and herpetic keratoconjunctivitis are the two autoinoculation complications to warn parents about; a red painful eye in a child with gingivostomatitis needs same day ophthalmology review rather than topical steroid.

subtopic_detail: early adolescent boy with breast tissue development and asymmetrical testicular size on examination
stem: A 13-year-old boy has had breast development for eight months. He takes no medications, supplements or creams and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: 3 cm of firm concentric glandular tissue beneath both areolae, mildly tender
data_table.Genital examination: Pubic hair Tanner stage 3; right testicular volume 12 mL, left 20 mL with a firm irregular upper pole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ultrasound of the testes with beta human chorionic gonadotrophin
options.rationale: The asymmetrical testicular volume with a firm irregular area is the finding that overrides the otherwise reassuring picture of pubertal gynaecomastia, because a testicular germ cell tumour secreting beta human chorionic gonadotrophin causes breast tissue. Imaging and the tumour marker are the immediate steps. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Referral for tamoxifen with review of response at three months
options.rationale: Medical therapy is occasionally considered for persistent painful gynaecomastia after a secondary cause has been excluded, not before. Starting it now would treat a symptom while leaving a possible testicular tumour undiagnosed for a further three months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Thyroid and liver function tests with a serum prolactin
options.rationale: Thyrotoxicosis, chronic liver disease and hyperprolactinaemia are all recognised secondary causes and would be reasonable in a boy with no localising findings. They do not explain a focal testicular abnormality and would delay assessment of it. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Reassurance that this is pubertal, reassessing in six months
options.rationale: Reassurance and review is right for the boy with symmetrical testes in mid puberty, and pubertal gynaecomastia does resolve in most within two years. An asymmetrically enlarged irregular testis is not part of that picture and must not be observed. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

options.text: Karyotype with morning testosterone and gonadotrophins
options.rationale: This panel is aimed at Klinefelter syndrome, the near pair, which also causes adolescent gynaecomastia but gives small firm testes of less than 6 mL bilaterally with tall stature. The large asymmetrical testes here point the opposite way. (Source: RCH CPG: Gynaecomastia)

explanation.summary: Pubertal gynaecomastia affects up to 60 per cent of adolescent boys and reflects a transient imbalance between oestradiol and testosterone as puberty proceeds, typically appearing at Tanner stage 3 to 4 and resolving spontaneously within one to two years. The clinical task is to identify the small minority with a secondary cause, and the examination that does most of that work is the testicular examination. Symmetrical volumes appropriate for pubertal stage support the physiological diagnosis, small firm testes suggest Klinefelter syndrome, and an asymmetrically enlarged or irregular testis raises a hormone secreting germ cell or Leydig cell tumour. Drugs are the other major group, with spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, antipsychotics and anabolic steroids among the common culprits, so a medication and supplement history is essential. Firm concentric subareolar tissue distinguishes true glandular gynaecomastia from the diffuse fatty pseudogynaecomastia of obesity.
key_points: Pubertal gynaecomastia is common, symmetrical and resolves within one to two years.
Testicular examination is the highest yield part of the assessment.
Asymmetrical or irregular testes suggest a hormone secreting tumour and need imaging.
Small firm bilateral testes with tall stature suggest Klinefelter syndrome.
Always take a medication and supplement history before attributing it to puberty.
explanation.pearls: Testicular volume measured with an orchidometer is the single most useful discriminator in adolescent gynaecomastia: under 6 mL bilaterally points to Klinefelter syndrome, a difference of more than 3 mL between sides points to a testicular mass, and symmetrical volumes above 8 mL support physiological puberty.

subtopic_detail: school aged boy with ballooning on voiding and a pale scarred ring at the tip of the foreskin
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9-year-old boy brought in by his father because the tip of his foreskin puffs up when he passes urine and the stream comes out as a thin spray that goes everywhere. Over the past year the opening has become progressively tighter and he has had two episodes of a red sore tip treated with oral antibiotics.

His father says the foreskin used to pull back a little further when he was younger than it does now. He is toilet trained, dry day and night, and has never had a urinary tract infection. On examination he is well grown and systemically well. The foreskin cannot be retracted at all, and the distal end has a firm pale ring of tissue that does not stretch when gentle traction is applied. The glans cannot be visualised. There is no surrounding erythema, discharge or tenderness today, and the testes are descended with no inguinal swelling.

data_table.Examination: Non retractile foreskin with a firm pale sclerotic ring at the preputial orifice, glans not visualised
data_table.Voiding: Ballooning of the prepuce with a thin spraying stream, no dysuria today
data_table.History: Two prior episodes of balanoposthitis, progressive loss of previously achieved retraction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the father that the foreskin separates naturally and review again in twelve months
options.rationale: Reassurance suits physiological non retraction, which is normal in most boys until later childhood and is not scarred. A foreskin that has gone backwards in retractability with a visible white ring is pathological and will not improve with time. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for circumcision and histological examination of the foreskin
options.rationale: A pale sclerotic ring with loss of previously achieved retraction, ballooning and recurrent balanoposthitis is balanitis xerotica obliterans, a pathological phimosis in which the scarring is irreversible. Circumcision is both the treatment and the way the diagnosis is confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Perform preputial adhesiolysis in the treatment room with topical anaesthetic gel applied
options.rationale: Separating congenital adhesions between the inner prepuce and the glans is a different problem from a scarred narrowed orifice, and forcing a sclerotic ring tears it and worsens the scarring. This near pair is distinguished by whether the narrowing is at the tip or is adherence to the glans. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Prescribe topical betamethasone with gentle daily retraction for six weeks then review
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid with gentle stretching is the correct first line for physiological phimosis and succeeds in most boys, but it cannot reverse established sclerotic scar tissue. Delaying referral for six weeks allows the meatus to become involved. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound with a urine culture before making a referral decision
options.rationale: Imaging and culture would be appropriate if there were recurrent urinary tract infection or a suspicion of upper tract involvement, and this boy has had neither. The diagnosis here is made by inspection of the prepuce. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Non retractility of the foreskin is normal in the majority of boys through early childhood and separation continues into adolescence, so physiological phimosis is a finding rather than a diagnosis. Balanitis xerotica obliterans, the genital form of lichen sclerosus, is the main pathological phimosis in boys and typically presents between the ages of seven and twelve. The distinguishing features are a firm pale sclerotic ring at the preputial orifice, loss of retraction that had previously been achieved, ballooning with a spraying stream, and recurrent balanoposthitis. It is one of the clear medical indications for circumcision in childhood, and the specimen is sent for histology because the condition can extend to the glans and meatus and needs ongoing surveillance. Untreated disease can progress to meatal stenosis and urethral involvement, so referral should not be delayed for a trial of topical steroid.
key_points: Physiological phimosis is soft, common and improves with topical steroid and time.
A pale sclerotic ring with regression of retraction indicates balanitis xerotica obliterans.
Ballooning with a spraying stream and recurrent balanoposthitis support the diagnosis.
It is a recognised medical indication for circumcision, with histology on the specimen.
Progression to meatal stenosis and urethral stricture follows untreated disease.
explanation.pearls: Meatal involvement occurs in roughly a fifth of boys with balanitis xerotica obliterans, so the meatus should be inspected at the time of circumcision and the boy followed for a spraying or narrowing stream afterwards rather than discharged as cured.

subtopic_detail: preschooler with a painless neck lump enlarging over six weeks and overlying violaceous thinning skin
stem: A 3-year-old girl has a painless lump under the right jaw that has grown slowly over six weeks. Courses of cefalexin and amoxicillin with clavulanate have not changed it.

data_table.Examination: Firm 3 cm non-tender right submandibular mass fixed to thinned violaceous skin; no other lymphadenopathy
data_table.History: No fever, night sweats or weight loss; no tuberculosis contact
