lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Incision and drainage in theatre with pus sent for culture
options.rationale: Incision and drainage is correct for a pyogenic abscess, which is hot, tender and rapidly evolving in a febrile child. Opening a mycobacterial node reliably produces a chronically discharging sinus that takes many months to close. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

options.text: Oral clarithromycin with rifampicin and reassess in one month
options.rationale: Combination macrolide based therapy is a genuine alternative when the node sits over the facial nerve or excision is otherwise unsafe, so it is a legitimate second choice rather than a wrong concept. Cure rates are lower and treatment runs for months, so surgery is preferred when the site allows. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Chest radiograph with an interferon gamma release assay
options.rationale: This pathway targets tuberculous lymphadenitis, the near pair, which is suggested by contact history, overseas residence, systemic symptoms or bilateral nodes. Interferon gamma release assays also cross react with some non tuberculous species and can mislead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Full blood examination with lactate dehydrogenase and oncology review
options.rationale: Malignancy deserves consideration in any persistent node, but lymphoma in this age group usually gives a rubbery mobile node with systemic symptoms or nodes at several sites rather than skin adherence and discolouration. The skin changes are close to specific for mycobacterial disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

options.text: Complete surgical excision of the node with mycobacterial culture
options.rationale: A painless enlarging node in a preschooler with violaceous adherent skin and no response to two antibiotic courses is non tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis, and complete excision gives both the highest cure rate and the diagnosis. Incisional approaches risk a chronically discharging sinus. (Source: RCH CPG: Cervical lymphadenopathy)

explanation.summary: Non tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis is a disease of immunocompetent children between one and five years, acquired from soil and water and presenting as a slowly enlarging unilateral submandibular or preauricular node. The child remains well, which is the feature that separates it from pyogenic adenitis, and the overlying skin classically thins and takes on a violaceous or parchment appearance before it breaks down. Failure to respond to two courses of conventional oral antibiotics is a common part of the referral history. Complete surgical excision cures around 95 per cent and provides tissue for culture, whereas incision and drainage leaves a chronically discharging sinus. Where the node overlies the facial nerve and excision carries an unacceptable risk, prolonged combination therapy with clarithromycin plus rifampicin or ethambutol is the alternative, accepting a slower and less certain resolution.
key_points: A well preschooler with a painless enlarging unilateral node and normal growth.
Violaceous thinning skin adherent to the node is close to specific.
Non response to two courses of conventional oral antibiotics is typical.
Complete excision is both diagnostic and therapeutic with the highest cure rate.
Incision and drainage causes a chronic sinus and should be avoided.
explanation.pearls: Tuberculin skin testing in non tuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis is often weakly positive at 5 to 10 mm because of shared antigens, so an intermediate reaction in a well Australian born preschooler with a single neck node points towards the environmental mycobacteria rather than towards tuberculosis.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Non tuberculous mycobacterial infections

subtopic_detail: immunised school aged child with a third episode of one sided swelling in front of the ear
stem: A 6-year-old boy has a tender 4 cm swelling over the left parotid that lifts the earlobe, developing over a day. The same happened twice in eighteen months, each settling in a week. He is fully immunised and afebrile.

data_table.Duct: Clear saliva expressed from the left Stensen duct, no pus
data_table.Investigations: Serum amylase 186 U/L (30 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Mumps polymerase chain reaction swab and public health notification
options.rationale: Mumps remains notifiable and would be the default for parotid swelling, but it is characteristically bilateral or sequential, occurs once, and is very unlikely in a child fully covered by the measles mumps and rubella schedule. A third episode on the same side is not mumps. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia)

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin for ten days with review in one week
options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal therapy treats acute suppurative parotitis, which occurs in dehydrated or debilitated children with a hot erythematous gland and frank pus expressible from the duct. Clear saliva in an afebrile well child argues against it, and two previous courses have already failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies with paediatric rheumatology referral
options.rationale: Juvenile Sjogren syndrome is the systemic mimic worth remembering and does cause recurrent parotid swelling, but it is far commoner in adolescent girls and is accompanied by dry eyes and a dry mouth. Normal salivary flow and no ocular symptoms make it improbable as a first line test. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Ultrasound of both parotid glands, with massage and sialogogues
options.rationale: Recurrent unilateral parotid swelling in a well immunised child with clear ductal saliva is juvenile recurrent parotitis, and ultrasound showing multiple small hypoechoic sialectatic areas confirms it without radiation. Management is conservative with hydration, gland massage and sialogogues during attacks. (Source: RCH CPG: Parotitis)

options.text: Serum lipase and abdominal ultrasound for the raised amylase
options.rationale: The amylase here is salivary in origin, which is the trap: any inflamed salivary gland raises total amylase without pancreatic disease, and this boy has no abdominal pain or vomiting. Lipase would be normal and the imaging would be negative. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

explanation.summary: Juvenile recurrent parotitis is the second commonest cause of parotid swelling in children after mumps and presents with repeated episodes of unilateral or alternating parotid inflammation between the ages of three and six. The pathology is non obstructive sialectasis with ductal ectasia, and each attack lasts days to a couple of weeks before settling spontaneously. Three conditions have to be reasoned past: mumps, which is usually bilateral and does not recur in an immunised child; acute suppurative parotitis, which is febrile with purulent ductal discharge; and an autoimmune sialadenitis, which brings sicca symptoms. A raised total amylase is expected and reflects the salivary isoenzyme, so it should not trigger a pancreatic workup. Ultrasound is the imaging of choice and most children outgrow the condition by puberty, with sialendoscopy reserved for frequent disabling attacks.
key_points: Recurrent unilateral parotid swelling in a well immunised child is rarely mumps.
Clear ductal saliva and an afebrile child argue against suppurative parotitis.
Total amylase rises from the salivary isoenzyme and does not indicate pancreatitis.
Ultrasound showing sialectasis confirms the diagnosis without radiation.
Most cases resolve spontaneously around puberty with conservative management.
explanation.pearls: Splitting total amylase into pancreatic and salivary isoenzymes, or simply checking a lipase, resolves the diagnostic confusion in minutes: lipase is normal in salivary disease because the salivary glands do not produce it.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

subtopic_detail: imaging a midline neck swelling before excision to confirm functioning thyroid tissue is present elsewhere
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 6 year old boy. His mother first noticed a soft painless lump in the middle of the front of his neck about three months ago and thought it would go away.

Two weeks ago it became red, tender and larger during a head cold, and a week of oral antibiotics from his general practitioner settled the redness and the tenderness. The lump itself remains. He has had no weight loss and no night sweats. When you ask him to swallow and then to poke his tongue out, the lump rides upwards with both.

data_table.Examination: Smooth 2 cm midline swelling just below the hyoid bone, moves superiorly on swallowing and on tongue protrusion, overlying skin now normal, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Referral for excision of the cyst and the central hyoid body now
options.rationale: Excision of the tract together with the central portion of the hyoid bone is the correct definitive operation and it will very likely be the eventual plan, but performing it before imaging risks removing the child's only thyroid tissue. The operation follows the scan rather than replacing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

options.text: Neck ultrasound to confirm normally positioned thyroid tissue is present
options.rationale: Imaging before any operation establishes that a normal gland sits in its usual position, because in a small proportion of these children the swelling contains the only functioning thyroid tissue they have and removing it renders them permanently hypothyroid. Normal thyroid function tests do not settle this question, since ectopic tissue can maintain euthyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

options.text: Incision and drainage of the lump under local anaesthetic today
options.rationale: Drainage is reserved for a genuinely fluctuant abscess that has not settled with antibiotics, and here the inflammation has already resolved. Opening the lesion also risks creating a discharging sinus and makes the later definitive excision considerably more difficult. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

options.text: Fine needle aspiration cytology of the lump at the next clinic visit
options.rationale: Cytology is used where malignancy is a genuine concern, signalled by a hard fixed mass, rapid painless growth or associated lymphadenopathy, none of which is present in a soft midline lesion that elevates on tongue protrusion. It carries the same risk of establishing a sinus tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Neck Lumps)

options.text: A further two weeks of oral antibiotics with review in the clinic after
options.rationale: The infective episode has already resolved and the residual swelling is the underlying structural lesion rather than persisting infection. Further antibiotics treat something that is no longer present and delay the definitive pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: A thyroglossal duct cyst is the commonest congenital midline neck swelling in childhood and arises from the embryological tract along which the thyroid descends from the foramen caecum at the base of the tongue to its final pretracheal position. Its attachment to that tract is what produces the diagnostic sign of elevation with tongue protrusion as well as with swallowing, distinguishing it from a dermoid cyst, which is also midline but does not move with the tongue, and from lymphadenopathy, which is lateral. Because descent can arrest anywhere along the tract, a minority of children have no orthotopic gland at all and the cyst contains their entire functioning thyroid, which is why ultrasound is performed before any excision and why normal thyroid function tests cannot substitute for it. These cysts often first present when they enlarge and become infected during an upper respiratory illness. Definitive management is the Sistrunk procedure, removing the cyst with the tract and the central hyoid body, since simple cystectomy has a high recurrence rate.
key_points: Elevation with tongue protrusion as well as swallowing is the discriminating sign
Ultrasound before excision confirms a normally sited gland is present
Normal thyroid function tests do not exclude the cyst containing the only thyroid tissue
Infection during an upper respiratory illness is the usual trigger for presentation
The Sistrunk procedure removes the central hyoid body to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: Removing a thyroglossal cyst that contains ectopic thyroid without preoperative imaging leaves the child permanently athyreotic and dependent on lifelong thyroxine, which is the single reason ultrasound is mandatory even when thyroid function tests are entirely normal.

subtopic_detail: first line management of a persistent head tilt with a palpable neck mass in early infancy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7 week old girl brought by her parents because her head is always tilted. She was delivered by forceps after a prolonged second stage.

Her parents noticed a firm pea sized lump in the right side of her neck at about three weeks of age, which has not changed since. Her head tilts to the right and her chin points to the left, and they find it hard to turn her face to the right when settling her. She is feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile, and moves all four limbs equally. Her eye movements are full in all directions.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted to the right with chin rotated to the left, firm non tender 1 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid, passive rotation of the head to the right limited to about 50 degrees, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed, red reflex present and symmetrical, hips clinically stable on Ortolani and Barlow testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for surgical release of the sternocleidomastoid within a month
options.rationale: Surgical release is considered only after a sustained conservative program has failed, conventionally not before twelve months of age. Operating at seven weeks removes the chance of the spontaneous resolution that most infants achieve. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for atypical features such as a tilt that is not accompanied by rotation to the opposite side, abnormal tone or reflexes, developmental regression, or failure to respond to an adequate physiotherapy program. Her examination is otherwise normal and imaging at this age would require sedation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a stretching and positioning program
options.rationale: Passive stretching, positioning to encourage active rotation toward the restricted side and parent education resolve the great majority of cases when started in the first few months. Earlier referral produces better and faster correction, which is why this is done now rather than after a period of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange botulinum toxin injection of the shortened neck muscle
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin has been used as an adjunct in resistant cases in older children, but it is not a first line intervention and the evidence in infancy is limited. It would be considered only well after a stretching program had failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Reassure the parents that no intervention is needed at this age
options.rationale: Untreated restriction leads to progressive facial asymmetry and positional flattening of the skull, and the window in which stretching works best is the first few months. Reassurance alone forfeits that window. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis presents in the first weeks to months of life with the head tilted toward the affected sternocleidomastoid and the chin rotated away from it, and a firm painless mass within the muscle is present in a proportion of cases and resolves over several months. Difficult instrumental delivery and intrauterine crowding are the usual antecedents. The two associations to check at the same visit are developmental dysplasia of the hip, which shares the crowding aetiology and occurs more often in these infants, and positional plagiocephaly, which develops because the infant persistently rests on the same part of the skull. Physiotherapy with passive stretching and active positioning resolves most cases, with better outcomes the earlier it starts. Features that should redirect the assessment include a tilt without contralateral chin rotation, abnormal tone, limitation that is painful, an eye movement abnormality suggesting ocular torticollis, or failure to improve over several months of an adequate program.
key_points: The head tilts toward the affected muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Start physiotherapy early rather than observing, because outcomes are time dependent
Check the hips at the same visit given the shared association with crowding
Watch for positional plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry developing
Reserve surgery for failure of conservative treatment after about twelve months
explanation.pearls: A head tilt without the expected chin rotation to the opposite side is not muscular torticollis and should prompt assessment for an ocular cause, a posterior fossa lesion or an atlantoaxial abnormality rather than a physiotherapy referral.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

subtopic_detail: timing of repair for a reducible groin swelling in a young ex preterm infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 6 week old boy born at 32 weeks gestation. His parents noticed a bulge in his right groin about ten days ago, which appears when he cries or strains and settles when he is asleep.

It is present when you examine him. He is feeding well, has had no vomiting, opens his bowels normally and his nappies are unremarkable. The swelling extends downwards from the groin toward the scrotum, and you are unable to feel a normal cord above it. It flattens with steady gentle pressure and the right testis is palpable separately below the swelling. The left side is normal.

data_table.Examination: Right groin swelling extending toward the scrotum, upper border not palpable, reducible with gentle sustained pressure, overlying skin normal in colour with no tenderness, right testis palpable separately in the scrotum, abdomen soft and not distended
data_table.Investigations: Weight tracking along the 25th centile, no investigations performed, no vomiting and no abdominal distension reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this resolves on its own by twelve months
options.rationale: Spontaneous closure over the first year is the natural history of a communicating hydrocele, which is why this option is tempting in an infant with a scrotal swelling. A hernia containing bowel does not close spontaneously, and the inability to feel normal cord above the swelling separates the two at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

options.text: Arrange a groin ultrasound and review in the clinic in three months
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical and ultrasound adds little when the examination findings are as clear as these. A three month delay in an infant of this age spans the period of greatest incarceration risk. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons)

options.text: Arrange emergency theatre tonight for exploration of the right groin
options.rationale: Emergency operation is required for an irreducible swelling, particularly with tenderness, discolouration, vomiting or abdominal distension, none of which he has. His swelling reduces with gentle pressure and he is feeding and passing stool normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for repair on the next available list
options.rationale: A reducible groin hernia in early infancy carries a high risk of incarceration, greatest in the first months of life and higher again in babies born preterm, so repair is arranged promptly rather than deferred. Referral while it remains reducible allows an elective operation instead of an emergency one. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

options.text: Advise observation with review only if the swelling becomes painful
options.rationale: Waiting for pain means waiting for incarceration, which presents with an irreducible tender lump and can progress to bowel and testicular ischaemia within hours. Emergency repair in that setting carries substantially higher complication rates than elective repair. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

explanation.summary: Inguinal hernia in infancy is almost always indirect and results from a patent processus vaginalis, the same embryological structure whose incomplete obliteration produces a communicating hydrocele. The clinical distinction rests on whether the upper border of the swelling can be felt: a hydrocele confined to the scrotum allows the examiner to palpate normal cord above it and typically transilluminates, whereas a hernia extends up through the inguinal canal so that no upper border is reachable. Prematurity is the strongest risk factor and incidence rises steeply with decreasing gestational age. The clinical urgency comes from incarceration, which is far more common in infancy than in later childhood and threatens both the bowel and the ipsilateral testis through compression of the gonadal vessels. Because of this, hernias in young infants are repaired promptly on an elective list, whereas hydroceles are observed and usually resolve by around two years without intervention.
key_points: A patent processus vaginalis underlies both infant hernia and communicating hydrocele
Inability to palpate normal cord above the swelling indicates a hernia
Prematurity markedly increases both incidence and incarceration risk
Incarceration threatens bowel and the ipsilateral testis within hours
Hydroceles are observed to about two years, hernias are repaired promptly
explanation.pearls: The risk of incarceration in an untreated infant inguinal hernia is highest in the first six months of life and is reported at around 30 per cent in infants under one year, which is why repair is arranged within weeks rather than deferred until the child is older and larger.

subtopic_detail: proceeding to division of a restrictive lingual frenulum after optimised attachment has failed
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9 day old breastfed boy in the assessment unit. His mother describes severe pain throughout every feed and her nipples are cracked and bleeding.

He feeds for about fifty minutes and wants to feed again within ninety minutes. A lactation consultant has seen the pair twice over the past four days and has worked on positioning and attachment at both visits, with no improvement in pain or in the pattern of feeding. His birth weight was 3480 g. On examination his tongue cannot be lifted above the level of the lower gum and the tip is notched when he cries.

data_table.Examination: Frenulum attached close to the tip of the tongue restricting elevation and lateral movement, tongue tip notched on crying, palate intact, no ankyloglossia of the upper lip, mother's nipples cracked with a compressed shape after the feed
data_table.Investigations: Weight 3090 g, representing 11 per cent below birth weight, serum bilirubin below the treatment threshold for age, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise cessation of breastfeeding and establish full formula feeding
options.rationale: Abandoning breastfeeding forecloses a problem with an effective and simple treatment. It should be a decision the mother reaches after the remediable cause has been addressed, not a first line clinical recommendation. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

options.text: Supply nipple shields for the mother and review the weight in one week
options.rationale: Shields can reduce pain in the short term but often reduce milk transfer further, which is the opposite of what a baby who has lost 11 per cent of his birth weight needs. Waiting a further week without addressing transfer risks continued weight loss. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

options.text: Commence formula top up feeds after each breastfeed and review weekly
options.rationale: Supplementation may well be needed in the short term to protect his weight and would reasonably run alongside the definitive step, but used alone it leaves the mechanical restriction and the maternal pain untreated and predictably ends breastfeeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding)

options.text: Treat both mother and baby for candida and review in one week
options.rationale: Candidal infection causes burning nipple pain that characteristically persists between feeds and is often accompanied by oral plaques in the infant, whereas her pain is confined to the feed and the nipple emerges compressed, which indicates a mechanical problem. There are no oral plaques. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for division of the tongue tie after the review of attachment
options.rationale: A frenulum that restricts tongue elevation, combined with nipple trauma, prolonged ineffective feeding and weight loss that has not responded to two skilled attachment reviews, is the specific situation in which frenotomy improves maternal pain and feeding effectiveness. Division is a brief procedure that allows immediate feeding afterwards. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia describes a lingual frenulum short or anteriorly attached enough to restrict tongue movement, and it is present in a meaningful minority of newborns, though only a fraction of those have any feeding problem at all. This distinction governs practice: the anatomical finding alone is not an indication to operate, and rates of division rose substantially in Australia before that point was re-emphasised. The indication combines a restrictive frenulum on examination with a genuine functional problem, meaning nipple pain and trauma, ineffective milk transfer with poor weight gain, or prolonged unsatisfying feeds, that has not resolved with skilled assessment of positioning and attachment. Weight loss beyond about 10 per cent of birth weight is itself a marker requiring prompt action regardless of cause. Frenotomy is performed without general anaesthesia in young infants, bleeding is usually minimal and the infant can feed immediately, with maternal pain scores improving most consistently in trials.
key_points: The anatomical finding alone is never the indication for division
Combine a restrictive frenulum with a documented functional feeding problem
Skilled attachment review must come first and be seen to fail
Weight loss beyond about 10 per cent of birth weight requires prompt action
Maternal nipple pain is the outcome that improves most consistently after frenotomy
explanation.pearls: A nipple that emerges compressed into a wedge or lipstick shape at the end of a feed indicates a mechanical compression problem rather than infection, and it distinguishes a restrictive tongue tie from candidal nipple pain, which burns between feeds as well as during them.

subtopic_detail: sequencing refractive correction before occlusion therapy in unilateral reduced vision found at screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred after a preschool vision screening visit. His parents had noticed nothing wrong and say he plays and draws normally.

He was born at term with no perinatal problems and there is no family history of childhood eye disease. On testing, the vision in his right eye is 6/6 and in his left eye is 6/24. The cover test reveals an inward shift of the left eye when the right eye is covered. The red reflex is present, symmetrical and normal in both eyes, and the fundus appears normal on both sides. Cycloplegic refraction has been performed in the clinic.

data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/6 right and 6/24 left, cover test shows an inward shift of the left eye on covering the right, red reflex symmetrical and normal bilaterally, fundi normal, ocular movements full
data_table.Investigations: Cycloplegic refraction plus 5.00 dioptres in the left eye and plus 0.75 dioptres in the right eye

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe spectacles for the refractive error and review in four months
options.rationale: Correcting a large difference in refractive power between the eyes is the necessary first treatment, because a substantial proportion of children recover normal vision on spectacles alone over a period of refractive adaptation lasting about three to four months. Occlusion is added only for the deficit that remains after that. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

options.text: Commence occlusion of the right eye for six hours daily from today
options.rationale: Patching the better eye before the blurred image is corrected asks the weaker eye to work through an uncorrected 5 dioptre error, which limits what occlusion can achieve and imposes an unnecessary burden on the child. It is the correct second step once spectacles have been worn and the deficit reassessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

options.text: Refer for surgical correction of the eye alignment within three months
options.rationale: Surgery addresses the cosmetic and sensory consequences of misalignment but does not itself restore vision in the affected eye. In this pattern the deviation is often driven by the uncorrected hypermetropia and improves substantially with spectacles alone. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.text: Commence daily atropine drops to the right eye as penalisation therapy
options.rationale: Pharmacological penalisation blurs the better eye and is a recognised alternative to patching with comparable outcomes, particularly where compliance with a patch is poor. Like patching, it belongs after refractive correction rather than before it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.text: Repeat the vision screening in twelve months at the school entry check
options.rationale: Visual development is plastic only through the first several years and treatment response falls progressively with age. Deferring for a year in a four year old spends a substantial part of the remaining treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Vision Screening)

explanation.summary: Amblyopia is reduced vision in an eye that is structurally normal, caused by the developing visual cortex suppressing a degraded or misaligned image during the sensitive period of visual development. The three mechanisms are a difference in refractive power between the eyes, misalignment, and deprivation from an obstruction such as a cataract or a ptosis, and the first two frequently coexist as they do here. It is the leading cause of monocular vision loss in Australian children and is usually asymptomatic, which is the rationale for preschool screening, since a child with one good eye reports nothing wrong. The normal symmetrical red reflex and normal fundus are important because they exclude deprivational causes including cataract and retinoblastoma, either of which would demand urgent rather than routine referral. Treatment begins with spectacles, worn for a period of refractive adaptation, before occlusion or atropine penalisation is added for residual deficit, and outcomes deteriorate steadily as treatment is started later in childhood.
key_points: Amblyopia is reduced vision in a structurally normal eye and is usually asymptomatic
A normal symmetrical red reflex excludes cataract and retinoblastoma as the cause
Correct the refractive error first and allow three to four months of adaptation
Add occlusion or atropine penalisation only for the residual deficit
Treatment response declines steadily with increasing age at presentation
explanation.pearls: Roughly a third of children with anisometropic amblyopia reach normal acuity on spectacles alone within about sixteen weeks of refractive adaptation, so patching started on the day of diagnosis subjects many children to occlusion they never needed.

subtopic_detail: identifying the treatable association behind stereotyped cyanotic episodes provoked by crying in a toddler
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 18 month old girl whose parents describe three frightening episodes over the past two months. The most recent happened yesterday when she was told she could not have a biscuit before dinner.

She cried hard, then went silent with her mouth open, her lips turned dusky blue and she went floppy and slid to the floor. She was unresponsive for about twenty seconds with a few jerks of her arms at the end, then cried, wanted a cuddle and was back to her usual self within a minute. Each of the three episodes has begun in exactly this way after she was upset or hurt. She is otherwise well, walks and runs normally and has around six bottles of cow's milk a day in addition to her meals.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, no murmur, normal heart sounds, femoral pulses palpable and symmetrical, neurological examination normal, development age appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105 to 135), mean cell volume 68 fL (70 to 86), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (15 to 150), electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography and refer to a paediatric neurologist
options.rationale: Brief jerking at the end of an episode reflects cerebral hypoperfusion rather than a primary seizure, and the constant provoking trigger of crying, the rapid complete recovery and the absence of any drowsy phase afterwards all argue against epilepsy. Investigation is reserved for episodes that occur without a trigger or that are followed by prolonged confusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

options.text: Commence oral iron with dietary advice and parental reassurance
options.rationale: These episodes are benign, stereotyped and reliably provoked by crying after an upset, and iron deficiency is a well established association that is present here on the blood film indices and ferritin. Correcting the deficiency reduces both the frequency and the severity of episodes, and excessive cow's milk intake is the usual dietary driver to address alongside it. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

options.text: Commence regular sodium valproate and review in the clinic in a month
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant therapy treats a condition she does not have and exposes a toddler to hepatotoxicity and other adverse effects for no benefit. These episodes do not respond to anticonvulsants. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer to paediatric cardiology for a 24 hour Holter monitor recording
options.rationale: Cardiac assessment is warranted when episodes occur during exertion, during swimming, without any provoking trigger, or where there is a family history of premature sudden death. Her electrocardiogram, cardiac examination and femoral pulses are all normal and every episode has followed an emotional trigger. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Advise the parents to avoid confrontation that triggers the episodes
options.rationale: Parents commonly begin to give in to avoid provoking an episode, and warning against this is an important part of counselling, so the advice is exactly backwards. Abandoning normal limit setting reinforces the behaviour without altering the underlying physiology. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells)

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect around one in twenty young children, typically begin between six and eighteen months and resolve by about five years of age. The cyanotic form follows a period of vigorous crying after pain, frustration or fright, with expiratory apnoea, colour change, loss of tone and brief loss of consciousness, while the less common pallid form follows a minor bump or fright and is mediated by a vagally driven asystolic pause. Brief tonic stiffening or a few clonic jerks occur in a substantial minority because of transient cerebral hypoperfusion and are frequently misread as a seizure, so the discriminating features are the invariable emotional or painful trigger, the crying that precedes the event, and rapid complete recovery without a postictal phase. Iron deficiency is associated with more frequent and more severe spells, and randomised evidence shows that iron supplementation reduces their frequency, which makes a full blood count and ferritin part of the standard assessment. Excessive cow's milk intake beyond about 500 mL a day in a toddler is the commonest dietary cause of the deficiency, and parents need explicit advice to maintain normal boundaries rather than avoid triggers.
key_points: Episodes are always preceded by crying after an upset, pain or fright
Brief jerking reflects cerebral hypoperfusion, not epilepsy
Check a full blood count and ferritin because iron deficiency worsens spells
Iron supplementation reduces both frequency and severity
Counsel parents to keep normal limits rather than avoid triggers
explanation.pearls: Cow's milk intake above about 500 mL a day in a toddler displaces iron rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss, and reducing it while giving three months of oral iron is what actually reduces breath holding spell frequency.

subtopic_detail: recognising that raised transaminases with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase are of muscle origin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred by a gastroenterology colleague for a second opinion. He was referred to that clinic three months ago after routine bloods taken during an episode of gastroenteritis showed raised liver enzymes, and repeat testing has shown the same pattern.

His parents mention that he is slower than the other children at kindergarten, falls frequently, and climbs the stairs at home one step at a time putting the same foot first. He walked at 19 months and his speech is also behind his peers. When you ask him to get up from sitting on the floor he turns onto his front and pushes on his own thighs with his hands to stand. His calves look bulky for his build.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral calf hypertrophy, proximal lower limb weakness, positive Gowers manoeuvre, waddling gait, reflexes present at the knees, no hepatomegaly and no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 35), gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits, bilirubin within normal limits, albumin within normal limits, creatine kinase 12400 U/L (less than 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps with immunohistochemical staining
options.rationale: Biopsy with dystrophin staining was formerly the standard confirmatory test and retains a role when genetic testing is negative despite a strong clinical picture. Performing it first subjects the child to a general anaesthetic for information that a blood test usually provides. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Liver ultrasound with viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen
options.rationale: This pursues the referral that has already been made in error. A gamma glutamyl transferase within normal limits alongside raised transaminases indicates that the enzymes are coming from skeletal muscle rather than from liver, since hepatocellular injury characteristically raises the gamma glutamyl transferase as well. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Dystrophin gene testing for deletions and duplications on a blood sample
options.rationale: Progressive proximal weakness with calf hypertrophy, a positive Gowers manoeuvre and a creatine kinase in the thousands is a dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and genetic testing on blood confirms the diagnosis in around seven in ten boys through deletion or duplication analysis. It avoids an operation and immediately informs carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the family. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Electromyography with nerve conduction studies under sedation
options.rationale: Electrophysiology can demonstrate a myopathic pattern but cannot identify which myopathy, so it does not reach a diagnosis. It has largely been displaced by genetic testing in this situation and is poorly tolerated by young children. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Repeat liver function tests and creatine kinase in three months
options.rationale: A further three months of observation delays a diagnosis that carries immediate implications for corticosteroid timing, cardiac and respiratory surveillance and genetic counselling for the family. The abnormality has already been confirmed on repeat testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Muscular Dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy affects roughly one in 3500 to 5000 boys and follows X linked recessive inheritance, with about a third of cases arising from new mutations so that a negative family history is common. Presentation is typically between two and five years with delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty with stairs and running, and a positive Gowers manoeuvre, and around a third of boys also have global developmental delay or language delay because dystrophin is expressed in brain as well as muscle. A recurring diagnostic detour is referral for liver disease, because damaged muscle releases alanine and aspartate aminotransferase and these are reported on standard liver panels, so a normal gamma glutamyl transferase alongside raised transaminases in a boy with motor difficulty should redirect thinking to muscle and prompt a creatine kinase. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started at the appropriate stage prolongs ambulation, and structured cardiac and respiratory surveillance changes long term outcome. Genetic confirmation also enables carrier testing of female relatives and access to mutation specific therapies.
key_points: Transaminases rise from damaged skeletal muscle and appear on standard liver panels
A normal gamma glutamyl transferase points away from a hepatic source
Creatine kinase in the thousands with a positive Gowers manoeuvre is the key combination
About a third of boys have associated developmental or language delay
Genetic testing on blood confirms most cases and avoids muscle biopsy
explanation.pearls: In any boy under five referred for unexplained raised transaminases, check the gamma glutamyl transferase and a creatine kinase before imaging the liver; a normal gamma glutamyl transferase with a creatine kinase above 2000 U/L redirects the entire workup to muscle.

subtopic_detail: discordance between pubic hair development and testicular volume in a tall adolescent boy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 15 year old boy referred by his school because of longstanding difficulty with reading and written work and because he finds it hard to make friends. His parents also wonder whether he is developing normally.

He is taller than both parents were at his age, and his height sits on the 97th centile against a mid parental centile of 40. His arm span exceeds his height by 7 cm. He has adult type pubic hair and has been shaving occasionally for a year. On examination his testes measure 4 mL on each side by orchidometer and he has firm breast tissue palpable behind both nipples. He takes no medication and uses no supplements.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 97th centile, arm span exceeding height by 7 cm, pubic hair Tanner stage 4, testicular volume 4 mL bilaterally and firm to palpation, bilateral glandular breast tissue, no abdominal or scrotal mass
data_table.Investigations: Luteinising hormone raised, follicle stimulating hormone raised, testosterone at the lower end of the reference range for age, prolactin within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat early morning testosterone with sex hormone binding globulin
options.rationale: Repeating the androgen measurement refines a number that is already consistent with the clinical picture, and the raised gonadotrophins have already localised the lesion to the testis. It delays the test that gives the answer. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated when gonadotrophins are low or inappropriately normal alongside a low testosterone, which indicates a central cause. Here the gonadotrophins are raised, which places the defect in the testis and makes the pituitary the wrong organ to image. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

options.text: Scrotal ultrasound to assess testicular volume and architecture
options.rationale: Ultrasound would confirm what the orchidometer has already established and is used principally to look for a testicular tumour, which would present with a discrete mass and typically with high oestrogen rather than raised gonadotrophins. It does not explain the tall stature or the learning profile. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Peripheral blood karyotype requested through the clinical genetics service
options.rationale: Small firm testes that have failed to enlarge despite advanced pubic hair development, tall stature with long limbs, gynaecomastia and raised gonadotrophins with a low testosterone indicate primary testicular failure with a chromosomal basis, and a karyotype is the definitive test. Making the diagnosis opens access to androgen replacement, fertility preservation counselling and educational support. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

options.text: Radiograph of the left hand and wrist to determine the bone age
options.rationale: Bone age is valuable when the question is the timing of puberty relative to growth, as in constitutional delay or precocity. His puberty has clearly begun and progressed, so the question is why the testes have not grown with it. (Source: RCH CPG: Puberty)

explanation.summary: Klinefelter syndrome, most often a 47,XXY karyotype, affects around one in 600 male births and is the commonest chromosomal cause of primary hypogonadism, yet the majority of affected men are never diagnosed. The reason is that puberty usually begins and progresses normally under adrenal and early testicular androgen drive, so pubic hair, voice change and body habitus develop on schedule, while progressive seminiferous tubule fibrosis prevents the testes from enlarging beyond about 4 to 6 mL. That discordance between advanced pubic hair and persistently small firm testes is the single most useful clinical clue and is easily missed if testicular volume is not measured. Additional features include tall stature with disproportionately long limbs from delayed epiphyseal closure, gynaecomastia, and a characteristic profile of language based learning difficulty with relatively preserved non verbal reasoning alongside social difficulties. Biochemically the picture is hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, and management involves testosterone replacement from mid puberty, discussion of fertility preservation because sperm retrieval rates fall with age, and educational and psychological support.
key_points: Advanced pubic hair with testes still at 4 mL is the discriminating discordance
Raised gonadotrophins localise the defect to the testis rather than the pituitary
Tall stature with long limbs reflects delayed epiphyseal closure
The learning profile is typically language based with preserved non verbal reasoning
Discuss fertility preservation early because sperm retrieval rates decline with age
explanation.pearls: Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer in any tall adolescent boy referred for learning or social difficulties; a volume that remains at or below 6 mL once pubic hair has reached Tanner stage 4 should prompt a karyotype rather than reassurance.

subtopic_detail: ear position distinguishing a fused suture from positional moulding in occipital flattening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6 month old girl whose parents are worried about the shape of the back of her head. They first noticed flattening on the right at about three months of age. She sleeps on her back as they were advised, and they have tried turning her head to the other side at night without any change.

She is meeting her developmental milestones, feeds well and has no vomiting or irritability. Looking down on the top of her head from above, you see that the right ear sits further back and lower than the left, and that the left side of her forehead is more prominent than the right. There is a firm ridge palpable running across the back right of her skull and a bulge behind the right ear.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening, right ear displaced posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the left, contralateral left frontal bossing, palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture, ipsilateral mastoid bulge, anterior fontanelle soft, head circumference tracking the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Neurological examination normal, red reflex present and symmetrical, no papilloedema visualised, developmental milestones age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretches and tummy time coaching
options.rationale: Neck restriction commonly drives positional flattening and physiotherapy is central to managing that pathway, which is why this option is plausible. Her neck movement is not described as restricted and the ear displacement here is backwards rather than forwards, which is the opposite of the positional pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Give repositioning advice and review the head shape in two months
options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for deformation caused by external pressure, and it has already been tried without effect. A fused suture cannot remodel in response to positioning, so two further months would be lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet to be fitted in the next four weeks
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is an option for moderate to severe positional deformity in selected infants within a defined age window. Applying a helmet to a skull with a fused suture does not correct the underlying restriction and delays the operation. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

options.text: Arrange plain skull radiographs and review the result in the clinic
options.rationale: Plain films are insensitive for sutural fusion in infancy and a normal film would not exclude the diagnosis, while an abnormal one would still be followed by specialist referral and dedicated imaging. The referral is what changes management. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Refer to the craniofacial surgical service for specialist assessment
options.rationale: A palpable sutural ridge with the ear displaced backwards and downwards, a mastoid bulge and bossing of the opposite forehead describes a trapezoid head shape that indicates a fused suture rather than external moulding. Premature fusion requires surgical assessment and operative correction is generally undertaken within the first year. (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal Head Shape)

explanation.summary: Occipital flattening in infancy is usually positional and has become much more common since back sleeping was adopted for sudden infant death prevention, but a small proportion represents premature fusion of the lambdoid suture, and the two are separated at the bedside by looking down on the skull from above. Positional deformity produces a parallelogram: the flattened occiput pushes the ear on that side forwards and the forehead on the same side becomes more prominent. Lambdoid synostosis produces a trapezoid: the ear on the affected side is pulled backwards and downwards, there is a compensatory bulge over the mastoid, and the bossing appears on the opposite forehead. A palpable ridge along the suture supports fusion, and the absence of any response to sustained repositioning is further evidence against a positional cause. Positional deformity is managed with repositioning, tummy time and treatment of any associated neck restriction, with helmet therapy for selected moderate to severe cases, whereas fusion requires craniofacial referral and surgical correction, typically within the first year, to prevent progressive asymmetry and to protect brain growth.
key_points: Look down on the skull from above to judge parallelogram against trapezoid
Positional flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear forwards and bosses the ipsilateral forehead
Lambdoid fusion pulls the ipsilateral ear backwards and downwards with a mastoid bulge
Contralateral frontal bossing and a palpable sutural ridge indicate fusion
Failure to respond to sustained repositioning argues against a positional cause
explanation.pearls: The direction of ear displacement is the single most reliable bedside discriminator in occipital flattening: an ear pushed forward means positional moulding, an ear pulled backward and down means lambdoid synostosis and a craniofacial referral.

subtopic_detail: biphasic noisy breathing unchanged by position in an ex preterm infant with previous intubation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 month old girl in the emergency department with noisy breathing. She was born at 27 weeks gestation and was ventilated through an endotracheal tube for three weeks in the neonatal unit.

Her parents say the noise started at about three weeks after she came home and has slowly become louder. It is present when she breathes in and also when she breathes out, and they have not been able to find any position that makes it better or worse. This is her third presentation in two months with what has each time been treated as croup, and on each occasion she improved for a day and then returned to her usual noisy breathing. She is feeding adequately and growing along the 25th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 52, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor audible at rest and unchanged by prone or supine positioning, mild intercostal and subcostal recession, no drooling, chest otherwise clear, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, no fever documented at any of the three presentations, growth tracking the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat for microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy
options.rationale: Stridor that is biphasic, unaltered by position and recurrent in an infant with prolonged neonatal intubation points to a fixed narrowing at or below the vocal cords rather than to a dynamic supraglottic collapse. Direct visualisation of the airway under anaesthesia is the only way to establish the site and severity and to plan treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor trial and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Acid reflux aggravates supraglottic collapse and antireflux treatment is sometimes used as an adjunct in that condition. It does nothing for a fixed structural narrowing, and six weeks of observation in an infant with recession at rest carries a real risk of decompensation during the next viral illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Reassure the parents that the noise resolves by eighteen months
options.rationale: Spontaneous resolution by around eighteen to twenty four months describes laryngomalacia, which is the commonest cause of infant stridor and the reason this reassurance is so tempting. That condition gives inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine, during feeding and when crying, and improves in the prone position, which is the opposite of what is described. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and review the film in the clinic
options.rationale: A chest film may show a vascular ring or a lower airway abnormality and is a reasonable adjunct, but it images below the level where the obstruction almost certainly lies and a normal film would not exclude it. It does not substitute for direct visualisation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Give nebulised adrenaline with oral dexamethasone and review after
options.rationale: This is the treatment for viral laryngotracheobronchitis and explains why she has transiently improved at each previous presentation, since reducing mucosal oedema temporarily widens an already narrowed lumen. Treating the recurring exacerbation again without investigating the fixed narrowing beneath it repeats the error of the previous two visits. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: The character and timing of stridor localise the obstruction: inspiratory stridor arises above the vocal cords, expiratory noise arises in the intrathoracic airway, and biphasic stridor indicates a fixed narrowing at the level of the glottis or subglottis where flow is limited in both phases of respiration. Laryngomalacia accounts for the majority of infant stridor and is distinguished by being inspiratory, worse supine and during feeding or crying, better prone, and by improving spontaneously over the first two years. Acquired subglottic stenosis follows prolonged or traumatic endotracheal intubation, which makes ex preterm infants the principal risk group, and it characteristically presents with biphasic stridor unaffected by position that becomes symptomatic during intercurrent viral illness. Recurrent croup, particularly more than twice in a year or in an infant under six months, is a recognised presentation of an underlying fixed narrowing and is an indication for airway assessment rather than for further episodic treatment. Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy establish the grade of stenosis, which determines whether observation, endoscopic dilatation or open reconstruction is appropriate.
key_points: Biphasic stridor indicates a fixed glottic or subglottic narrowing
Laryngomalacia is inspiratory, worse supine and better prone, and resolves by about two years
Prolonged neonatal intubation is the main risk factor for acquired subglottic stenosis
Recurrent croup under six months of age warrants airway assessment
Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy grade the stenosis and direct treatment
explanation.pearls: Two or more episodes of croup before six months of age, or any croup that does not fully settle between episodes, should prompt referral for airway endoscopy rather than another course of dexamethasone, because acquired subglottic stenosis presents exactly this way.
