subtopic_detail: extrahepatic features redirecting a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia away from the default diagnosis
stem: A 7-week-old girl has been jaundiced since day four with pale stools and dark urine. Her weight has fallen from the 50th to the 3rd centile.

data_table.Examination: Deep set eyes, broad forehead, pointed chin; ejection systolic murmur radiating to the back; posterior embryotoxon
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 168 micromol/L, conjugated 110 micromol/L; gamma glutamyl transferase 620 U/L (less than 100); alpha 1 antitrypsin normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Extrahepatic biliary atresia of the perinatal type
options.rationale: This is the diagnosis that must be excluded urgently in any infant with pale stools and conjugated jaundice, and it remains the default until the extrahepatic features are noticed. It does not cause peripheral pulmonary stenosis, posterior embryotoxon, butterfly vertebrae or the facial phenotype, all of which are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Syndromic paucity of the intrahepatic bile ducts
options.rationale: Conjugated jaundice with a markedly raised gamma glutamyl transferase occurring alongside peripheral pulmonary stenosis, posterior embryotoxon, a butterfly vertebra and the characteristic facial appearance identifies a multisystem disorder rather than isolated liver disease. The combination of cardiac, ocular, skeletal and facial features is what distinguishes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency of the PiZZ phenotype
options.rationale: This is a genuine cause of neonatal cholestasis and is part of the standard workup, but the serum level is within normal limits here. It also produces no cardiac, ocular, skeletal or facial abnormality. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2
options.rationale: The inherited canalicular transport defects of types 1 and 2 present with severe cholestasis and intense itch, but characteristically with a gamma glutamyl transferase that is low or within normal limits, which is the opposite of the markedly raised value here. That single enzyme separates them from the other intrahepatic causes. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection of the liver
options.rationale: Congenital infection can produce conjugated jaundice and hepatomegaly and belongs in the differential, but it is typically accompanied by microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and intracranial calcification. It does not produce the cardiac, ocular and vertebral combination described. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced at two weeks of age, or at three weeks if preterm and breastfed, needs a split bilirubin, because a conjugated fraction is never physiological and always requires investigation. The immediate priority is to exclude biliary atresia, since the success of the Kasai portoenterostomy falls sharply after about sixty days of life, and pale stools with dark urine make that the working diagnosis until proven otherwise. Alagille syndrome is the principal alternative and arises from mutations in JAG1 or NOTCH2 affecting the Notch signalling pathway, producing paucity of interlobular bile ducts together with abnormalities in several organ systems. The recognised features are cholestasis, peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot, posterior embryotoxon on slit lamp examination, butterfly vertebrae on a spine or chest film, and a characteristic facies with a broad forehead, deep set eyes and a pointed chin. Distinguishing it from biliary atresia matters because these infants do not benefit from a Kasai procedure and may be harmed by it, and the gamma glutamyl transferase is the enzyme that separates both from the low enzyme familial cholestasis syndromes.
key_points: Any jaundice persisting past two weeks requires a split bilirubin
A conjugated fraction is never physiological and demands urgent assessment
Exclude biliary atresia first because Kasai success falls after about sixty days
Peripheral pulmonary stenosis, posterior embryotoxon and butterfly vertebrae define the syndromic alternative
A low gamma glutamyl transferase points instead to the familial canalicular transport defects
explanation.pearls: A markedly raised gamma glutamyl transferase excludes progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis types 1 and 2, in which the enzyme is characteristically normal or low despite severe cholestasis, making that one enzyme the fastest way to narrow a neonatal cholestasis differential.

subtopic_detail: exertional collapse with a borderline corrected QT interval and a family history of unexplained sudden death
stem: A 14-year-old girl collapsed during a 400 m race, unresponsive for 40 seconds with a few limb jerks, then spoke normally, with no tongue biting or postictal confusion. Two years ago she collapsed diving into a pool. Her father died at 33 in an unexplained single-vehicle crash.

data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm 62 /min, corrected QT 468 ms, no delta wave

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that the corrected QT is not diagnostic
options.rationale: It is true that a corrected QT of 468 milliseconds falls below the 480 millisecond threshold that is diagnostic on the electrocardiogram alone, and this is precisely the trap. Diagnosis rests on a weighted score that combines the interval with syncope during exertion and a family history of unexplained sudden death before 30, and a borderline interval with those features reaches a high probability. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography and neurology review
options.rationale: Brief myoclonic jerks occur commonly in cerebral hypoperfusion from any cause and do not indicate a seizure, and the absence of tongue biting, incontinence and any postictal phase argues strongly against epilepsy. Pursuing the neurological pathway is the classic route by which these children are misdiagnosed for years. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Refer to a cardiac genetic service for evaluation
options.rationale: Two exertional collapses, one on entering water, together with a father who died in an unexplained single vehicle crash before 35 and a borderline corrected QT interval, constitute a high probability inherited arrhythmia syndrome that requires specialist evaluation with genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives. Competitive sport is withheld and beta blockade commenced through that service while the assessment proceeds. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Arrange a 24-hour Holter monitor and clinic review
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring over a single day is unlikely to capture an event that has occurred twice in two years and a normal recording would provide false reassurance. Exercise testing with recovery phase measurement is more informative in this syndrome, and both belong within a specialist assessment rather than instead of one. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Commence propranolol with review in six months
options.rationale: Beta blockade is the correct pharmacological treatment and starting it is not the error, but doing so without specialist evaluation leaves the genotype unknown, the family unscreened, the need for an implantable defibrillator unassessed and the sports restriction unaddressed. Relatives at identical risk remain undiagnosed. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Syncope during exertion is a red flag that separates a cardiac cause from the far commoner reflex faint, which occurs on standing, in heat or after a painful stimulus and is preceded by a warning of nausea, greying vision and sweating. Brief myoclonic jerking occurs in up to two thirds of ordinary faints and is not evidence of epilepsy, so the discriminating features are the absence of a postictal phase, of tongue biting and of incontinence, with rapid complete recovery. The congenital long QT syndromes are diagnosed by the Schwartz weighted score rather than by the interval alone, combining the corrected QT, symptom pattern and family history, so an interval between 450 and 480 milliseconds may still indicate disease when it sits alongside exertional syncope and unexplained premature sudden death in a first degree relative. Trigger specificity helps subtype the condition: exertion and swimming point to LQT1, auditory startle and the postpartum period to LQT2, and events during sleep to LQT3. An unexplained single vehicle crash or drowning in a young relative should be recorded as a possible arrhythmic death, since these are the ways sudden arrhythmic deaths are commonly misclassified, and cascade screening of first degree relatives is part of managing the index case.
key_points: Syncope during exertion or on entering water is a cardiac red flag
Myoclonic jerks occur in ordinary faints and do not establish a seizure
Diagnosis uses a weighted score, not the corrected QT interval alone
A corrected QT of 450 to 480 milliseconds can still be diagnostic with supporting features
Unexplained single vehicle crashes and drownings in young relatives may be arrhythmic deaths
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether any relative died young in a single vehicle crash, a drowning or a cot death, because these are the three ways inherited arrhythmic deaths are routinely misclassified and the answer can move a borderline corrected QT of 460 to 480 milliseconds from equivocal to diagnostic.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: the narrow window in which a sample can still distinguish congenital from postnatally acquired infection in a newborn who failed hearing screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 19 day old boy referred after he did not pass the newborn hearing screen in either ear on day two and again on a repeat test on day fourteen.

He was born at term with a birth weight on the tenth centile. His mother had a mild flu like illness with sore throat and fatigue at around sixteen weeks of pregnancy and did not seek medical attention. He is feeding and growing, and his mother reports no fevers. On examination he has scattered petechiae over his trunk that his mother says have been present since birth, and his liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. His anterior fontanelle is soft and his neurological examination is otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Weight tenth centile, head circumference third centile, scattered petechiae, liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows platelets 88 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haemoglobin 148 g/L (140 to 220), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 45)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M serology taken from the infant now
options.rationale: Neonatal immunoglobulin M is insensitive because the infant's antibody response is unreliable, and maternally transferred immunoglobulin G confuses interpretation further, so serology neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis. Direct viral detection is required instead. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Polymerase chain reaction on the stored newborn screening dried blood spot
options.rationale: Testing the stored card is the fallback once the infant is beyond three weeks of age and the window for a definitive sample has closed, but its sensitivity is only moderate so a negative result cannot exclude the diagnosis. At nineteen days the better sample is still obtainable. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Urine collected for viral polymerase chain reaction within the next two days
options.rationale: Detection of virus in urine or saliva before twenty one days of age establishes that the infection was acquired before birth rather than afterwards, and urine carries a high viral load making it the sample of choice. The age of the infant is the whole point: after three weeks a positive result could reflect acquisition through breast milk or contact. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any laboratory testing is done
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is part of the assessment once infection is confirmed, because periventricular calcification and migrational abnormality inform prognosis and the decision to treat, but it cannot establish the causative organism. Sequencing it first also consumes the remaining days of the diagnostic window. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Repeat automated auditory brainstem response testing at three months of age
options.rationale: Formal diagnostic audiology is certainly needed, but deferring everything to three months abandons the only window in which the cause can be established and delays treatment that must start early to protect hearing. Audiology tells you the deficit, not the aetiology. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health Newborn Hearing Screening)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health Newborn Hearing Screening

explanation.summary: Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest congenital infection and the leading non genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, yet the majority of infected babies look entirely well at birth. The diagnosis rests on detecting virus in urine or saliva within the first three weeks of life, because after that a positive result cannot distinguish infection acquired before birth from the common postnatal acquisition through breast milk or close contact. Symptomatic disease presents with small size for gestational age, microcephaly, petechiae from thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, raised transaminases and chorioretinitis. Maternal primary infection during pregnancy is often a trivial or entirely silent illness, so the absence of a remembered illness never excludes it. Hearing loss may be present at birth or appear over the first years, which is why confirmed cases need audiological surveillance for years rather than a single test.
key_points: Urine or saliva viral detection before twenty one days of age is required for a definitive diagnosis
Neonatal immunoglobulin M serology is unreliable and is not used
The dried blood spot is the fallback after three weeks but lacks sensitivity
Most infected infants are asymptomatic at birth and still risk later hearing loss
Maternal infection is frequently silent or a trivial illness
explanation.pearls: Valganciclovir started within the first month of life and continued for six months improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes in symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus, which is why the three week diagnostic window is a genuine emergency rather than an administrative deadline.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline
Australian Government Department of Health Newborn Hearing Screening

subtopic_detail: which hip imaging modality is reliable once the femoral head has begun to ossify in a seven month old with limited abduction
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 7 month old girl brought by her mother, who has noticed that one leg does not seem to move out to the side as easily as the other when she changes her nappy.

She was the first baby and was breech from thirty two weeks until delivery by caesarean section at term. There is no family history of hip problems. She was examined in the newborn period and again at six weeks and no abnormality was documented on either occasion. She is not yet pulling to stand. On examination the right hip abducts to eighty degrees and the left to fifty degrees, there is an extra skin crease on the left thigh, and the left knee sits lower than the right when both hips and knees are flexed with the feet together on the couch.

data_table.Examination: Limited left hip abduction to 50 degrees, asymmetrical thigh creases, Galeazzi sign positive on the left, no leg length discrepancy on standing assessment
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips with dynamic stress views performed by a sonographer
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the modality of choice under about four to six months because the cartilaginous femoral head is sonographically visible, but once the ossific nucleus appears it casts an acoustic shadow over the acetabulum and the study becomes unreliable. Her age is what moves the answer away from this otherwise standard test. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips performed under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess reduction after closed or open surgical treatment rather than to make the initial diagnosis, and it requires sedation or anaesthesia for an infant. It answers a later question than the one being asked now. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons)

options.text: Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis with the hips in neutral position
options.rationale: From around four to six months the ossific nucleus makes the bony landmarks measurable, so a plain anteroposterior pelvic film with Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines and the acetabular index becomes the reliable investigation at this age. The same film that would be uninformative at six weeks is the correct study at seven months. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Computed tomography of the pelvis reconstructed in three planes for planning
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantial gonadal radiation dose to an infant girl and adds nothing to a plain film for the initial diagnosis, so it is reserved for complex surgical planning. The relevant contrast with the plain radiograph is dose rather than diagnostic capability. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons)

options.text: No imaging at this stage with a repeat clinical examination at twelve months
options.rationale: Limited abduction with asymmetrical creases and a positive Galeazzi sign in a breech born first born girl is a high risk combination that requires imaging now, and the results of treatment deteriorate sharply with every month of delay after walking age. Normal newborn examinations do not exclude the condition because a proportion present late. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip covers a spectrum from a shallow acetabulum to frank dislocation, and the aim of screening is to detect it before walking begins because treatment becomes progressively more invasive with age. The clinical signs change with age: the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are informative only in the first few months, after which limited abduction, asymmetrical skin creases and a positive Galeazzi sign become the useful findings. Risk factors are breech presentation in the third trimester, female sex, first born status and a positive family history, with breech and family history carrying the most weight. A normal neonatal examination does not exclude the condition because some hips become dysplastic after the newborn period, so persisting parental concern warrants examination rather than reassurance. The imaging choice is determined entirely by age, and getting it wrong produces a falsely reassuring study.
key_points: Ultrasound is the modality under four to six months, plain radiography after it
The ossific nucleus obscures the acetabulum on ultrasound once it appears
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign replace Ortolani and Barlow after the newborn period
Third trimester breech presentation is the single strongest risk factor
A normal newborn examination does not exclude late presenting dysplasia
explanation.pearls: Pavlik harness treatment is effective up to about six months of age, after which closed reduction under anaesthesia with a spica cast is usually required, so the difference between diagnosing at four months and at nine months is the difference between a brace and an operating theatre.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: a teenager with a meat bolus obstruction who has quietly adapted his eating for years, and what is needed to establish the cause
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12 year old boy who came in three hours ago unable to swallow after a mouthful of steak. While he was waiting the obstruction resolved spontaneously and he is now drinking comfortably.

His mother mentions that he is always the last to finish a meal, cuts everything very small, drinks a full glass of water with every few mouthfuls and will not eat bread crusts. He has had eczema since infancy and uses a preventer inhaler for asthma. He has not lost weight and his growth is tracking on the fiftieth centile. He has no heartburn, no regurgitation and no nocturnal cough. There is no history of caustic ingestion and no previous oesophageal surgery.

data_table.Examination: Comfortable, no drooling, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender, weight and height on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Barium swallow to assess the calibre and motility of the oesophagus
options.rationale: A contrast study can show a narrowed or ringed oesophagus and is useful for defining a stricture before dilatation, but a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis and it cannot provide tissue. The characteristic mucosal findings are frequently absent even when inflammation is dense. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Gastroscopy with multiple biopsies from the proximal and distal oesophagus
options.rationale: The diagnosis is histological and requires a threshold density of eosinophils on biopsy, and because the infiltrate is patchy, samples must be taken from at least two levels of the oesophagus even when the mucosa looks normal. Endoscopy also allows a stricture to be identified and treated at the same sitting. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks with review of his symptoms
options.rationale: A proton pump inhibitor was formerly used as a diagnostic filter, but current consensus treats response to it as a treatment outcome rather than as something that excludes the diagnosis, so biopsies are taken regardless. His absence of heartburn or regurgitation also argues against reflux as the primary problem. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Empirical elimination of dairy and wheat with a dietitian and review in twelve weeks
options.rationale: Dietary elimination is a legitimate treatment once the diagnosis is established, but starting it first removes the abnormality that the biopsy needs to demonstrate and commits a growing child to restriction without a diagnosis. Response to elimination is assessed by repeat endoscopy, not by symptoms alone. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise the pattern of contraction
options.rationale: Manometry is the investigation for achalasia and other primary motility disorders, which typically cause dysphagia to liquids as well as solids and progressive weight loss. His difficulty is confined to solid textures with normal growth, which points to a mucosal rather than a motor problem. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune mediated disease in which an eosinophil rich infiltrate produces oesophageal dysfunction, and it has become the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in children and young adults. It is strongly associated with the other atopic conditions, so a history of eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis or food allergy raises the pretest probability considerably. Children rarely complain of dysphagia and instead develop adaptive behaviours over years, such as prolonged mealtimes, excessive chewing, drinking with every mouthful, avoiding dry textures like bread and meat, and lubricating food with sauces, so the history must be sought from the parent as well as the child. Diagnosis requires oesophageal biopsy showing at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field in the setting of symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction. Treatment options are a proton pump inhibitor, swallowed topical corticosteroid, or dietary elimination, and untreated disease progresses to fibrostenotic remodelling with stricture formation.
key_points: Adaptive eating behaviours are the history, since children seldom report dysphagia
Biopsies from at least two oesophageal levels are needed because disease is patchy
A normal looking mucosa at endoscopy does not exclude the diagnosis
Response to a proton pump inhibitor no longer excludes the diagnosis
Untreated disease remodels the oesophagus and causes strictures
explanation.pearls: Fifteen eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy is the diagnostic threshold, and because the infiltrate is patchy at least six biopsies split between proximal and distal oesophagus are taken to reach an acceptable sensitivity.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: unexplained bruising with a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio and normal platelets in a six week old whose parents declined the birth injection
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department seeing a 6 week old boy brought in by his parents because of bruising over his back and thighs that appeared over the past two days.

He is exclusively breastfed, feeding well and gaining weight along the fiftieth centile. His parents declined all injections at birth and he has had no immunisations. He bled from the heel prick site for about twenty minutes at his newborn screening. He is alert, afebrile and interactive, with a soft anterior fontanelle and a normal neurological examination. His mother took no medication during pregnancy and there is no family history of bleeding. His stools are yellow and his urine is pale.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 142, blood pressure 76/44, respiratory rate 40, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bruises over the back and both thighs, no petechiae, fontanelle soft and flat, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 6.4 (0.9 to 1.3), activated partial thromboplastin time 78 seconds (25 to 38), platelets 312 x10^9/L (150 to 400), fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (1.5 to 4.0), haemoglobin 108 g/L (100 to 140), bilirubin and alanine aminotransferase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Transfuse platelets and repeat the coagulation profile after the transfusion
options.rationale: His platelet count is normal at 312 x10^9/L, so a platelet transfusion has no target and does not correct a clotting factor deficiency. The normal count alongside a grossly prolonged clotting time is precisely what localises the defect to the factors rather than to the platelets. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma as the sole treatment and observe him overnight
options.rationale: Plasma replaces the missing factors immediately and is added when bleeding is life threatening, but its effect lasts only hours and it does not restore the body's ability to make functional factors. Using it alone means the coagulopathy returns once the transfused factors are consumed. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)

options.text: Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics after taking blood cultures
options.rationale: Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation is a genuine differential for a coagulopathic infant, but it would consume fibrinogen and platelets and produce an unwell febrile baby, and here both are normal and he is alert and afebrile. The isolated factor deficiency pattern points elsewhere. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection before treating him
options.rationale: Unexplained bruising in a non mobile infant rightly raises this question, but a coagulopathy that fully explains the bruising must be identified and treated first, and delaying treatment to arrange imaging risks an intracranial bleed. Investigation for inflicted injury proceeds if the bleeding is not explained by the correctable deficiency. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K slowly and recheck the clotting profile afterwards
options.rationale: A prolonged prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin time with normal platelets, normal fibrinogen and normal liver enzymes in an exclusively breastfed infant who received no birth prophylaxis is the deficiency of the vitamin dependent factors, and replacing the vitamin corrects it within hours. Correction after administration also confirms the diagnosis. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding is classified as early within the first day, classic between days two and seven, and late between two weeks and six months, with the late form carrying the highest risk of intracranial haemorrhage and the highest mortality. Breast milk contains very little vitamin K while infant formula is supplemented, so exclusively breastfed infants who did not receive prophylaxis are the group at risk. Australian practice is a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth, and parents who decline the injection may be offered a three dose oral schedule, which is less effective and depends on the later doses actually being given. The laboratory signature is prolongation of both clotting times with preserved platelets and fibrinogen and normal liver function, which distinguishes it from disseminated intravascular coagulation and from liver disease. Late presentation also demands consideration of underlying cholestatic liver disease impairing absorption, so a conjugated bilirubin and an assessment of stool colour belong in the workup.
key_points: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurs from two weeks to six months and often bleeds intracranially
Normal platelets and fibrinogen separate it from disseminated intravascular coagulation
Exclusive breastfeeding without prophylaxis is the risk combination
Plasma is an adjunct for major bleeding, not a substitute for the vitamin
Consider cholestatic liver disease as a cause of impaired absorption in late cases
explanation.pearls: Correction of the international normalised ratio within four to six hours of parenteral vitamin K is itself diagnostic, so a repeat coagulation profile at that point answers the question without any further testing.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: daily soiling in a five year old with a palpable faecal mass, and the consequence of starting maintenance laxative without clearing the load first
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 year old boy whose prep teacher has sent a note home about a smell in the classroom. His mother is exasperated and says he is soiling his underwear most days and has started hiding the dirty pairs behind the couch.

She says he passes an enormous hard stool in the toilet about once every seven to ten days, and that he sometimes goes up on his toes, crosses his legs and holds onto furniture when he looks like he needs to go. He has a good appetite and drinks water and milk. He was toilet trained at three without difficulty and the soiling began about nine months ago after a painful episode with an anal fissure. His growth is tracking along the fiftieth centile, he has never had delayed passage of meconium, and his neurological and spinal examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with a firm non tender mass palpable in the left lower quadrant and suprapubically, normal anal position, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, no sacral dimple or hair tuft
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology and thyroid stimulating hormone both within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in treatment?

options.text: Increase dietary fibre and fluid intake and review his progress in four weeks
options.rationale: Dietary measures alone do not shift an established faecal mass and are insufficient as initial treatment once retentive posturing and overflow have developed, though they support maintenance later. Offering them alone here means another month of daily soiling. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange an abdominal radiograph to assess the extent of the faecal loading
options.rationale: Constipation is a clinical diagnosis and a plain film adds radiation without changing management when the mass is already palpable and the history is characteristic. Imaging is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty rather than for confirming what the hand has found. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer to a child psychologist for behavioural management of the soiling
options.rationale: The soiling is overflow of liquid stool past a retained mass rather than a behavioural problem, and the hiding of underwear reflects shame about an involuntary event. Psychological input helps with toilet avoidance and family distress once the bowel has been cleared, not instead of clearing it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Give an escalating macrogol regimen for disimpaction before daily maintenance
options.rationale: An established faecal mass must be cleared with a short high dose oral macrogol course before a maintenance dose begins, because maintenance dosing alone leaves the mass in place and the overflow soiling continues or worsens. Warning the family that soiling increases during disimpaction is what stops them abandoning treatment in the first week. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Administer a phosphate enema in the clinic and start maintenance macrogol after
options.rationale: Rectal treatment is distressing for a child whose problem began with painful defaecation and carries a risk of phosphate absorption with electrolyte disturbance, so it is reserved for failure of the oral route. The oral approach achieves the same clearance without reinforcing the fear of the anus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for the overwhelming majority of childhood constipation and typically begins with a single painful or frightening defaecation that establishes a cycle of withholding, progressive rectal distension and loss of the normal urge to defaecate. Overflow incontinence is the consequence of liquid stool passing around a retained mass, and parents and teachers frequently interpret it as laziness or defiance, so explaining the mechanism is a therapeutic act in itself. Red flags that point away from a functional cause include delayed passage of meconium beyond forty eight hours, onset in the first month of life, failure to thrive, abnormal anal position, a sacral dimple or hair tuft, and abnormal lower limb neurology. Treatment has two phases that must be kept distinct: disimpaction with high dose macrogol over several days, then a maintenance dose continued for months rather than weeks. The commonest reason for treatment failure in Australian practice is stopping maintenance too soon, before the dilated rectum has regained normal sensation.
key_points: Overflow soiling is a sign of retention, not a behavioural problem
Disimpaction and maintenance are separate phases and the order matters
Soiling typically worsens during disimpaction and families must be warned
Abdominal radiography is not needed when the mass is palpable and the history is typical
Maintenance continues for months, and stopping early is the usual cause of relapse
explanation.pearls: Maintenance macrogol is continued for at least six months and until the child has had a normal soft stool pattern without soiling for several months, then weaned slowly, because the stretched rectum needs that long to recover normal sensation.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: choosing between a hydrolysed and an amino acid based formula for an infant with blood streaked stools, eczema and centile loss
stem: A 4-month-old girl changed from breast to cow's milk formula at six weeks has since vomited after most feeds and passes six or seven loose stools daily with blood-streaked mucus. Her eczema has not improved on moisturiser and hydrocortisone. Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 15th centile.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C-reactive protein normal; stool culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her feeding?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula
options.rationale: An extensively hydrolysed formula is the first line replacement for non immunoglobulin E mediated cow's milk protein allergy and is tolerated by around nine in ten affected infants, so it is the trial that both treats and confirms the diagnosis. Symptoms of the gastrointestinal type typically settle within two to four weeks, which sets the review interval. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to a soy protein based formula
options.rationale: Soy formula is not recommended under six months of age, and a substantial minority of infants with the non immunoglobulin E mediated form react to soy protein as well, so the trial frequently fails. It has a limited place in older infants whose families decline a hydrolysate. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to an amino acid based formula
options.rationale: An amino acid formula is reserved for infants who fail an extensively hydrolysed formula, or who have anaphylaxis, severe enteropathy or faltering growth with hypoalbuminaemia, because it costs several times more and tastes markedly worse. Starting with it skips the step that succeeds in the large majority. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Change to a lactose free cow's milk formula
options.rationale: Removing lactose leaves the cow's milk protein in the feed, and it is the protein that drives the blood streaked stools and the eczema. Primary lactose intolerance is vanishingly rare in infancy and would not cause rectal bleeding or a skin manifestation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Change to a thickened anti-reflux formula
options.rationale: Thickening reduces the volume of visible posseting but does nothing for the colitis causing the blood and mucus or for the eczema, and reflux alone does not cause centile loss of this degree. The blood streaked stool is the finding that moves the diagnosis away from uncomplicated reflux. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Cow's milk protein allergy splits into an immunoglobulin E mediated form with rapid onset urticaria, angioedema, vomiting or anaphylaxis, and a non immunoglobulin E mediated form with delayed gastrointestinal and skin manifestations, of which proctocolitis and enteropathy are the commonest patterns in infancy. Skin prick testing and specific immunoglobulin E are useful only for the immediate form and are normal in the delayed form, so the diagnosis rests on an elimination and challenge sequence rather than on a laboratory test. Improvement on elimination must be followed by a planned reintroduction, because a substantial proportion of infants labelled allergic on elimination alone are not, and unnecessary formula restriction is expensive and nutritionally limiting. Where a mother is still breastfeeding, maternal dairy exclusion with calcium and vitamin D supplementation is preferred over stopping breastfeeding. Most children outgrow the non immunoglobulin E mediated form by two to three years of age, so a structured reintroduction plan is part of initial management rather than an afterthought.
key_points: Delayed gastrointestinal and skin symptoms define the non immunoglobulin E mediated form
Specific immunoglobulin E testing is normal in the delayed form and does not exclude it
Extensively hydrolysed formula is first line and works for around ninety per cent
Soy is avoided under six months and cross reacts in a significant minority
Confirm the diagnosis with a planned reintroduction rather than leaving the label unchallenged
explanation.pearls: Blood streaked mucous stools in an otherwise thriving, afebrile infant is the signature of allergic proctocolitis, and it characteristically resolves within two to four weeks of removing the protein, which is much faster than the eczema improves.

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: the silent sight threatening complication that must be screened for in a young girl with a persistently swollen knee and a positive antinuclear antibody
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 year old girl who has limped for four months. Her mother says she is at her worst first thing in the morning and hobbles for about an hour before loosening up, and that she is back to running by the afternoon.

There was no injury. She has had no fevers, no rash, no weight loss and no night pain that wakes her. Her right knee has been visibly swollen throughout and she has begun to keep it slightly bent when standing. She has no eye pain, no redness and no photophobia, and her mother has noticed nothing wrong with her vision. The rheumatology team has confirmed a diagnosis of oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and is starting an intra articular corticosteroid injection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm with an effusion and a 10 degree fixed flexion deformity, no other joint involved, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, white eyes with no injection
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count within normal limits, antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 320, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What additional step is most important in her ongoing care?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the right knee to assess for synovial thickening
options.rationale: Imaging can characterise synovitis and is used where the diagnosis is uncertain or a single joint behaves unusually, but the diagnosis is already established and the result would not change treatment. It also requires sedation at this age for no additional benefit. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Aspiration of the knee effusion for cell count, Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.rationale: Aspiration is essential when infection is a possibility, but four months of morning stiffness that eases through the day in an afebrile child with a mildly raised inflammatory marker is not a septic picture. Fluid will be obtained in any case when the joint is injected. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Testing for human leucocyte antigen B27 to define the arthritis subtype further
options.rationale: This marker is associated with enthesitis related arthritis, which typically affects older boys with lower limb enthesitis and sacroiliac involvement and causes an acute painful red eye rather than a silent one. It would not alter the surveillance that this girl's own subtype demands. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist arranged within the next few weeks
options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in this subtype is asymptomatic with a white eye and normal vision until irreversible damage has occurred, so it is detectable only on slit lamp examination and is screened for regardless of symptoms. Young age at onset, oligoarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody together place her in the highest risk group. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Visual acuity assessment at each clinic visit performed by the practice nurse
options.rationale: Acuity remains normal until the uveitis has already produced posterior synechiae, cataract or band keratopathy, so relying on it means detecting the complication only once sight has been lost. The distinction from the correct answer is that only the slit lamp can see the anterior chamber cells that come first. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

explanation.summary: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is defined as arthritis beginning before the sixteenth birthday and persisting for at least six weeks with no other identified cause, and the oligoarticular subtype involving four or fewer joints is the commonest presentation in Australian children. It characteristically affects young girls, favours the knee, and produces morning stiffness that improves with activity, which is the opposite of the pattern seen in mechanical or malignant bone pain. Chronic anterior uveitis complicates up to a fifth of cases in this subtype and is uniquely dangerous because it is entirely asymptomatic, with a white quiet eye and preserved acuity, until complications develop. Risk is highest in girls, in those under seven at onset, in oligoarticular disease and in those with a positive antinuclear antibody, and these factors determine screening frequency rather than whether to screen at all. Untreated uveitis causes posterior synechiae, cataract, glaucoma, band keratopathy and permanent visual loss, and remains a leading cause of avoidable childhood blindness.
key_points: Morning stiffness easing with activity distinguishes inflammatory from mechanical joint pain
Chronic anterior uveitis in this subtype is asymptomatic with a white eye
Only slit lamp examination detects it early; acuity is normal until damage is done
Positive antinuclear antibody, young onset and oligoarticular disease mark the highest risk group
A red painful photophobic eye instead suggests the enthesitis related subtype
explanation.pearls: Highest risk children, meaning those under seven at onset with a positive antinuclear antibody, need slit lamp screening every three months for the first four years, not annually, and screening continues for years after the arthritis itself has gone quiet.

subtopic_detail: whether a sleep study is required before surgical referral in an otherwise well preschooler with classic obstructive symptoms and large tonsils
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5 year old boy whose parents are worried about his breathing at night. He has snored every night for two years and they now hear him stop for several seconds and then gasp, several times an hour.

He sleeps with his neck extended and his mouth open, thrashes about, and sweats through his pyjamas. He was dry at night for eight months and has been wetting the bed again for the past four. His kindergarten teacher has raised concerns that he is inattentive and cannot sit still at mat time. His weight and height are both on the fiftieth centile. He has no craniofacial abnormality, no neuromuscular disorder and no chromosomal condition, and his tonsils touch in the midline on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tonsils meeting in the midline, mouth breathing, no adenoid facies, chest clear, heart sounds dual with no murmur, body mass index on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry at home and refer only if desaturations are recorded
options.rationale: Oximetry has reasonable specificity but poor sensitivity in children, so a normal study is uninterpretable and cannot be used to withhold referral. Making referral conditional on it means a proportion of genuinely affected children are turned away. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange laboratory polysomnography and refer once the study confirms the diagnosis
options.rationale: A formal sleep study is required where the picture is atypical or where surgery carries higher risk, meaning children under two, obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial anomaly or neuromuscular disease, none of which applies to him. Insisting on it in a straightforward case adds months of waiting for a study that would not change the plan. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence an intranasal corticosteroid with montelukast and review in three months
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory treatment has a role in mild disease or in children awaiting surgery, and montelukast carries a recognised risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects that must be discussed with families. Witnessed apnoea with secondary enuresis is beyond the severity at which a medical trial is appropriate as the sole plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Refer to an otolaryngologist for consideration of adenotonsillectomy without delay
options.rationale: In an otherwise healthy child over two with a classic obstructive history and tonsils meeting in the midline, adenotonsillectomy is the first line treatment and the diagnosis can be made clinically, so referral proceeds without a sleep study. Surgery resolves symptoms in the large majority and improves the behavioural and nocturnal enuresis features as well. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer to a sleep physician for assessment for nocturnal continuous positive pressure
options.rationale: Positive airway pressure is the treatment for children who have residual disease after surgery or who cannot have surgery, and adherence in preschoolers is difficult. It is not offered before the adenotonsillar tissue that is causing the obstruction has been dealt with. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects around two to four per cent of children and peaks between two and eight years when adenotonsillar tissue is largest relative to the airway. The nocturnal history is the diagnostic core: habitual snoring every night, witnessed pauses, gasping, restless sleep, sweating, unusual sleeping positions with the neck extended, and secondary nocturnal enuresis after a period of dryness. Daytime consequences in children are more often inattention, hyperactivity and irritability than the frank sleepiness seen in adults, and children are not infrequently assessed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder before the breathing is considered. Australian practice accepts a clinical diagnosis in the otherwise well child over two with a typical history and large tonsils, reserving polysomnography for the higher risk groups in whom surgical risk and the likelihood of residual disease are greater. Untreated disease causes growth impairment, behavioural and learning difficulty, and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain.
key_points: Habitual snoring with witnessed apnoea and restless sleep is the diagnostic history
Secondary nocturnal enuresis after established dryness is a recognised feature
Children present with inattention and hyperactivity rather than daytime sleepiness
Polysomnography is reserved for under twos, obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial and neuromuscular disease
Adenotonsillectomy is first line in the otherwise healthy child with large tonsils
explanation.pearls: Children under three, and those with severe disease or comorbidity, need overnight postoperative monitoring after adenotonsillectomy because respiratory complications cluster in the first night, so day surgery is not appropriate for that group.

subtopic_detail: separating nutritional from inherited phosphate wasting rickets in a toddler with worsening bow legs using the parathyroid hormone level
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 20 month old boy in Melbourne whose mother is worried that his legs are becoming more bowed rather than less. He began walking at seventeen months and tires quickly.

He was breastfed exclusively until fourteen months and has never received a vitamin supplement. He now eats family foods but refuses dairy. His mother has deeply pigmented skin and wears clothing that covers her arms and legs when outdoors, and he spends most days indoors at home. There is no family history of short stature, bone disease or bowed legs in either parent. On examination his wrists are widened, there are palpable beading swellings along his costochondral junctions, and his forehead is prominent. His length is on the third centile having previously tracked along the twenty fifth.

data_table.Examination: Widened wrists, costochondral beading, frontal bossing, symmetrical genu varum with an intercondylar distance of 7 cm, no limb asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.13 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20 to 2.20), alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (100 to 350), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 16 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone 16.4 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of both legs with review of the angle in six months
options.rationale: The deformity is a consequence of unmineralised growth plate cartilage and it remodels once the metabolic defect is corrected, so bracing treats the visible sign while the bone disease continues. Orthopaedic input is reserved for deformity that persists after biochemical correction. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence high dose colecalciferol with adequate dietary or supplemental calcium
options.rationale: A 25 hydroxyvitamin D of 16 nmol/L with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone, low phosphate and a high alkaline phosphatase is nutritional deficiency, and replacing the vitamin with sufficient calcium substrate heals the growth plate over weeks to months. Calcium must accompany the vitamin because rapid remineralisation otherwise drives the calcium down further. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence oral phosphate supplements with calcitriol and monitor renal ultrasound
options.rationale: This is the treatment for inherited phosphate wasting rickets, in which vitamin D and parathyroid hormone are both normal and the phosphate is low in isolation. Here both the profoundly low vitamin D level and the elevated parathyroid hormone point to a nutritional rather than a renal tubular cause. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence an oral calcium supplement alone and repeat his biochemistry in three months
options.rationale: Calcium alone does not correct the underlying deficiency of the vitamin needed to absorb it, so the parathyroid drive and the growth plate disease persist. Calcium is a necessary companion to the vitamin rather than a treatment in its own right here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Reassure that this is physiological bowing and arrange review at three years of age
options.rationale: Physiological genu varum is symmetrical, painless, improves after about eighteen months and comes with entirely normal biochemistry and no metaphyseal signs. Widened wrists, costochondral beading, falling length centiles and an alkaline phosphatase of 1180 U/L are incompatible with it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains present in Australia despite abundant sunlight, concentrated in children with deeply pigmented skin, in those whose mothers were deficient during pregnancy, in prolonged exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, and in families whose cultural dress or indoor lifestyle limits ultraviolet exposure. Breast milk contains very little vitamin D, so an exclusively breastfed infant depends on maternal stores and on supplementation. The biochemical sequence is a fall in vitamin D leading to reduced calcium absorption, a compensatory rise in parathyroid hormone that defends the calcium at the expense of phosphate wasting, and a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase from the unmineralised growth plate. That pattern of low or low normal calcium with low phosphate and high parathyroid hormone is what separates it from inherited phosphate wasting disease, where parathyroid hormone and vitamin D are normal. Radiographs of the wrist or knee show cupping, fraying and widening of the metaphysis and confirm the diagnosis when it is in doubt.
key_points: Low vitamin D with a raised parathyroid hormone defines the nutritional form
Normal parathyroid hormone with isolated low phosphate suggests inherited phosphate wasting
Alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised and is the most sensitive screening test
Calcium must be given with the vitamin to avoid a fall during remineralisation
Deformity remodels after biochemical healing and rarely needs orthopaedic correction
explanation.pearls: Australian guidance recommends 400 international units of vitamin D daily for infants at risk, including exclusively breastfed babies of mothers who are deficient, and the same at risk groups need maternal supplementation through pregnancy and lactation.

subtopic_detail: persistent delayed sleep onset in an autistic school aged child after a documented adequate trial of behavioural sleep measures
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8 year old autistic boy whose parents say bedtime has become the hardest part of the day. Lights go out at half past seven and he is still awake at half past nine or later, almost every night.

Over the past three months the family has worked with a psychologist on a written plan: the same routine every night, screens off an hour before bed, a dark and quiet bedroom, no daytime naps, morning outdoor light and a consistent wake time. His parents have kept a diary showing they followed it and that sleep onset latency has not changed. Once asleep he stays asleep and wakes at half past five. He does not snore, has no witnessed pauses in breathing and has no urge to move his legs at night. He takes no regular medication, his ferritin is normal and he has never had a stimulant prescribed.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils small, body mass index on the fiftieth centile, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 48 micrograms/L (20 to 200), full blood count and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before considering any medication for sleep
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when the history suggests sleep disordered breathing or a periodic limb movement disorder, and the absence of snoring, apnoea and leg symptoms with small tonsils and a normal ferritin makes those unlikely. His problem is initiating sleep rather than maintaining it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe promethazine at bedtime and review his sleep diary again in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines produce tolerance within weeks, cause daytime drowsiness and can paradoxically agitate children, and they do not act on the circadian mechanism driving delayed sleep onset. They are not recommended for chronic paediatric insomnia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reinforce the existing behavioural plan and review his sleep diary in three months
options.rationale: Behavioural measures are the correct first line and must be in place before and alongside any drug, but a documented three month trial with a diary showing adherence and no change has already tested them. Repeating an intervention that has failed costs the family another term of broken evenings. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Trial melatonin given before bedtime while continuing the behavioural measures
options.rationale: Melatonin has the strongest evidence for delayed sleep onset in autistic children who have not responded to an adequate behavioural program, reducing sleep latency by around half an hour and increasing total sleep time. It is added to the behavioural measures rather than replacing them, because the combination outperforms either alone. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe clonidine at night and monitor his blood pressure and pulse at review
options.rationale: Clonidine is used for paediatric sleep problems, particularly where there is coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder being treated with a stimulant, but it requires cardiovascular monitoring and causes rebound on abrupt cessation. It sits behind melatonin in the sequence for an otherwise well child. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Sleep problems affect the majority of autistic children and are among the strongest predictors of parental distress and of daytime behavioural difficulty, so they are worth asking about at every review rather than waiting for them to be raised. Delayed sleep onset is the commonest pattern and is thought to reflect a combination of altered melatonin secretion, heightened arousal and sensory sensitivity. Behavioural intervention is the first line at every age and includes a fixed routine, a consistent wake time, removal of evening screens, attention to bedroom sensory features and management of daytime activity. Before attributing insomnia to autism itself, treatable contributors are excluded: obstructive sleep apnoea, iron deficiency driving restless legs, gastro oesophageal reflux, pain, constipation, epilepsy, anxiety and the effect of stimulant medication given too late in the day. Melatonin is the best studied pharmacological option in this group and is continued alongside rather than instead of the behavioural plan, with periodic trials off treatment.
key_points: Behavioural measures come first and continue after any drug is added
Exclude sleep disordered breathing, iron deficiency, reflux, pain and late stimulant dosing
A normal ferritin makes restless legs an unlikely contributor
Melatonin is the best evidenced pharmacological option for delayed sleep onset in autism
Sedating antihistamines produce tolerance and can cause paradoxical agitation
explanation.pearls: Melatonin is most effective when given about thirty to sixty minutes before the intended bedtime rather than at the time the child currently falls asleep, because the aim is to advance the circadian phase rather than simply to sedate.

subtopic_detail: separating recurrent wheeze occurring only with colds from asthma needing a daily preventer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 2 year old boy brought by his father after a fourth episode of wheeze in twelve months. Each episode has begun with a runny nose and a cough, lasted about five days, and settled completely.

His father says that between episodes he runs around the park without stopping, sleeps through the night, and has never coughed at night or after running when he is well. He has no eczema and no food allergies, and neither parent nor either sibling has asthma, hay fever or eczema. He attends childcare three days a week. He was born at term and has never been admitted to hospital. Today he is at the end of an episode, is not distressed, and his chest is clear on auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Speaking in phrases and playing, no accessory muscle use or tracheal tug, chest clear with no wheeze audible today, no eczema, growth tracking along the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start a daily inhaled corticosteroid preventer and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: A daily preventer is indicated where there are interval symptoms between illnesses, frequent severe episodes or a strong atopic background, none of which he has. Trials in this pattern of wheeze show daily inhaled corticosteroid does not reduce episode frequency or severity, so it commits a toddler to continuous treatment without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Start a daily oral leukotriene receptor antagonist taken through the winter months
options.rationale: Montelukast has been trialled both continuously and intermittently in this age group with modest and inconsistent benefit, and it carries a recognised risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects including sleep disturbance and behavioural change in young children. It is not a first line answer for a child with no interval symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to aeroallergens before deciding on any preventer
options.rationale: Allergy testing contributes to the assessment of a child with interval symptoms or eczema where an atopic phenotype would change the threshold for preventer treatment. In a child with no personal or family atopy and no symptoms between illnesses it will not alter the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Provide an inhaled bronchodilator with a spacer and a written action plan
options.rationale: Wheeze confined to viral illnesses with complete freedom between them and no atopic background is the pattern that resolves in most children by school age, so treatment is directed at episodes rather than at maintenance. Salbutamol through a spacer with a written plan setting out dosing and when to seek help gives the family control of the episodes without exposing him to continuous therapy that has not been shown to help this phenotype. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone for the family to begin at each illness
options.rationale: Parent initiated oral corticosteroid has been studied in this pattern of wheeze and does not reduce hospital admission or symptom duration, while repeated courses in a preschooler carry growth and bone effects. Oral corticosteroid is reserved for an episode severe enough to require medical assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze divides into a viral triggered pattern and a multiple trigger pattern, and the distinction determines whether maintenance treatment is worthwhile. This boy wheezes only with viral illnesses, is entirely well between them, and has no personal or family atopy, which places him firmly in the viral triggered group that usually resolves by school age. Randomised evidence shows that daily inhaled corticosteroid does not reduce the frequency or severity of episodes in this phenotype. Management is therefore episodic, with a bronchodilator delivered by spacer and a written action plan so the family knows what to give and when to seek review. Interval symptoms, atopy or escalating severity would change that assessment and prompt a preventer trial.
key_points: Complete freedom from symptoms between illnesses characterises viral triggered wheeze.
Daily inhaled corticosteroid does not reduce episode frequency or severity in this phenotype.
A personal or family history of atopy raises the likelihood of asthma and lowers the threshold for a preventer.
A spacer is as effective as a nebuliser for delivering bronchodilator in preschool children.
Parent initiated oral corticosteroid has not been shown to shorten episodes or prevent admission.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child coughs at night or after running when completely well, because interval symptoms are what separate asthma from viral triggered wheeze and determine whether a daily preventer will do anything at all in a child under three.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

subtopic_detail: recognising heavy proteinuria in a preschooler whose facial swelling has been treated as an allergy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old girl referred by her general practitioner. Her mother first noticed puffiness around both eyes three weeks ago, worst on waking and easing through the day, and a locum prescribed an antihistamine for presumed allergy.

The swelling has not improved and over the past week her abdomen has become distended and her ankles swollen, so that her shoes no longer fit. She has had no rash, no urticaria and no wheeze, and there has been no new pet, detergent or food. She has passed normal coloured urine throughout and has had no dysuria and no fever. She had a sore throat about six weeks ago that settled without treatment. Her blood pressure is normal for her age and her growth is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked periorbital oedema, pitting oedema to both mid shins, abdominal distension with shifting dullness, no rash or purpura, no joint swelling, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 4 plus with no blood, urine protein creatinine ratio markedly raised, serum albumin 16 g/L (35-50), total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L (less than 5.5), creatinine 32 micromol/L (20-50), complement C3 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue the antihistamine and add a short course of topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Antihistamine treatment addresses histamine mediated angioedema, which appears over minutes to hours, is often asymmetrical and is usually accompanied by urticaria or a trigger. Three weeks of progressive symmetrical oedema with 4 plus proteinuria and an albumin of 16 g/L is a renal problem rather than an allergic one. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent percutaneous renal biopsy before commencing any drug treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for features that make minimal change disease unlikely, such as age under one or over twelve years, macroscopic haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function or low complement, and for children who fail to respond to corticosteroid. None of those applies here, so biopsy would add an invasive procedure to a presentation with a predictable histology. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous albumin with furosemide and observe the diuretic response
options.rationale: Albumin with a diuretic is used for severe symptomatic oedema causing respiratory compromise, scrotal or vulval oedema, or skin breakdown, and it carries a risk of pulmonary oedema and rebound fluid shift. She is comfortable with normal oxygen saturation, so it treats a complication she does not yet have rather than the disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Start oral penicillin and await antistreptolysin O titres before further treatment
options.rationale: A preceding sore throat raises post streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is the intended distractor, and that condition produces a nephritic picture with haematuria, hypertension, oedema and a low complement C3. Her urine contains no blood, her blood pressure is normal and her C3 is normal, which excludes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone daily with a planned taper after four weeks
options.rationale: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia in a child between one and twelve years with normal blood pressure, no haematuria and normal renal function is minimal change disease in the great majority of cases, and around nine in ten such children enter remission on corticosteroid alone. Treatment is therefore started empirically without histology, with daily dosing for four weeks followed by an alternate day taper, alongside pneumococcal protection and counselling about the risk of peritonitis and thrombosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

explanation.summary: Periorbital oedema that is worst on waking is regularly misattributed to allergy, and the distinguishing features are that it is symmetrical, progressive over weeks, unaccompanied by urticaria or a trigger, and associated with dependent oedema later in the day. The diagnostic combination is heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia. In a child aged one to twelve with normal blood pressure, no haematuria, normal renal function and normal complement, minimal change disease accounts for the great majority of cases and responds to corticosteroid, so treatment is empirical and biopsy is not required. The preceding sore throat is a deliberate lead towards post streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is excluded by the absent haematuria, normal blood pressure and normal complement C3. Children need counselling about infection and thrombosis, since urinary loss of immunoglobulin and antithrombin drives both.
key_points: Proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia together define the nephrotic syndrome.
Minimal change disease predominates between one and twelve years and responds to corticosteroid in about nine in ten children.
Biopsy is indicated for atypical age, haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment, low complement or steroid resistance.
A nephritic picture with haematuria, hypertension and a low complement C3 suggests post streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and antithrombin causes susceptibility to pneumococcal peritonitis and to thrombosis.
explanation.pearls: Dipstick the urine of every child presenting with periorbital swelling before accepting an allergic explanation, because nephrotic syndrome is regularly treated with antihistamines for weeks, and swelling that is worst on waking with no urticaria and no trigger is renal until the dipstick says otherwise.

subtopic_detail: choosing between oral and intravenous glucose for a large newborn of a diabetic mother whose repeat sugar stays low
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward at two hours of age. The baby is a term boy born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery weighing 4 420 g to a mother whose pregnancy was complicated by insulin treated gestational diabetes.

He was put to the breast at thirty minutes and fed briefly. A routine pre feed blood glucose at one hour was 1.9 mmol/L, so the midwife gave 0.5 mL/kg of 40 percent oral glucose gel and a breastfeed, and the repeat pre feed level one hour later is 1.6 mmol/L. He is pink and well perfused, has a normal cry, has not had a seizure and is not jittery at present. His temperature has been stable since birth and there are no respiratory signs.
