data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142/min, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well perfused with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, normal tone and normal cry, anterior fontanelle soft, no respiratory distress, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Pre feed blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L at one hour, repeat pre feed blood glucose 1.6 mmol/L at two hours, formal laboratory glucose sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: A second dose of 40 percent oral glucose gel with a further breastfeed
options.rationale: Buccal glucose gel with a feed is the correct first response and may be repeated, but it has now been given once and the level has fallen rather than risen, which is the point at which repeating it becomes a delay rather than a treatment. Most protocols permit at most two gel doses and none accept a falling level as a reason to repeat. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Top up with expressed breast milk hourly and recheck in three hours
options.rationale: Increasing enteral intake is the mainstay while levels are responding, and a three hour gap is far too long once a level below 2.0 mmol/L has failed to correct. Neuroglycopenic injury in the newborn is not signalled reliably by symptoms, so the interval between checks must shorten rather than lengthen. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give an intramuscular glucagon dose and continue to feed on the ward
options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and is reserved for hypoglycaemia where intravenous access has failed or hyperinsulinism is established, and in a hyperinsulinaemic infant it produces a brief rise followed by a rebound fall. It is a holding measure rather than the definitive answer when a drip can be sited. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after cultures
options.rationale: Sepsis does cause neonatal hypoglycaemia and would demand exactly this, but it requires a risk factor or an unwell infant, and this baby is afebrile, well perfused and has a wholly sufficient alternative explanation in maternal diabetes. Treating an infection you have no evidence for leaves the glucose uncorrected. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Admit for intravenous 10 percent glucose with hourly glucose monitoring
options.rationale: A level that falls despite buccal gel and feeding has failed enteral management, and a blood glucose of 1.6 mmol/L carries a risk of neurological injury that does not depend on the baby looking symptomatic. Intravenous 10 percent glucose titrated against hourly levels is the definitive correction, and the admission also allows a true hypoglycaemia screen to be drawn if the requirement turns out to be high. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of diabetic mothers are macrosomic and hyperinsulinaemic because maternal glucose crosses the placenta while maternal insulin does not, driving fetal islet hyperplasia that persists after the cord is cut. Screening with pre feed levels and treating with buccal glucose gel plus a feed is correct initial practice. The decision point in this question is that the repeat level has fallen rather than risen despite that treatment, which means enteral management has failed. A well appearing baby is not reassuring, because neonatal neuroglycopenia is frequently silent. Intravenous glucose with hourly monitoring is the answer, and persistent high glucose requirements should prompt a formal hypoglycaemia screen.
key_points: Fetal hyperinsulinism from maternal hyperglycaemia is the mechanism, and it resolves over the first days of life.
Buccal glucose gel with a feed is first line and is generally limited to two doses.
Absence of jitteriness, seizure or poor feeding does not make a low neonatal glucose safe.
A level that falls after treatment, rather than simply remaining low, signals failure of enteral management.
High intravenous glucose requirements suggest persistent hyperinsulinism and warrant a formal hypoglycaemia screen.
explanation.pearls: Escalate from buccal glucose gel to intravenous 10 percent glucose when the repeat pre feed level falls rather than rises, and draw the hypoglycaemia screen at the time of a low level rather than afterwards, because insulin, cortisol, growth hormone and ketones are only interpretable in the hypoglycaemic sample.

subtopic_detail: investigating an adolescent girl with heavy periods since menarche and lifelong easy bruising
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 14 year old girl referred with heavy periods. She reached menarche at twelve and says every period since then has been heavy, requiring a change of pad every hour on the first two days and causing her to miss school.

She has also had nosebleeds since early childhood, two of which needed nasal packing, and she bruises on her thighs without recalling any injury. She bled for several hours after a dental extraction at age ten. Her mother describes her own periods as heavy and had a postpartum haemorrhage after her second child. She takes no aspirin, no anti-inflammatory medication and no herbal preparations. On examination she has scattered bruises of differing ages over both thighs, no petechiae, no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, bruises of varying age on both thighs, no petechiae or purpura, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no joint swelling or deformity
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (120-160), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (30-300), prothrombin time 12 seconds (11-14), activated partial thromboplastin time 41 seconds (25-38)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess megakaryocyte number and morphology
options.rationale: Marrow examination is directed at a production failure, which would show as cytopenias in one or more lineages with an abnormal film. Her platelet count is normal at 268 x10^9/L and her only cytopenia is a microcytic anaemia entirely explained by chronic menstrual iron loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity with a factor VIII level
options.rationale: A lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding pattern of menorrhagia, epistaxis, bruising and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction, with a normal platelet count, a normal prothrombin time and a mildly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time in a family with affected women, is von Willebrand disease until proven otherwise. The specific panel is needed because the screening tests are frequently normal in mild disease, and factor VIII is measured alongside because von Willebrand factor carries it and its reduction is what prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Factor IX assay with genetic testing for a haemophilia B carrier state
options.rationale: Haemophilia is X linked and produces deep bleeding into joints and muscles rather than a mucocutaneous pattern, and carrier females are usually only mildly affected. The absence of any joint bleeding and the strong female to female family pattern both point away from an X linked disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to identify a structural cause for her menstrual bleeding
options.rationale: Imaging looks for fibroids, polyps or adenomyosis, which are uncommon at fourteen and would not explain nosebleeds, bruising or bleeding after dental extraction. A structural diagnosis cannot account for bleeding at three separate anatomical sites since early childhood. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Antinuclear antibody with antiphospholipid antibodies and a lupus anticoagulant
options.rationale: A lupus anticoagulant does prolong the activated partial thromboplastin time and so is a reasonable thought when that test is abnormal, but it causes thrombosis rather than bleeding. Testing for it would explain the coagulation result while contradicting the entire clinical history. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, affecting around one percent of the population, and it is substantially underdiagnosed in adolescent girls whose heavy menstrual bleeding is accepted as normal. The pattern is mucocutaneous: menorrhagia, epistaxis, easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after dental or surgical procedures, in contrast to the deep joint and muscle bleeding of haemophilia. Autosomal inheritance means affected women appear across generations, which is why the maternal history matters. Screening tests are unreliable, since the platelet count is normal and the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged only when factor VIII falls appreciably, so specific assays are required. Iron deficiency is almost universal and must be treated alongside, with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tranexamic acid or desmopressin used to control the bleeding.
key_points: Mucocutaneous bleeding suggests a platelet or von Willebrand factor problem rather than a coagulation factor deficiency.
A normal platelet count and a normal or only mildly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time do not exclude the diagnosis.
Von Willebrand factor stabilises factor VIII, so factor VIII falls in more severe disease and prolongs the clotting time.
Autosomal inheritance means affected mothers and daughters are common, unlike X linked haemophilia.
Levels rise with stress, pregnancy and oestrogen, so repeat testing may be needed when suspicion is high.
explanation.pearls: Ask about nosebleeds and dental extractions in every adolescent with heavy periods, because a lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding history with a normal platelet count warrants specific von Willebrand assays rather than a pelvic ultrasound, and a single normal set of levels does not exclude the diagnosis since they rise with stress and oestrogen.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: advising a family about the single highest yield change when several sudden infant death risk factors are present together
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 week old boy for his immunisations. He was born at 35 weeks and is feeding well and gaining weight.

His mother mentions that she is exhausted. She tells you she smokes ten cigarettes a day outside the house, that the baby sleeps in a bassinet beside her bed on his back, and that when he wakes at three in the morning she feeds him lying down on the sofa in the lounge room and they both usually fall asleep there until the morning. She uses a light muslin wrap and the bassinet has a firm mattress and no bumpers or soft toys. She asks whether a home apnoea monitor would let her relax, because a friend has offered to lend one.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure not recorded, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and well grown, weight tracking along the 25th centile, chest clear, heart sounds normal with no murmur, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: Which single change would you advise first to reduce this baby's risk of sudden unexpected death?

options.text: Borrow the home apnoea monitor and use it whenever the baby sleeps
options.rationale: Domestic monitors detect central apnoea and bradycardia, and trials have never shown that they reduce sudden unexpected death, because the mechanism is not a detectable apnoea that a parent can interrupt. They also generate false alarms that worsen the exhaustion driving the unsafe sleeping in the first place. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Swaddle the baby more firmly with arms contained during every sleep
options.rationale: Firm wrapping with the hips able to flex and abduct is acceptable practice for a young infant sleeping on the back, but it is not the problem here and it becomes hazardous once a baby can roll. Adjusting the wrap addresses none of the three genuine risks in this history. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Feed the baby on a bed and return him to his own cot before sleeping
options.rationale: Sharing a sofa or armchair for sleep carries a far higher risk than any other sleep surface, because an infant wedges into the cushion gap or against the adult and cannot reposition, and this risk is multiplied by prematurity and maternal smoking, both present here. The practical advice is to move night feeds to a bed cleared of pillows and duvets so that falling asleep is survivable, and to return the baby to the bassinet in the parental room. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Move the bassinet out of the bedroom into a separate quiet nursery
options.rationale: This reverses the recommendation, since room sharing without bed sharing for the first six to twelve months is protective and separate room sleeping is associated with increased risk. The mother is already doing the right thing for the first part of the night. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Position the baby on his side with a rolled towel to stop him rolling
options.rationale: Side positioning was advised historically and has since been shown to be unstable, since infants roll from the side to the front, which is the highest risk position. Any device or prop used to maintain a position adds a suffocation hazard of its own. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

explanation.summary: Three risk factors stack in this history: prematurity at 35 weeks, maternal smoking, and unplanned sofa sleeping during night feeds. The mother has already got the supine position, the firm flat mattress and room sharing right, which is what makes the sofa the highest yield target. Sofa sharing carries a substantially greater risk than bed sharing, and it most often happens by accident when an exhausted parent feeds in a chair rather than as a planned arrangement. Advising a safer place to feed at night is therefore more useful than telling a tired mother simply not to fall asleep. Home apnoea monitors have no evidence of benefit and should not be offered as reassurance.
key_points: Supine positioning, a firm flat mattress, a clear cot and room sharing without bed sharing are the core protective measures.
Sofa and armchair sleeping carries the highest risk of any sleep surface for an infant.
Maternal smoking and prematurity are independent risk factors that multiply the risk of an unsafe sleep surface.
Home apnoea monitors have not been shown to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy.
Side lying is not a safe alternative to supine because infants roll from the side onto the front.
explanation.pearls: Ask every exhausted parent where they actually feed at three in the morning rather than where the baby sleeps, because accidental sofa sleeping during night feeds is the commonest unrecognised high risk exposure and the fix is to move the feed to a cleared adult bed rather than to promise to stay awake.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sudden unexpected death in infancy

subtopic_detail: responding to a request for contraception from a young adolescent who does not want her parents informed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old girl who has come to the clinic alone and asks for the contraceptive pill. She tells you she does not want her parents to know and asks whether you have to tell them.

She explains that she has been in a relationship for eight months with a boy in her year at school who is sixteen, that they have not yet had sex, and that she wants to be prepared before they do. She describes the relationship as happy and says there has been no pressure, no violence and no exchange of money or gifts. She can explain how the pill works, what happens if she misses one, and that it does not protect against sexually transmitted infection. She is attending school regularly, is not using alcohol or other drugs, and her mood and weight are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well grown with body mass index on the 50th centile, no bruising or injury, engaged and articulate throughout the consultation, no features of low mood
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, no other investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Decline to prescribe until at least one parent attends with her in person
options.rationale: Requiring a parent removes her ability to access care and is not what the law requires, since a young person who understands the treatment may consent to it themselves. Refusing on age alone predictably leads to unprotected intercourse rather than to parental involvement. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health

options.text: Notify child protection services because of her age before prescribing anything
options.rationale: Mandatory reporting is triggered by a reasonable belief of abuse or neglect, and indicators include a large age difference, coercion, exchange of money or gifts, violence or an inability to consent. A consensual relationship with a peer of similar age, with none of those features, does not meet that threshold. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health

options.text: Prescribe the pill without exploring the relationship or discussing confidentiality
options.rationale: Providing contraception is the right outcome, and doing it without the assessment misses the point of the consultation, because the risk screen is what distinguishes a safe peer relationship from exploitation. It also leaves her unclear about the limits of confidentiality, which is the information she specifically asked for. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health

options.text: Provide condoms only and review her request again when she turns sixteen
options.rationale: Barrier protection should certainly be discussed and supplied for infection prevention, and offering it instead of effective contraception substitutes a method with a much higher failure rate. Age alone is not a reason to withhold hormonal contraception from a competent young person. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health

options.text: Assess her competence and capacity to consent, then provide confidential care
options.rationale: A young person who understands the nature, purpose and consequences of a treatment can consent to it independently, and she has demonstrated that understanding by explaining how the method works and what to do if a dose is missed. The consultation must also screen for exploitation using age difference, coercion and violence, explain that confidentiality holds unless there is a risk of serious harm, encourage but not require parental involvement, and offer sexually transmitted infection protection alongside the contraception. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health

explanation.summary: A young person under 18 who demonstrates sufficient understanding and intelligence to comprehend fully what is proposed may consent to their own treatment, a principle that applies across Australian jurisdictions although the statutory detail varies. Competence is assessed for the specific decision rather than assumed from age, and this girl demonstrates it by explaining the method, its failure mode and its limitations. The consultation must nonetheless screen for sexual exploitation, where the relevant indicators are a significant age difference, coercion or pressure, violence, exchange of money or gifts, and an inability to consent. A consensual relationship with a similarly aged peer without those features does not trigger mandatory reporting. Confidentiality should be explained clearly, including that it would be broken only where there is risk of serious harm, and parental involvement encouraged without being made a condition of care.
key_points: Competence is decision specific and is assessed rather than inferred from chronological age.
Exploitation indicators include age disparity, coercion, violence, exchange of money and inability to consent.
Confidentiality should be explained explicitly, including the circumstances in which it would be broken.
Parental involvement is encouraged but cannot be made a condition of providing care to a competent minor.
Contraceptive provision should be accompanied by sexually transmitted infection prevention and screening.
explanation.pearls: Ask the age of the partner and about coercion, money and violence in every adolescent sexual health consultation, because those answers rather than the patient's own age determine whether this is confidential care for a competent young person or a child protection matter.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Confidentiality and adolescent health
Family Planning Australia: Contraception for young people

subtopic_detail: choosing an anticonvulsant when brief staring episodes coexist with early morning jerks in an adolescent
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric neurology clinic seeing a 13 year old girl referred after a convulsion at school. Her mother reports that for the past two years she has had brief episodes at home where she stops mid sentence and stares for a few seconds, then carries on as though nothing happened.

Her mother adds that for the past six months she has been dropping her cereal spoon at breakfast and has smashed two bowls, always within an hour of waking, and that she is fully aware when this happens. The convulsion at school followed a sleepover at which she had about four hours of sleep. She takes no regular medication and is not sexually active. Her electroencephalogram shows generalised polyspike and wave discharges that increase markedly on photic stimulation.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal with no focal deficit, no neurocutaneous stigmata, normal fundi, normal gait and coordination
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram shows generalised polyspike and wave at 4 to 6 Hz with a photoparoxysmal response, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Levetiracetam titrated to effect with monitoring of mood and behaviour
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is effective against both the myoclonic jerks and the generalised tonic clonic seizures of this syndrome and avoids the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate, which is why it is preferred for an adolescent girl who may become pregnant. Irritability and low mood are its characteristic adverse effects and are the reason the counselling and review are built into the prescription. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Sodium valproate at a standard weight based dose with liver function testing
options.rationale: Valproate is the most effective drug for this syndrome, and its use in a girl of childbearing potential is restricted because of a dose related risk of neural tube defects and a substantial risk of neurodevelopmental impairment in exposed children. It is reserved for when other agents have failed, under a pregnancy prevention program. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Carbamazepine as a modified release preparation with slow upward titration
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is a sodium channel blocker suited to focal epilepsy and it characteristically aggravates generalised syndromes, worsening both myoclonus and absence seizures. Prescribing it here would be expected to increase seizure frequency rather than reduce it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ethosuximide with a review of seizure frequency after four weeks of therapy
options.rationale: Ethosuximide is first line for childhood absence epilepsy occurring alone, where it has the best balance of efficacy and tolerability, but it treats only the absences and leaves myoclonic and generalised tonic clonic seizures uncovered. The morning jerks and the convulsion are what make it insufficient here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Sleep hygiene advice with a plan to review before starting any medication
options.rationale: Avoiding sleep deprivation, alcohol and flashing lights genuinely reduces seizures in this syndrome and is part of every management plan, but it is an adjunct rather than a substitute once a generalised tonic clonic seizure has occurred. Non pharmacological measures alone would leave her at continued risk and affect her eligibility to drive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: This is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and the history of early morning jerks with preserved awareness is the finding that reclassifies what otherwise looks like childhood absence epilepsy. The triad is myoclonic jerks soon after waking, generalised tonic clonic seizures often provoked by sleep deprivation, and absences in about a third of patients. Generalised polyspike and wave with a photoparoxysmal response supports the syndrome. Valproate is the most effective agent but is restricted in girls and women of childbearing potential because of teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harm, so levetiracetam is the practical first choice. Carbamazepine and other sodium channel blockers aggravate the syndrome and must be avoided.
key_points: Myoclonic jerks within an hour of waking with retained awareness are the defining feature of the syndrome.
Sleep deprivation, alcohol and photic stimulation are the principal seizure triggers.
Carbamazepine, phenytoin and other sodium channel blockers aggravate generalised myoclonic and absence seizures.
Ethosuximide covers absences only and does not protect against myoclonic or tonic clonic seizures.
Remission is uncommon and treatment is usually lifelong, unlike childhood absence epilepsy which frequently resolves.
explanation.pearls: Ask every adolescent with absences whether they drop things at breakfast, because early morning myoclonus converts childhood absence epilepsy into juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and changes the drug from ethosuximide to levetiracetam, with valproate withheld in girls of childbearing potential unless other agents have failed.

subtopic_detail: planning the follow up that matters after a palpable purpuric rash with arthralgia in a school aged child
stem: A 6-year-old boy developed a rash on his buttocks and legs four days ago, a week after a sore throat. He has colicky abdominal pain and swollen tender ankles.

data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura over buttocks and extensor legs, none above the waist; no scrotal swelling
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 386 x10^9/L, normal coagulation profile, urinalysis 1 plus blood, no protein

lead_in: Alongside analgesia, what most matters in his ongoing management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin to shorten the rash
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used in Kawasaki disease to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk and has no established role in this condition. The rash resolves spontaneously over weeks and its duration is not what determines outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Oral corticosteroid to prevent later kidney disease
options.rationale: Corticosteroid helps significant abdominal pain and arthritis and is used for those indications, and randomised evidence shows it does not prevent the onset of nephritis. Prescribing it as renal prophylaxis is a common misconception and would give no protection while adding adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Referral for renal biopsy now to grade involvement
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for persistent heavy proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, hypertension or impaired renal function, which would indicate significant nephritis requiring immunosuppression. Isolated microscopic haematuria with normal protein, blood pressure and creatinine does not meet that threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Scheduled blood pressure and urinalysis for six months
options.rationale: Nephritis is the only complication that threatens long term outcome and it commonly appears weeks to months after the rash has faded, when the child appears entirely well, so surveillance rather than treatment is what protects the kidneys. The accepted schedule checks blood pressure and urinalysis at defined intervals for at least six months, and new proteinuria or hypertension is what triggers nephrology referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Empirical antibiotics for the preceding throat infection
options.rationale: A preceding upper respiratory infection is a common trigger and antibiotics are given only where an active bacterial infection is confirmed, which has not been demonstrated here. Treating the trigger retrospectively does not alter the course of the vasculitis or the risk of nephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Henoch Schonlein purpura is the commonest childhood vasculitis and is diagnosed clinically from palpable purpura distributed over the buttocks and lower limbs in a child with a normal platelet count, accompanied by arthritis, abdominal pain or renal involvement. The normal platelet count and coagulation screen are what exclude thrombocytopenic and coagulopathic causes of a non blanching rash. Most of the illness is self limiting, and corticosteroid is used for troublesome abdominal pain or arthritis rather than for renal protection, since trials show it does not prevent nephritis. Nephritis is the complication that determines long term outcome and may declare itself weeks to months after the rash resolves, which is why scheduled blood pressure and urinalysis monitoring for at least six months is the central element of care. Intussusception is the important abdominal complication and should be considered if pain becomes severe or a mass appears.
key_points: A normal platelet count distinguishes this vasculitis from thrombocytopenic causes of non blanching purpura.
The rash is characteristically distributed over the buttocks and extensor surfaces below the waist.
Corticosteroid treats abdominal pain and arthritis but does not prevent the development of nephritis.
Nephritis may appear weeks to months after the rash, requiring at least six months of surveillance.
Intussusception is the important abdominal complication and is typically ileoileal rather than ileocolic.
explanation.pearls: Give the family a written schedule of blood pressure and urine checks before they leave, because nephritis in this condition often appears six to eight weeks after the rash has gone and will be missed entirely if follow up is left to depend on the child looking unwell.

subtopic_detail: recognising anterior horn cell disease in a floppy infant whose face and eyes remain fully active
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 month old boy referred because he cannot hold his head up. His mother says he moved vigorously in the womb but has become less active over the last two months and no longer kicks the play mat.

She describes his cry as quieter than it was and says he takes longer to finish a bottle and sweats while feeding. He smiles readily at her, follows her across the room with his eyes and babbles. He has had no fever and no seizures, and his weight is tracking along the 10th centile having been on the 50th at birth. On examination he lies with his hips abducted and externally rotated, has no head lag correction on pull to sit, and the deep tendon reflexes cannot be elicited at the knees, ankles or biceps. His tongue shows fine rippling movements at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked hypotonia with a bell shaped chest and paradoxical breathing, absent deep tendon reflexes throughout, fine tongue fasciculations, full facial expression and full extraocular movements, alert and socially responsive
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 142 U/L (60-305), full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Methylation testing of the chromosome 15 imprinted region on a blood sample
options.rationale: Methylation studies diagnose Prader Willi syndrome, which is a leading cause of neonatal hypotonia with poor feeding, but those infants have a weak suck with global developmental delay, characteristic facies and preserved reflexes rather than areflexia with fasciculations. Cognitive and social development here is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Survival motor neuron gene deletion testing with urgent neurology referral
options.rationale: Areflexia with tongue fasciculations, a normal creatine kinase and preserved facial and eye movements localise the lesion to the anterior horn cell, and homozygous deletion of exon 7 of the survival motor neuron 1 gene confirms it on a blood sample within days. Urgency matters because disease modifying therapy works by preserving motor neurons that have not yet died, so weeks of delay translate directly into lost function. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Central causes of hypotonia are sought with imaging, and they characteristically produce a depressed conscious state, developmental delay, brisk reflexes or upgoing plantars. A bright socially engaged infant with absent reflexes and fasciculations has a lower motor neuron problem, and anaesthesia carries real respiratory risk in this state. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Serum lactate with urine organic acids and plasma amino acid quantification
options.rationale: Metabolic screening is appropriate where hypotonia comes with encephalopathy, regression across multiple domains, organomegaly or acidosis, none of which is present. It is a reasonable parallel test in an undifferentiated floppy infant but not the one that will name this diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Repetitive nerve stimulation with an edrophonium test performed at the bedside
options.rationale: Neuromuscular junction disorders are identified this way, and they characteristically involve the extraocular and facial muscles, producing ptosis and a fatigable weak facial expression along with fluctuation through the day. Full facial expression and full eye movements argue strongly against the junction as the site of the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

explanation.summary: This is spinal muscular atrophy, and the localising value of the examination is the whole point. Areflexia with tongue fasciculations places the lesion at the anterior horn cell, a normal creatine kinase argues against a muscular dystrophy, and full facial and extraocular movement argues against a neuromuscular junction disorder. Alert, socially normal development in a profoundly weak infant is characteristic and separates this from central causes of hypotonia. Diagnosis is by survival motor neuron 1 gene testing on blood, which is fast and does not require biopsy. Disease modifying therapies work by rescuing motor neurons that are still alive, so the referral is urgent rather than routine.
key_points: Anterior horn cell disease gives profound weakness with areflexia, fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase.
Preserved facial expression and eye movements argue against a neuromuscular junction disorder.
Normal social and cognitive development distinguishes lower motor neuron causes from central hypotonia.
Paradoxical breathing with a bell shaped chest reflects intercostal weakness with a spared diaphragm.
Prader Willi syndrome causes neonatal hypotonia but with preserved reflexes and global developmental delay.
explanation.pearls: Look at the tongue at rest and test the reflexes in every floppy infant, because fine tongue fasciculations with absent reflexes and a normal creatine kinase point to spinal muscular atrophy and justify same week genetic testing, since disease modifying treatment preserves only the motor neurons that have not yet been lost.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

subtopic_detail: blue episodes provoked by frustration in a toddler whose milk intake has displaced solid food
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18 month old girl whose mother describes six episodes in three months. Each begins when she is hurt or told no, she cries hard, stops breathing out, turns blue around the lips and goes limp for about twenty seconds, then wakes irritable.

Her mother says two of the episodes ended with a few seconds of stiffening of the arms. There has never been an episode during sleep, during exercise or without an obvious trigger, and she has never been incontinent or drowsy for long afterwards. She walks, runs and says twenty words. She drinks about 1.4 litres of cow milk each day and eats very little meat or cereal. There is no family history of sudden death or of fainting, and her electrocardiogram taken last week was reported as normal with a corrected QT interval of 410 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no murmur, femoral pulses equal, neurological examination normal, weight on the 25th centile and length on the 50th
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with corrected QT interval 410 ms (below 440), no bloods taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Supply buccal midazolam for the parents to give during the longer episodes
options.rationale: The episodes are self limiting within a minute and terminate as breathing resumes, so a rescue anticonvulsant treats nothing and exposes a toddler to sedation and airway risk. Rescue medication belongs with prolonged epileptic seizures, not with hypoxic events of this kind. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.text: Reassure the parents that the episodes are harmless and need no further assessment
options.rationale: Reassurance about the benign natural history is correct as far as it goes and is part of the consultation. It is incomplete here because the pallor and the milk intake point to a treatable contributor that reassurance alone will leave in place. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a sleep deprived electroencephalogram to characterise the stiffening movements
options.rationale: Brief stiffening or a few jerks at the end of a prolonged episode is a hypoxic phenomenon and does not indicate epilepsy when every episode has an emotional or painful trigger. An electroencephalogram in this setting is normal or shows non specific findings that risk an incorrect diagnosis. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.text: Refer for 24 hour ambulatory cardiac monitoring before any other investigation
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring is directed at episodes occurring without warning, during exercise or during sleep, or where the family history raises the possibility of an inherited arrhythmia. A normal corrected QT interval with a consistent emotional trigger and no relevant family history makes this a low yield test. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.text: Take a full blood count with iron studies and replace iron if the stores are low
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is found in a large proportion of children with these episodes and treating it reduces both their frequency and their severity, which is the only intervention shown to change the natural history. Her milk intake of 1.4 litres daily displaces iron rich food and inhibits absorption, and she is pale, so the deficiency is likely and worth confirming before it is treated. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Blue episodes triggered by pain or frustration in a toddler, with a short recovery and no episodes during sleep or exertion, describe a hypoxic event rather than a seizure or an arrhythmia. Terminal stiffening is common once the episode lasts long enough to cause cerebral hypoxia and does not change the diagnosis. The feature that should change management here is the combination of pallor and a milk intake that has displaced iron rich solids, because iron deficiency is strongly associated with these episodes and its correction reduces them. Confirming the deficiency before treating avoids committing a child to iron on the basis of appearance alone. A normal corrected QT interval and the absence of exertional or sleep related episodes make cardiac investigation low yield.
key_points: Every episode following a trigger, with recovery in under a minute, argues against epilepsy.
Terminal stiffening reflects cerebral hypoxia and does not warrant an electroencephalogram.
Cow milk above about 500 mL daily in a toddler displaces iron rich foods and impairs absorption.
Correcting iron deficiency reduces the frequency and severity of these episodes.
Episodes during sleep or exertion, or a family history of sudden death, shift the workup to cardiac.
explanation.pearls: Ask the daily milk volume in every toddler presenting with these episodes, because intake above 500 mL a day makes iron deficiency likely, and replacing iron for three months is the one intervention that reduces how often the episodes happen.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

subtopic_detail: deciding whether repeated nosebleeds in a well child need a bleeding disorder workup
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 year old boy who has had about eight nosebleeds in the past two months. His mother says each one comes from the right nostril, starts while he is watching television or soon after he has been picking his nose, and stops within ten minutes when she pinches the bridge of his nose for him.

He has never bled from the gums or into a joint, has never bruised without an injury, and had a tonsillectomy at five without excessive bleeding. No relative has a bleeding problem or has needed transfusion after surgery. The family has recently started using ducted heating through the winter. On examination the anterior part of the right septum is crusted and reddened, and the rest of the examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Crusted excoriated area on the anterior right nasal septum, no petechiae, no bruises beyond both shins, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Correct the pressure technique and prescribe an antiseptic nasal ointment for two weeks
options.rationale: Bleeding from one nostril in a well child with a visible excoriated area on the anterior septum is local in origin, and treatment is directed at the mucosa and at the technique. Pressure belongs on the soft part of the nose rather than the bony bridge, and an antiseptic ointment reduces crusting and staphylococcal colonisation, which shortens the run of bleeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for chemical cautery of the septal vessels
options.rationale: Cautery is reserved for bleeding that continues despite mucosal treatment and correct first aid, and it carries a risk of septal injury when the mucosa is already excoriated. It is a second line step rather than the opening move in a child having short self limiting bleeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Advise a saline spray alone and review him again only if the bleeding worsens
options.rationale: Saline addresses dryness from heated indoor air and is a reasonable adjunct, but on its own it leaves the colonised excoriated area untreated and the family still pinching the wrong part of the nose. The technique correction is the part of this consultation that most reliably shortens each episode. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Request a full blood count, coagulation profile and von Willebrand factor studies
options.rationale: A haemostatic workup is indicated when bleeding comes from both nostrils, lasts beyond about ten minutes despite correct pressure, involves other sites, or where surgery or family history suggests a disorder. None of those apply, and he bled normally at tonsillectomy, which is a substantial haemostatic challenge. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Arrange nasal endoscopy to exclude a mass in the posterior nasal space
options.rationale: Endoscopy is warranted for unilateral obstruction, foul discharge or profuse posterior bleeding, particularly in an adolescent boy where a vascular nasal tumour is a consideration. Short anterior bleeds with a visible septal cause in a 7 year old do not raise that possibility. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Epistaxis)

explanation.summary: Most childhood nosebleeds arise from the anterior septum, where a superficial vascular plexus sits close to the surface and is easily damaged by picking and by dry heated air. The features that separate this local pattern from a bleeding disorder are the single nostril, the short duration with pressure, the absence of bleeding at other sites, and an uneventful tonsillectomy. Management is mucosal treatment plus correcting the first aid, because families very commonly pinch the bony bridge, which does not compress the bleeding point. Antiseptic ointment reduces crusting and colonisation and is a reasonable first line in Australian practice. Cautery and haematological investigation both sit downstream of this step.
key_points: The anterior septum is the source of the great majority of childhood nosebleeds.
Pressure must be applied to the soft part of the nose, not the bony bridge.
Bleeding from both nostrils or at other sites shifts the assessment toward a haemostatic disorder.
Normal haemostasis at tonsillectomy is strong evidence against an inherited bleeding disorder.
Unilateral obstruction with profuse bleeding in an adolescent boy warrants imaging and endoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to demonstrate how they hold the nose, because most families compress the bony bridge where no bleeding vessel lies, and ten minutes of correctly applied pressure to the soft part settles nearly all anterior bleeds without any prescription at all.

subtopic_detail: anterior knee pain in a growing athlete where the site of tenderness decides the management
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13 year old boy who plays basketball four times a week and has had three months of pain at the front of his right knee. He says it is worst going up stairs and during jumping drills, settles within a day of rest, and has never woken him at night.

He has grown 9 cm in the past year. He has not had fevers, weight loss or night sweats, and the knee has never given way, locked or swollen. On examination he is tender over a prominent bony lump below the kneecap, the joint line is not tender, and there is no effusion. Extending the knee against resistance reproduces his pain, and hip rotation is full and painless on both sides.

data_table.Examination: Prominent tender tibial tubercle on the right, no joint effusion, no joint line tenderness, full painless internal rotation of both hips, no warmth or erythema
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for consideration of excision of the bony prominence
options.rationale: Surgery to remove a residual ossicle is confined to skeletally mature patients whose symptoms have persisted well beyond the end of growth despite full conservative treatment. Operating during the growth spurt risks the tubercle and is never the first response. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

options.text: Request plain radiographs of the knee in two planes before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for night pain, rest pain, systemic symptoms, an effusion or a history of significant trauma, because those raise the possibility of bone tumour or an internal derangement. Focal tenderness over the tubercle with pain reproduced by resisted extension is a clinical diagnosis and radiographs add nothing. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

options.text: Inject corticosteroid around the tender prominence and allow return to sport
options.rationale: Corticosteroid placed near a tendon insertion weakens the collagen and risks avulsion of the apophysis, which is precisely the structure already under traction stress. There is no role for injection in this condition at any stage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children

options.text: Request pelvic radiographs including frog lateral views of both hips today
options.rationale: Referred pain from a slipped upper femoral epiphysis genuinely can present as knee pain in this age group, which is why hip rotation must be examined in every adolescent with knee pain. Full and painless internal rotation of both hips makes that diagnosis very unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Advise relative rest with a quadriceps stretching program and simple analgesia
options.rationale: Traction apophysitis at the tibial tubercle is a self limiting overuse condition of the growth spurt, and load modification with a stretching program addresses the tight extensor mechanism that drives it. Complete withdrawal from sport is neither necessary nor helpful, so activity is reduced to a level that does not provoke pain while flexibility improves. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

explanation.summary: Anterior knee pain in a rapidly growing adolescent athlete, with tenderness localised to the tibial tubercle and pain reproduced by resisted knee extension, is traction apophysitis at the patellar tendon insertion. The absence of night pain, rest pain, systemic features and effusion removes the presentations that require imaging, and full painless hip rotation removes the referred pain from a slipped epiphysis that must always be considered. Treatment is load modification rather than cessation of sport, combined with stretching of the quadriceps and hamstrings, because reduced flexibility during the growth spurt increases traction on the apophysis. The condition resolves as the apophysis fuses, and families need to be told the prominence itself will remain. Persisting symptoms after skeletal maturity are the only situation in which surgery is discussed.
key_points: Tenderness confined to the tibial tubercle with a normal joint line indicates apophysitis, not internal derangement.
Every adolescent with knee pain needs hip rotation examined to exclude referred pain.
Night pain, rest pain or systemic symptoms mandate radiographs to exclude bone tumour.
Load is reduced to a pain tolerable level rather than stopped altogether.
The bony prominence persists after symptoms resolve and does not indicate treatment failure.
explanation.pearls: Tell the family at the first visit that the lump is permanent even though the pain is not, because otherwise they return repeatedly for the unchanged prominence and are offered imaging that was never indicated.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children

subtopic_detail: responding to parental refusal of the newborn intramuscular prophylaxis without losing the protection entirely
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward asked to see the parents of a healthy boy born two hours ago at 39 weeks by normal vaginal birth, weighing 3480 g. They have declined the intramuscular vitamin K injection after reading that the dose is far larger than a newborn would receive naturally, and they say they will not consent to an injection under any circumstances.

They are articulate, have asked good questions, and say they will accept anything given by mouth. The mother took no medications in pregnancy, has no liver disease, and plans to breastfeed exclusively. The baby has fed once, has normal tone and colour, and his examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 140/min, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 98% in air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, blood pressure not indicated
data_table.Examination: Term male infant, normal tone and cry, no bruising or cephalohaematoma, red reflex present bilaterally, femoral pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What should you do next?

options.text: Notify child protection services because refusal places the infant at risk of harm
options.rationale: Notification is reserved for refusal of treatment for an established life threatening condition, not for declining prophylaxis where a reasonable alternative is accepted. Escalating at this point damages a relationship these parents have engaged with and would not change the outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.text: Advise the mother to take a daily supplement so that her breastmilk supplies enough
options.rationale: Maternal supplementation raises breastmilk concentrations only modestly and unpredictably, and breastmilk is inherently a poor source, which is why exclusively breastfed infants carry the highest risk of late bleeding. It cannot be relied on as the infant prophylaxis. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

options.text: Offer the three dose oral regimen and document the discussion of the residual bleeding risk
options.rationale: Where an injection is refused, the oral schedule of three doses given at birth, at three to five days and at four weeks is the recognised alternative for a breastfed infant and preserves most of the protection. It is less effective than the single intramuscular dose, particularly against late bleeding, so the discussion and the residual risk are recorded and the parents are told the later doses are essential. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

options.text: Give the injection once the parents have left the room and record it in the notes
options.rationale: Treating a child against an explicit parental refusal without legal authority is an assault and destroys the trust on which every subsequent conversation depends. The strength of the clinical case for the injection does not create consent. (Source: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.text: Accept the refusal and arrange close follow up with the child health nurse instead
options.rationale: Surveillance does not prevent bleeding, and late haemorrhagic disease presents as intracranial bleeding without warning signs in a previously well infant. Declining the injection is the parents right, but leaving the infant with no prophylaxis at all when an oral alternative is available is not an equivalent plan. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

explanation.summary: Newborn bleeding from vitamin K deficiency has an early form in the first week and a late form at two to twelve weeks that typically presents as intracranial haemorrhage, and the late form is almost confined to exclusively breastfed infants who received no prophylaxis. A single intramuscular dose is the most effective prevention, but when parents refuse it the oral schedule of three doses is the accepted alternative and is markedly better than nothing. Because oral prophylaxis fails more often, especially in infants with unrecognised cholestasis, the later two doses must be arranged explicitly rather than left to chance. Accepting outright refusal, giving the injection covertly and relying on maternal supplementation are all unsafe responses in different ways. The conversation and the residual risk belong in the record.
key_points: Late bleeding occurs at two to twelve weeks and often presents as intracranial haemorrhage.
Exclusively breastfed infants who receive no prophylaxis carry the highest risk.
The oral alternative is three doses, at birth, at three to five days and at four weeks.
Oral prophylaxis fails more often than intramuscular, particularly with undiagnosed cholestasis.
Treating a child over an explicit parental refusal without legal authority is unlawful.
explanation.pearls: When parents accept the oral route, book the four week dose before they leave the ward, because the third dose is the one families forget and it is the dose that covers the window in which late intracranial bleeding actually occurs.

sources.label: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K
RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

subtopic_detail: deciding on removal versus observation for a swallowed metallic object using its position and appearance
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 3 year old girl brought in ninety minutes after her brother saw her put a coin from his money box into her mouth and swallow it. She coughed twice at the time and has been entirely well since, running around the waiting room and asking for food.

She is drooling no more than usual, is swallowing her own saliva, and has no stridor, wheeze or chest pain. Her chest and abdomen are unremarkable on examination. A single plain radiograph of the neck, chest and abdomen shows a uniform round metallic disc, about 20 mm across, lying below the left hemidiaphragm with no surrounding halo or step on either view.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Handling secretions normally, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender, no subcutaneous emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Plain film shows a uniform round metallic disc 20 mm diameter in the left upper abdomen, no double ring or step off, no free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent endoscopic removal from the stomach within the next two hours
options.rationale: Urgent removal from the stomach is reserved for a button battery, for a sharp or elongated object, and for multiple magnets, each of which causes injury while it sits there. A single smooth coin in the stomach of a well child does none of that. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Refer for oesophagoscopy because a coin of this size lodges above the diaphragm
options.rationale: Coins of 20 mm and above do lodge more often in a small child, which is why the oesophagus must be imaged, but this one has already passed the narrow points and lies in the stomach. The site on the film, not the diameter alone, determines the risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Give a stimulant laxative and keep her fasted until the object has been passed
options.rationale: Laxatives do not accelerate the passage of an ingested foreign body and fasting a toddler for days is both unnecessary and unkind. Normal diet encourages normal transit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal foreign bodies)

options.text: Discharge her with advice to watch the stools and to return if pain or vomiting develops
options.rationale: A blunt object that has reached the stomach in an asymptomatic child of this size passes without intervention in the great majority of cases, so management is observation at home with clear return advice. The radiograph excludes the two appearances that would change this, a lodged oesophageal position and the double ring that identifies a battery. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Admit for observation with repeat radiography in four hours to confirm it is moving
options.rationale: Serial films are used when an object remains in the stomach on a repeat film taken after some weeks, which is the point at which retrieval is considered. Imaging a well child again the same day exposes her to radiation without any decision depending on the result. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

explanation.summary: The two questions that decide the management of a swallowed metallic disc are where it is and what it is. An object still in the oesophagus needs removal because it causes pressure necrosis and cannot be expected to pass, whereas a blunt object that has reached the stomach passes spontaneously in almost all children. The appearance on the film distinguishes a coin from a button battery, which shows a double ring on the frontal view and a step at the edge on the lateral, and a battery in the oesophagus is a surgical emergency because it burns through the wall within hours. This child has a smooth uniform disc below the diaphragm and no symptoms, so she can go home with return advice. Repeat imaging has a role only if the object has still not passed after several weeks.
key_points: A blunt object that has reached the stomach passes spontaneously in the great majority of children.
A button battery shows a double ring on the frontal film and a step on the lateral.
A battery lodged in the oesophagus causes mucosal burns within two hours and needs immediate removal.
Sharp objects, elongated objects and multiple magnets warrant retrieval even from the stomach.
Laxatives do not speed transit and serial same day films change nothing.
explanation.pearls: Look for the double ring on the frontal film before you call anything a coin, because a 20 mm lithium battery and a coin are the same size and shade, and mistaking one for the other costs the child an oesophageal perforation within hours.

subtopic_detail: timing of first exposure to a high risk food in an infant whose eczema places her in the highest risk group
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 month old girl for her immunisations. Her mother mentions that she has had moderate eczema since eight weeks of age, currently controlled on a daily moisturiser and intermittent hydrocortisone 1 per cent ointment, and asks when it would be safe to give her peanut butter.

The infant has never eaten peanut or tree nuts and has never had a reaction to any food. She has had smooth cereal, pureed vegetables and yoghurt over the past three weeks without any problem. The mother has a sister with a peanut allergy and has been avoiding peanut herself while breastfeeding because she read that it would help. The infant is thriving, growth is tracking along the 50th centile, and her skin today shows mild dryness with no active flare.

data_table.Examination: Dry skin at the antecubital fossae with no excoriation or weeping, growth on the 50th centile for weight and length, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What advice should you give about introducing peanut?

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to peanut and introduce it only if the result is negative
options.rationale: Testing before introduction in a child who has never reacted generates positive results that reflect sensitisation rather than clinical allergy, and acting on them delays or prevents an introduction that would have been tolerated. Testing is indicated after a reaction, not before a first exposure. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Have the mother resume eating peanut so the infant is exposed through the breastmilk
options.rationale: Maternal avoidance during breastfeeding is unnecessary and her diet can return to normal, but exposure through breastmilk is not the mechanism that induces tolerance. The infant needs to eat the food herself in a form she can manage. (Source: NHMRC: Infant Feeding Guidelines)

options.text: Defer peanut until the eczema has been clear for three months and then introduce it
options.rationale: Waiting for clear skin postpones introduction past the window in which it is protective, and moderate eczema in infancy often persists for years. Eczema raises the risk of allergy, which is a reason to introduce sooner rather than later. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Give smooth peanut paste at home in the next week and continue it regularly thereafter
options.rationale: Introducing peanut in the first year and continuing it regularly reduces the development of peanut allergy, and the benefit is greatest in infants with eczema because they carry the highest baseline risk. She has already tolerated other solids and has no history of reaction, so the introduction happens at home in the usual way with a smooth form appropriate to her age. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Refer to an immunologist for the first dose to be given under supervised observation
options.rationale: Supervised introduction is reserved for an infant who has already reacted to that food or who has a sibling with anaphylaxis and a positive test. Routine referral for every infant with eczema would delay introduction by months and is not what the risk justifies. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

explanation.summary: Australian guidance is that all infants should be given the common allergenic foods, including peanut and egg, in the first year of life and preferably by around six months, once solids have begun. Infants with eczema have the highest risk of food allergy and therefore stand to gain the most, so eczema is a reason to introduce earlier rather than to delay. Screening tests before a first exposure are counterproductive because sensitisation without clinical allergy is common and a positive result leads to unnecessary avoidance. Whole nuts are a choking hazard at this age, so peanut is given as a smooth paste thinned into food the infant already takes. Regular ongoing intake matters, because tolerance is maintained by continued exposure rather than by a single successful feed.
key_points: Introduce common allergenic foods in the first year, preferably around six months.
Eczema raises the risk of food allergy and argues for earlier, not later, introduction.
Screening tests before a first exposure detect sensitisation and cause unnecessary avoidance.
Whole or chopped nuts are a choking hazard until about four years of age.
Regular continued intake is needed to maintain tolerance once the food is introduced.
explanation.pearls: Tell the family to keep peanut in the diet at least twice a week after the first successful feed, because a single tolerated exposure followed by months of avoidance does not maintain tolerance and allergy can still develop.

sources.label: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

subtopic_detail: scaly scalp and flexural rash in a young infant where the absence of itch redirects the diagnosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10 week old boy whose parents are distressed by thick yellowish scale that has built up over his scalp during the past month and has spread to his eyebrows and the creases of his neck. They have been told by relatives that it is eczema and that he needs a special formula.

He is exclusively breastfed, feeds well and has gained weight along the 60th centile since birth. He does not scratch, rub his head or cry when the areas are touched, and he sleeps through his night feeds. There is no family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever, and no blood or mucus in his stools. On examination the scale is greasy and adherent with mild underlying redness, there are salmon coloured patches in both axillae and the nappy flexures, and the skin elsewhere is soft with no excoriation, weeping or crusting.

data_table.Examination: Greasy adherent scale over the vertex, eyebrows and neck creases, salmon coloured patches in the axillae and nappy flexures with no satellite lesions, no excoriation, no petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly, weight on the 60th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and stop breastfeeding for a two week trial
options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial belongs to suspected cow milk protein allergy, which presents with blood or mucus in the stools, vomiting, poor weight gain or an itchy eczema that fails standard treatment. Advising a thriving breastfed infant to stop breastfeeding for a rash of this appearance causes real harm for no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Soften the scale with an emollient before washing, using a mild shampoo regularly
options.rationale: Greasy adherent scale on the scalp and face with flexural involvement in a comfortable infant who does not scratch is a self limiting condition of the first months that resolves without active treatment. Loosening the scale with an emollient such as white soft paraffin or a bath oil before gentle washing is all that is required, and the parents need to know it settles by around a year. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.text: Refer urgently to dermatology for skin biopsy to exclude an infiltrative condition
options.rationale: Urgent referral is warranted when a scaly scalp rash is petechial or purpuric, fails to respond to simple measures, or occurs with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or faltering growth, because Langerhans cell histiocytosis can present this way. A thriving infant with typical greasy scale and none of those features does not need a biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin because the thick adherent crust indicates bacterial infection
options.rationale: Bacterial infection complicating an infant rash produces honey coloured crusting, weeping, surrounding erythema and often fever, none of which is present. Greasy scale without any of those features is not an infection and antibiotics treat nothing. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.text: Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid to the scalp and the flexures twice daily
options.rationale: A topical corticosteroid is the treatment for atopic dermatitis, which itches intensely, spares the nappy area and appears later in infancy on the cheeks and the outer limbs. This infant does not scratch and has flexural and nappy involvement, so the diagnosis is different and a moderately potent steroid on facial and flexural skin risks atrophy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

explanation.summary: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis are both common in the first year and are frequently confused, but they separate cleanly on three features. Seborrhoeic dermatitis appears in the first weeks to months, produces greasy adherent scale on the scalp, face and flexures including the nappy area, and above all does not itch, so the infant is comfortable. Atopic dermatitis appears later, itches intensely enough to disturb sleep, spares the nappy area and favours the cheeks and extensor surfaces. Getting this right matters because it determines whether the family leaves with reassurance and an emollient or with a corticosteroid, a formula change and an unnecessary interruption to breastfeeding. Referral is reserved for the infant whose scalp rash is petechial or purpuric, fails simple treatment, or comes with organomegaly or faltering growth.
key_points: Seborrhoeic dermatitis in infancy does not itch and the infant is comfortable.
It involves the nappy area and flexures, which atopic dermatitis characteristically spares.
Atopic dermatitis appears later in infancy and disturbs sleep through itch.
Treatment is emollient softening and gentle washing, and it resolves by around a year.
Petechial scale with organomegaly or faltering growth warrants urgent assessment.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the baby scratches or wakes because of the rash, because a comfortable infant with a florid scaly scalp has seborrhoeic dermatitis and needs paraffin, while an infant who rubs his face on the sheets has atopic dermatitis and needs a steroid.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

subtopic_detail: why a scaly scalp patch with broken hairs will not respond to the treatment used for body ringworm
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old boy whose mother has been applying a topical antifungal cream to a patch on his scalp for the past four weeks with no improvement. The patch has grown and a second smaller one has appeared behind his ear.

He is otherwise well, has no fever and no pain, and attends a school where two other children have had something similar. He has no eczema and no history of hair pulling. On examination there is a 4 cm scaly patch on the vertex with hairs broken off a few millimetres above the scalp surface, a further 1 cm patch behind the right ear, and two small mobile tender nodes at the back of his neck. There is no boggy swelling and no pustulation.

data_table.Examination: Two scaly scalp patches with hairs broken close to the surface, mild occipital lymphadenopathy, no boggy mass, no pustules, no scarring, nails normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid because the appearance suggests scalp psoriasis
options.rationale: Psoriasis produces thick silvery scale on a well demarcated plaque and characteristically spares the hair, whereas hairs broken off close to the scalp indicate the shaft itself is infected. A corticosteroid without an antifungal allows a dermatophyte to spread more widely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Change to a stronger topical antifungal cream applied twice daily for eight weeks
options.rationale: Potency is not the problem, penetration is. No topical preparation reaches the fungal elements within the hair shaft, which is why four weeks of cream produced nothing and why another eight weeks would do the same. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Take hair and scale samples for fungal studies and begin oral griseofulvin
options.rationale: Fungal infection of the scalp sits within the hair shaft, where topical agents cannot reach, so systemic treatment for several weeks is required and topical therapy alone predictably fails. Samples are taken before treatment starts because the course runs for six to eight weeks and the species identified guides the choice and duration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin because the tender neck nodes indicate bacterial infection
options.rationale: Reactive occipital nodes are an expected part of scalp fungal infection and do not by themselves indicate bacterial disease. A tender boggy mass with pustules would suggest the inflammatory form, which still needs an antifungal and is treated with an added corticosteroid rather than an antibiotic alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Use an antifungal shampoo twice weekly and keep him home from school until it clears
options.rationale: Shampoo reduces surface spores and is a useful adjunct that limits spread to others, but it does not cure the infection within the shaft. Exclusion from school is not required once systemic treatment has started. (Source: RCH CPG: Skin infections)

explanation.summary: Hairs broken off a few millimetres above the scalp identify an infection inside the hair shaft rather than on the skin surface, and that anatomical fact drives the entire management. Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the shaft, so scalp disease requires an oral agent for six to eight weeks, and the four weeks of failed cream in this history is the expected outcome rather than a sign of resistance. Samples for microscopy and culture are taken before treatment because the responsible species influences the drug choice and because a long course should not rest on a clinical guess. Reactive occipital nodes are typical and do not indicate bacterial infection, while a boggy pustular mass represents the inflammatory form that additionally risks scarring alopecia. Antifungal shampoo is an adjunct that reduces transmission to household and school contacts.
key_points: Hairs broken close to the scalp indicate infection within the shaft.
Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the hair shaft and reliably fail on the scalp.
Oral treatment runs six to eight weeks and samples are taken before it starts.
Reactive occipital lymphadenopathy is expected and does not mean bacterial infection.
A boggy pustular mass is the inflammatory form and risks permanent scarring alopecia.
explanation.pearls: Any scalp scale with broken hairs and palpable occipital nodes gets an oral antifungal and a specimen, never a cream, because every week of topical treatment is a week the shaft infection keeps spreading and the culture takes up to four weeks to come back.

subtopic_detail: treating an itchy infestation across a household where only one child has symptoms
stem:
