You are the general practitioner seeing a 2 year old girl whose parents report three weeks of an itchy rash that is much worse at night and wakes her repeatedly. Her mother has begun to notice an itch on her own wrists over the past week.

The child attends family day care. She has had no fevers and is eating and playing normally. On examination there are excoriated papules on the trunk and thin wavy tracks in the web spaces of both hands and along the inner wrists, with a few papules on the soles. Her father and her 5 year old brother have no symptoms at all. There is no weeping, crusting or surrounding cellulitis.

data_table.Examination: Linear tracks in finger web spaces and on the flexor wrists, excoriated papules on the trunk, papules on both soles, no honey coloured crusting, no fever
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the child alone and treat other family members only if they develop an itch
options.rationale: Itch arises from a delayed hypersensitivity response that takes four to six weeks after a first infestation, so an asymptomatic contact is very often already infested. Waiting for symptoms is what produces the cycle of repeated treatment failures families describe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Prescribe oral ivermectin for the child as a single weight based dose
options.rationale: Oral treatment is reserved for crusted disease, for outbreaks in institutions and for people in whom topical treatment has failed or cannot be applied. It is not used as first line for ordinary infestation in a small child, where topical treatment is effective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid to the itchy areas for two weeks
options.rationale: A corticosteroid may be added after the infestation has been treated, because itch commonly persists for a fortnight once the mites are dead. Given alone it suppresses the inflammatory response, allows the mites to multiply and produces the widespread crusted form in a vulnerable child. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Treat every member of the household on the same day and repeat the application in one week
options.rationale: Treating only the symptomatic child guarantees reinfestation, because contacts carry mites for weeks before itch begins, which is why the father and brother being well does not exclude them. Simultaneous treatment of the whole household with a second application a week later covers eggs that survive the first, and permethrin is applied to the whole body including the scalp and soles in a child of this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin because the excoriated lesions are likely to be infected
options.rationale: Secondary bacterial infection does complicate scratched lesions and is treated when honey coloured crusting, surrounding erythema or systemic features appear. This child has excoriation without any of those signs, so antibiotics address nothing and leave the cause untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

explanation.summary: Night predominant itch with linear tracks in the web spaces and on the flexor wrists is the classic distribution of this infestation, and involvement of the soles is characteristic in infants and toddlers. The single most common reason treatment fails is that asymptomatic household contacts are not treated, because itch is a hypersensitivity phenomenon that takes four to six weeks to develop after a first infestation. Everyone in the household is therefore treated on the same day, whether or not they itch, and the application is repeated a week later to kill mites that hatch from eggs surviving the first treatment. In children under two the cream is applied to the scalp and face as well as the body, and to the palms and soles at every age. Bedding and clothing from the preceding days are washed hot or sealed for several days.
key_points: Itch develops four to six weeks after a first infestation, so contacts are infested before they are symptomatic.
All household members are treated on the same day regardless of symptoms.
Application is repeated after seven days to cover eggs surviving the first treatment.
In infants and toddlers the scalp, face, palms and soles are all treated.
Itch persisting up to two weeks after treatment does not indicate failure.
explanation.pearls: Warn the family before they leave that the itch will continue for up to two weeks after successful treatment, or they will return convinced it has failed and be tempted into a third and fourth application that only causes irritant dermatitis.

subtopic_detail: bone deformity in a toddler where the dietary and sun exposure history points away from a physiological cause
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20 month old boy whose mother is worried that his legs have become more bowed rather than less over the past six months, and that he is slow to walk any distance.

He was born at term and is still breastfed four times a day with small amounts of family food. The family covers up outdoors for cultural reasons and rarely spends time in direct sunlight. He has had no fractures and no bone pain that the family has noticed, and his bowels are regular with no diarrhoea or greasy stools. On examination he has symmetrical bowing of both tibiae, palpable widening at both wrists, and a row of small bony prominences along the costochondral junctions. His height has fallen from the 50th to the 10th centile over the past year while his weight has stayed on the 25th.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical tibial bowing, widened wrists, costochondral prominences, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, waddling gait, height dropping across centiles
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone
options.rationale: Wrist widening and costochondral prominences are the signs of unmineralised growth plate rather than of physiological bowing, and this biochemical panel confirms the metabolic pattern and shows how far it has progressed. A raised alkaline phosphatase with a low phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone identifies the deficiency state and distinguishes it from the inherited phosphate wasting forms. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Send coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A as the first line test
options.rationale: Malabsorption is a genuine cause of this bone disease and coeliac serology belongs in the workup if the first line biochemistry is abnormal and the dietary history does not explain it. Here the combination of prolonged breastfeeding with minimal solids and near complete sun avoidance explains the deficiency directly, and his stools are normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a bone density scan to quantify the degree of bone loss
options.rationale: Densitometry in a toddler is difficult to interpret because results must be corrected for bone size and skeletal maturity, and it does not distinguish the cause. The diagnosis here is biochemical and radiographic, not densitometric. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Start high dose oral vitamin D now and reassess the legs in three months
options.rationale: Treatment is indeed high dose vitamin D with adequate calcium intake, but starting before baseline biochemistry removes the ability to confirm the diagnosis and to detect the inherited phosphate wasting forms that will not respond. Baseline results also allow the response to be measured. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Request standing long leg radiographs to measure the tibiofemoral angle
options.rationale: Alignment films are used when bowing is the only abnormality and the question is physiological bowing against a growth plate disorder of one side. Wrist widening, rib changes and height crossing centiles have already moved this beyond an alignment problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Physiological bowing is symmetrical, painless and improves after the second birthday, and it is not accompanied by changes elsewhere in the skeleton. Widening at the wrists, prominences along the costochondral junctions, a delayed fontanelle and height crossing centiles all point instead to failure of mineralisation at the growth plate. The risk factors here are prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation beyond six months, minimal dietary intake and almost no ultraviolet exposure, which together deplete vitamin D stores. Baseline biochemistry confirms the metabolic picture and separates nutritional deficiency, in which parathyroid hormone rises and phosphate falls, from the inherited phosphate wasting disorders that require a different treatment. Treatment follows the results and is high dose vitamin D with adequate calcium, since replacing vitamin D alone in a child with poor calcium intake gives an incomplete response.
key_points: Wrist widening and costochondral prominences distinguish metabolic bone disease from physiological bowing.
Physiological bowing is symmetrical and improves after about two years of age.
Prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation plus minimal sun exposure depletes vitamin D stores.
A raised alkaline phosphatase with low phosphate and raised parathyroid hormone indicates the deficiency state.
Calcium intake must be adequate or vitamin D replacement alone gives an incomplete response.
explanation.pearls: Run your thumb along the costochondral junctions of any toddler with bowed legs, because a palpable row of beads turns an orthopaedic referral into a blood test and a treatable deficiency that also affects the mother and the next baby.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

subtopic_detail: resisting acid suppression in a thriving infant whose vomiting distresses the parents more than the child
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 month old boy whose parents describe vomiting after almost every feed since about three weeks of age. They have been given a proton pump inhibitor prescription by an after hours service and want your view before starting it.

The vomiting is effortless, happens within twenty minutes of a feed, and is milk that looks unchanged. He does not arch, scream or refuse feeds, and he settles quickly afterwards. There is no blood or green colour in the vomit, no constipation and no fevers. He is formula fed, taking 180 mL every three hours, which the parents have been increasing because they assume he is bringing most of it back up. His weight has tracked steadily along the 75th centile since birth, and examination including the abdomen is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, blood pressure not indicated
data_table.Examination: Alert and settled, abdomen soft with no mass, anterior fontanelle normal, weight on the 75th centile tracking since birth, no dehydration
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula for a two week trial of dairy exclusion
options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial is reasonable where vomiting occurs with blood or mucus in the stools, eczema, faltering growth or marked feed refusal, since cow milk protein allergy can mimic reflux. None of those features is present and a formula change adds cost and complexity without a target. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Explain the natural history, reduce the feed volume per feed and do not start the medicine
options.rationale: Effortless vomiting of unchanged milk in a thriving infant who feeds happily is a normal developmental phenomenon that resolves as the infant spends more time upright and takes solids. He is being offered around 200 mL per kilogram per day, well above requirement, and overfeeding is the reversible driver here, so reducing the volume per feed while keeping the frequency is the intervention that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Advise raising the head of the cot and putting him down to sleep on his left side
options.rationale: Positional measures reduce measured reflux episodes but any sleep position other than supine increases the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy, so the trade is not acceptable. Cot elevation has not been shown to reduce symptoms and can cause the infant to slide into an unsafe position. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Request an abdominal ultrasound to assess the pylorus before changing anything
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis presents with forceful vomiting during or straight after a feed in a hungry infant who loses weight, and it declares itself between two and eight weeks. Effortless vomiting with steady growth at three months does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting in infants)

options.text: Start the proton pump inhibitor for a four week trial and review the response
options.rationale: Trials in infants show acid suppression does not reduce crying or vomiting more than placebo, and it is associated with increased gastrointestinal and respiratory infection. Its place is in proven oesophagitis or in reflux with faltering growth, neither of which describes a settled infant on the 75th centile. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

explanation.summary: Effortless posseting of unchanged milk in an infant who feeds willingly, settles afterwards and grows along a centile is physiological and needs explanation rather than treatment. The feed volume matters: 180 mL every three hours in a baby of this age is well above the usual requirement of about 150 mL per kilogram per day, and overfeeding is one of the few reversible contributors. Acid suppression has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for crying and vomiting in infants and carries a real infection risk, so it is reserved for proven oesophagitis or for reflux with faltering growth. Features that should redirect the assessment include bile or blood in the vomit, faltering growth, feed refusal, blood in the stools and fever. Side or prone sleeping is never recommended because the risk of sudden unexpected death outweighs any reduction in reflux.
key_points: Effortless vomiting with normal growth and settled behaviour needs explanation, not treatment.
Requirement is about 150 mL per kilogram per day and exceeding it worsens posseting.
Acid suppression does not outperform placebo for infant crying or vomiting.
Bile, blood, faltering growth, fever or feed refusal each redirect the assessment.
Supine sleeping is maintained regardless of reflux because of sudden death risk.
explanation.pearls: Work out the millilitres per kilogram per day before you write anything, because a baby taking over 200 mL per kilogram daily will keep vomiting on any dose of any acid suppressant, and reducing the volume per feed usually settles it within a week.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

subtopic_detail: night waking maintained by the conditions under which a toddler falls asleep
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the exhausted mother of a 2 year old girl who wakes three or four times every night and will not resettle unless a parent lies on the floor beside her cot until she is asleep again. This has been the pattern for eight months and the mother is now falling asleep at work.

The child falls asleep at bedtime only with a parent lying next to her. She snores only with colds, has never been seen to stop breathing, and has no mouth breathing or daytime sleepiness. She naps once for an hour in the early afternoon, is dry overnight, has no pain, and her tonsils are not enlarged. Growth and development are normal and her behaviour during the day is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils small, no adenoidal facies, nasal airway clear, ears normal, growth and development appropriate for age
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the mother that this resolves with age and review again in six months
options.rationale: Learned sleep associations of this kind persist for years without intervention rather than resolving on their own, and the maternal sleep deprivation described is itself a safety issue at work and on the road. Reassurance without a plan leaves a treatable problem in place. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Teach a graduated settling approach so she learns to fall asleep without a parent present
options.rationale: She wakes normally between sleep cycles as every toddler does, but she can only return to sleep by recreating the conditions present when she first fell asleep, which is a parent lying beside her. Changing what happens at bedtime is therefore the intervention that changes the night waking, and graduated settling with progressively delayed responses has the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Prescribe melatonin at bedtime for four weeks to consolidate the overnight sleep
options.rationale: Melatonin shortens the time taken to fall asleep and has a place in neurodevelopmental conditions where the sleep phase is genuinely delayed. It does not address a learned sleep association and does not reduce night waking of this type, and it is not first line in an otherwise well toddler. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Refer for overnight sleep study to assess for obstructive sleep apnoea
options.rationale: A sleep study is directed at habitual snoring, witnessed pauses, mouth breathing, restless sleep with sweating or daytime behavioural change. Snoring only with intercurrent colds and a clear airway on examination does not meet that threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Advise dropping the daytime nap so that she builds more sleep pressure by bedtime
options.rationale: One early afternoon nap is developmentally appropriate at two years and removing it usually produces an overtired child who settles worse. Nap timing matters if the nap runs late into the afternoon, which is not the case here. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

explanation.summary: Brief arousals between sleep cycles happen in every young child several times a night, and whether they become a presenting problem depends on what the child needs in order to fall back asleep. A child who falls asleep at bedtime with a parent beside her requires that same parent at each arousal, which converts normal physiology into repeated calls for help. The effective intervention therefore targets bedtime rather than the night waking itself, teaching the child to fall asleep independently through graduated settling with progressively longer intervals before responding. Snoring only during colds, a clear nasal airway and small tonsils argue against obstructive sleep apnoea, which is the differential that would require a very different pathway. Parental exhaustion of this degree deserves acknowledgement in its own right and makes deferral an unsatisfactory answer.
key_points: Night waking becomes a problem when the child cannot return to sleep unaided.
The conditions present at sleep onset must be recreated at each normal arousal.
Graduated settling targets bedtime and has the strongest evidence at this age.
Habitual snoring, witnessed pauses or mouth breathing indicate assessment for obstructive sleep apnoea.
A single early afternoon nap remains developmentally appropriate at two years.
explanation.pearls: Ask exactly what is happening in the room at the moment the child first falls asleep, because that detail predicts what she will demand at two in the morning better than anything else in the history, and changing it is what fixes the nights.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

subtopic_detail: how background rheumatic fever risk changes the threshold for treating a sore throat before the swab returns
stem:
You are the doctor at a remote clinic in the Northern Territory seeing a 9 year old Aboriginal boy with two days of sore throat and fever. His community has a high rate of acute rheumatic fever and two children from his school were diagnosed with it last year.

He has no cough and no runny nose. He is drinking, has no drooling, no trismus and no neck swelling, and his voice is normal. On examination his tonsils are enlarged and red with exudate on the left, and there are two tender anterior cervical nodes. He has no rash and no joint pain or swelling, and there is no history of a previous episode of rheumatic fever. A throat swab has been taken and the laboratory is four days away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Enlarged erythematous tonsils with left sided exudate, two tender anterior cervical nodes, no rash, no murmur, joints normal, hydration adequate
data_table.Investigations: Throat swab taken and sent, no result available for four days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and treat the fever, starting treatment only if the swab is positive
options.rationale: Waiting for a result is the correct approach in a low risk urban setting, where most sore throats are viral and rheumatic fever is rare. Here it leaves a child in a high incidence community untreated for four days during the window in which treatment prevents rheumatic fever. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin as secondary prophylaxis
options.rationale: The long acting injection is the mainstay of secondary prophylaxis, given four weekly to a child who has already had rheumatic fever or has established rheumatic heart disease. A single dose is also an option for treating this episode if adherence to oral treatment is doubtful, but calling it prophylaxis misplaces it, since he has had no previous episode. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for seven days to cover resistant organisms
options.rationale: The organism responsible remains uniformly susceptible to penicillin, so broadening the spectrum adds adverse effects and selection pressure with no gain. A seven day course would also fall short of the duration needed to prevent rheumatic fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)

options.text: Prescribe oral azithromycin for three days to improve the chance of completing treatment
options.rationale: A macrolide is the alternative for a child with genuine penicillin allergy, and shorter courses are attractive for adherence. Macrolide resistance among these organisms is rising and the shorter course has not been shown to prevent rheumatic fever, so it is a second line choice rather than a convenience option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pharyngitis and tonsillitis)

options.text: Start oral phenoxymethylpenicillin now for ten days without waiting for the swab result
options.rationale: Where rheumatic fever is common, every sore throat in a child of school age is treated as streptococcal from the moment it presents, because the purpose of treatment is preventing rheumatic fever rather than shortening the illness. A full ten day course is required for that purpose, and stopping early on a negative swab is not recommended in a high risk setting. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

explanation.summary: The decision to treat a sore throat with antibiotics in Australia depends on where the child lives rather than on the appearance of the throat. In most urban settings sore throats are managed symptomatically because rheumatic fever is rare and antibiotics shorten symptoms by less than a day. In communities with a high incidence of acute rheumatic fever, every sore throat in a child of school age is treated empirically and immediately, because the aim is preventing a disease that follows untreated infection weeks later. Oral penicillin for ten days is the standard course, with the long acting injection used when adherence to a ten day oral course is uncertain, and a macrolide reserved for genuine penicillin allergy. Treatment is not stopped if the swab later returns negative in a high risk setting.
key_points: Background rheumatic fever incidence, not throat appearance, determines whether to treat empirically.
The aim of treatment is preventing rheumatic fever rather than shortening the sore throat.
Ten days of oral penicillin is required, since shorter courses do not prevent rheumatic fever.
The long acting intramuscular injection is an option when oral adherence is uncertain.
Secondary prophylaxis applies to children who have already had rheumatic fever or have rheumatic heart disease.
explanation.pearls: In a high incidence community, treat the sore throat the day it walks in and finish all ten days, because the rheumatic fever that follows arrives two to four weeks later in a child who has long since felt better and stopped the tablets.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever

subtopic_detail: Sticky eyes with lid swelling first appearing on day ten of life in a baby born vaginally at term
stem:
A 10 day old baby girl is brought to your general practice because both her eyes have been gluey since yesterday and her lids look puffy. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and her mother had no antenatal screening swabs taken.

She is feeding well and gaining weight. Her mother mentions that she has been a little snuffly but has no cough. On examination the conjunctivae are injected with a copious sticky discharge and moderate lid oedema, and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining. You take a swab for nucleic acid testing before starting treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure 72/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctival injection with copious sticky discharge, moderate lid oedema, clear corneas on fluorescein staining, red reflex present bilaterally
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.6 kg, tracking along the birth centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin for the baby and referral of both parents for testing and treatment
options.rationale: Onset at the end of the first week with copious discharge and lid oedema points to a genitally acquired organism, which needs systemic rather than topical therapy because it also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause pneumonitis. Treating the parents prevents reinfection and addresses their own untreated infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol eye drops for the baby with review arranged in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Topical therapy does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage and so does not prevent the later respiratory complication. It would be reasonable for an uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis in an older infant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Saline eye toilet and reassurance, with review only if the discharge has not settled
options.rationale: Saline toilet alone is appropriate for a blocked tear duct, which presents with watering rather than this degree of purulent discharge and lid swelling. Withholding treatment here risks progression. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

options.text: Admit for intravenous cefotaxime and hourly saline irrigation of both eyes
options.rationale: This intensity of treatment is reserved for the hyperacute presentation of a different genital organism, which characteristically appears in the first days of life with marked chemosis and corneal risk. The timing and corneal findings here do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral aciclovir for the baby with urgent ophthalmology review the same day
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is directed at a vesicular or dendritic presentation, and the fluorescein stain here shows no dendritic ulcer. Copious purulent discharge is not the expected pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Conjunctivitis)

explanation.summary: Neonatal conjunctivitis is stratified by the day of onset because that determines the likely organism and therefore the route of treatment. Presentation within the first few days with marked chemosis suggests gonococcal infection and is a sight threatening emergency needing parenteral therapy. Onset towards the end of the first week or in the second week suggests chlamydial infection, which requires oral macrolide therapy because the organism also colonises the nasopharynx and can produce an afebrile pneumonitis at four to twelve weeks. Diagnosis of either in a neonate is also a diagnosis in the parents, so contact testing and treatment are part of the management.
key_points: Day of onset is the primary discriminator in neonatal conjunctivitis
Chlamydial infection needs oral not topical therapy because of nasopharyngeal carriage
Untreated chlamydial carriage can cause an afebrile pneumonitis weeks later
A swab for nucleic acid testing is taken before treatment starts
Parental testing and treatment are part of managing the neonate
explanation.pearls: Chlamydial conjunctivitis typically declares itself between day five and day fourteen, and the oral macrolide is given to prevent the pneumonitis that can follow at four to twelve weeks, not merely to clear the eye.

subtopic_detail: Oral iron dose and duration for a toddler drinking large volumes of cow milk with microcytic anaemia
stem:
An 18 month old boy is brought to your clinic because he is pale and his parents feel he tires easily at playgroup. He drinks about a litre and a half of cow milk each day and eats very little solid food. He was born at term and his development is age appropriate.

His parents are both well and there is no family history of anaemia or blood disorders. His examination is unremarkable apart from pallor, with no organomegaly and no dysmorphic features. His blood film is reported as showing hypochromic microcytic red cells without target cells or basophilic stippling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 64 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (20-200), C-reactive protein within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Pallor of conjunctivae and palmar creases, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily ceased as soon as the haemoglobin has returned to normal
options.rationale: Stopping at haemoglobin normalisation leaves stores depleted and the anaemia predictably recurs. The haemoglobin recovers well before ferritin does. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Dietary modification alone with reduced milk intake and review of the blood count in three months
options.rationale: Diet alone is too slow to correct an established deficiency of this degree, though it is essential to prevent recurrence. It would be appropriate for borderline iron status without anaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion arranged as a day case with dietary advice given at the same visit
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is reserved for failed or not tolerated oral therapy, malabsorption, or ongoing losses, none of which has been established here. Oral therapy has not yet been tried. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Packed red cell transfusion followed by oral iron and outpatient haematology review
options.rationale: Transfusion is for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic severe anaemia, and this child is stable with a haemoglobin well above that threshold. It would also delay the diagnostic value of the response to iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises
options.rationale: Replacement corrects the haemoglobin within weeks but the stores take far longer, so treatment continues past normalisation to refill ferritin and prevent early relapse. Reducing milk volume and increasing iron rich solids is given alongside the supplement. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow milk intake is the classic driver, displacing iron rich solids and causing occult gut blood loss. The diagnosis rests on a microcytic hypochromic picture with a low ferritin, remembering that ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal during inflammation. Treatment is oral elemental iron with a deliberate continuation phase after the haemoglobin corrects, because haemoglobin recovery precedes store repletion by months. Failure to respond should prompt review of adherence, of ongoing losses, and of alternative diagnoses such as thalassaemia trait.
key_points: Cow milk intake above about 500 mL daily in toddlers displaces dietary iron
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be falsely normal with inflammation
Haemoglobin corrects within weeks but stores need months of continued therapy
A reticulocyte rise within a week supports the diagnosis
Persistent failure to respond prompts review for thalassaemia trait or blood loss
explanation.pearls: Continue oral iron for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation: stopping the day the count is normal is the single commonest reason a toddler is back with the same microcytic anaemia six months later.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Alarm versus desmopressin choice for a nine year old with bedwetting only and a normal daytime pattern
stem:
A 9 year old boy is brought to your practice because he still wets the bed most nights, which is now stopping him accepting invitations to sleep at friends' houses. He has never had a sustained period of dry nights.

He passes urine four to five times during the day with no urgency, no daytime wetting and no pain. He opens his bowels daily without straining. His examination including abdominal, genital, spinal and lower limb neurological assessment is normal, and his urine dipstick and blood glucose are normal. His parents are motivated and ask what will give him the best chance of lasting dryness, mentioning that a school camp is scheduled in eight months.

data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal, genital and spinal examination, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose protein blood and leucocytes, random blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: Enuresis alarm used consistently every night, with review of progress at four weeks
options.rationale: The alarm produces the highest rate of sustained dryness after treatment stops, which matches this family's stated goal and their capacity to persist. The timeframe before camp comfortably allows a full alarm course. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Oral desmopressin taken each night, with review of progress at four weeks
options.rationale: Desmopressin suppresses wetting while it is being taken but relapse on stopping is common, so it suits short term cover such as a single camp rather than a durable cure. Here there is ample time for definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Fluid restriction after the evening meal with a scheduled lift to the toilet overnight
options.rationale: Lifting a sleeping child does not teach the arousal response and simply empties the bladder, and severe evening fluid restriction is not effective as sole therapy. These measures support but do not replace definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Oral oxybutynin at night with a bladder diary kept over the following four weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergic therapy targets detrusor overactivity, which typically shows as daytime urgency and frequency, and this boy has an entirely normal daytime pattern. It would be considered where alarm and desmopressin have both failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

options.text: Referral for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic studies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for daytime symptoms, abnormal examination, or treatment resistant cases, none of which applies to uncomplicated monosymptomatic bedwetting. His assessment is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis means bedwetting with a normal daytime voiding pattern and no other urinary symptoms, and it is distinguished from non-monosymptomatic enuresis because the two are managed differently. Constipation must be excluded and treated first because it is a common reversible contributor. The alarm and desmopressin both work but differ in what they achieve: the alarm conditions arousal and gives the best chance of dryness that persists after treatment ends, while desmopressin acts only while it is taken and is best used for short term cover of specific events. Choosing between them therefore depends on whether the family wants a durable cure or immediate cover, and on their capacity to persist with a device that wakes the household.
key_points: Monosymptomatic enuresis requires a normal daytime voiding pattern
Treat coexisting constipation before starting enuresis specific therapy
The alarm gives the highest sustained dryness after treatment stops
Desmopressin suits short term cover such as camps and sleepovers
Imaging is reserved for daytime symptoms or abnormal examination
explanation.pearls: Alarm training needs a minimum of six to eight weeks of consistent nightly use before it is judged to have failed, so it is the wrong choice when a family needs dryness for an event only days away.

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice and timing for a newborn girl with a family history of hip problems and a stable clinical examination
stem:
You review a 3 day old girl on the postnatal ward before discharge. She was born at term in a cephalic presentation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth, and she is feeding and behaving normally.

Her mother mentions that her own sister was in a harness as a baby for a hip problem. On your examination the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative, hip abduction is full and symmetrical, and leg lengths and skin creases are equal. The rest of the newborn examination including the spine is normal. Her mother asks whether anything further needs to be arranged.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres negative bilaterally, full symmetrical hip abduction, equal leg lengths and symmetrical skin creases, normal spine
data_table.Birth history: Term cephalic vaginal birth, birth weight 3.4 kg, uncomplicated pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound before discharge from the postnatal ward this week
options.rationale: Scanning in the first days of life commonly shows physiological immaturity from maternal hormones and generates false positives with unnecessary follow up. The examination timing, not the modality, is what is wrong here. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound at six weeks of age and review her with the result
options.rationale: A first degree family history is a risk factor that warrants imaging even when the examination is normal, because dysplasia can be present without instability. Scanning is deferred to about six weeks so that normal neonatal laxity has resolved and the study is interpretable. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a pelvic radiograph at six weeks of age and review her with the result
options.rationale: The femoral head is not ossified at this age so radiography cannot assess the joint reliably, and ultrasound is the modality of choice. Radiography becomes useful once the ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Provide double nappy padding and arrange clinical review at six weeks of age
options.rationale: Double nappies are not an effective treatment or substitute for imaging and may falsely reassure the family. Clinical review alone will miss dysplasia without instability. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Give routine discharge advice with no imaging and rely on child health checks
options.rationale: Relying on serial examination alone misses the dysplastic but stable hip, which is exactly the pattern that a family history predicts. Risk factors change the screening pathway even when examination is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened clinically in every newborn, but clinical examination detects instability rather than dysplasia and therefore misses a proportion of affected hips. Selective ultrasound is added for recognised risk factors, principally a first degree family history and breech presentation in later pregnancy. The timing of the scan matters as much as the decision to order it, because maternal hormone mediated laxity in the first weeks produces immature appearances that resolve spontaneously and generate false positives. A frankly dislocated or dislocatable hip on examination is a different situation and needs urgent orthopaedic referral rather than a routine scan.
key_points: Clinical examination detects instability but can miss dysplasia without instability
First degree family history and breech presentation prompt selective ultrasound
Ultrasound is deferred to around six weeks to avoid physiological false positives
Radiography is unhelpful until the femoral head ossifies at four to six months
An abnormal examination needs orthopaedic referral rather than routine imaging
explanation.pearls: A positive Ortolani or Barlow test at the newborn check bypasses the six week ultrasound pathway entirely and goes straight to orthopaedic referral, because a dislocatable hip is a treatment decision rather than a screening question.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Newborn hip screening

subtopic_detail: Spiral tibial fracture in a newly walking toddler with a witnessed low fall and no other injuries
stem:
A 16 month old boy is brought to your emergency department after his father saw him trip on the edge of a rug while running and twist as he fell onto carpet. He has refused to bear weight on the right leg since.

He began walking independently at 12 months. He is consoled easily and his father's account has been consistent each time it has been taken. On examination there is mild swelling over the lower right shin with tenderness, no bruising anywhere on his body, and full painless movement at the knee, hip and ankle. His skin, frenulum, ears and scalp are normal, and his growth and development are age appropriate. The radiograph shows an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft with an intact fibula.

data_table.Examination: Mild swelling and tenderness over the distal right tibia, no bruising or other skin injury, normal frenulum ears and scalp, full painless movement of knee hip and ankle
data_table.Imaging: Undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal right tibial shaft with an intact fibula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Above knee cast with a child protection notification made before the child leaves
options.rationale: Notification is driven by a mismatch between injury and explanation rather than by fracture type alone, and no such mismatch exists here. A spiral configuration is not by itself an indicator of inflicted injury in a mobile child. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Admit for a skeletal survey and ophthalmology review before any definitive fracture treatment
options.rationale: A skeletal survey is indicated for children under two when the injury is unexplained or inconsistent, which is not the case with this witnessed and congruent account. It would be correct had he been pre-mobile. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Above knee cast with routine fracture clinic review, without a child protection notification
options.rationale: A spiral fracture of the distal tibia in an independently walking toddler is a recognised accidental pattern produced by rotation on a planted foot, and the mechanism, mobility and consistent history fit it. There are no other injuries and no features that would make the account implausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Below knee backslab with fracture clinic review and blood tests for bone fragility
options.rationale: Metabolic bone investigation is prompted by multiple fractures, blue sclerae, wormian bones or a family history, none of which is present. A below knee cast also fails to control rotation at this level. (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

options.text: Simple analgesia with weight bearing as tolerated and general practitioner review in one week
options.rationale: This fracture needs immobilisation to control rotational forces and to provide pain relief, so symptomatic management alone is inadequate. It would suit an undisplaced buckle fracture of the distal radius. (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

explanation.summary: Deciding whether a fracture is accidental rests on whether the injury, the explanation, and the child's developmental stage are congruent, not on the fracture configuration alone. The spiral tibial fracture of early walking, sometimes described as a toddler's fracture, is produced by a twisting force through a planted foot and is a common accidental injury once a child is independently mobile. The features that should raise concern are a fracture in a child who is not yet mobile, an absent or changing explanation, delayed presentation, injuries of differing ages, or associated bruising in sites that do not take the impact of ordinary falls. Every child under two with a suspicious fracture warrants a skeletal survey, and inflicted injury should be considered alongside metabolic bone disease rather than instead of it.
key_points: Congruence of injury, explanation and developmental stage drives the assessment
Spiral tibial fractures are a recognised accidental pattern in walking toddlers
A fracture in a pre-mobile infant is the strongest single red flag
Skeletal survey is indicated under two years when the account is inconsistent
Metabolic bone disease is considered alongside, not instead of, inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: The developmental question that reframes a toddler fracture is whether the child walks independently: the same spiral tibial fracture that is unremarkable at sixteen months demands a skeletal survey in a six month old who cannot yet cruise.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and poor feeding in a two week old with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia after a normal newborn check
stem:
A 14 day old baby is brought to your emergency department with three days of vomiting after feeds and increasing sleepiness. The parents describe the vomit as milky and not green, and say the baby has been taking progressively less at each feed.

The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and the newborn examination was documented as normal. Weight today is 8 per cent below birth weight. On examination the baby is lethargic with dry mucous membranes and a capillary refill of three seconds, the abdomen is soft with no palpable mass, and the external genitalia appear unremarkable. Venous gas and electrolytes are taken while intravenous access is obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 54/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill three seconds, soft abdomen with no palpable mass, unremarkable external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 7.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-6.0), venous pH 7.24 (7.32-7.42), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with correction of the alkalosis and surgical referral
options.rationale: This is the pathway for gastric outlet obstruction, which produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis and a palpable mass rather than this electrolyte pattern. The acid base and potassium findings here point the opposite way. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with broad spectrum antibiotics after blood and urine cultures
options.rationale: Sepsis is a reasonable parallel consideration and cultures should be taken, but antibiotics alone do not address the hormone deficiency that is driving the electrolyte derangement. Treating only for sepsis risks a fatal outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with hydrocortisone after a sample is taken for hormone assay
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a collapsing neonate indicates mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency, which needs fluid resuscitation and immediate steroid replacement. Taking the diagnostic sample first preserves the ability to confirm the diagnosis without delaying treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia)

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with hypertonic saline to raise the sodium concentration rapidly
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or coma attributable to hyponatraemia, and rapid correction in a chronically adapted neonate risks osmotic injury. The sodium here will correct as the underlying deficiency is treated. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride bolus with a trial of a hydrolysed formula and dietitian review
options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy causes vomiting and poor feeding but does not produce hyperkalaemia with hypoglycaemia and acidosis. The metabolic picture excludes it as the explanation. (Source: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

explanation.summary: The vomiting neonate presenting in the second week of life is a high stakes presentation because the common benign diagnoses and the lethal ones share a surface appearance. The electrolyte pattern does most of the discriminating work: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis indicates gastric outlet obstruction, whereas hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and acidosis indicates adrenal insufficiency. Salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically declares itself between day seven and day twenty one, after the newborn check and often after discharge, and virilisation may be obvious in an affected girl but absent in a boy, so normal looking genitalia offer no reassurance. Treatment is fluid resuscitation with immediate hydrocortisone, and the diagnostic sample is drawn before the first steroid dose so that confirmation remains possible.
key_points: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia in a neonate suggests adrenal insufficiency
Gastric outlet obstruction produces the opposite acid base and potassium picture
Salt wasting crisis typically presents after the newborn check in the second week
Normal appearing genitalia do not exclude the diagnosis in a male infant
Take the diagnostic sample before the first hydrocortisone dose
explanation.pearls: A male infant with salt wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia has no virilisation to give the diagnosis away, so the second week presentation of vomiting with a potassium above 6 mmol/L and a sodium below 130 mmol/L is the finding that must trigger hydrocortisone.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

subtopic_detail: Child with stridor that returns forty minutes after nebulised adrenaline with a rising fever and toxic appearance
stem:
A 3 year old girl was brought to your emergency department with a barking cough and stridor at rest that began two days after a runny nose. She received oral dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline, and her stridor settled well over the following twenty minutes.

Forty minutes later you are called back because the stridor has returned and is now present at rest with moderate chest wall recession. She looks unwell and is not interested in her parents or the toys, and her temperature has climbed since arrival. She is sitting upright but is drooling only minimally and her voice is hoarse rather than muffled. She is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168/min, blood pressure 92/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest with moderate intercostal and subcostal recession, hoarse voice, toxic appearance with reduced interaction, minimal drooling
data_table.Treatment so far: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 given on arrival

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline and continue observation for a further two hours
options.rationale: Repeat adrenaline is appropriate for recurrent stridor in an otherwise well child with viral croup, but here the fever and toxic appearance signal a different pathology. Repeating it treats the symptom while the underlying process progresses. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone and admit to the general paediatric ward
options.rationale: Corticosteroid has already been given and a further dose does not address a bacterial process, while ward admission without airway assessment misjudges the risk. Steroid dosing is not the limiting factor here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Arrange a lateral neck radiograph to assess the airway before involving other teams
options.rationale: Sending a child with a compromised airway to the radiology department removes them from immediate help and delays definitive assessment. Imaging does not change the need for inspection under controlled conditions. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone and commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy
options.rationale: High flow therapy does not relieve a fixed upper airway obstruction and may delay recognition of deterioration, and the steroid route is not the issue. Neither addresses the likely bacterial cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Urgent anaesthetic and ENT review for airway inspection, with intravenous flucloxacillin
options.rationale: A toxic child with rising fever whose stridor recurs rapidly after adrenaline has moved outside the expected course of viral croup and suggests bacterial infection of the trachea. Definitive assessment is airway inspection in a controlled setting with antistaphylococcal cover started. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Viral croup follows a predictable course in which dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline produce reliable improvement, with adrenaline wearing off over two to three hours rather than forty minutes. Departure from that course is the signal to reconsider the diagnosis, and the specific combination of high fever, a toxic appearance and poor or short lived response to adrenaline suggests bacterial tracheitis. This is a bacterial infection of the trachea, most often staphylococcal, that produces adherent purulent membranes and can obstruct the airway abruptly. Management is urgent airway inspection by anaesthetics and ENT in a controlled environment with antistaphylococcal antibiotics, since these children frequently require intubation and toilet of the airway. Epiglottitis remains in the differential but is now rare in immunised children and classically produces a muffled voice with marked drooling rather than a hoarse voice and barking cough.
key_points: Nebulised adrenaline should give two to three hours of improvement in croup
A toxic appearance with high fever is not part of uncomplicated viral croup
Bacterial tracheitis is most often staphylococcal and may need intubation
Airway inspection belongs in theatre, not in the radiology department
Epiglottitis gives a muffled voice and drooling rather than a barking cough
explanation.pearls: Recurrence of stridor within an hour of nebulised adrenaline, rather than at the expected two to three hours, alongside a rising fever is the combination that should move bacterial tracheitis ahead of croup and trigger a call to anaesthetics.

subtopic_detail: Persistent night waking thigh pain in an adolescent with a lamellated periosteal reaction on plain film
stem:
A 14 year old boy is brought to your clinic with four months of pain above his right knee that has been attributed to growing pains and then to a football injury. The pain now wakes him at night several times a week and is no longer relieved by paracetamol.

He has lost 3 kg over that period without dieting. His mother has noticed a firm fullness over the lower thigh in the past three weeks. On examination there is a firm, deep, tender swelling over the distal femur with overlying warmth, and the knee joint itself has a full painless range of movement. He is afebrile and his inflammatory markers are only mildly raised. The radiograph shows a poorly defined lesion of the distal femoral metaphysis with a lamellated periosteal reaction and cortical destruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Firm deep tender swelling over the distal right femur with overlying warmth, full painless knee range of movement, no regional lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (<5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (60-450)
data_table.Imaging: Poorly defined distal femoral metaphyseal lesion with lamellated periosteal reaction and cortical destruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an open biopsy locally and refer once the histological diagnosis is available
options.rationale: A locally placed biopsy tract can cross compartments that the definitive resection would otherwise spare and may convert a salvageable limb into an amputation. The diagnosis is not what determines where the biopsy happens. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange bone scintigraphy to assess the lesion
options.rationale: Osteomyelitis is the main alternative but would be expected to produce fever with markedly raised inflammatory markers rather than this indolent four month course with weight loss. Treating empirically would delay oncological staging. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Arrange outpatient magnetic resonance imaging and review him with the result in six weeks
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is part of staging but a six week wait is far too long given an aggressive radiographic appearance and progressive symptoms. Timeliness is the problem rather than the modality. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

options.text: Prescribe a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and review him in four weeks for reassessment
options.rationale: Marked relief with a non-steroidal agent suggests osteoid osteoma, which produces a small sclerotic lesion with a lucent nidus rather than cortical destruction. A therapeutic trial here would waste critical time. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

options.text: Refer to a specialist bone tumour unit for staging before any biopsy is undertaken
options.rationale: Night pain, weight loss, a soft tissue mass and an aggressive periosteal reaction indicate a primary bone malignancy, and the biopsy tract itself becomes part of the tissue that must later be resected. Performing it outside the treating unit can compromise limb salvage, so referral precedes biopsy. (Source: eviQ: Osteosarcoma)

explanation.summary: Bone pain in adolescents is common and almost always benign, so the discriminating features matter: pain that wakes the child from sleep, pain that persists beyond the expected course of an injury, systemic symptoms such as weight loss, and a palpable mass all argue against a mechanical cause. Osteosarcoma has a peak incidence during the adolescent growth spurt and arises most often in the metaphyses around the knee and proximal humerus. The radiographic hallmarks are an aggressive periosteal reaction, either lamellated or spiculated, with cortical destruction and a soft tissue component. The single most consequential management point is that biopsy must be planned and performed by the unit that will carry out the definitive resection, because a poorly sited tract contaminates tissue planes and can cost the patient their limb.
key_points: Night waking pain and weight loss are the features that reframe adolescent bone pain
Osteosarcoma favours the metaphyses around the knee during the growth spurt
Aggressive periosteal reaction with cortical destruction suggests malignancy
The biopsy tract is excised at definitive surgery and must be sited by that unit
Osteomyelitis usually produces fever and markedly raised inflammatory markers
explanation.pearls: Refer a suspected primary bone tumour before biopsy rather than after: a tract placed outside the sarcoma unit crosses compartments that the definitive resection would have spared and is a recognised reason limb salvage becomes impossible.

subtopic_detail: Jaundice still present at three weeks of age in a breastfed baby whose stools have become pale
stem:
A 23 day old breastfed baby girl is brought to your practice because she still looks yellow. Her mother was told at the maternity hospital that breastfed babies often stay a little jaundiced and not to worry.

She is feeding well and has regained her birth weight, and she is alert and active. Her mother mentions in passing that her nappies have been staining a dark colour and that her stools have turned a pale putty colour over the last week. Examination confirms jaundice to the abdomen with a soft abdomen and a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Her newborn screening test was normal.

data_table.Examination: Jaundice visible to the abdomen, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable, alert and well perfused
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.9 kg, regained birth weight by day 12 and tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother that breast milk jaundice is common and review the baby in one month
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires an unconjugated picture with normally pigmented stools, and pale stools exclude it outright. Reassurance here would delay a time critical diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Measure the conjugated bilirubin fraction urgently on a sample taken today
options.rationale: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days requires the bilirubin to be fractionated, because a raised conjugated fraction indicates cholestasis and demands urgent investigation. Pale stools with dark urine make this imperative, since the outcome of biliary atresia surgery deteriorates sharply with age. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Measure the total serum bilirubin alone and plot the value on the phototherapy chart
options.rationale: A total level without fractionation cannot distinguish cholestasis from unconjugated jaundice, and phototherapy charts do not apply beyond the early neonatal period. Fractionation is the step that changes management. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Advise interrupting breastfeeding for 48 hours and reassess the degree of jaundice afterwards
options.rationale: Interrupting feeding to observe a fall in bilirubin is an outdated approach that risks undermining breastfeeding and wastes time. It does not address the possibility of an obstructive cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange a direct antiglobulin test and blood group to investigate ongoing haemolysis
options.rationale: Haemolytic disease presents in the first days of life with an unconjugated picture and anaemia, not at three weeks with pale stools. The stool colour points to an obstructive rather than haemolytic mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Prolonged neonatal jaundice is defined as jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant or twenty one days in a preterm infant, and it mandates fractionation of the bilirubin rather than reassurance. The purpose of that single test is to separate the common and benign unconjugated causes, principally breast milk jaundice and hypothyroidism, from conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, which is always pathological. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that drives the urgency, because the success of the Kasai portoenterostomy falls substantially once the infant is beyond about sixty days of age, and an infant who looks well and is feeding normally can still have it. Pale stools and dark urine are the classic accompanying features and should never be attributed to breast milk jaundice. Other conjugated causes include neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, metabolic disease and sepsis.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term infant requires bilirubin fractionation
A raised conjugated fraction is always pathological and needs urgent workup
Pale stools with dark urine exclude breast milk jaundice
A well looking, thriving baby can still have biliary atresia
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes deteriorate sharply beyond about sixty days
explanation.pearls: The Kasai portoenterostomy achieves far better bile drainage when performed before sixty days of age, which is why a three week old with pale stools needs the conjugated fraction measured the same day rather than at the next routine visit.

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first retinopathy of prematurity examination in a preterm infant weaned to room air by day three
stem:
You are the registrar on the neonatal unit preparing a preterm girl for her discharge planning meeting. She is feeding fully from the breast in an open cot and has gained weight steadily over the past fortnight, with no apnoeic or desaturation episodes recorded in that time.

Her cranial ultrasound and newborn hearing screen were both normal, and she has not needed any supplemental oxygen since her first two days of life. Her mother asks which tests still need to be arranged before they go home.

data_table.Current age: 28 days, corrected age 33 weeks and 4 days
data_table.Respiratory support: Continuous positive airway pressure for 48 hours, in room air since day three

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to retinal examination?

options.text: Defer the first examination until she reaches 36 weeks corrected gestational age
options.rationale: The first examination is timed to four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever falls later, so waiting until 36 weeks would step over the window in which treatable disease usually declares itself. A 36 week timing belongs to a more mature infant being checked for late structural sequelae rather than for evolving disease. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Examine only if she needs supplemental oxygen again before she is discharged
options.rationale: Oxygen exposure modifies risk but does not define eligibility, and disease occurs in preterm infants who never receive supplemental oxygen at all. Eligibility is set by gestation and birthweight, which she meets on both counts. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Arrange the first retinal examination now, at four weeks after her birth
options.rationale: She was born below 31 weeks with a birthweight below 1250 g, so she qualifies for screening, and the first examination falls at four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later. At 33 weeks and 4 days corrected the four week point governs, which is today. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Arrange one retinal examination on the day her discharge is planned
options.rationale: Screening is a serial process with examinations every one to two weeks until the retina is fully vascularised, not a single snapshot. A single examination tied to a discharge date would miss disease that progresses after she goes home. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: Omit retinal examination because her birthweight was above one kilogram
options.rationale: The birthweight threshold for screening is 1250 g rather than 1000 g, so a weight of 1180 g sits inside the criteria rather than outside them. Her gestation below 31 weeks would qualify her independently in any case. (Source: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity is a proliferative retinal vascular disease of preterm infants whose natural history is time critical, because the treatable stage occupies a narrow window and untreated progression causes retinal detachment and irreversible blindness. Australian screening criteria select infants by gestation below 31 weeks or birthweight below 1250 g, and deliberately do not use oxygen exposure as an entry criterion because disease occurs without it. The first examination is timed at four weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later, which protects the most immature infants from being examined before disease could plausibly appear. Examinations then repeat at one to two week intervals, with the interval determined by the zone and stage found, until vascularisation reaches the periphery.
key_points: Screening eligibility is gestation below 31 weeks or birthweight below 1250 g
Supplemental oxygen exposure modifies risk but is not an entry criterion
First examination at four weeks postnatal or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later
Examinations repeat every one to two weeks until peripheral vascularisation completes
Screening continues after discharge and must be handed over explicitly
explanation.pearls: The later of four weeks postnatal age and 31 weeks postmenstrual age sets the first examination, so a baby born at 24 weeks waits until 31 weeks postmenstrual age while a baby born at 30 weeks is examined at four weeks of age.

sources.label: RANZCO: Guidelines for the Screening of Retinopathy of Prematurity
Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity

subtopic_detail: Febrile encephalopathy with transaminitis in the second week of life without any vesicular rash
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 9 day old boy who has been feeding poorly since yesterday and is now difficult to rouse. During your assessment he has a two minute focal seizure affecting the right arm.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and his mother has never had any genital lesions or blistering rash. His skin is examined carefully under good light and shows no vesicles, and his anterior fontanelle is soft. Blood cultures and a lumbar puncture are taken, and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and cefotaxime are commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 58/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes, no rash or vesicles, soft fontanelle, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Blood results: Alanine aminotransferase 640 U/L (less than 45), platelets 74 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count within normal limits
data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 68 x10^6/L with lymphocyte predominance, protein 1.4 g/L (0.2-0.8), glucose within normal limits, Gram stain negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his management?

options.text: Continue the intravenous antibiotics alone and review when the cultures return
options.rationale: A lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid with a negative Gram stain, marked transaminitis and thrombocytopenia points away from a pyogenic bacterial cause that antibiotics alone would cover. Waiting for cultures wastes the interval in which antiviral therapy changes outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Add intravenous ganciclovir and arrange a urine sample for viral culture
options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus, which in the congenital form presents at birth with growth restriction, microcephaly and a positive urine test in the first three weeks, not with an acute febrile encephalopathy at day nine. The acute disseminated picture here fits a different virus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Add intravenous dexamethasone before the next dose of antibiotic is given
options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroid is used in older children with proven or suspected Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis and is not recommended in neonates, where evidence of benefit is absent. It would not address the viral process suggested by these results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Add high dose intravenous aciclovir now and send samples for viral testing
options.rationale: Disseminated neonatal herpes presents in the first two weeks with seizures, hepatitis and thrombocytopenia, and fewer than half of affected babies ever develop a rash or have a mother with a known history. Empirical high dose aciclovir is started on suspicion because mortality rises steeply with every hour of delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Withhold antiviral therapy until the cerebrospinal fluid result is available
options.rationale: Cerebrospinal fluid viral testing can be falsely negative early in the illness and takes time to return, so a negative or pending result does not justify withholding therapy. Treatment is started empirically and stopped later if testing and the clinical course exclude the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

explanation.summary: Neonatal herpes simplex infection is acquired around the time of birth and presents in three overlapping patterns: disease limited to skin, eye and mouth, central nervous system disease, and disseminated disease with hepatitis and coagulopathy. The trap for clinicians is that the absence of a maternal history and the absence of vesicles are both common, because most transmission comes from asymptomatic shedding during a first infection the mother never recognised. Any neonate with fever, seizures, an unexplained transaminitis or a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid should receive empirical high dose aciclovir alongside antibacterial cover while testing proceeds. Delay is the main determinant of death and of neurological disability among survivors.
key_points: Most mothers of affected babies have no history of genital herpes
Vesicles are absent in a large proportion at presentation
Unexplained transaminitis with thrombocytopenia suggests disseminated disease
Empirical aciclovir is started on suspicion, not after confirmation
Antibacterial cover continues until bacterial sepsis is excluded
explanation.pearls: Neonatal herpes needs 20 mg/kg of intravenous aciclovir every eight hours, which is well above the dose used in older children, and disseminated or central nervous system disease is treated for at least 21 days.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

subtopic_detail: Operative referral timing once a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale stools is established at seven weeks
stem:
A 7 week old girl is reviewed in your general practice because she is still yellow. She was born at term, is exclusively breastfed and is gaining weight along her birth centile.

Her mother has photographed several nappies over the past fortnight, and the stools in them are a pale putty colour while the wet nappies look dark. The split bilirubin you requested last week has returned, and her newborn screening test and thyroid function were both normal. She is alert and feeding well, and there is no bruising.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae, soft abdomen with a liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no bruising
