data_table.Bilirubin: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 92 micromol/L
data_table.Other results: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 45), international normalised ratio within normal limits, newborn screening and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the split bilirubin in two weeks and refer only if it remains elevated
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction this high is already abnormal and never physiological, so repeating it adds no information while consuming the operative window. Watchful repetition is appropriate for unconjugated jaundice in a thriving breastfed baby, which is a different problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Refer today to a paediatric liver unit for cholangiogram and possible Kasai
options.rationale: Pale stools with a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total demand same day specialist referral, because the outcome of portoenterostomy falls sharply once the infant passes about 60 days of age and she is already 49 days old. Definitive assessment is an intraoperative cholangiogram, so referral is to a unit able to proceed to surgery on the same admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and arrange outpatient review in three weeks
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid is an adjunct for cholestatic symptoms once a cause is known and does nothing for an obstructed biliary tree. Starting it here creates the appearance of treatment while the operative window closes. (Source: GESA: Paediatric liver disease)

options.text: Arrange a sweat test and metabolic screen before making any surgical referral
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis and metabolic disorders do belong in the wider cholestasis workup, but they are pursued in parallel with urgent referral rather than ahead of it. Sequencing them first delays the one diagnosis whose treatment is time critical. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Reassure that breast milk jaundice resolves and review again at three months
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and by definition has a normal conjugated fraction, so it cannot explain a conjugated bilirubin of 92 micromol/L or pale stools. Attributing conjugated jaundice to breastfeeding is the classic reason these infants present too late. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any infant still jaundiced beyond 14 days of age needs a split bilirubin, and a conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total defines cholestasis that requires urgent investigation. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that sets the clock, because the Kasai portoenterostomy restores bile drainage in most infants operated before about 60 days but in far fewer after 90 days, and those who fail drainage need transplantation in infancy. Pale stools and dark urine are the classic combination but are frequently missed because parents are not asked to look, and the baby otherwise thrives. The broader cholestasis workup for infection, metabolic and endocrine causes proceeds alongside referral rather than before it.
key_points: Jaundice beyond 14 days needs a split bilirubin, not reassurance
A conjugated fraction above 20 per cent of the total is always pathological
Kasai outcomes deteriorate sharply beyond about 60 days of age
Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and cannot explain pale stools
Other cholestasis investigations run in parallel with urgent referral
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to photograph a nappy rather than describe the stool colour, because pale stools are reported as normal by most parents who have never been shown a comparison chart.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing confirmatory testing after strongly positive coeliac serology in a child still eating gluten
stem:
A 6 year old girl is reviewed in your general practice after her serology returned. She was tested because her weight has drifted from the 50th to the 10th centile over eighteen months and she complains of a sore tummy and feeling puffy after meals.

Her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease and has already bought gluten free products, asking whether she should start them today. The girl has continued her usual diet up to this appointment. Her abdomen is soft with no organomegaly and her iron studies show mild deficiency.

data_table.Growth: Weight tracking down from the 50th to the 10th centile over eighteen months, height on the 25th centile
data_table.Serology: Tissue transglutaminase IgA strongly positive at more than ten times the upper limit of normal, total IgA within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Keep gluten in her diet and refer for endoscopic small bowel biopsy
options.rationale: Histological confirmation remains the standard in Australian paediatric practice, and the mucosal changes begin to heal within weeks of gluten withdrawal, so removing gluten before biopsy can make the diagnosis impossible to secure. A lifelong dietary restriction warrants a firm diagnosis before it is imposed. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

options.text: Start a gluten free diet now and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Symptomatic improvement on withdrawal is not diagnostic, because many children without coeliac disease feel better on the diet, and the change forecloses confirmatory biopsy. An empirical trial is reasonable only where coeliac disease has already been formally excluded. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

options.text: Repeat the antibody level after four weeks of a gluten free diet
options.rationale: Antibody titres fall with gluten withdrawal in both affected and unaffected children, so a falling level after four weeks discriminates nothing. Serial titres have a role in monitoring adherence once the diagnosis is established. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease clinical update)

options.text: Arrange HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing to confirm the diagnosis before referral
options.rationale: The genetic test is useful for its negative predictive value, since absence of both alleles effectively excludes the disease, but roughly half the general population carries one and a positive result confirms nothing. It cannot substitute for histology. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

options.text: Reassure the family and repeat her growth measurements in six months
options.rationale: Faltering growth with iron deficiency and a strongly positive antibody is an indication to complete the diagnostic pathway rather than to observe. Six months of further growth failure would be difficult to recover. (Source: RCH CPG: Coeliac disease)

explanation.summary: Coeliac disease in Australian children is diagnosed on the combination of positive serology and duodenal histology obtained while the child is still consuming gluten. The single most common preventable error is starting the diet before biopsy, because villous architecture recovers quickly and the family is then left choosing between an unconfirmed lifelong restriction and a gluten challenge that nobody wants to undertake. Tissue transglutaminase IgA is the screening test of choice but must be paired with a total IgA, since selective IgA deficiency is over ten times more common in coeliac disease and produces a falsely negative result. Associated autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, raise the pre-test probability and appear frequently in the family history.
key_points: Biopsy is taken while the child is still eating gluten
Total IgA must accompany tissue transglutaminase IgA to exclude IgA deficiency
HLA typing excludes rather than confirms the diagnosis
Faltering growth and iron deficiency are common presenting features
Serology is used after diagnosis to monitor dietary adherence
explanation.pearls: If a family has already removed gluten before testing, a formal challenge of at least four weeks of gluten daily is needed before serology and biopsy become interpretable again.

subtopic_detail: Preoperative biochemical correction before pyloromyotomy in an infant with hypochloraemic alkalosis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 5 week old boy whose ultrasound has just been reported. His mother says he brings the whole feed back forcefully, sometimes clearing the edge of the change table, and then wants to feed again straight away.

He has lost 200 g since his two week check and his nappies have been drier than usual for three days. He is alert with a sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. The surgical registrar telephones to say a theatre slot is free this evening and asks whether to take him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 172/min, blood pressure 74/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Ultrasound: Pyloric muscle thickness 4.6 mm, channel length 19 mm
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer to theatre now because the obstruction needs urgent surgical relief
options.rationale: The obstruction is mechanical but not strangulating, so there is no ischaemic emergency and nothing is gained by operating on an alkalotic infant. Anaesthesia in uncorrected metabolic alkalosis carries a recognised risk of postoperative apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Give a bolus of five per cent dextrose and book theatre for this evening
options.rationale: Dextrose without sodium and chloride does not replace the losses that generated the alkalosis and risks worsening the hyponatraemia. Correction requires chloride specifically, which this fluid lacks. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Rehydrate with sodium chloride and added potassium until the biochemistry corrects
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting of gastric contents strips hydrogen and chloride, producing a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that the kidney sustains until chloride is replaced. Pyloromyotomy is an elective procedure performed only once the chloride and bicarbonate have normalised, because uncorrected alkalosis depresses the central respiratory drive under anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Pass a nasogastric tube and start intravenous antibiotics before theatre
options.rationale: There is no infective process here, and continuous nasogastric drainage removes yet more gastric chloride and worsens the alkalosis. Free drainage is used for a distal obstruction with bilious aspirates, which is a different clinical problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Start oral rehydration solution and recheck the electrolytes in twelve hours
options.rationale: Oral fluid will not be retained past a mechanically obstructed pylorus, so the deficit persists while the delay accumulates. Oral rehydration is the route of choice in gastroenteritis, where the gut remains patent. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents in the third to sixth week with non bilious forceful vomiting in a baby who remains hungry, and the diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound by muscle thickness above about 3 mm with a channel longer than 15 mm. The metabolic consequence is the part that kills: loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, which the kidney perpetuates by exchanging hydrogen for sodium once chloride is unavailable, generating the paradoxical aciduria. Pyloromyotomy is therefore never an emergency, and operating before correction exposes the infant to postoperative apnoea from a centrally depressed respiratory drive. Resuscitation with sodium chloride and potassium typically takes 24 to 48 hours, and surgery follows once the chloride exceeds about 100 mmol/L and the bicarbonate has fallen below about 30 mmol/L.
key_points: The vomiting is non bilious and the infant remains hungry afterwards
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria is the signature
Pyloromyotomy is elective and follows biochemical correction
Chloride replacement is what allows the kidney to excrete bicarbonate
Uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea
explanation.pearls: Aim for a chloride above 100 mmol/L and a bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L before pyloromyotomy, which usually takes 24 to 48 hours of sodium chloride with added potassium once the infant is passing urine.

subtopic_detail: Choosing urate lowering prophylaxis for tumour lysis risk when glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is known
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 6 year old boy with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. He is alert and well perfused, and induction chemotherapy is planned to start tomorrow morning.

His presenting blood film and counts show a heavy circulating blast burden, and his biochemistry already shows a raised urate before any treatment. He was investigated for prolonged jaundice as a newborn and was found then to have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, confirmed on enzyme assay after the jaundice settled. The haematology consultant asks you to write up his tumour lysis prophylaxis.

data_table.Full blood count: White cell count 184 x10^9/L with 88 per cent blasts, haemoglobin 76 g/L (115-135), platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Biochemistry: Urate 0.58 mmol/L (0.12-0.32), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), phosphate 1.9 mmol/L (1.0-1.8), creatinine 74 micromol/L (30-60)
data_table.Past history: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency confirmed on enzyme assay in infancy

lead_in: Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Give rasburicase now because the urate and white cell count are both high
options.rationale: The risk profile does argue for aggressive urate control, but rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide as it degrades urate and precipitates severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in enzyme deficient patients. His deficiency makes this an absolute contraindication rather than a relative one. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Give rasburicase at half the usual dose with close monitoring of haemoglobin
options.rationale: The haemolytic reaction is not dose dependent in a way that makes reduction safe, and monitoring detects the injury rather than preventing it. Dose reduction is a strategy for renal clearance issues, not for an enzymatic contraindication. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Withhold urate lowering therapy and rely on intravenous hydration alone
options.rationale: Hydration is the backbone of prophylaxis but is insufficient by itself when the urate is already elevated with this blast burden. Hydration alone suits a low risk tumour with a normal baseline urate. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Start urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and give rasburicase
options.rationale: Alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate deposition in the tubules while the patient is already hyperphosphataemic, and it is redundant alongside effective urate lowering. The rasburicase component remains contraindicated regardless. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Start allopurinol with generous intravenous hydration and monitor the urate
options.rationale: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase and prevents further urate formation without any oxidative stress on red cells, making it the safe choice when rasburicase cannot be used. Combined with high volume intravenous hydration it protects renal function while the blast burden falls, accepting that existing urate is cleared more slowly than with the enzyme. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome follows the rapid breakdown of a large tumour burden, releasing potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids that are metabolised to urate, with acute kidney injury the feared endpoint. Risk stratification in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia rests on the white cell count, the baseline urate and renal function, and this child is high risk on all three. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts existing urate to the far more soluble allantoin and is the agent of choice for high risk disease, but the reaction liberates hydrogen peroxide, which red cells lacking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase cannot detoxify. The result is brisk haemolysis with methaemoglobinaemia, so the enzyme deficiency converts the preferred drug into a contraindicated one and allopurinol with aggressive hydration becomes the fallback.
key_points: High white cell count, raised baseline urate and renal impairment define high risk
Rasburicase degrades existing urate; allopurinol only prevents new formation
Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended and worsens phosphate deposition
Hydration underpins every regimen regardless of the agent chosen
explanation.pearls: Screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before rasburicase in any patient of African, Mediterranean or Southeast Asian ancestry, because the resulting haemolysis with methaemoglobinaemia does not respond to methylene blue in these patients.

subtopic_detail: Deciding on prophylactic fixation of the unaffected hip when a slip occurs with an underlying endocrinopathy
stem:
You are the registrar in the orthopaedic clinic seeing an 11 year old boy referred with three weeks of left knee ache and a limp that his mother says has slowly worsened. There was no injury.

He was diagnosed with hypothyroidism two years ago and takes thyroxine, though his mother admits doses are often missed. On examination the left leg lies in slight external rotation and the hip rolls outwards as you flex it. Plain films of both hips are reviewed with the consultant, who confirms a mild stable slip on the left and asks you to consent the family for surgery.

data_table.Examination: Left leg externally rotated, obligate external rotation on hip flexion, able to weight bear with a limp
data_table.Growth: Weight above the 97th centile, height on the 25th centile
data_table.Imaging: Mild stable slip of the left capital femoral epiphysis, right epiphysis not displaced with an open physis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative plan?

options.text: Pin the affected hip alone and review the other hip clinically each year
options.rationale: Clinical surveillance alone is the default for an otherwise healthy adolescent with a unilateral slip, where the contralateral risk is roughly one in five and presentation is usually symptomatic. It underprotects a child whose endocrinopathy raises that risk substantially. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Pin the affected hip and pin the opposite hip during the same anaesthetic
options.rationale: An underlying endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism raises the rate of a subsequent contralateral slip towards and beyond half, which is the accepted threshold for prophylactic fixation. Doing both hips under one anaesthetic avoids a second operation and prevents a slip that could present late with avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Pin the affected hip and arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the other hip
options.rationale: Imaging the asymptomatic side can identify a pre slip but does not alter the decision in a child who already meets the criteria for prophylactic fixation on endocrine grounds. It adds cost and a further anaesthetic in a young child without changing the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Attempt closed reduction of the slip before any internal fixation is done
options.rationale: Forceful reduction of a stable slip disrupts the retinacular vessels and is the principal iatrogenic cause of avascular necrosis in this condition. Fixation is performed in situ, accepting the existing deformity. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Treat in traction without weight bearing and delay any operative fixation
options.rationale: Non operative management allows progression of the slip and does not stabilise the physis, so it is not used for a diagnosed slip. Traction has no role once the diagnosis is radiologically confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: A slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and classically presents with knee or thigh pain rather than hip pain, which is why a limping adolescent needs the hip examined and imaged regardless of where the pain is felt. Treatment is in situ screw fixation, since attempting to reduce the slip strips the posterior retinacular blood supply and causes avascular necrosis. The contested decision is the opposite hip: baseline contralateral slip rates sit near 20 per cent and most units accept clinical follow up, but prophylactic fixation becomes the recommended course when the risk is markedly elevated. The recognised high risk groups are children with endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency or renal osteodystrophy, and those presenting at a young chronological age relative to their skeletal maturity.
key_points: Knee or thigh pain with a limp requires hip imaging in an adolescent
Fixation is performed in situ because reduction risks avascular necrosis
Contralateral slip occurs in about one in five otherwise healthy children
Endocrinopathy or young age at presentation justifies prophylactic fixation
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the classic examination finding
explanation.pearls: Suspect an underlying endocrinopathy when a slip occurs below ten years of age or in a child whose height is well below the weight centile, and check thyroid function before discharge.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions

subtopic_detail: Antiviral decision for a symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection confirmed within the first three weeks
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing a 12 day old girl on the postnatal ward whose newborn hearing screen failed on both sides and was not passed on repeat.

She was born at term but was small, and the midwives noted a scattered rash of pinpoint red spots on her trunk that does not blanch. Her head circumference sits well below her weight centile. A urine sample collected on day 10 has returned positive for cytomegalovirus on nucleic acid testing, and her cranial ultrasound shows scattered calcification. Her mother recalls a flu like illness in the second trimester.

data_table.Growth: Birthweight below the 3rd centile, head circumference below the 3rd centile
data_table.Examination: Non blanching petechial rash over the trunk, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Urine cytomegalovirus nucleic acid test positive on day 10, alanine aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 45), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400), cranial ultrasound shows periventricular calcification
data_table.Hearing: Automated auditory brainstem response failed bilaterally on initial and repeat screening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with audiology follow up alone because antiviral therapy has no benefit
options.rationale: Observation is the correct course for asymptomatic infection detected incidentally, where treatment has not been shown to help and carries toxicity. This baby has multisystem disease, which is precisely the group in whom treatment improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Give intravenous ganciclovir for six weeks and then stop all antiviral therapy
options.rationale: Six weeks of intravenous ganciclovir was the older regimen and is now used only for the initial phase when oral therapy is not tolerated, because six months of oral treatment produces better hearing and developmental outcomes. Stopping at six weeks forfeits that additional benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Start oral valganciclovir only if the hearing loss progresses over the first year
options.rationale: The treatment benefit depends on starting within the first month of life, so deferring until progression is documented moves therapy outside the window in which it works. Later deterioration is managed with amplification and implantation rather than with antivirals. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Start oral valganciclovir now and continue it for six months with monitoring
options.rationale: Symptomatic congenital infection confirmed within the first three weeks of life is treated with six months of oral valganciclovir begun before one month of age, which improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes compared with shorter or later therapy. Neutropenia is the dose limiting toxicity, so the full blood count is monitored weekly at first and then monthly. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Give cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin as a single dose and monitor her hearing
options.rationale: Hyperimmune globulin has been studied mainly as an antenatal intervention to prevent transmission and has not shown benefit as postnatal treatment of established disease. It does not replace antiviral therapy in a symptomatic newborn. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

explanation.summary: Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest congenital infection and the leading non genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, which is why a failed newborn hearing screen should prompt consideration of it. Diagnosis must be established on urine or saliva nucleic acid testing within the first three weeks of life, because a positive sample after that point cannot distinguish congenital infection from postnatal acquisition through breast milk or saliva. Treatment is reserved for symptomatic disease, defined by features such as growth restriction, microcephaly, petechiae, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification or sensorineural hearing loss. Six months of oral valganciclovir started within the first month improves both hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes, while asymptomatic infants are followed with serial audiology rather than treated.
key_points: Confirmation requires urine or saliva testing within the first three weeks of life
Only symptomatic infants are treated with antivirals
Six months of oral valganciclovir beats six weeks of intravenous therapy
Therapy must begin within the first month to achieve benefit
Neutropenia is the dose limiting toxicity and requires scheduled counts
explanation.pearls: A positive cytomegalovirus test after 21 days of age cannot distinguish congenital from postnatally acquired infection, so retrieve the stored newborn screening card for testing if the diagnosis is raised later.

subtopic_detail: First line agent for epileptic spasms when hypopigmented macules point to an underlying neurocutaneous disorder
stem:
A 6 month old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents, who have filmed what they describe as him suddenly bending forward and throwing his arms out, over and over, in runs of twenty or so just after he wakes. He cries afterwards.

His mother says he used to reach for toys and babble but has stopped doing both over the past month. Under the Wood lamp you find four pale oval patches on his trunk and thigh. His neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable and his head circumference is on the 50th centile. An urgent electroencephalogram is reported as showing a chaotic high amplitude pattern with multifocal spikes.

data_table.Examination: Four hypopigmented oval macules on the trunk and thigh, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Development: Loss of previously acquired reaching and babbling over the past month
data_table.Electroencephalogram: Chaotic high amplitude background with multifocal spikes

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start vigabatrin as the initial agent and arrange specialist follow up
options.rationale: The hypopigmented macules indicate tuberous sclerosis complex, and vigabatrin is markedly more effective than hormonal therapy for spasms in that specific setting, with response rates well above those achieved in other causes. It is therefore chosen first rather than as a second line agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone as the initial agent and review shortly
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy with prednisolone is the first line choice for spasms without an identified structural or genetic cause, and it would be right had the skin examination been normal. The neurocutaneous findings here shift the preferred agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Start sodium valproate and arrange outpatient neurology review in two weeks
options.rationale: Valproate is a later option with substantially lower rates of spasm cessation and carries hepatotoxicity risk in infants with undiagnosed metabolic disease. An outpatient timeframe also underestimates the urgency of stopping the spasms. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Start levetiracetam and repeat the electroencephalogram in four weeks
options.rationale: Conventional anticonvulsants including levetiracetam are relatively ineffective against epileptic spasms, and a four week delay allows continued developmental regression. The distinction from focal or generalised seizures matters because the drug classes that work are different. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Observe without treatment because these episodes often settle spontaneously
options.rationale: Spasms do eventually remit but at the cost of permanent developmental loss, and the duration of untreated spasms is the strongest predictor of poor cognitive outcome. Observation is never appropriate once the diagnosis is made. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

explanation.summary: Epileptic spasms present between three and twelve months as clusters of brief symmetrical flexion or extension, typically on waking, and are far too often mistaken for colic or reflux until developmental regression brings the child back. The triad of spasms, the chaotic high amplitude electroencephalogram pattern called hypsarrhythmia and developmental arrest defines West syndrome, and time to treatment is the main modifiable determinant of cognitive outcome. First line therapy is hormonal, usually high dose oral prednisolone in Australian practice, except where tuberous sclerosis complex is identified, in which case vigabatrin is clearly superior. Every infant with spasms therefore needs a careful skin examination under ultraviolet light, since the hypopigmented macules of tuberous sclerosis may be the only external clue and they directly change the drug chosen.
key_points: Clusters on waking with developmental regression suggest epileptic spasms
Hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram completes the West syndrome triad
Hormonal therapy is first line except in tuberous sclerosis complex
Vigabatrin is the preferred first agent when tuberous sclerosis is present
Time from onset to effective treatment predicts developmental outcome
explanation.pearls: Vigabatrin causes an irreversible concentric visual field constriction in roughly a third of treated patients, so baseline and serial ophthalmological assessment is arranged and the duration of therapy is kept as short as the response allows.

sources.label: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

subtopic_detail: Avoiding percutaneous sampling of a large intrarenal mass in a preschool child before definitive surgery
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3 year old girl whose mother felt a firm lump in her left tummy while bathing her two days ago. The girl has been well in herself, eating normally and playing as usual, with no fevers, bone pain or weight loss.

On examination there is a smooth firm mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline and moves little with respiration. Her blood pressure is above the 95th centile for age and height, and urinalysis shows blood without protein. Cross sectional imaging has been reported and the surgical team has been contacted. Her catecholamine metabolites are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Smooth firm left flank mass not crossing the midline, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows blood without protein, urinary catecholamine metabolites within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Large mass arising within the left kidney with a claw of surrounding renal parenchyma, no tumour thrombus in the renal vein or inferior vena cava, no pulmonary lesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Percutaneous core biopsy of the mass to establish the histological diagnosis
options.rationale: Needle sampling breaches the tumour capsule and seeds the track, which upstages the disease and commits the child to flank radiotherapy she would otherwise avoid. Biopsy is reserved for unresectable or bilateral disease or when imaging suggests a different tumour type. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Percutaneous biopsy followed by chemotherapy before any surgical resection
options.rationale: This sequence combines the staging penalty of biopsy with delayed surgery and is not used for a resectable unilateral tumour. It carries the same track seeding problem as biopsy alone. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Refer for primary nephrectomy without a preoperative percutaneous biopsy
options.rationale: Imaging showing an intrarenal mass with a claw sign of surrounding renal parenchyma in a preschool child, with normal catecholamine metabolites excluding the main alternative, is sufficient to proceed to upfront radical nephrectomy, which provides both the diagnosis and the staging. Australian practice follows the North American approach of immediate surgery for resectable unilateral disease, with chemotherapy then guided by the operative stage and histology. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Start chemotherapy based on imaging alone and defer any surgical referral
options.rationale: Preoperative chemotherapy without histology is the European protocol approach and is a defensible strategy internationally, but it is not the pathway followed in Australian units for resectable unilateral disease, where upfront surgery preserves accurate staging. The two approaches differ mainly in whether stage is assigned before or after chemotherapy. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Observe with repeat imaging in six weeks before deciding on any intervention
options.rationale: A solid renal mass of this size in a child of this age requires definitive management rather than surveillance, and delay allows local progression and metastatic spread. Interval imaging has no role once a solid intrarenal tumour is identified. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

explanation.summary: A painless abdominal mass in a well preschool child, often discovered by a parent during bathing, is a Wilms tumour until proven otherwise, and the key clinical discriminator is that it arises within the kidney and does not cross the midline. The main differential is neuroblastoma, which characteristically does cross the midline, encases rather than displaces vessels, produces a child who looks unwell and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites. Hypertension occurs in roughly a quarter of children with Wilms tumour through renin mediated mechanisms, and microscopic haematuria is common. The management principle that carries the most weight in an examination is that percutaneous biopsy is avoided, because tumour spill upstages the disease and adds radiotherapy to the treatment burden of a child who is otherwise highly curable.
key_points: Wilms tumour arises within the kidney and does not cross the midline
Neuroblastoma crosses the midline and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites
Hypertension and microscopic haematuria are common accompanying features
Percutaneous biopsy seeds the track and upstages otherwise curable disease
Australian units proceed to upfront nephrectomy for resectable unilateral tumours
explanation.pearls: Handle the abdomen as little as possible once a Wilms tumour is suspected and document that in the notes, because repeated deep palpation risks capsular rupture with the same staging consequence as a biopsy.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass in children

subtopic_detail: Timing of corticosteroid initiation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy while motor function has plateaued
stem:
You are the registrar in the neuromuscular clinic reviewing a 5 year old boy whose genetic testing last year confirmed a deletion in the dystrophin gene. His parents have read about steroids and ask whether he should be on them.

His mother says he still runs and manages the playground but he pushes on his thighs to stand up from the floor and asks to be carried on longer walks. Serial timed testing in the clinic shows his rise from the floor and ten metre walk times have been unchanged over the last three visits, having improved steadily before that. His cardiac and respiratory assessments are within normal limits and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Examination: Calf hypertrophy, positive Gowers manoeuvre, proximal weakness of the hip girdle
data_table.Functional testing: Time to rise from the floor and ten metre walk time unchanged across three consecutive visits
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram and spirometry within normal limits, dystrophin gene deletion confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about corticosteroid therapy?

options.text: Defer corticosteroids until he loses the ability to walk independently
options.rationale: Waiting until walking is lost forfeits the main benefit, which is prolonging ambulation and delaying scoliosis. Steroids started after loss of ambulation still have a role for respiratory and cardiac function but no longer preserve walking. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Start corticosteroids only once his forced vital capacity begins to fall
options.rationale: Respiratory decline occurs years after the ambulatory phase, so using it as the trigger would delay treatment well past the window in which walking can be preserved. Spirometry guides later respiratory management rather than steroid initiation. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Avoid corticosteroids because the adverse effects outweigh any benefit
options.rationale: Weight gain, growth suppression, reduced bone density and behavioural change are real and require active monitoring, but the evidence for prolonged ambulation, delayed scoliosis and preserved cardiorespiratory function is strong enough that steroids are standard care. The adverse effects are managed rather than used as a reason to withhold. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Start corticosteroids at the time of genetic diagnosis regardless of function
options.rationale: Starting during the phase when a young boy is still gaining motor skills exposes him to years of additional toxicity without added benefit, since the gains continue regardless. The genetic diagnosis defines who will need treatment, not when it begins. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Start daily corticosteroids now while his motor function has plateaued
options.rationale: The accepted trigger is the plateau phase, when motor skills have stopped improving but have not yet begun to decline, which his serial timed testing demonstrates across three visits. Starting at this point maximises the years of preserved ambulation and delays scoliosis and cardiorespiratory decline. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy typically declares itself between three and five years with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and a Gowers manoeuvre, and a markedly raised creatine kinase should trigger genetic testing rather than a muscle biopsy in the first instance. Corticosteroids remain the only intervention shown to prolong independent ambulation, and the decision that matters clinically is when to start rather than whether to start. Australian and international consensus times initiation to the plateau phase, identified on serial timed function testing as the point at which motor skills stop improving but have not yet declined, which usually falls between four and six years of age. Treatment brings a predictable burden of weight gain, growth suppression, reduced bone mineral density and behavioural change, so bone health, blood pressure, glucose and immunisation status are addressed before and during therapy.
key_points: Serial timed function tests identify the plateau phase that triggers treatment
Corticosteroids prolong ambulation and delay scoliosis and cardiac decline
Starting during the improving phase adds toxicity without added benefit
Bone density, growth, glucose and behaviour need scheduled monitoring
Live vaccines should be completed before immunosuppressive doses begin
explanation.pearls: Check varicella immunity and complete live vaccines before starting corticosteroids, because daily prednisolone at these doses makes subsequent live vaccination unsafe and varicella exposure then requires immunoglobulin.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Post exposure prophylaxis choice for an unimmunised infant four days after a measles contact
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by the parents of a 7 month old boy. Four days ago they sat in a waiting room with a child who has since been confirmed as having measles, and the public health unit has contacted them as part of contact tracing.

Their son has had his scheduled immunisations for his age but has not yet had a measles containing vaccine. He is entirely well today with no fever, rash, cough or red eyes, and he is feeding and behaving normally. His mother was born overseas and does not know whether she had measles or was ever vaccinated. He has no immune deficiency and takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no conjunctivitis, no coryza, no buccal lesions, chest clear
data_table.Exposure: Shared indoor waiting room with a confirmed case four days ago
data_table.Immunisation status: Age appropriate schedule complete, no measles containing vaccine given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post exposure management?

options.text: Give normal human immunoglobulin and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Vaccine provides protection only when given within 72 hours of exposure, and at four days that window has closed, leaving immunoglobulin as the effective option up to six days after contact. Measles is a notifiable disease, so the public health unit coordinates contact management alongside the clinical decision. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give measles mumps rubella vaccine now as post exposure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Vaccine is the preferred option for an immunocompetent contact aged six months or older, but only within 72 hours of exposure, because it must generate immunity faster than the wild virus replicates. At four days it is too late to prevent disease. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Reassure the family that maternal antibody will protect him at this age
options.rationale: Transplacental maternal antibody wanes over the first six to nine months and its presence depends on the mother's own immunity, which is unknown here. Infants in this age band are among the most vulnerable to severe measles. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Start oral vitamin A and review only if a rash or fever develops
options.rationale: Vitamin A is given as an adjunct to treatment once measles is established, particularly in young children admitted to hospital, and has no prophylactic role. Waiting for a rash forfeits the prophylaxis window entirely. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Arrange serology now and decide on prophylaxis once it has returned
options.rationale: Serology at this point reflects his pre exposure status rather than infection, and the turnaround time would push him beyond the six day limit for immunoglobulin. The decision must be made on exposure history and immunisation status. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Measles is among the most transmissible infections known, with airborne spread persisting in a room for up to two hours after an infectious person leaves, which is why shared waiting room exposure counts as significant contact. Post exposure prophylaxis is chosen by the interval since exposure and by the susceptibility of the contact. A measles containing vaccine is preferred for immunocompetent contacts aged six months and over when given within 72 hours, while normal human immunoglobulin covers the period up to six days and is also used for infants under six months, pregnant women without immunity and immunocompromised contacts regardless of timing. Measles is notifiable in every Australian jurisdiction, and contact tracing is run by the public health unit. Infants who receive a measles vaccine before twelve months of age still require the routine doses at twelve and eighteen months, because early vaccination produces a less durable response.
key_points: Airborne spread persists for up to two hours after the case leaves a room
Vaccine works as prophylaxis only within 72 hours of exposure
Immunoglobulin extends the prophylaxis window to six days
Immunoglobulin is preferred for infants under six months and immunocompromised contacts
A dose given before twelve months does not replace the routine scheduled doses
explanation.pearls: A measles vaccine given to an infant under twelve months for outbreak control does not count towards the schedule, so both routine doses at twelve and eighteen months must still be given.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles national guidelines
